# Ten Toes Down: The Viet Telling

*Bell Street rewrite. Creative direction: Nolan. New prose: Codex.*

# Book I: The Price of Standing

## Chapter 1: Money at the Curb

The first man who handed me money had mistaken me for my father.

The second knew exactly who I was and apologized for giving me less than the first.

By the time Shawna got out of the car, I had nine thousand dollars, a gold watch, and somebody's parking space for the rest of my life.

We had come to Bell Street for noodles.

“Don't put any of that in my purse,” she said.

“We could buy another purse.”

“I already like this one.”

The man with the parking space was still holding his hands together. He had white hair, a purple tracksuit and a small dog wearing the same tracksuit. The dog looked like it had objections to the arrangement.

“You remember me?” he asked.

“Mr. Flores.”

He slapped his chest. The dog barked.

“He remembers!”

People outside the barber shop applauded.

Shawna looked at them, then at me.

“You told me you were weird in high school.”

“I was very good at geometry.”

“He threw a refrigerator at my landlord,” Mr. Flores said.

“The refrigerator was empty.”

“The landlord wasn't.”

“He moved.”

“Both of us did,” Mr. Flores said happily. “I got the downstairs unit.”

Bell Street ran six blocks downhill toward the port, and every block appeared to have been informed that my wife and I were coming. A butcher stood in his doorway holding a package the size of a mattress. Two boys had put a banner between a bus stop and a palm tree. It said WELCOME BACK, GREAT CHIGGA. The word GREAT had been painted over something longer. My cousin's old nickname for me had survived six years, three changes of bar ownership and, apparently, an unsuccessful attempt at spelling it on a bedsheet.

“You didn't approve the sign?” Shawna asked.

“I would have asked for a picture.”

“Of yourself.”

“So people know which great one.”

Somebody shouted my name from upstairs. A paper bag fell from a window. I caught it against my chest.

Inside were two hot pork buns and five hundred dollars.

“Auntie Loan says don't get skinny!” the woman at the window shouted.

“That's a lot of encouragement,” Shawna said.

I put one bun in her hand. She took a bite and stopped objecting to the neighborhood for almost four seconds.

Then a man in a cream tracksuit came sprinting out of Bishop's carrying a wireless microphone.

“Ladies and gentlemen, the motherfucking prodigal nigga has arrived!”

“Saint,” I said.

He threw both arms around me. He had gained a beard, a diamond tooth and enough cologne to qualify as an indoor weather system. When we were fourteen, he had tried to book me for a paid appearance at his own birthday party. We had argued about the deposit until his mother cut the cake.

He stepped back and held the microphone beneath my mouth.

“Say something for the people.”

“Your microphone isn't on.”

Saint glanced at it. His smile remained in place while he worked the switch with his thumb.

“That's why the people love you. Technical support.”

The speaker outside Bishop's screamed. Three pigeons left a roof. A bus driver stopped his bus halfway through the intersection, opened the doors and leaned out.

“Aiden?”

I waved.

“Look at this nigga!”

He started clapping. His passengers joined him because they were on a bus and something was happening. A woman in the front seat held up a baby. I waved at the baby too. The driver closed the doors and took the whole applauding bus downhill.

Saint watched it go with professional interest.

“I should have sold tickets.”

“To public transportation?” Shawna asked.

“I'm meeting my best friend's wife for the first time. Please don't attack my business model.”

She hugged him with her free arm. He called her Mrs. Greatness. She told him she had an actual name. He immediately announced Shawna Nguyễn to the street with more ceremony than he'd used for me.

The butcher brought the meat over.

“For your wedding,” he said.

“We got married last year,” I said.

“I wasn't invited.”

“It was very small.”

He looked at the meat in his arms.

“So was the cow when I started saving it.”

Shawna thanked him and opened the trunk. He laid it beside our suitcases, bowed to her, then whispered something in Saint's ear. Saint whispered back. The butcher took a photograph of me next to his business card.

“What was that?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“Darius.”

“He can say you eat there.”

“I haven't.”

“You got a whole animal in your trunk. Eventually the claim becomes true.”

I put an arm around his shoulders and steered him toward Bishop's. Shawna walked on my other side, checking a message from the driver carrying the dress forms and sewing machines for her new atelier. She'd spent the flight home sketching a jacket on the back of a customs form. When I asked whether the jacket was for me, she said it was for someone who knew when to stop talking.

I still had hopes.

Bishop's had the same red chairs, the same tiled counter and the same woman behind it pointing at me before I reached the door.

“Don't you bring that suitcase in here,” Denise Bishop said. “I just mopped.”

“Auntie, it's good to see you too.”

She came around the counter, grabbed my face in both hands and kissed my forehead. Then she did it to Shawna, whom she had previously met only on video calls and already preferred.

“Look what she did to you. You got a collar. Shoes match. Teeth clean.”

“I had teeth before.”

“You also had a rat tail.”

“For eleven days.”

“I counted.”

She gave us the booth by the window. Saint slid in beside me before she could tell him where to sit. She told him to get out. He got out. She put a bowl in front of him at the counter, and he accepted this change of status without argument.

There were framed photographs above the booth. A baseball team. A graduation. My mother and Denise holding a cake shaped like a car. My father standing beside an actual car, one hand under its rear bumper, while Denise changed the tire.

The picture had been taken in 2008. He was wearing the same blue work shirt he still wore on Sundays.

“He charges everybody else,” Denise said, following my eyes. “Tell your daddy that.”

“For changing tires?”

“For acting like he doesn't want his picture taken.”

I had just picked up my chopsticks when Shawna's delivery driver pulled up outside.

He parked behind a black van that hadn't been there a minute earlier. Four men got out of the van. One carried a clipboard. Another carried a baseball bat. The other two were large enough to carry most of their conversations without props.

The clipboard man spoke to the driver. The driver pointed at Bishop's. Shawna stood up.

“Sit down,” I told her. “I'll see what they want.”

She looked at me.

“Those are my sewing machines.”

She went out first.

Saint left his bowl at the counter. Denise put a lid on mine.

“You just got home,” she said.

“I know.”

“And I used the good broth.”

The clipboard man was explaining a delivery fee. He had a narrow face, a bright white shirt and the expression of a man who charged for bad news by the syllable.

“Six hundred to unload,” he told Shawna.

“I've paid for delivery.”

“To the street. Unloading is separate.”

“The building is on the street.”

“That's convenient.”

The driver held his phone toward him. “Man, I work for the moving company.”

“Then you should know the rules.”

Shawna reached for the clipboard. The man pulled it back.

“You don't touch this.”

“Then you don't get paid.”

I came down the restaurant steps.

The man with the bat recognized me. His eyes moved from my face to the banner above the street. He leaned toward the clipboard man and said something very quietly.

“Who?” the clipboard man asked.

The bat man said it again.

I stopped beside my wife.

“You've got about six seconds to make this a welcome-home joke.”

The clipboard man glanced at Saint. Saint had both hands over the microphone, which made me suspect it was on.

“We're with the Wharf Circle,” the man said.

“Four seconds.”

He looked me over. His mouth tightened when he reached the slippers on my feet. I had changed out of my plane shoes in the car. Shawna said they made me look like I was escaping a hotel fire.

“You somebody important?”

Saint lifted the microphone.

“That's a very expensive question, nigga.”

The clipboard hit my chest.

The man hadn't swung it hard. He was making a point. Behind him, one of the large men smiled and reached for the delivery truck's latch.

I took the clipboard, folded it across my knee and gave the two halves back.

“Put it on separate invoices.”

The bat man dropped his bat.

The bigger man at the truck did the opposite of what a sensible person would have done. He grabbed Shawna's wrist.

She drove the heel of her free hand into his nose. He let go and staggered against the truck. She stepped backward, out of my way, without looking to see if I was coming.

I caught his jacket at the shoulder and belt, turned him sideways and threw him through the open sliding door of the black van.

He hit the far door hard enough to push it off its track.

Both doors now opened.

The second big man charged me from the left. I stepped toward him. His fist passed over my right shoulder. I put my left hand behind his elbow and drove my right fist into the soft space beneath his ribs.

Air came out of him in a long flat note.

I held his elbow so he didn't land on Shawna's shoes. When his knees reached the pavement, I let go.

The clipboard man had made it to the driver's door. He dragged a pistol from beneath his shirt, snagged the muzzle in the fabric and pulled harder. I crossed the distance before the shirt tore.

I trapped his gun hand against the roof of the van.

He squeezed the trigger.

The shot punched through the roof. Everyone outside Bishop's ducked. Saint ducked behind a flowerpot that covered neither his head nor his body.

I pushed the gunman's wrist backward over the edge of the roof. Something clicked in his arm. He screamed and let go of the pistol. I caught it by the barrel, put it on top of the van and drove his forehead into the window.

The glass broke on the second impact.

I let him slide down the door.

Behind me, the bat man held his empty hands above his head.

“I told him,” he said.

“You did.”

“I'm from Alder Street. I know your dad.”

“Then why are you holding your hands like that?”

He lowered them halfway.

“You shot?” Shawna asked.

“No.”

She checked my chest anyway. Her hand shook once against my shirt, then steadied. I closed mine over it.

The man I'd thrown into the van crawled out through the new opening on the other side. He took one look around the vehicle at me and sat down on the curb.

The moving driver had been recording. His phone was still aimed at the sky.

“Get the machines inside,” Shawna told him. “I'll show you where.”

She took the keys out of her bag and walked him toward the empty storefront two doors below Bishop's. The driver hurried after her.

For a moment the whole block was quiet except for the clipboard man trying to breathe through his nose.

Then Mr. Flores started clapping.

The barber shop joined in. The butcher lifted both hands above his head. Somebody upstairs shouted that I'd done the window wrong and could have used the man's elbow.

“He's rusty!” Saint shouted back. “Let the nigga warm up!”

A woman handed me a tissue for my knuckles. Another put twenty dollars in my shirt pocket.

“Auntie, you don't have to—”

“Take it.”

I took it.

Denise stood at her door with the lid from my bowl in one hand.

“Your food,” she said, “is getting disrespectful.”

I looked at the bat man. He was already helping his boss into the van.

“Leave the gun,” I said.

“Absolutely.”

“And the bat.”

“Wasn't mine anyway.”

They left slowly. The displaced door rattled against the side of the van every time it hit a bump.

I picked up the bat and carried it into Bishop's. Denise pointed at the umbrella stand. I put it there.

Saint sat across from me when Shawna returned. He had found a napkin and was making a list.

“What's that?” I asked.

“Welcome-home expenses.”

“You owe me money?”

“No, I'm trying to work out how much more we could have charged.”

Shawna took his pen.

I finally got a mouthful of noodles.

Outside, a white sedan stopped beside the damaged glass on the pavement. A woman in a dark green suit got out. She spoke briefly to Mr. Flores, who pointed at the restaurant with both hands.

She entered, nodded to Denise and laid a cream envelope beside my bowl.

“Mr. Lâm would like to see you tonight.”

“I'm eating.”

“I can see that.”

“Then you're already doing better than the last guy.”

Her eyes flicked toward the bat in the umbrella stand.

“Mr. Lâm would like to apologize for the misunderstanding.”

I opened the envelope.

There was an address, a time and a check for a hundred thousand dollars.

Saint put his napkin over the check so Denise couldn't see it. She lifted the napkin, looked, then set a second bowl in front of me.

“On the house,” she said.

Shawna put down her chopsticks.

“For what?”

Denise pointed at the check.

“Whatever the hell he's doing, I want him to remember who fed him.”

## Chapter 2: Shoes Off

My mother opened the front door, looked at the meat in my arms and shut it again.

“Mom.”

The mail slot lifted.

“Did you call first?”

“You told me to come at five.”

“Then why do you have a cow?”

“Wedding present.”

“You got married last year.”

“Nobody is happy about that, apparently.”

The door opened. She wore a black shirt, gray trousers and the expression she used when someone ordered wedding invitations without knowing whom they intended to marry. Behind her, the house smelled of fried garlic and the laundry powder she'd been buying since I was little.

She hugged Shawna first. Then she took the meat from me and pointed at my feet.

“Shoes.”

“They're slippers.”

“They're outside slippers. Now they're making outside in my house.”

I took them off.

Saint arrived behind us with my suitcase. He'd insisted on helping after I told him he couldn't expense a microphone to my welcome-home account.

“Auntie Mai! Looking magnificent.”

“You look expensive, Darius. Who owes you money?”

“Nobody. That's the problem.”

She took his face in one hand and turned it toward the window.

“Is that a diamond in your tooth?”

He smiled wider.

“That's crazy, nigga. What happens when you eat corn?”

“With respect, Auntie, not everything is an engineering problem.”

“Until something gets stuck.”

She gave him a bag of recycling to take outside. He accepted it with a little bow. Shawna watched him retreat down the steps.

“Does everyone on this street work for your mother?”

“Usually only when they come inside.”

Mom kissed me hard enough to hurt my cheek, held me for a second and then slapped the back of my head.

“I saw the video.”

“Already?”

“Denise sent it before you finished. Why were you wearing hotel slippers to fight people?”

“Grip.”

“One of them came off.”

“That was the weak one.”

She made a sound that meant she loved me and didn't intend to admit I'd said anything funny.

My father was in the kitchen, holding the refrigerator.

I don't mean he was leaning against it. The refrigerator was sideways in his arms. Its doors faced the ceiling. A bowl of uncovered marinating pork sat on the upper door while my mother's rice cooker steamed on the counter beneath it.

He looked over the refrigerator at me.

“Come help.”

I went around the table and reached for the other end.

“With the mop,” he said.

There was water under his feet. A supply hose lay beside the wall.

I found the mop in the closet and cleaned under the refrigerator while he held it. Shawna came into the kitchen. My father shifted the appliance onto one arm and held out his free hand.

“Good flight?”

“Long,” she said, shaking it. “Is that comfortable?”

He glanced at the refrigerator.

“It was in the way.”

“I can see that.”

“Aiden, you missed the corner.”

I moved the mop.

Saint came back in, saw my father and the refrigerator, and quietly took a photograph.

“Darius,” Dad said.

Saint put away the phone.

“It was for the warranty, Uncle.”

“Good. You can call them.”

Dad set the refrigerator upright, caught the bowl before it slid off the door and passed it to Mom as she came through the kitchen. She took it without breaking her conversation with Shawna about commercial sewing machines.

I put away the mop. When I turned around, Dad was looking at me.

I went over, bent from the waist and bowed. We had done this since I was six and he'd caught me announcing myself as head of the household because I could reach the thermostat. He'd said the job came with bills. I'd bowed and returned the title.

He put a hand on the back of my neck and brought me into a hug.

“Welcome home, son.”

For a moment I was small enough to fit under his arm again.

Then he stepped back, took my right hand and turned my knuckles toward the light.

“Window glass.”

“A little.”

“You should have used his elbow.”

Saint slapped the kitchen counter.

“I knew that was you upstairs!”

Dad looked at him.

“I was at work.”

“Then why did—”

“Because it was stupid,” Mom said, taking plates out of the cupboard. “Several people can notice the same stupid thing.”

Shawna laughed into her hand. I pointed at her.

“You're supposed to be on my side.”

“I'm in your mother's house. I haven't established voting rights yet.”

The back door opened. A man in a straw hat came through carrying a bag of oranges and a folding chair.

“Who's stupid?” he asked.

“Your grandson,” Mom said.

Granddad Hòa looked at me.

“Which one?”

“You only have one here.”

“Then why ask me?”

He put the oranges on the counter and hugged us both. He smelled faintly of chalk, though he'd retired from teaching years before. His shirt pocket held two pens, a folded grocery list and a metal ruler with one corner missing.

He set up his folding chair at the end of the table.

“We have chairs,” Mom told him.

“This one knows me.”

Saint studied it. One leg was bent inward, and the seat had been repaired with bright blue cord.

“That's a historical chair, Uncle.”

“It will be if you stop touching it.”

Saint took his hand off the back.

Dad brought the rice to the table. Mom arranged vegetables around the pork. Shawna reached to help and was given something useful to do, which was how I knew Mom had accepted her. Everyone else got told to sit down.

I took the chair beside Shawna.

Dad put his hand on its back.

“Move it left.”

I moved it left.

“More.”

I moved it again. The table leg was now between my knees.

“Dad.”

“Your great-grandfather sits there.”

“I thought he was coming tomorrow.”

“I thought you were arriving without punching a van,” Mom said. “People surprise you.”

A horn sounded outside. It was the high, furious horn of the tiny electric cart Great-Grandpa used when he wanted strangers to think he needed assistance.

Saint was already standing.

“I'll get him.”

“Don't offer to carry his bag,” Granddad said.

Saint stopped at the door.

“Why?”

“Find out.”

We heard the gate click, Saint's bright greeting, and the prolonged grunt of a man discovering something unfortunate about luggage.

Great-Grandpa Tín came through the front door in a white linen shirt, dark trousers and sunglasses bigger than his face. Saint followed him sideways, both arms wrapped around a canvas bag. The bag dragged a little on the floor.

“Put that down, nigga,” Great-Grandpa said. “You're making it tired.”

Saint set it down with a thump that shook the spoons.

“What's in there?” he whispered.

“My things.”

“Your things weigh more than me.”

“Then get some better things.”

Great-Grandpa took off his sunglasses. His hair was white, clipped close around the ears, and his face had so many fine lines that each smile arrived with reinforcements. He inspected me from the doorway.

“You got handsome.”

“Thank you.”

He inspected Dad.

“Where did he get it?”

Mom made a delighted noise. Dad pulled out Great-Grandpa's chair.

“Please sit.”

“Don't say please like you're closing a door.”

He hugged Shawna, accepted her compliment on his shirt and told her he'd bought it to annoy his doctor. Then he sat down and reached for the nearest dish.

Mom caught his wrist with her chopsticks.

“We haven't started.”

“I've started.”

Granddad moved the dish closer to him. Mom pointed her chopsticks at her father instead. He peeled an orange with great concentration.

We made it through half the meal before the check came up.

Saint did it. He had been trying not to do it for twelve minutes, which was a personal record.

“Uncle Minh, how well do you know Bảo Lâm?”

Dad kept eating.

“Enough.”

“He gave Aiden a hundred thousand dollars.”

“For what?” Mom asked.

“Coming to a party,” I said.

Shawna looked at me. I added the part about the Wharf Circle. Dad set down his bowl.

“Are you going?”

“Yes.”

“Then don't take their car home.”

“That's it?”

“You wanted directions?”

Mom put more vegetables on my plate.

“He wanted you to tell him not to go so he could explain his independence,” she said.

“I did not.”

“You took a breath for it.”

“I breathe regularly.”

Great-Grandpa snorted. Granddad put a piece of orange on his father's plate, and the old man ate it without looking down.

“You two are very calm,” Great-Grandpa said to my parents. “Twenty-six years ago, one of you came home with blood on his wedding shoes and the other wanted to know whether he'd saved the receipt.”

“That wasn't the same,” Mom said.

“No. Your dress cost more.”

Dad reached for the serving spoon.

“He'll make his own decisions.”

“Listen to this nigga,” Great-Grandpa said to Shawna. “When he was twenty-seven, his decisions arrived at my house on a tow truck.”

Shawna rested her chin on her hand.

“I would like to hear that story.”

“After he eats,” Mom said quickly.

I grinned at Dad. He looked at me for a long moment, then slid the pork dish to my end of the table.

“Eat.”

The front doorbell rang.

Saint started to get up again. Great-Grandpa touched one finger to his sleeve.

“You already met the bag. Let somebody else have a turn.”

Dad went to the door. A man outside asked for me. His voice was loud, cheerful and completely wrong for our porch.

“Mr. Lâm sent a courtesy vehicle.”

“He has a car,” Dad said.

“This one's bulletproof.”

“He has a car.”

I stood up and went into the hall. The driver wore a black suit with a purple pocket square. He had one foot across the threshold. Dad looked down at it.

“Take that out.”

“Sir, I'm just here to—”

Dad took him by the front of the jacket, lifted him six inches off the floor and turned him around. He held him over the porch while reaching past him to open the screen door.

The man hung rigidly with both hands pressed to his trouser seams.

Dad set him on the top step, brushed a wrinkle out of his lapel and nodded toward the driveway.

“Tell Bảo thank you.”

The man walked to the car without bending either knee very much.

I watched him get in.

“You could have let me answer,” I said.

Dad closed the door.

“My house.”

I put a hand against the door before it latched. He glanced at it.

“Son.”

I pushed. He kept one finger on the brass knob. The door didn't move.

I planted my feet and pushed harder.

He looked past me toward the kitchen.

“Mai, did you put ginger in this?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

I put my shoulder against the door. The wooden frame creaked. Dad took his finger off the knob, caught my shirt as I stumbled forward and set me back where I'd started.

“Don't break the house,” he said.

From the kitchen, Great-Grandpa called, “Nigga, you broke that same frame in 2003!”

Dad shut his eyes for half a second.

I returned to dinner smiling.

Granddad had put his folding chair in my old place. Its bent leg was straight now. I looked at it, then at him.

He held up an orange segment.

“Want one?”

Under the table, Great-Grandpa nudged the chair's leg with his shoe. Granddad nudged it back. Neither looked down.

The thick oak table moved an inch toward the wall.

Mom slapped its top.

“Both of you. I have hot soup.”

The table stopped moving.

Granddad handed me the orange. Great-Grandpa winked at Shawna. Dad ate another mouthful of rice.

Saint leaned close to me.

“I need you to ask who's paying to fix my back.”

I looked at the canvas bag beside the door.

“What did he put in it?”

“I opened it while he was arguing.”

“And?”

Saint swallowed.

“A hat.”

## Chapter 3: Spring

The address on the invitation belonged to a boxing gym called Honest Work.

There was no sign explaining the joke.

Saint parked across the street and turned off the engine. He had changed into a black suit, replaced his diamond stud with a larger diamond stud and brought a second microphone in case an opportunity survived the first.

“You're staying in the car,” I said.

“Nigga, I have been waiting twenty years to say we're on the list.”

“We're on a different kind of list.”

“Every list is a different kind when you haven't been on it.”

I got out. He got out. I looked over the roof at him.

“My mother will kill you.”

“Your mother likes my initiative.”

“She gave you recycling.”

“And trusted me to complete it.”

Two men stood outside the gym beneath a yellow light. The older one recognized me and opened the door before I reached him. The younger one put a hand on Saint's chest.

“Just Mr. Trần.”

Saint pointed at me.

“I'm his—”

“Publicist,” I said.

Saint paused for half a beat.

“Publicist. Thank you.”

The younger man looked at his colleague, who shrugged. We went inside.

“You just invented my job,” Saint whispered.

“Try to keep it for ten minutes.”

The gym smelled of leather, bleach and money that had been counted with wet fingers. There was a boxing ring in the center, tables where exercise machines should have been and a bar built beneath photographs of men in trunks holding belts. Most of the tables were full. Some men stopped talking when I entered. Others leaned closer to the men who'd stopped.

A woman in the green suit from Bishop's came toward us.

“Aiden. Trinh Lê.”

“You didn't introduce yourself earlier.”

“You were enjoying lunch.”

“You could tell?”

“You had broth on the check.”

She led us between the tables. Saint walked as if somebody might be filming from either side. He greeted a man he didn't know, complimented a watch he couldn't afford and accepted a drink that hadn't been offered to him.

At the far end of the room, Bảo Lâm sat in a red barber chair. A woman was trimming the hair above his ears. He wore a charcoal suit, no tie and a white towel across his shoulders. A bowl of peeled grapes rested on the arm of the chair.

He held out one hand.

“Aiden.”

I shook it. He had rings on four fingers, each carefully arranged to avoid getting squeezed.

“My apologies for today.”

“Put them in writing next time. It keeps the van intact.”

His mouth twitched. The woman with the scissors smiled into his hair.

He pointed at a chair beside him.

I stayed standing.

“You wanted to see me.”

“I did.”

“I'm here.”

Bảo looked at Trinh. She took a slim folder from beneath her arm and put it on the table. Saint immediately found a place to set his drink.

“You know what the Circle does,” Bảo said.

“Takes money from delivery drivers.”

“A misunderstanding.”

“I'm getting a lot of those lately.”

He took a grape from the bowl.

“We run clubs. Games. Private events. We settle certain disputes before people make them public. We have enemies, naturally.”

“Naturally.”

“And occasionally we find somebody we would rather invite than inconvenience.”

Saint nodded as though he had personally developed this strategy.

“You have a remarkable family,” Bảo continued.

“They're busy tonight.”

The woman cutting his hair stopped moving her scissors. Bảo looked at me for a moment, then laughed.

“Your father said something like that to me once.”

“How much did it cost you?”

He put down the grape.

“Would you like to make money, Aiden?”

I tapped the check in my jacket pocket.

“I'm having a good day already.”

Trinh opened the folder. There was a photograph of a room with green felt tables, a narrow stage and a stained-glass window above the bar.

“The upstairs floor of the Pearl,” she said. “Games three nights a week. Fully staffed. A share of the house.”

“What share?”

“Twenty percent.”

“Forty.”

Saint took a slow drink.

Bảo smiled at him, then at me.

“You're confident.”

“You keep paying me for conversations.”

“Aiden, everyone here went through an introduction.”

I looked at the ring.

“There it is.”

Bảo lifted one shoulder beneath the towel.

“A little entertainment. People have heard stories. They'd like to meet the man.”

“The man brought a publicist,” Saint said. “So appearances are separate.”

Trinh looked at him with genuine interest for the first time.

“What does he charge?”

“Depends what he has to take off.”

I pointed at the photograph.

“Forty percent. And if I win, those four men leave my wife's deliveries alone.”

“Of course.”

“All her deliveries. All the drivers. All the little imaginary fees.”

Bảo's eyes went flat for a second. Then he nodded.

Trinh took a pen out of her pocket and amended the page. I read it. Saint read over my shoulder, moving his lips only at the numbers.

“You can read,” I told him.

“I like hearing good news twice.”

The room began to fill around the ring before I took off my jacket. A man in a sleeveless black shirt climbed between the ropes. He had a shaved head, a thick neck and scar tissue above both eyebrows. His hands were wrapped, but he wasn't wearing gloves.

“Who's that?” I asked Trinh.

“Milo Voss.”

“What does he do?”

“This.”

Voss jumped once, rolled his shoulders and hit a hanging bag beside the ring with a short right hand. The chain snapped at its top link. The bag dropped flat on the floor.

Men at the nearest table stopped pushing money toward my side of the betting sheet.

Saint watched the bag, then me.

“It's probably old equipment.”

A broad man standing at the foot of the ring snorted. He held a tray of bottled water and a hot dog wrapped in a napkin.

“They put that bag up yesterday.”

Saint leaned toward him.

“You work here, nigga?”

“Sometimes.”

“Then show a little customer service.”

The man looked at me. “Hậu Phạm.”

“Aiden.”

“I know.”

He gave me a bottle and lowered his voice.

“Watch the left elbow. He broke a man's jaw with it last month. Said he slipped.”

“Did he?”

“Afterward. There was blood everywhere.”

I handed the unopened bottle to Saint and climbed through the ropes.

Voss stood in the opposite corner. He watched my feet.

“No slippers?”

“My mother saw the video.”

He grinned. He had a gold tooth near the back of his mouth and a gap beside it.

“You ever fought somebody who can hit back?”

“My wife plays tennis.”

The bell rang while he was still deciding whether that was an insult.

Voss crossed the ring in three steps and threw his right hand at my head.

I leaned left. His fist passed close enough to brush my ear. He used the missed punch to turn his hips, brought his left elbow around and aimed it at my jaw.

I ducked underneath it and hit him twice in the ribs.

He grunted. His stomach tightened against my fists. He shoved me backward with his forearm and followed with a knee.

I caught the knee on both palms. The force pushed my feet six inches across the canvas.

Voss smiled wider.

I kicked the inside of his standing ankle.

His leg bent. He dropped his raised foot, recovered and swung at me with both hands. I slipped the first punch and blocked the second against my forearm. Pain ran to my elbow. His fist had the weight of a thrown brick.

He drove me toward the ropes.

Behind him, Bảo had stopped eating grapes.

Voss stepped on my right foot and punched my cheek with his left hand.

My head snapped sideways. I tasted blood. Saint shouted something that began as advice and ended as a complaint to the referee, who had never entered the ring.

Voss pulled back his right fist.

I planted my left foot, bent my knee and jumped to get my trapped foot out from under him.

I overdid it.

The top rope dropped away beneath me. Voss's punch passed under my ankle. For a moment I was level with the bottom of the gym's clock, eight feet above the canvas, looking directly into the face of a man on the upstairs balcony.

He had a shrimp halfway to his mouth.

“Excuse me,” I said.

Then I came down.

I landed behind Voss with both knees bent. The canvas sagged. A board beneath it cracked. I caught the back of his shirt before he could turn, pulled him backward and drove my knee between his shoulder blades.

He hit the mat on his hands and knees.

The room erupted.

Somebody shouted that I'd used a wire. The man on the balcony dropped his shrimp over the railing.

Voss lunged up from the canvas and caught me around the waist.

He drove us into the corner. My back struck the turnbuckle. He lifted me, pinned my thighs against his chest and tried to fold me over the top rope.

I hooked my right foot behind the corner post. The rope dug into my lower back. He pushed harder. The post tilted toward the audience.

People jumped away from their table.

I put both hands around the back of his head and pulled his face into my forehead.

His nose broke against it.

He let go of my legs. I dropped to the canvas, stayed low and drove my shoulder under his ribs. He hit the tilted post sideways. I stepped out, caught his left wrist and pulled him across the ring.

He tried to turn with the pull. I let him.

His feet crossed.

I hit his jaw with my right hand.

The punch lifted both feet off the canvas. He struck the middle rope back first, stretched it three feet toward the crowd, then fell forward onto his knees.

He blinked at me. His mouth opened.

“Stay there,” I said.

He reached for my leg.

I hit him again.

He lay down.

Hậu climbed through the ropes with a towel. He knelt beside Voss, checked him and rolled him onto his side. The noise in the room kept getting louder. Men who'd bet against me were loudly explaining why they'd always intended to change their bets.

Saint climbed onto the apron and held out my jacket.

“We need to talk about the flying.”

I spat blood into Hậu's towel.

“Spring.”

“What?”

“Bent my knee. Used the spring.”

He looked at the clock.

“Nigga, knees are not supposed to come with a second floor.”

A man in a white dinner jacket pushed toward the ring with a stack of cash. He pressed it into my hand before I stepped down.

“For the show.”

Another man added his watch. A third asked whether I would attend his daughter's graduation.

“Is she graduating from a casino?” Shawna asked through Saint's phone.

I looked at him.

He held up the screen.

“She called. I couldn't ignore family.”

Shawna studied my face.

“You got hit.”

“A little.”

“Move the camera.”

Saint pointed it at Voss, whom two men were now helping onto a stool.

She considered him.

“Fine. Ice before you come home. And don't let anybody give you livestock.”

Bảo stood beside the ring, clapping slowly. He'd had time to remove the towel and smooth his hair. Trinh held the amended agreement.

“Welcome,” he said, “to the Wharf Circle.”

I took the pen, signed and handed it back.

Across the room, a lean man in a maroon shirt wasn't clapping. He had his arms folded and a dark bruise on one knuckle. The clipboard man from the afternoon sat beside him, holding a bag of ice against his face.

“Who's the unhappy one?” I asked.

Bảo followed my eyes.

“Vinh. He manages collections.”

“He should collect better employees.”

Bảo smiled without showing his teeth.

Vinh unfolded his arms and came toward us.

He stopped close enough that I could smell peppermint on his breath.

“You made a mess of my van.”

“Your van made a mess of my afternoon.”

His eyes moved to the signed agreement in Trinh's hands.

“Enjoy your room.”

“I intend to.”

He leaned closer.

“Things catch fire in this neighborhood.”

I took the watch the man in the dinner jacket had given me and placed it in Vinh's shirt pocket.

“There. Now you can tell me what time.”

The man in the dinner jacket began applauding again.

Vinh looked down at the watch, then back at me. I smiled at him until he left.

Hậu stepped down from the ring behind us. His hot dog was still on the water tray. He picked it up, examined it and sighed.

“You hungry?” I asked.

“Always.”

“Come with us.”

He glanced at Bảo.

I opened my jacket to show him the new agreement.

“Forty percent of upstairs. That should cover fries.”

Hậu put the hot dog in the trash and followed me out.

## Chapter 4: The King Has a Receipt

By nine the next morning, somebody had painted wings on my welcome-home banner.

By ten, Saint was selling shirts.

He brought one to our apartment above the unfinished atelier. It showed a cartoon of me jumping over a terrified man. The words BELL STREET AIRLINES curved around my head.

“Forty dollars,” he said.

Shawna held it up to the light.

“This is my husband's face.”

“I know. I got a bulk discount.”

“You owe him money.”

“He gets one free.”

“I get fifty percent,” I said from the bathroom.

Saint looked toward the open door.

“Of what?”

“The shirt operation.”

“You didn't even design the wings.”

I came out with a cold pack against my cheek. Shawna had made me hold it there for twenty minutes. The swelling was mostly gone. She kept checking anyway, moving my face with one finger whenever she passed me.

“Fifty percent,” I said.

Saint took back the shirt.

“I'll have to raise prices.”

“People will understand,” Shawna said. “It's difficult being exploited by somebody's actual face.”

Hậu arrived carrying breakfast and wearing one of the shirts. He put the bags on the kitchen counter, accepted a cup of coffee and waited while Saint tried to charge him for the shirt again.

“I paid downstairs,” Hậu said.

“That was wholesale.”

“You sold it to me personally.”

“I'm a versatile company.”

Hậu looked at me. I shook my head. He took a breakfast sandwich out of the bag and ate it in two bites.

Shawna watched him.

“Do you have somewhere else to be?”

“No.”

“Then the sandwich can stay a minute.”

He looked embarrassed and slowed down on the second one.

I liked him more for that than for the warning he'd given me at the ring. He was built like a refrigerator in a hoodie, with heavy shoulders and hands that made paper cups look like medicine measures. He had worked collections for Bảo for four years. Before that he'd unloaded trucks, repaired restaurant equipment and spent six months attempting to become a professional wrestler under the name Hank the Thank.

“The Thank?” Shawna asked.

“They spelled Tank wrong on my first poster.”

“And you kept it?”

“People remembered.”

Saint sat down beside him.

“That's branding, nigga.”

Hậu pointed a finger at him.

“You don't get a percentage of that too.”

We left Shawna supervising the installation of her cutting table and went to the Pearl. It occupied a narrow brick building between a jewelry shop and a pharmacy. The downstairs restaurant was closed until lunch. Upstairs, the green felt tables waited beneath brass lamps, and a woman in a white shirt was using a vacuum cleaner with the fury of someone who had lost an argument before breakfast.

Trinh stood at the bar counting glasses.

“You're early.”

“I own part of it.”

“That doesn't usually make people early.”

She showed me the room. Six tables, twelve cameras, a bar with a cracked mirror and a stage big enough for a singer who didn't need to move. The stained-glass window overlooked Bell Street. A blue heron spread its wings across the upper panes.

Saint stopped under it.

“We could put your face there.”

“We could put yours outside,” Trinh said.

He looked at her.

“I'm the publicist.”

“Then advertise quietly.”

She took me behind the bar and opened a drawer. Bundles of cash sat inside, wrapped in paper bands.

“Your welcome,” she said.

I looked at her.

“Another one?”

“The men who watched last night asked for tables tonight. They paid in advance. Your presence appears to be worth more than our liquor.”

“How much more?”

“Fifty-eight thousand.”

Saint coughed into his fist.

“I need to stop selling cotton.”

I took a bundle from the drawer and put it in Trinh's hand.

“Fix the mirror. Pay the woman with the vacuum whatever you're thinking of paying me to stop talking.”

Trinh smiled slightly.

“She's my aunt.”

“Then double it.”

The vacuum stopped.

“I heard that,” her aunt called.

“He meant double the work,” Trinh said.

“Nigga, I speak English.”

Saint laughed so hard he had to lean against the bar.

I walked out onto the small balcony. From there I could see the atelier, Bishop's, the barber shop and a flatbed truck turning into the street. The truck carried something tall wrapped in blue plastic.

Saint came to stand beside me. He watched the truck with the careful blank expression he used when a surprise had cost more than expected.

“What did you do?” I asked.

“The neighborhood wanted to honor you.”

“The neighborhood has been very generous.”

“Exactly. We needed a central place to express it.”

Hậu joined us and squinted at the truck.

“Is that the statue from Bảo's old banquet hall?”

Saint turned to him.

“You know too many things.”

The driver stopped outside Bishop's. Four men got out. One wore a work shirt with the words ROYAL OCCASIONS stitched over the pocket. He waved at Saint, then looked expectantly at the empty space beside the restaurant steps.

“You bought Bảo's statue?” I asked.

“Borrowed the concept.”

“That sounds like stealing the object.”

“It's legally complicated.”

We went downstairs.

The statue stood seven feet tall on its plinth. Somebody had put sunglasses on it and draped a new jacket across its bronze shoulders. Its hair had been painted black. Its right hand held an enormous fish.

“Why am I holding a fish?” I asked.

Saint looked at the fish as though seeing it for the first time.

“Prosperity.”

“Bảo won a fishing tournament,” Hậu said.

“We all have our little journeys,” Saint said quickly.

People were gathering on both sides of the street. A boy had set up a folding table with more shirts. Denise came outside, took one look at the statue and turned around.

“No,” she said.

Saint hurried after her.

“Auntie, we discussed a neighborhood installation.”

“You said a bench.”

“This encourages standing.”

“Not in front of my window.”

The Royal Occasions man put a clipboard on the flatbed and asked who was paying the remaining delivery charge. Shawna came out of the atelier with a tape measure around her neck. She saw the clipboard and stopped.

“Not again.”

“Legitimate invoice,” the man said immediately. “I saw the video. We're insured.”

I paid him.

The men lowered the truck's lift. Its motor whined, slowed and stopped halfway to the pavement. The driver hit the switch again. The platform shuddered beneath the statue.

Everybody stepped back except the man holding its base steady.

The left lift arm snapped.

The platform tilted toward him.

I caught the plinth with both hands. The weight drove one knee to the asphalt. Bronze ground against steel. The worker scrambled backward on his hands, leaving a shoe beneath the leaning platform.

“Get away from the truck,” I said.

The crowd scattered to the sidewalk.

I pushed upward until the broken platform cleared the man's shoe. Hậu dragged the steel ramp out from beneath the base. The driver stood beside the cab with both palms pressed to his head.

“What do you want me to do?” he shouted.

“Move the truck.”

He climbed in, started the engine and eased forward. I kept my hands beneath the edges of the plinth as the flatbed rolled away. The whole statue settled against my arms.

My right shoe split along the sole.

I took three short steps and set the statue down in the gutter.

The fish pointed accusingly at the pharmacy.

Saint was the first to clap. Then everybody did. The rescued worker limped over, hugged me around the waist and started crying into my shirt.

“You're good,” I told him. “You're good.”

He nodded against me.

Shawna crouched by my feet.

“Your shoe is dead.”

“It served bravely.”

“I bought those.”

“Then it had a beautiful childhood.”

She took my wrist and checked it. Hậu retrieved the worker's shoe and handed it back. Denise brought water for the men. Saint used the temporary confusion to move the shirt table closer to the statue.

The Royal Occasions driver tried to return my delivery money.

“Keep it,” I said.

“Please.”

“Fix the lift.”

He put the money away, then gave me two hundred dollars out of his own wallet.

I looked at it.

“For what?”

“My cousin was under there.”

“He's still your cousin.”

“Exactly.”

He shoved the money into my hand and went back to the truck before I could give it back.

Shawna stood beside me and looked from the statue to the crowd.

“How long have you been home?”

“Twenty-six hours.”

“This city is going to need a budget.”

A tall man in a pale blue shirt emerged from a silver car farther down the block. He had close-cropped hair, soft brown eyes and a smile that arrived before the rest of him. Two men followed him carrying boxes.

“Leon Mercer,” Hậu said quietly.

I watched him approach.

“Sunday,” Saint murmured.

The name carried along the sidewalk. A few people moved their children behind them. Others came forward to shake his hand. He greeted everyone by name and stopped to admire a woman's new glasses before reaching me.

“Aiden Trần.”

“Mr. Mercer.”

“Sunday. Everybody calls me Sunday.”

He looked at the statue and smiled.

“You made a strong entrance.”

“Some assembly required.”

He laughed, then introduced himself to Shawna with both hands visible and none of the touching men like Bảo considered a privilege.

“I hear you're opening an atelier. My sister needs a dress. I'll send her over.”

“I'll give her my rates,” Shawna said.

“I'm sure she'll deserve them.”

He signaled to the men with the boxes. They opened them on the hood of his car. Inside were two pairs of handmade shoes, one black and one dark brown.

“I saw yours go,” Sunday said. “A lucky coincidence.”

I looked from the shoes to his face.

“You keep these in your car?”

“I keep gifts.”

Saint whispered, “That's a rich-nigga sentence.”

Sunday heard him and laughed again. He gave me a card with a telephone number embossed in silver.

“Call if you need anything. Bell Street's always been good to my family.”

He left without mentioning the Circle. I watched his car go uphill, away from the port.

Hậu waited until it turned the corner.

“Don't wear the shoes.”

“Why?”

“You'll start owing him places to walk.”

I closed the boxes.

“Get a good price for them.”

Saint already had his phone out.

By lunchtime the statue had been moved to a patch of concrete beside the barber shop. Denise had refused it, Shawna had refused it, and Auntie Loan had accepted it on the condition that people buying shirts also buy a haircut.

We went upstairs at the Pearl to look at the stage. Shawna was considering renting it for her first private showing. She measured the width, checked the light from the stained glass and told Saint he'd have to stand somewhere else if he intended to keep wearing that much cologne.

I was holding the other end of her tape measure when Hậu's phone rang.

He listened, looked toward the window and stopped chewing the mint he'd taken from the bar.

“The statue's gone,” he said.

Saint blinked.

“Gone where?”

“Two men with a truck. Said Bảo wanted his face back.”

Trinh put down the glass she was drying.

“Bảo's on a plane to San Diego.”

My phone buzzed.

A photograph arrived from an unknown number. The statue lay on its side in the back of a truck. Somebody had removed the sunglasses and painted a red X across its chest.

Beneath the photograph was one sentence.

*Bring the thing from underneath, or we start with your wife's window.*

I looked at Saint.

He held up both hands.

“I have a receipt,” he said.

## Chapter 5: Heavy Delivery

Rafa Ortiz brought a tow truck because he'd heard we were stealing something back and wanted to be useful.

Saint had asked for a discreet car.

The tow truck was orange. Its doors showed a cartoon gorilla holding a broken sedan. A speaker above the cab played a recording of Rafa's uncle shouting that breakdowns were opportunities.

“Turn that off,” I said as I climbed in.

Rafa reached over the dashboard and pulled a wire loose. The shouting stopped halfway through the word opportunity.

“He made that recording in 1998,” Rafa said. “He's been dead four years and still books more work than me.”

Hậu climbed into the back seat. The truck settled lower on that side. Saint squeezed in beside him, immediately objected to the amount of space available and was handed a socket wrench to hold.

“Why?”

“So your hands have a job,” Rafa said.

I called Shawna as we pulled away.

“Loan and Denise are coming over,” I told her. “Keep the door locked until they're there.”

“They already are.”

In the background, Auntie Loan asked whether the threatened window was laminated. Denise asked whether the men threatening it were.

“I'll be home before dinner,” I said.

“You said that yesterday.”

“I was.”

“You came home with boxing money in a takeout bag.”

“It was a clean bag.”

“Call me when you have a better argument.”

She hung up. I smiled at the phone, then put it away.

The boy selling shirts had filmed the statue being loaded. He'd been annoyed because the thieves wouldn't wait for him to move his table. The truck's rear plate was visible for three seconds. Hậu recognized the bent bumper before I finished looking at the numbers.

“Kenny Vale,” he said. “Used to move equipment for the Circle. Now he moves equipment for whoever pays him.”

“Where?”

“Old cold-storage place by the Blue Cut.”

Rafa took the next right.

“I know it. They owe my uncle for a recovery.”

Saint leaned forward.

“Your uncle's dead.”

“The invoice isn't.”

The city flattened as we approached the water. Brick buildings gave way to corrugated steel, fenced yards and long concrete channels carrying brown river water toward the harbor. A red drawbridge stood ahead of us with its center span raised. Behind it, cranes moved above the port like enormous bent fingers.

The cold-storage building sat beside a lane ending at the river. A faded fish painted on its wall grinned at the loading bays. The truck from the video was backed into the middle bay, engine running.

Two men stood beside it.

One was Kenny Vale, if the embroidered name on his jacket could be trusted. The other wore a tight gray T-shirt and had a neck as wide as my thigh. His right hand rested on the truck's rear door. The door was dented beneath his fingertips.

Hậu stopped moving in the back seat.

“That's Rhett King.”

“I know the name.”

“You should know the rest of him.”

Rafa parked around the corner. I got out before Saint could begin explaining why publicists needed to stay near their clients.

Hậu followed me.

“Stay with Rafa,” I told Saint.

“To coordinate?”

“To sit.”

He stayed.

We walked through the open gate. Kenny saw us first. His face changed, and he put a hand on King's arm.

King looked up slowly.

He was taller than I'd expected. Six and a half feet, maybe more, with heavy forearms and a pale scar running from his left ear to the corner of his mouth. A thick silver chain hung against his shirt. He had no rings, no watch and no visible weapon.

Kenny had a pistol. He drew it immediately, which told me who had the weaker argument.

“Stay there.”

I stopped ten feet from the loading bay. Hậu stopped beside me.

“You took my fish,” I said.

Kenny blinked.

“What?”

“Big bronze fish. Attached to an ugly man.”

King looked through the open rear door of the truck. A corner of blue plastic hung over the loading ramp.

“That's supposed to be you?” he asked.

“The paperwork says so.”

“You got robbed twice.”

I laughed before I could help it.

Kenny didn't. His pistol shook slightly as he pointed it between Hậu and me.

“Where's the box?”

“What box?”

“Don't do that.”

“You stole a statue and sent me a picture. I don't think I'm the one being cryptic.”

King took his hand off the truck. Four shallow fingerprints remained in the aluminum panel.

“Under the base,” he said. “Small red box. It was there when the statue left the banquet hall. It isn't there now.”

I thought of the delivery platform tilting, the plinth dragging against steel, Hậu pulling the ramp out. I hadn't seen a box.

“Then you should ask the moving company.”

Kenny lifted his pistol toward my face.

Hậu grabbed his wrist and shoved it upward. The shot went into the loading-bay roof. I stepped past Hậu and drove my fist into Kenny's stomach.

He folded around my arm. Hậu took the gun, twisted Kenny's wrist once more and knocked him against the truck with his shoulder.

King hit me before Kenny reached the ground.

His fist caught the side of my head. I stumbled sideways, struck the bay's concrete pillar with one shoulder and saw the yard tilt white for half a second.

King came after me.

I ducked under his next punch. His knuckles hit the pillar. A piece of concrete broke off beside my ear.

I drove three punches into his body, left, right, left. The last one made him step back. I kicked his knee from the side.

His leg moved. The rest of him didn't.

He caught my ankle before I could bring it back and swung me into the truck.

My back struck the open door. Its lower hinge tore loose. I hit the loading ramp on one hip and rolled beneath it as his foot came down where my chest had been.

The steel ramp bent in the middle.

Hậu hit King across the back with a length of pipe.

King turned around.

Hậu looked at the bent pipe in his hands.

“That's some bullshit.”

He hit him again, this time across the side of the knee. King grunted and shifted his weight. I came out from under the ramp and drove my shoulder into the back of that knee.

King dropped to one leg.

Hậu threw the pipe at his face and jumped back. King raised an arm to block it. I caught the silver chain at his neck, pulled backward and wrapped the loose length around the truck's door handle.

King reached for my hand.

I kicked the broken loading ramp out from beneath his planted foot.

He fell sideways. The chain snapped. Its links flew across the concrete like coins.

I grabbed Hậu's sleeve.

“Truck.”

We ran around opposite sides of the cab. Kenny was crawling toward the gate. Hậu kicked the pistol farther away from him before climbing into the passenger seat. I opened the driver's door, found the keys still in the ignition and started the engine.

King hit the rear of the truck as I pulled out.

The impact shoved the whole vehicle forward. I saw him in the mirror, one hand gripping the torn rear door.

I floored the accelerator.

He held on for three strides. His shoes scraped across the yard. Then the remaining hinge tore out, and he was left standing with the door in his hands.

We hit the street at an angle. Hậu braced his palm against the dashboard.

“That nigga is going to be upset.”

I checked the mirror.

King threw the door.

It spun across the road and struck the rear corner of the truck. The vehicle lurched left. I corrected, clipped a trash bin and scattered crushed ice across the lane.

Rafa's tow truck pulled out behind us. Saint leaned out of its window, shouting something that disappeared beneath the engine noise.

My phone rang. Hậu answered it on speaker.

“Why is there a door in the road?” Saint demanded.

“Change of management,” I said.

“Rafa says you can't go straight.”

The drawbridge ahead was beginning to lower. Red lights flashed at the crossing. Beyond it, a tug pushed a barge slowly through the channel.

“We can,” I said.

Hậu looked at the descending bridge, then at the truck's speedometer.

“We absolutely cannot.”

I pressed harder on the accelerator.

The bridge had thirty feet to travel. The truck had a hundred and ninety. Its suspension bounced beneath the statue's weight. The left side of the raised roadway disappeared behind the cab roof as we approached.

“Aiden.”

“I can see it.”

“Can you see the river?”

“Also yes.”

The front bumper struck the crossing barrier and snapped it at its hinge. We hit the bottom of the bridge span just as it came level enough to take our wheels.

The truck launched upward.

Hậu's head struck the ceiling. The statue slammed against the rear of the cargo compartment. For one long moment the windshield showed nothing but pale sky.

Then the front wheels hit the far side of the span.

The dashboard cracked. My teeth clicked together. I wrestled the wheel straight as the truck bounced once, twice, and landed fully on the road beyond the channel.

Hậu sat with both hands flat against the ceiling.

His phone was still on speaker.

Saint had stopped shouting.

“You alive?” I asked Hậu.

“I'm deciding.”

Behind us, the bridge settled into place. Rafa drove across at a perfectly reasonable speed.

Saint found his voice.

“The bridge was coming down, nigga! You could have waited!”

I glanced in the mirror. There was no sign of King.

“Traffic,” I said.

Hậu turned his head very slowly toward me.

“You are buying lunch.”

We abandoned Kenny's damaged truck in Rafa's yard and covered the statue with a tarp. Rafa walked around the vehicle, whistling softly at the torn hinges and the dents in the side.

“You know,” he said, “my uncle would've called that an opportunity.”

Saint opened the truck's rear compartment and looked at the statue. Its sunglasses were gone. The fish's tail had bent upward during the bridge landing.

“It's more dynamic now.”

I sat on a stack of tires while Hậu looked at the cut behind my ear. He pressed a clean cloth against it.

“You need stitches.”

“Later.”

He pressed harder.

“Now is usually before later.”

Saint paced in front of us, scrolling through his phone. A message made him stop.

“Oh.”

I looked at him.

“What?”

“There was a box.”

Hậu took the cloth away from my ear.

“Say that carefully.”

Saint held up a photograph. Auntie Loan stood in the barber shop holding a small red metal box. Its lid had a brass star stamped into the center.

“It fell off when the lift broke,” Saint said. “One of the kids picked it up. Loan thought it was a donation box.”

I stared at the photograph.

“Where is it now?”

“She's trying to open it with haircut scissors.”

I stood up.

Rafa came out of his office with an envelope.

“Before you go.”

He handed it to me. Inside were three hundred dollars and his uncle's old unpaid invoice.

“What is this?”

“Kenny owes us. You got him out of the truck. That's more progress than we've made in five years.”

“Rafa.”

He closed my hand around the envelope.

“Take the money, nigga. Let my uncle rest.”

## Chapter 6: The Woman Who Charged Full Price

Shawna charged me six hundred dollars to enter my own apartment.

She had a receipt ready.

“What's this?” I asked.

“Blood on the stair runner. Replacement shirt. Emergency alterations to whatever you've done to those trousers.”

“We share a bank account.”

“Then you'll enjoy watching it move.”

Hậu stood behind me with the red box under one arm. Saint had remained at the barber shop to help Auntie Loan deny that he'd ever suggested she could keep half of whatever was inside.

Shawna looked at Hậu.

“Are you bleeding too?”

“Not on anything.”

“Come in.”

She made me sit on the closed toilet lid while she cleaned the cut behind my ear. I told her a warehouse had gotten personal. She told me warehouses didn't usually leave knuckle marks on people's faces.

When she pressed the antiseptic pad against the cut, I hissed.

“The great one suffers,” she said.

“The great one is considering another doctor.”

“The great one's mother is downstairs.”

I held still.

Mom had brought a stack of price cards for the atelier and a sandwich press she insisted was essential to doing business. By the time I came out of the bathroom, she'd plugged the press in, opened a window and told Hậu he was cutting the sandwiches too small.

“People should be able to hold them,” he said.

“They have two hands.”

She handed me a price card. It was thick cream paper with Shawna's name embossed across the top.

“Looks good,” I said.

“I know. Take these downstairs. Your wife has a client.”

“I'm helping Hậu with—”

“Nigga, she's the one who makes you look employable.”

I took the cards.

The atelier had changed while I was out. The machines were in place along the left wall. A long cutting table occupied the center. Shawna had hung three finished jackets near the window and positioned a mirror where the afternoon light struck it. The empty storefront now looked like somebody had plans for it and expected the rest of the world to dress accordingly.

A woman in a red coat stood by the mirror.

She was tall, broad-shouldered and wore enough gold at her wrists to ring when she moved her hands. A younger woman beside her held a garment bag and an expression of permanent caution.

“Estelle Mercer,” the woman said when she saw me.

“Your brother mentioned you.”

“My brother mentions everybody. It's how he keeps track of who thinks they matter.”

I liked her immediately, which was probably a family skill.

She gave me a slow look from my taped ear to the ruined seam at my knee.

“You're the one who jumped over that boxer.”

“I was avoiding the elbow.”

“I'd have hit him with the bell.”

“I'll remember that.”

Shawna came down the stairs carrying a notebook. Estelle turned toward her and opened the garment bag.

Inside was a silver dress with a ripped sleeve and a neckline that looked as if it had lost a negotiation.

“I need this fixed.”

Shawna examined it without touching it.

“For when?”

“Saturday.”

“This Saturday?”

“I like my deadlines near enough to frighten people.”

Shawna took the dress out, laid it on the cutting table and looked at the inside seam. She turned the sleeve over, checked the lining and asked the younger woman whether she had a photograph of the original fitting.

The younger woman produced three before Estelle could answer.

“Thank you,” Shawna said. “What's your name?”

“Nia.”

“You're about to save both of us some time.”

Estelle watched Shawna compare the pictures with the dress.

“My brother says your husband is a friend.”

“Then he can come to the show,” Shawna said.

“I thought there might be a family rate.”

“There is.”

Estelle smiled.

“Family gets told what it actually costs.”

I coughed into my hand. Estelle looked at me.

“You knew she was like this?”

“I married her on purpose.”

Shawna wrote a number in her notebook and turned it around.

Estelle stared.

“For a sleeve?”

“For a sleeve, a rebuilt shoulder, a corrected lining and the two days you're asking me to remove from my week.”

“That's a very expensive shoulder.”

“It belongs to a very demanding woman.”

Nia looked down so quickly I knew she was smiling.

Estelle leaned against the table. For a moment I thought she might make it ugly. Then she laughed, opened her bag and put down a stack of cash.

“Fix the neckline too. I want the photographer to feel unprepared.”

Shawna counted the deposit, wrote a receipt and asked Estelle to step onto the fitting platform.

“Aiden,” she said, “upstairs.”

Estelle raised an eyebrow.

“He's not staying?”

“He's very distracting.”

I spread my hands.

Estelle looked at my knee again.

“In several directions.”

I went upstairs.

Hậu had finished the sandwiches. Mom had gone to the printshop after telling him twice not to let me eat over the red box. Saint arrived carrying a small plastic crown from a children's party shop.

“Don't,” I said.

He put it on the table anyway.

“The statue's out of commission. We need continuity.”

“We need the box open.”

“Loan tried scissors, pliers and a man who said he used to do safes.”

“Did he?”

“He sells furniture now. Nobody asked why.”

I turned the box over in my hands. It was about the size of a paperback, made from red-painted steel with a recessed latch and no visible keyhole. The brass star in the lid had eight points. A line of small black dots ran along one edge.

Hậu watched my thumbs settle against the lid.

“Don't squeeze the contents.”

“I know.”

“Last time you said that, we landed on a bridge.”

I braced the box against the table, hooked my fingers beneath the lip and pulled. The steel gave a long squeal. The latch tore free. I lifted the lid without bending the bottom.

Saint leaned closer.

“Very advanced.”

Inside lay a black drive, a folded card and a small ivory carving of a heron. I took out the card first.

Two words had been written on it.

*Beautiful dies.*

Hậu stopped chewing.

“Mr. Beautiful,” he said.

I turned the card over. Nothing on the back. The carving had no mark I could see. The drive had a silver star etched into its casing.

Saint picked up the crown, set it down again and moved his chair away from the table.

“I should have ordered the bench.”

My phone buzzed with another message from the unknown number.

*You should have stayed in the gym.*

Then a picture of our front window.

Taken from across the street.

I went to the window and looked down.

The silver car that had brought Estelle was still at the curb. A delivery cyclist waited at the intersection. Two men in work jackets stood outside the pharmacy, both looking at their phones.

One looked up.

I stepped back from the glass.

“Hậu. Downstairs.”

He was already moving.

The atelier door opened before we reached the bottom step.

The taller of the two men came in holding a paper bag. The second stayed near the entrance with one hand inside his jacket.

“Delivery,” the tall man said.

Shawna stood beside Estelle on the fitting platform. Nia sat near the window, holding the red coat. Shawna looked at the bag, then at the man's shoes.

“Put it on the floor.”

“Needs a signature.”

“So does a lease. You don't see me carrying one in a lunch bag.”

The second man drew his pistol.

Estelle stepped off the platform and grabbed Nia by the back of her jacket. Shawna shoved the rolling mirror between them and the door.

The first shot shattered the mirror.

I hit the tall man from the side before he could bring the bag around. His shoulder struck the cutting table. I drove my elbow across his jaw and pushed him down over its edge.

The bag fell open. A bottle rolled out with a strip of cloth stuffed into its neck.

Shawna caught it with her foot, rolled it under the table and kicked the metal waste bin over it.

Hậu slammed the second man against the doorframe. The gun went off again. Plaster burst from the wall above the stairs. Hậu trapped the man's forearm between both hands and bent it backward until the pistol dropped.

The man screamed.

I punched the tall man in the temple. His knees folded. I caught his collar and lowered him just far enough to keep his head from hitting Shawna's machine pedal.

From behind the fallen mirror, Estelle shouted, “Nia, are you hit?”

“No.”

“Then stop trying to save the coat.”

The door gunman tried to bite Hậu's shoulder.

Hậu looked personally offended.

“Nigga.”

He lifted the man by his belt and jacket, carried him outside and put him headfirst into the empty recycling cart beside the entrance. The lid bounced once against the man's back.

I searched the tall man's pockets. Phone. Keys. Two hundred dollars. A brass lighter shaped like a pistol.

“That would've been confusing,” Saint said from the stairs.

I looked up at him.

He held both hands in front of him.

“I called your mother.”

“Why?”

“She told me to if somebody tried to burn down the shop.”

“When did she tell you that?”

“This morning. You were outside discussing the fish.”

Shawna came around the table. I stood to meet her. She took my face in both hands, checked my eyes and then looked past me at the ruined mirror.

“Three days,” she said.

“I'll replace it.”

“I have owned that mirror for three days.”

“I'll get the same one.”

She looked down at the unconscious man beside her cutting table.

“No. He will.”

Estelle emerged with Nia, both unharmed. A strip of silver lining hung loose from the dress she'd been trying on. She looked at it, then at Shawna.

“Add it to the bill.”

Shawna met her eyes.

“Your brother gave my husband shoes this morning.”

Estelle's expression changed.

“Did he wear them?”

“No,” I said.

“Good.”

She took out her phone and walked to the far corner of the shop. She spoke quietly, but I heard her brother's name and several words that made Saint look impressed.

Outside, Denise and Loan had arrived with my mother. The man in the recycling cart was trying to climb out. Loan pushed the lid down with one hand while Denise demanded his home address so she could send his family the video.

Mom came in, took one look around and went to Shawna.

She hugged her without speaking. Shawna held on for a few seconds. Then Mom stepped back and picked a piece of glass off her sleeve.

“Come to the printshop tonight,” she said. “You can work there until this is fixed.”

Shawna nodded.

Mom turned to me.

“Make the phone stop ringing.”

I looked at the tall man's phone in my hand.

The screen was lighting up.

An incoming call from someone saved as SUNDAY SCHOOL.

I answered.

For a second there was no sound.

Then a man said, “Is it done?”

I looked at the broken mirror, the waste bin over the bottle and Shawna holding the torn silver dress against her chest.

“No,” I said. “But I'm getting started.”

## Chapter 7: The Easy Problem

The man on the phone hung up before I could ask whether Sunday school offered refunds.

I called back.

The number was already disconnected.

Saint looked at the screen over my shoulder.

“Fast service.”

I put the phone in my pocket. Hậu dragged the unconscious man out from under the cutting table. Outside, a small crowd had gathered to watch his partner argue with the lid of the recycling cart.

Estelle Mercer finished her call and came toward me.

“My brother says he doesn't know anything about this.”

“Does he?”

“He knows I'm here. That should concern somebody.”

She handed Shawna a business card.

“My driver will take you anywhere you need to go. He works for me.”

Shawna glanced at the street, where Mom was directing two men with a sheet of plywood.

“I'm going next door.”

“Then he'll carry things.”

Estelle pressed the card into her hand anyway. She left with Nia and the ruined dress, passing the recycling cart without slowing down. The man inside stopped trying to escape when she looked at him.

I made a note of that.

We took the red box and the drive upstairs at the Pearl. Trinh locked the door behind us. Her aunt had finished vacuuming and was counting the bottles beneath the bar with a pencil tucked behind one ear.

“Somebody tried to burn the atelier,” I said.

Trinh looked up sharply.

“Shawna?”

“Unhurt.”

She put down the tray she was holding.

“What do you need?”

“A table. A power outlet. Somewhere Saint can't touch anything.”

“I heard that,” Saint said.

“Then the system works.”

Rafa brought my equipment case from the apartment. It was small enough to fit beneath an airline seat, though security people usually wanted to discuss it. Inside were a folding screen, a compact machine with no manufacturer's logo and three cables I had marked with tape because knowing mathematics doesn't prevent you from plugging in the wrong cable when you're tired.

Saint watched me set it up on a card table.

“That's the famous thing?”

“One of them.”

“I expected more lights.”

“I built it for work.”

“That's your problem. You're always missing the merchandise.”

Trinh stood beside me as I connected the drive.

“What does it do?”

“Finds answers.”

“Google does that.”

“Google asks whether you meant another question.”

When I was twenty, I'd proved P equaled NP. The argument had filled notebooks, then a paper, then several months of people telling other people the paper must be wrong. Making a machine that could use the result had taken another year. The machine on the table was that year's work, packed into a black box with a fan that whined whenever I gave it something entertaining.

Hậu looked at the blank screen.

“What's NP?”

“Nondeterministic polynomial time.”

He thought about that.

“You could've said you didn't want to tell me.”

The drive's opening screen appeared. A silver star turned slowly against a black background. Beneath it was a box asking for a passphrase.

Saint leaned closer.

“Try password.”

I looked at him.

“It works on my aunt's Wi-Fi.”

I told the machine what I wanted. It began its work. No waterfall of green symbols appeared. No skull grinned at us. The fan made a noise like a small irritated hair dryer.

Thirteen seconds later, the silver star vanished.

A list of files filled the screen.

Saint stared.

“That's it?”

“That's it.”

“Nigga, you solved a thing with letters in it to open a folder?”

“I also use it to organize photographs.”

“You need a publicist so badly.”

I opened the first file. It showed Bảo sitting at a table in a white suit, signing a document while a man out of frame held the paper flat. The next image showed Vinh standing beside the same man. His face was turned toward the camera.

It was the tall gunman from Shawna's shop.

Trinh leaned in until her shoulder touched mine.

“That's Curtis Ames. He used to drive for Vinh.”

I opened another file.

A video began. The camera had been hidden low, looking past a bottle toward a restaurant booth. Vinh sat on the left. Kenny Vale sat on the right. Between them was the red box, still intact.

“Bảo gets the stage,” Kenny said in the recording. “Mercer gets the water. What do I get?”

Vinh slid an envelope across the table.

Kenny opened it, counted the first few bills and grinned.

“I like water.”

The recording continued. There were dates, names and a reference to a private show at the Pearl. Vinh said Bảo would stand in front of the stained-glass window when the guests arrived. Kenny asked whether the wife would be there too.

“She's the designer,” Vinh said. “She's useful until the doors open.”

I stopped the video.

Saint's grin had disappeared.

Trinh looked toward the blue heron in the window above the room.

“Saturday,” she said.

“Shawna's show.”

She nodded.

Hậu put both hands on the back of a chair. The wood cracked under his fingers.

“Vinh told me he wanted extra security here,” he said. “Asked who had keys.”

I copied the files onto my own storage and disconnected the drive. On the screen, the frozen image of Vinh smiled above an envelope full of money.

“Can you call Bảo?” I asked Trinh.

“He'll be back tonight.”

“Tell him I want to see him before anybody else does.”

She took out her phone.

Her aunt came over from the bar and looked at the machine.

“Can it find my brother?”

We all turned toward her.

“He owes me two thousand dollars,” she said. “Nobody is dead. Don't make those faces.”

Saint pulled out a chair for her.

“Auntie, we may have a premium service.”

I shut the machine down before he could invent a price.

Trinh couldn't reach Bảo. She tried twice, left a message and called the man responsible for his airport car. He said Bảo's flight had been delayed and then asked whether Aiden would still be at the Pearl that night.

“Why?” she asked.

He talked for nearly a minute. Trinh closed her eyes and pinched the bridge of her nose.

“No,” she said. “Nobody can pay extra to touch him.”

Saint's head came up.

I pointed at him until it went down again.

The first guests arrived at seven. Trinh had intended to postpone the evening, but I told her to open. Vinh expected me to hide the box, panic about the threat and wait for someone older to tell me what to do. I put on a fresh jacket and stood beneath the heron window where he could find me.

Saint borrowed a microphone from the stage. This one worked.

“Ladies and gentlemen, please respect the man's personal space. Photographs are welcome. Flash photography is fifteen dollars more.”

Trinh took the microphone from him.

“Flash photography is free.”

He looked wounded.

“You keep doing this to me in front of customers.”

The room filled in half an hour. Men shook my hand, pressed envelopes on me and asked whether I'd remember their names. Women told me I looked better in person and then asked where Shawna had bought her jacket. I gave out her business cards until I ran out.

A jeweler offered me a ring with a blue stone the size of a thumbnail.

“For good luck.”

“What do you want?” I asked.

He looked offended.

“To be generous.”

I waited.

“And perhaps you wear it in one photograph.”

I put it on. He took the photograph. Saint appeared beside him with a notebook, and the jeweler immediately stopped smiling.

Near eight, a man entered with two friends supporting him by the elbows.

Milo Voss wore a gray tracksuit and had a strip of white tape across his nose. His jaw was swollen. When he saw me, he detached himself from his friends and came across the room alone.

The conversations nearest us quieted.

Voss stopped in front of me and held out a small velvet box.

I looked at it.

“You people have a serious problem with gifts.”

He opened it. Inside lay his gold tooth.

“Found it in my bag.”

Saint made a delighted sound.

“That's collectible.”

Voss ignored him.

“I heard you met King.”

“Briefly.”

“He still got both arms?”

“Last I checked.”

Voss closed the box.

“My sister used to work at one of Mercer's clubs. King broke her hand when she tried to leave with her tips.”

I said nothing.

He looked past me toward the window, then back.

“I want to be there when you see him again.”

“Can you stand without your friends?”

He set the box on the table, straightened and took a full step backward. Pain crossed his face. He stayed upright.

“Yeah.”

“Then heal first.”

Hậu brought him a chair. Voss sat slowly. Saint put a glass of water in front of him without trying to sell it.

At the far end of the room, one of the card dealers stood up suddenly. A man at his table had grabbed his wrist. The man's companions rose with him.

“He dealt from the bottom,” the man shouted.

Trinh crossed the room. I followed her.

The dealer was young, with a neat mustache and a white shirt too large at the collar. His trapped hand had begun to turn red.

“Let him go,” Trinh said.

“I lost twenty thousand dollars.”

“Then you're having an expensive evening.”

The man looked up at me.

“You own this place now?”

“Part of it.”

“Then fix it.”

I looked at the cards spread across the table, the chips and the man's face. He had palmed a card under his right thigh. Its corner showed against the dark fabric of his trousers.

“Stand up,” I said.

He didn't.

I put my hand on the back of his chair and lifted it, with him still sitting in it, until his feet left the floor.

The hidden card fell onto the table.

His companions sat down.

I held the chair there for another second while everyone looked at the card. Then I set him down carefully enough that his drink didn't spill.

He released the dealer's wrist.

“A misunderstanding,” he said.

I looked at Trinh.

“Do you sell those here?”

“Only to regulars.”

The man took a thick envelope from his jacket and placed it on the table.

“For the inconvenience.”

I slid it to the dealer.

The room applauded. Somewhere behind me, Saint shouted that standing ovations were now included with the cover charge.

My phone vibrated.

A message from Trinh's airport driver.

*Mr. Lâm is back. He says come downstairs alone.*

I looked toward the stairs.

Bảo stood at the bottom in a white suit. Beside him was Vinh.

Both men were looking up at me.

## Chapter 8: Everybody Wants a Picture

Bảo wanted me to get into his car.

I heard my father's voice so clearly that I almost looked behind me.

“We can talk here,” I said.
