The three of us stood beneath the Pearl's striped awning. Upstairs, people were laughing. Somebody had begun playing the little piano beside the stage with enough enthusiasm to compensate for having no relationship with the song.

Vinh watched me from Bảo's left. His maroon shirt had been replaced by a black one. He wore the watch I'd put in his pocket.

I pointed at it.

“You got it fitted.”

He looked down, then tucked his wrist behind his back.

Bảo opened the rear door of the car.

“Private conversation.”

“Your man threatened my wife. We've gone public.”

Vinh stepped toward me. Bảo held out an arm without looking at him.

“I'm told you stole a truck.”

“It was carrying my statue.”

“Your statue.”

I nodded.

“The one with my face.”

“We're making changes.”

He stared at me, then laughed once through his nose.

“Come to my house tomorrow. We can resolve this.”

“You should look at something tonight.”

I held up my phone and played the video from the drive. Vinh's recorded voice came out of the speaker.

*She's useful until the doors open.*

Bảo stopped smiling.

Vinh knocked the phone out of my hand.

I caught his wrist before he could step back. The phone struck the sidewalk and slid beneath the car.

“You should've watched the rest,” I said.

He tried to pull free. I tightened my grip. His fingers opened involuntarily.

Bảo looked from my hand to his face.

“Vinh.”

“He made it,” Vinh said. “He's the computer boy. He makes pictures talk.”

“That's a very nervous sentence,” I said.

Vinh drove his free fist toward my throat.

I turned, brought his trapped arm across his own chest and pushed him against the car. His shoulder hit the open door. The hinges groaned.

Bảo stepped backward into the street.

An engine revved behind him.

I looked over his shoulder and saw a dark sedan coming downhill without lights. Its passenger window was open. A gun muzzle rose inside it.

I grabbed Bảo by the jacket and threw him behind the Pearl's concrete planter.

The first shots struck the car.

Vinh dropped flat. I went over him, landed beside Bảo and pulled his head below the planter's rim. Bullets shattered the awning lights above us. The piano upstairs stopped in the middle of a chord.

The sedan swept past.

I stood, tore the heavy clay pot out of the planter and hurled it at the rear window.

It hit squarely. The glass collapsed inward. Soil and broken clay filled the car. The driver swerved into a parked pickup, bounced off it and kept going with one rear wheel wobbling.

I looked back at the sidewalk.

Vinh was running.

He reached the alley beside the pharmacy, vanished between the buildings and left the watch lying in the gutter where its strap had broken.

Bảo sat behind the planter with one hand pressed to his upper arm. Blood ran between his rings.

“He shot you,” I said.

Bảo looked at the blood.

“I noticed.”

Hậu came through the Pearl's door, followed by Trinh. Saint appeared in the upstairs window, saw the broken lights and disappeared again.

“Ambulance,” Trinh said into her phone.

Bảo caught her sleeve.

“No.”

She looked at him.

He pointed at his car.

“My doctor.”

“Your car is full of holes,” she said.

Hậu opened the rear door and inspected the seat.

“This side's mostly okay.”

I helped Bảo stand. He looked smaller with one arm clamped to his body and dirt in his hair. He noticed me noticing and straightened before he reached the car.

“Come with me.”

“No.”

“Aiden.”

“You need a doctor. I need Vinh.”

For a second his face twisted with anger. Then he looked at the planter, the bullet marks and the street where Vinh had disappeared.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

Hậu drove him away in the damaged car. Trinh went with them. I stood on the curb and called Shawna.

She answered on the first ring.

“I heard.”

“Stay at Mom's.”

“I am at your mother's. She's looking for her car keys.”

“Don't let her leave.”

“You tell her that.”

Mom took the phone.

“Are you bleeding?”

“No.”

“Is Darius?”

I looked up. Saint was back at the window, now wearing a reflective vest he'd found somewhere.

“No.”

“Good. Stop standing in the road.”

I looked toward the printshop. She stood in the doorway half a block away with Shawna beside her.

I stepped onto the sidewalk.

Behind me, a man from the card room came outside holding a leather envelope.

“Mr. Trần.”

“Not now.”

He put it on the planter anyway.

“For getting Mr. Lâm out of the way.”

I stared at him.

“People were shooting.”

“Yes. I saw. That's why it's a generous amount.”

He hurried back inside before I could decide what to say.

Saint came down the stairs with a dustpan and a broom.

“Everybody's asking whether the party is over.”

“The party is over.”

“I said that. They asked whether you're coming to the next one.”

“Darius.”

He started sweeping glass.

“I'm just reporting demand, nigga.”

We closed the Pearl for the night. Trinh's aunt walked each guest to the stairs, thanked them for coming and reminded several of them that they still owed for drinks. By ten, the street had quieted. The police took statements from people who had developed remarkably poor eyesight during the shooting.

One detective stayed after the others left.

She was in her forties, with short dark hair, a gray jacket and a black notebook she never opened. She introduced herself as Elena Pike and looked at the broken clay across the road.

“You threw that?”

“The car was leaving.”

“Most people wave.”

“They'd been rude.”

She looked at my taped ear.

“You seem to be having a difficult week.”

“It's Wednesday.”

“Then pace yourself.”

She gave me a card. Her eyes moved past me to Saint, who had begun taking down the damaged awning fabric with a pair of kitchen scissors.

“You know Leon Mercer?”

“He gave me shoes.”

“That's friendly.”

“We didn't exchange sizes.”

She held my gaze for a moment, then put the notebook away unopened.

“Call if you remember anything useful.”

Her car was parked across the street. Before she got into it, she looked up at the stained-glass window. I watched until she drove away.

Shawna waited in the printshop with a length of silver fabric across her lap. Mom had given her the largest worktable. A portable machine hummed beneath the overhead lamps. Denise sat nearby eating crackers and criticizing a television host.

I stood in the doorway until Shawna looked up.

“You're doing the sad face,” she said.

“I have several.”

“This is the one where you want me to be mad so you can stop waiting.”

Denise turned up the television.

I sat across from Shawna.

“We should move the show.”

“I've already moved it.”

“Where?”

She turned her notebook around. On the page was a sketch of the old cinema on Alder Street, three blocks inland. She'd marked the aisle, the backstage space and the rows she intended to remove.

“The owner owes your mother for menus.”

“It's a cinema.”

“He had a restaurant before that.”

Mom called from the back room, “And a terrible understanding of invoices.”

Shawna tapped the drawing.

“Nobody gets the new address until Friday. The Pearl stays on the printed invitation. Your mother is handling the corrected cards.”

I looked at the fabric in her hands.

“You still want to do it?”

“I have six clients, four models, a photographer and a woman who has paid me enough to make her shoulder a landmark. Yes.”

I took her hand.

“I'll keep them away.”

She squeezed once.

“Keep them away from everyone. I'm not the only person with a window.”

She let go and fed the fabric back beneath the needle.

I stayed while she worked. Mom brought me rice in a bowl and set it at the far end of the table where a spilled grain couldn't get into the dress. Denise asked whether I intended to pay for her broken flowerpot. I said yes. She said she hadn't decided which price she remembered paying for it.

At eleven, Hậu returned.

Bảo was alive. The bullet had passed through the fleshy part of his upper arm. His doctor had told him to rest. Bảo had responded by trying to fire two people from a treatment chair.

“He wants you at his house at noon,” Hậu said.

“I know.”

“He wants Vinh before then.”

“So do I.”

Hậu sat down beside me. His hands smelled of soap. There was a bloodstain on one sleeve where he'd helped Bảo out of the car.

“Vinh called me.”

I put down my bowl.

“When?”

“At the doctor's. Said I should remember who gave me work.”

“What did you say?”

Hậu looked at Shawna's machine moving steadily across the table.

“I said I was busy.”

“Will he call again?”

“Probably.”

I nodded.

“Answer.”

He looked back at me.

“You want me to tell him where you are?”

“Tell him you want your job back.”

Hậu held my eyes for a moment. Then he leaned back in the chair.

“I should ask for a raise.”

“Absolutely.”

Denise turned from the television.

“Get dental.”

Saint arrived carrying a large framed photograph.

We all looked at him.

“Before you get upset,” he said, “this was already paid for.”

He turned it around.

It showed me in midair above Voss, both feet clear of the ring, while the man on the balcony stared at me with his shrimp halfway to his mouth. Someone had printed BELL STREET'S OWN beneath it in gold letters.

Shawna studied the picture.

Then she started laughing.

It began quietly, with one hand over her mouth. She tried to stop, looked at the man with the shrimp and lost the fight completely. Mom came out from the back room, saw it and joined her. Denise took off her glasses to wipe her eyes.

I looked at Saint.

“How much?”

“For you? Free.”

He leaned closer.

“For the shrimp nigga, we're negotiating.”

## Chapter 9: My Father's Day Off

Dad's shop had a sign saying CLOSED THURSDAYS.

There were eleven people waiting outside it on Thursday morning.

One of them had brought a chair. Another had brought a box of pastries. A third stood beside a red sports car holding an envelope against his chest as if he was waiting for a medical diagnosis.

Dad was inside, sharpening a kitchen knife.

“Your customers are here,” I said.

“They're early for Friday.”

He drew the blade across the stone with a soft, even scrape. The shop was cleaner than I remembered. Tools hung in straight rows along the wall. Two motorcycles stood on lifts. An engine block sat on the counter beside a mug with my baby picture on it.

Somebody had written MASTER CHIGGA across the mug in gold paint.

I picked it up.

“You still use this?”

“It holds coffee.”

“I was eight when I made it.”

“You've improved at writing.”

I turned the mug around. My painted letter G looked like a bent fishhook.

“The title was Saint's idea.”

“Most expensive mistakes in this family begin with that sentence.”

Outside, the man with the pastries tapped lightly on the glass. Dad didn't look up.

“What do you need?” he asked me.

“A car that doesn't look like a tow truck.”

“You have a car.”

“Mine is at the apartment.”

“That's where you should keep it.”

“Dad.”

He put down the knife and finally looked at my face.

“New bruise.”

“Same face.”

“Your mother saw the bridge.”

I leaned against the counter.

“Does everybody in this city film traffic?”

“When it flies.”

He took a key from a hook and tossed it to me.

“Blue sedan. Bring it back with fuel.”

“Thank you.”

“And all four doors.”

The man with the sports car knocked on the glass. Dad glanced at the clock, set the knife aside and opened the shop door.

The man stepped forward immediately.

“Mr. Trần, I know you're closed.”

“Good.”

“But I've got a meeting in an hour, and the engine's making a noise.”

“Engines do that.”

The man held out the envelope.

“Five thousand.”

Dad looked at the red car.

“To fix it?”

“To look at it.”

Dad took the envelope, walked around the car once and looked through the driver's window.

“Handbrake,” he said.

The man's face went blank.

Dad opened the door, released the handbrake and closed it again.

“Try now.”

The man got in, started the engine and moved forward six feet. The noise was gone. He sat there for a moment, staring through the windshield.

Then he got out and applauded.

The people waiting outside applauded with him.

I watched from the doorway.

“Five thousand dollars,” I said when Dad came back inside.

He put the envelope in a drawer.

“He asked me to look.”

“You could have charged ten.”

“Nigga, it's my day off.”

He went back to sharpening the knife.

The man with the pastries put the box on the doorstep and left without asking for anything. The woman with the chair settled in more comfortably. She had a book and the patient expression of someone who had been married to a difficult man for forty years.

I went out to the blue sedan.

Hậu waited beside it with two coffees. He handed me one and looked at the crowd.

“Your dad signing something?”

“Apparently people pay him to notice them.”

Hậu glanced at the envelopes in several hands.

“You come by it honest.”

Before I could unlock the car, a black pickup rolled into the space in front of the shop. Its tires were too large for its body, and its body was too large for the space. The driver parked across two customers' cars and stepped out wearing sunglasses and a sleeveless vest.

A second man climbed down from the passenger side. He carried a broken motorcycle frame with both hands. They set it on the pavement between them.

The driver pointed at Dad through the glass.

“You Minh?”

Dad kept working.

The driver tried the door. It opened because Dad hadn't locked it after dealing with the sports car. He went inside, leaving his partner beside the frame.

I handed my coffee back to Hậu.

Hậu shook his head.

“I think we should watch.”

Through the open door, I heard the driver tell Dad that a repair had failed. Dad asked for the invoice. The man said he didn't need an invoice because his friend knew somebody who'd brought the bike there.

Dad looked at the frame outside.

“That's a bicycle.”

“Electric.”

“Still a bicycle.”

The man took off his sunglasses.

“You think I'm stupid?”

Dad said nothing.

The silence lasted long enough for the woman with the chair to lower her book.

“I want compensation,” the driver said.

Dad pointed at the sign on the window.

“Friday.”

The man slammed his palm on the counter. The mug with my baby picture jumped, tipped and rolled toward the edge.

Dad caught it with the hand holding the sharpening stone. He set both down. Then he looked at the man's palm on his counter.

“Take that off.”

The man reached inside his vest.

Dad picked up the engine block with one hand and put it in his arms.

The man's knees buckled.

He made a short, shocked noise and fell backward onto the shop stool. The stool bent beneath him. His boots scraped the floor as he tried to keep the engine from crushing his lap.

Dad took the pistol from the man's open vest, removed it from sight beneath the counter and folded his arms.

“Who sent you?”

The man couldn't answer. His face had turned red.

Dad lifted the engine two inches.

The man sucked in air.

“Mercer,” he gasped.

Dad let the engine settle again.

Outside, the passenger had begun edging toward the pickup.

I put a hand on its door.

“Stay.”

He looked at me, recognized me and shut his eyes.

“Fuck.”

“Busy family,” Hậu said sympathetically.

Dad brought the driver outside with the engine still in the man's arms. The man shuffled along, bent nearly double. Every few steps Dad supported the engine with two fingers so he could breathe.

The waiting customers moved their chairs and boxes out of the way.

Dad stopped beside the pickup.

“Tell Mercer he can bring his own complaint.”

The driver nodded desperately.

Dad took the engine, set it gently in the truck bed and then caught the rear bumper with one hand.

He lifted.

The rear wheels rose off the pavement. The truck's nose dipped until the front bumper touched the curb. Loose tools slid against the cab. The passenger grabbed the open door to keep from falling.

Dad looked at me over the tilted bed.

“Get the bicycle.”

I picked up the broken frame and laid it in the back beside the engine.

Dad lowered the truck. All four tires met the street with a soft bounce.

He took the engine back out, tucked it under one arm and pointed the driver toward his seat.

“Go.”

The two men climbed in. The pickup left with the broken frame rattling in its bed.

The waiting customers applauded again.

The woman with the chair stood up and handed Dad a foil-covered dish.

“For your wife.”

He accepted it with his free hand.

“Thank you.”

“Don't eat it yourself.”

“I won't.”

She looked at the engine under his arm.

“And stop encouraging idiots. They bring more.”

Dad nodded as if she had made a useful point about the weather.

When he returned to the shop, I followed him.

“Mercer sent them because of me.”

He set the engine down.

“Mercer sends people because he likes sending people.”

“I can deal with him.”

“Then deal with him.”

He put the dish beside the mug and looked at my hand, still wrapped around the car key.

“You wanted a car. You have a car.”

I nodded.

As I reached the door, he called my name.

I turned.

“Your mother wants you at dinner on Sunday.”

“I'll be there.”

“And Shawna.”

“She'll be there.”

“She's invited even if you're stupid.”

I smiled.

“I figured.”

Hậu was waiting with my coffee.

“Did he ever fight your great-grandfather?” he asked as we got in.

“I've heard stories.”

“Who won?”

“Depends who starts telling them.”

We drove uphill to Bảo's house.

It had a white wall, a black gate and a driveway long enough to make visitors think about whether they'd worn the right shoes. Two guards opened the gate when they saw me. One looked at Dad's blue sedan with the uncertain expression people get when an important guest arrives in something practical.

Bảo sat beside his pool beneath a striped umbrella. His arm was in a sling. A woman in enormous sunglasses lay on a lounger nearby reading a magazine upside down.

“That's Phương,” Hậu murmured. “His wife.”

“The magazine's upside down.”

“She likes knowing who's paying attention.”

Bảo waved us over. A young man stood behind his chair holding a tray of drinks and looking angry about it.

“My son, Baojun,” Bảo said.

The young man nodded at me without smiling.

I took a drink from the tray.

“Thank you.”

He looked at his father as if I'd insulted a hereditary office.

Phương lowered the magazine.

“He said thank you, baby. That's the polite part.”

Baojun went inside.

Bảo watched him go, then turned back to me.

“You saved my life.”

“Vinh tried to end it.”

“I heard the recording.”

“Good.”

“Trinh sent it.”

He pushed an envelope across the small table with his good hand.

I didn't pick it up.

“What's this one for?”

“Last night.”

“And the next one?”

He looked at me steadily.

“Bring me Vinh.”

“Alive?”

“Breathing.”

Phương turned a page of her upside-down magazine.

“He'll want to talk for an hour first,” she said. “Make sure the man can hear.”

Bảo ignored her.

“Vinh knows every room I own. Every driver. Every weakness.”

“He also knows you were putting Shawna in front of a window for him.”

“I didn't know.”

“You know now.”

He reached for his drink, winced at the wrong arm and used the other.

“What do you want?”

I leaned forward.

“The Pearl outright. The games, the rooms, the building. Your men stop collecting on Bell Street. Anyone who wants my help asks me directly.”

Hậu became very still beside me.

Bảo set down his glass.

“You joined yesterday.”

“You've had a difficult twenty-four hours.”

Phương smiled behind the magazine.

Bảo looked toward the house where his son had disappeared. Then he looked back at me.

“Bring me Vinh.”

I took the envelope and stood.

“Have the keys ready.”

As we walked away, Phương called my name.

I turned.

She held up her phone.

“One picture. My sister doesn't believe you can jump.”

“I'm not jumping into your pool.”

“Good. The cleaner just left.”

She took the photograph with me standing beside her lounger. Then she pressed a folded hundred-dollar bill into my hand.

“For your wife,” she said.

I looked at the money.

“Everybody keeps saying that.”

“Maybe listen.”

## Chapter 10: Front Row

By Friday afternoon, I had bought three mirrors, two windows, a new flowerpot and a dinner jacket I hadn't been allowed to choose.

Shawna held the jacket against my chest while I stood on her fitting platform.

“Arms out.”

I put my arms out.

“Stop flexing.”

“I'm standing.”

“Then stand less proudly.”

She marked the sleeve with a pin. Behind her, Estelle Mercer sat in the chair Denise had brought over and inspected the repaired shoulder of her silver dress.

“He always like this?” Estelle asked.

“He gets worse when people applaud.”

“Then you're in the wrong neighborhood.”

Hậu stood by the new window talking quietly into his phone. Vinh had called twice since Thursday. Both times he promised Hậu money, a better position and the chance to stop being somebody else's heavy bag. Both times Hậu asked where to meet him. Vinh said he'd call back.

Bảo had sent a message every four hours.

*Have you found him?*

After the fifth, I sent back a photograph of an empty chair.

He stopped for six hours.

Shawna turned me around and smoothed the jacket between my shoulders.

“You can wear this tomorrow.”

“Do I get paid?”

“You'll get to go home married.”

Estelle applauded softly.

I pointed at her.

“You're making it worse.”

The old Alder Cinema smelled of velvet seats, dust and expensive flowers when we arrived Saturday evening. Shawna had kept the screen down and used it as a pale backdrop. A narrow runway extended over the front rows. Two rows of guests sat on either side, close enough to see the stitching and complain about the price.

Saint wore an earpiece connected to nothing.

“Professional appearance,” he told me when I asked.

“Can you hear anything through it?”

“My ambitions.”

Hậu checked the side doors with Rafa. Milo Voss sat near the rear aisle in a dark jacket. His jaw was still swollen, but he had insisted on helping. I gave him a job that involved sitting still and telling me if anybody came through the wrong door.

“I can do more than sit,” he said.

“You can heal.”

He looked annoyed, then adjusted the chair so he could see both exits.

Mom stood beside the entrance with the corrected invitations. Denise greeted guests as if she owned the cinema. Auntie Loan had somehow acquired the cloakroom and was charging people to leave coats they hadn't intended to remove.

“It's warm inside,” she told a man in a short-sleeved shirt.

He looked down at himself.

“Auntie.”

“Then buy a program.”

The programs were free. He gave her ten dollars anyway.

Shawna worked behind the screen with Nia and the models. Estelle had loaned Nia to the show after discovering she knew more about organizing clothes than the people Estelle actually paid to organize clothes.

I found my wife kneeling to adjust a hem.

She looked up at me and stopped for a second.

“Good,” she said.

“The jacket?”

“You listened.”

I turned slowly.

“No livestock. No sunglasses indoors. No visible weapons.”

“No microphone.”

“Saint has that disease.”

She stood, brushed a thread from my lapel and pulled me down for a kiss.

“Sit in the front row,” she said. “Try to be handsome without making an announcement.”

“That's a difficult balance.”

“I made you a jacket for it.”

I went out to the runway.

People stood when they saw me.

It started with the jeweler from the Pearl. He rose, clapped and called my name. His wife stood beside him because she wanted a photograph of the jacket. A man three seats down joined them. Within seconds half the room was on its feet.

I pointed toward the screen.

“My wife's show.”

They applauded harder.

Saint hurried onto the runway with the microphone.

“Thank you. Thank you. Please save some of that for the clothes.”

Mom took the microphone from him as she passed.

“Sit down, niggas. The women have been working.”

Everybody sat.

The lights dimmed.

The first model came out in a dark green coat with a silver lining that flashed when she turned. The room quieted in a different way. People leaned forward. A woman near me whispered that she'd take it in blue. Her husband whispered back that she already owned blue. She put a hand on his knee, and he stopped talking.

Shawna's work moved through the room in clean lines and small surprises: a sleeve opening into a different color, a jacket fastening off-center, a dress that looked almost plain until the model walked and the skirt unfolded around her legs.

I watched my wife in the gap beside the screen. She wasn't watching the audience. She watched the clothes, the way the models held their shoulders and whether a fastening stayed where she'd put it.

Estelle came out halfway through the show in the repaired silver dress.

She hadn't been on the model list. She'd told Shawna that if she was going to pay that much, she intended to be seen walking in it.

She reached the end of the runway, turned toward me and lifted one shoulder.

It looked perfect.

The photographer nearly fell off his stool trying to get the shot.

Estelle pointed at him as she turned back.

“That's the reaction I bought.”

The room laughed and applauded.

Then Voss stood at the rear aisle.

I saw him through the space between two guests. He wasn't looking at the runway. He was looking at the upper projection booth.

The booth's little window had opened.

Something black rested on its lower edge.

I stood.

The man in the booth fired.

I hit the runway with both hands and shoved upward.

The nearest section flipped onto its side between the guests and the booth. The bullet struck the wood with a flat crack. Estelle jumped backward off the runway. Hậu caught her under the arms and pulled her behind a row of seats.

The room screamed.

“Down!” I shouted.

A second shot tore through the raised platform. I grabbed its supporting brace, kept it upright and looked toward the back of the cinema.

Voss was already climbing the narrow stairs beside the booth.

Two men burst through the side entrance near the screen. One carried a short club. The other had a knife and a grin that disappeared when he saw me.

Shawna pulled the nearest model behind the screen. Nia dragged a rolling clothes rack across the opening.

The man with the club swung at the rack. Hangers flew. He stepped through them and caught his foot in the hem of a long coat.

Shawna yanked the coat from the other side.

He fell forward onto both hands.

I left the platform braced against the seat row, jumped over two chairs and landed beside him.

The knife man lunged at my stomach.

I caught his wrist with my left hand, shoved it outward and punched him in the throat with my right. He gagged. His free hand clawed at my jacket. I turned his knife hand toward the floor and drove his shoulder against the end of the runway.

His arm dislocated with a thick pop.

The knife fell.

The man with the club got up behind me and hit my left arm.

Pain burst from the bone above my elbow. I spun toward him. He swung again, aiming at my head. I stepped inside the arc, caught the club against my shoulder and hit him twice in the face.

His nose flattened. He stumbled backward into the clothes rack. I grabbed the rack's horizontal bar and drove the whole thing into him.

He hit the screen support hard enough to bend it. The screen shuddered overhead.

Another shot came from the booth.

Voss shouted. I looked up.

The gunman had backed into the doorway with his pistol raised. Voss hung from the handrail below him, one foot braced against the wall. The gun swung toward his head.

I picked up the fallen club and threw it.

It crossed the cinema and struck the gunman's wrist against the doorframe. The pistol dropped into the aisle. Voss hauled himself upward, caught the man around the waist and drove him into the booth.

Glass broke inside.

I turned back toward the screen just as its loosened support gave way.

The long metal roller at the top tilted forward.

Shawna stood beneath it with two models and Nia.

I jumped onto the runway, caught the falling roller with both hands and let it drive me to one knee. The weight tore through the muscles of my injured arm. The screen billowed over my head and draped across the front rows.

“Go!” I shouted.

Shawna pushed Nia toward the side exit. The models followed. Hậu came through the hanging screen, got his shoulder beneath the roller and took enough weight for me to move my left hand.

Together we lowered it onto the raised edge of the runway.

Behind us, the audience had begun moving toward the rear doors. Mom stood in the aisle directing people with the same voice she'd used to send them to their seats. Denise had a frightened woman by each arm. Loan carried the cloakroom cash box and three abandoned coats.

Saint ran past me with the microphone.

“No refunds,” he blurted, then looked at my face. “On the coats. I meant the coats.”

I grabbed his shoulder.

“Get everyone out.”

He nodded and kept moving.

The knife man tried to crawl beneath the runway. I caught his ankle and dragged him back into the light. His injured arm hung uselessly against his chest.

“Who sent you?”

He spat at me.

I put my foot on his good hand.

He screamed before I pressed down.

“Vinh!”

“Where?”

“Crown Billiards. Back room. Please.”

I moved my foot and kicked the knife farther away.

Shawna came back through the side door.

“Everyone's outside,” she said. “One woman twisted her ankle. Nia's calling an ambulance.”

She saw my arm.

Blood had soaked through the sleeve where the club's metal cap had torn the fabric and skin. She pulled the jacket away carefully.

“I liked this jacket,” she said.

“So did I.”

She looked around the ruined cinema. Her mouth tightened. I waited.

Then she took a pair of scissors from the pocket at her waist and cut the damaged sleeve free.

“Hold still.”

She wrapped the strip of fabric around my arm, pulled it tight and tied it with two sharp movements. I watched her face while she worked.

“I'm sorry,” I said.

“I know.”

She finished the knot, pressed her forehead briefly against my chest and stepped back.

Outside, somebody began applauding.

We both looked toward the doors.

Saint stood on the cinema steps with the microphone, addressing the shaken guests gathered beneath the marquee.

“The woman made a coat that caught a motherfucker,” he announced. “Tell me that isn't quality.”

Estelle stood beside him in the silver dress, one heel in her hand. She took the microphone.

“I have bought worse evenings for more money,” she said. “If you promised this woman an order, keep it.”

The jeweler's wife raised her hand.

“The green coat. In blue.”

Another woman called out a dress number.

Shawna looked at me once, wiped her face with the back of her hand and went outside with her notebook.

I watched the guests close around her.

Hậu stood beside me, holding the red box under one arm and the captured gun under the other side of his jacket.

“Crown Billiards,” he said.

I looked at the blood on my sleeve.

“Call Vinh back.”

## Chapter 11: The Man Under the Table

Vinh offered Hậu a ten-percent raise.

Hậu said he'd need twenty.

We sat in Dad's blue sedan behind the cinema while the argument went on. My left arm throbbed beneath Shawna's improvised bandage. Rafa had brought a clean shirt, and Saint had brought five different suggestions for what to call the evening on social media.

I told him to call it Saturday and put the phone away.

Hậu listened to Vinh for another minute.

“Dental too,” he said.

There was a pause.

Hậu looked at me and shrugged.

“Because I have teeth.”

Saint turned toward the window to laugh silently.

When Hậu finally hung up, he put the phone on the dashboard with care.

“Back entrance. Fifteen minutes. Alone.”

“You don't have to go in,” I said.

He looked at me.

“I know.”

“He'll search you.”

“I know.”

“He might already know you're with me.”

Hậu rolled his shoulders against the seat.

“Then he'll be expecting a better performance.”

I looked at his hands. They were steady.

“What do you want from him?”

For a moment he didn't answer.

“Four years ago he gave me work,” he said. “I was sleeping in my cousin's laundry room. I thought carrying money in a nice car meant I had a nice job.”

“And now?”

He flexed one hand, looked at the scar across its knuckles and closed it again.

“Now I want him to hear me quit.”

We parked two blocks from Crown Billiards. The building had blacked-out windows and a gold crown painted above the entrance. An actual crown would have looked less suspicious.

Saint stayed in the car with Rafa. Voss arrived in his own car and took up a position across the street, still looking annoyed that I wouldn't let him sprint anywhere with his jaw half-healed.

Hậu walked around to the back.

I went through the front door.

The room was long and narrow, with six pool tables arranged in two rows. Green lamps hung low above each one. A bar ran along the left wall. At the far end, a pair of saloon doors led to the private room.

Four men looked up when I entered.

One held a cue. Another sat on the edge of a table counting money. The other two stood near the saloon doors with their hands empty and their jackets hanging open.

The man with the cue recognized me.

“Fuck.”

“People keep greeting me like that,” I said.

He set the cue down carefully.

The man counting money swept the bills into his jacket and slid off the table. He moved toward the side door without saying anything.

The two men at the back stayed where they were.

“Private event,” one said.

“I'm invited.”

“Not through here.”

“Then show me the red carpet.”

He drew a pistol.

I shoved the nearest pool table sideways.

Its legs scraped across the floor. The table struck his knees before he could aim properly. He fired into the ceiling as he fell over the edge. The green lamp above him shattered.

The second man reached inside his jacket.

I picked up the cue the first player had set down and jabbed the butt into his mouth.

His head snapped back. He dropped to one knee. I caught his wrist, pulled the gun free and threw it behind the bar.

The man trapped against the table tried to crawl backward. I kicked the pistol out of his hand and stepped over him.

Behind the saloon doors, someone shouted Hậu's name.

I pushed through.

The private room had one table, a leather couch and a large television showing a horse race with the sound off. Vinh stood behind the table with a pistol pointed at Hậu's stomach.

Hậu had both hands open at his sides.

Two more men flanked him. One had a short shotgun. The other held a knife against the seam beneath Hậu's ribs.

Kenny Vale sat on the couch with his wrist wrapped in a dirty bandage. He saw me and closed his eyes.

“Again?” he said.

Vinh didn't turn.

“Stop there.”

I stopped beside the door.

“You're hard to get on the phone.”

“You're easy to find in a crowd.”

He shifted the pistol toward Hậu's chest.

“He didn't come alone.”

“I told you,” Hậu said, “I wanted a better position.”

Vinh hit him across the face with the pistol.

Hậu's head turned. He spat blood onto the floor, looked back at Vinh and smiled with red teeth.

“That's not it.”

The shotgun man glanced at Hậu's face.

I moved.

I grabbed the pool table's near corner with my right hand and heaved upward. The heavy slate top rose between us. Balls rolled across the felt and spilled toward Vinh's feet.

The shotgun fired into the underside of the table.

Hậu caught the knife man's wrist, stepped across his body and threw him over his hip. The man landed on the couch with enough force to knock Kenny off the other end.

I drove the raised table forward.

Its far edge hit the shotgun man in the chest and pinned him against the wall. The gun dropped from his hands. I let the table fall flat again and climbed over it as Vinh fired.

The shot passed beneath my right arm and tore a strip from the felt.

I landed on his side, caught the gun hand and shoved it into the corner pocket.

Vinh pulled back. The pistol snagged in the leather netting. I hit his elbow with the heel of my hand.

His arm bent the wrong way.

He screamed and let go.

Hậu had the knife man by both ankles now. He swung him off the couch and into the shotgun man, who had just pushed himself away from the wall. They hit the floor together beneath a shower of broken plaster.

Kenny crawled toward the door.

I put one foot in his path.

He looked up.

“I just drive trucks.”

“Badly.”

I stepped past him to reach Vinh.

Vinh had a second knife.

He slashed at my injured arm. The blade cut through the loose bandage and opened the skin beneath it. Pain flashed hot and immediate. I pulled back, caught the edge of the table with my hip and nearly fell.

He came at me again, low, driving the point toward my stomach.

I turned sideways. The knife scraped across my shirt. I clamped his wrist under my right arm and hit him in the ear with my left fist.

The impact sent pain all the way up my own arm. I hit him again anyway.

He sagged against me.

I drove his head into the table cushion, once, then twice. His knees gave out. The knife fell to the floor. I kicked it beneath the couch.

Vinh hung from my grip with blood running over his mouth.

“You sent men into my wife's shop.”

He spat blood at my shoes.

“You walked into our business.”

“Now I'm staying.”

I let him fall.

Hậu stood over the other two men with a broken cue in his hand. Neither was trying to get up. Kenny sat against the wall, both hands visible, breathing quickly through his nose.

I pulled out my phone and called Bảo.

He answered before the second ring.

“Is he alive?”

“He's complaining.”

“Bring him.”

“Have the keys.”

I hung up.

Vinh laughed from the floor. It came out wet and ugly.

“You think he gives things away?”

I crouched beside him.

“He gave me you.”

His eyes moved to Hậu.

“You stupid fuck. He'll use you the same.”

Hậu came over and knelt on the other side of him.

For a second neither man spoke.

Then Hậu took Vinh's phone out of his pocket and placed it on the table.

“I quit,” he said.

Vinh tried to raise his head.

Hậu pushed it gently back to the floor with one hand.

“You can keep the dental.”

We carried Vinh outside wrapped in the leather couch cover. Saint looked from the bundle to my bleeding arm and opened the rear door without making a joke.

Rafa followed us to Bảo's house in the tow truck. Kenny rode with him, seated between Voss and a box of chain. He had volunteered to remain available after Voss explained that walking home might become tiring very suddenly.

Bảo met us in his garage.

He wore a silk robe over his trousers. His sling was gone, though his left arm stayed close to his body. Three men stood behind him. Baojun hovered in the doorway to the house with a phone in his hand.

We lowered Vinh onto a folding chair.

Bảo looked at his face for a long time.

“Fourteen years,” he said.

Vinh stared at the floor.

“You ate at my table.”

“You charged me for the chair,” Vinh said.

Bảo slapped him with his good hand.

Vinh's head snapped sideways. He laughed again.

I put out my hand.

“The keys.”

Bảo turned toward me.

“We're having a conversation.”

“You can have it after you pay.”

Baojun lowered his phone.

“You don't talk to my father like that.”

Hậu looked at him. Baojun raised the phone again, then thought better of it and put it away.

Bảo went to a cabinet, opened a drawer and took out a ring of keys. He threw them to me.

I caught them.

“Documents?”

He stared.

“You want a ribbon too?”

“Only if it's tied around the building.”

Phương appeared in the doorway behind her son.

“They're on the kitchen counter,” she said. “I told you he would ask.”

Bảo's jaw tightened.

Hậu went inside with Phương. I stayed beside Vinh.

The men behind Bảo shifted closer to the chair. One held a length of electrical cord. Another had taken off his jacket.

I looked at the cord, then at Bảo.

“Ask what you need to ask.”

“This isn't your concern.”

“He knows Mercer. That part is.”

Bảo held my gaze, then turned back to Vinh.

“What did Sunday offer you?”

Vinh wiped his mouth against his shoulder.

“Your rooms.”

“My rooms.”

“And a piece of the ferry.”

Bảo's face changed at the last word.

I noticed.

Vinh noticed me noticing.

“There it is,” he said. “The boy doesn't know about the water.”

Bảo hit him again.

Vinh fell out of the chair.

I caught Bảo's wrist before he could follow him down.

The garage went quiet.

Bảo looked at my hand on his arm.

“Careful,” he said.

I let go slowly.

“He's answered one question.”

Hậu returned with a folder. Phương came behind him, took one look at the scene and pulled Baojun back into the house by his sleeve.

I checked the documents. Trinh's name appeared beside mine on the operating agreement. The building transfer was ready for signatures. Bảo had kept enough of his promise to think he'd finished keeping it.

“Tomorrow night,” he said. “At Honest Work. We finish it in front of the Circle.”

I closed the folder.

“I'll be there.”

As we walked out, Vinh called after me from the garage floor.

“He'll make you kneel.”

I turned back.

Bảo stood over him with the three men behind his shoulder.

“He can buy a ticket,” I said.

Saint opened the car door for me. Hậu got in on the other side. I sat between them because neither intended to let me pretend my arm was fine.

Rafa leaned through the driver's window with a clean towel.

“For the seat,” he said.

I pressed it against my arm.

“My dad's car.”

“Exactly. I know who frightens me.”

## Chapter 12: Membership Fees

The doctor put nine stitches in my arm and asked what had happened.

“A fashion event,” I said.

He looked at Shawna.

She nodded.

“Very competitive industry.”

He didn't laugh. He finished the stitches, wrapped the arm and told me to avoid lifting anything heavy for at least a week.

Shawna looked at me before I could answer.

“He heard you.”

The doctor handed her the instructions instead of handing them to me.

We got home after two. She helped me out of the ruined shirt, put it in a bag for the tailor she intended to become angry at later, and made me drink water before I could ask for anything else.

“Did the orders come through?” I asked.

She sat on the edge of the bed and looked at her phone.

“Twenty-three confirmed. Four deposits already paid. Estelle ordered two more dresses.”

“Good.”

“One woman wants the coat you used in the fight.”

“The actual coat?”

“She said it has provenance now.”

I laughed, then stopped when my arm pulled.

Shawna put the phone down. She leaned over me carefully and kissed the unbruised side of my mouth.

“You looked good before they shot at us.”

“I looked good after.”

“You looked expensive after.”

She turned off the lamp. I reached for her with my good arm. She settled against me, warm and tired, and for a few hours nobody asked me to come anywhere or gave me anything made of bronze.

Sunday morning arrived with a delivery of twelve flower arrangements, a pair of cufflinks and an envelope containing tickets to a private aquarium.

Saint brought the last one upstairs.

“The fish community is reaching out.”

Shawna pulled the blanket over her head.

“Make him leave.”

I pointed at the door.

Saint put the envelope on the counter and left with two pastries he claimed had been addressed to him.

By afternoon, the Pearl belonged to me on paper.

Trinh brought the completed documents to the apartment. Bảo had signed. The games, the upstairs room and the building were ours, divided between my new ownership and the operating share I'd insisted she keep.

She read that section twice.

“You didn't have to do that.”

“You run the room.”

“Bảo paid me to run it.”

“I'm paying you to care whether it burns down.”

She put the folder on her lap.

“He's going to ask you to kneel tonight.”

I looked up.

“Vinh mentioned it.”

“He's making it a ceremony. Cameras. Witnesses. He gives you the keys in front of everyone. You thank him. You accept the Circle's authority.”

“On my knees.”

She nodded.

Shawna came out of the bedroom carrying the jacket she'd started altering around my bandage.

“Is this a thing people actually do?” she asked.

“It's a thing Bảo saw in a film,” Trinh said. “He liked the furniture.”

I leaned back in the chair.

“Does he have a throne?”

Trinh didn't answer immediately.

I closed my eyes.

“Of course he has a throne.”

We ate at my parents' house before going to Honest Work. Dad looked at the bandage, looked at my clean shirt and chose not to ask in front of the food. Mom asked anyway. Great-Grandpa Tín listened while I explained the cinema, then asked whether the silver-dress woman had kept both shoes.

“One came off,” Shawna said.

“Then she had a real evening.”

Granddad Hòa sat beside the window peeling an apple with the small knife he carried everywhere. One long strip of skin curled onto his plate. When I mentioned Bảo's ceremony, he cut the strip neatly and looked up.

“Take a handkerchief.”

“Why?”

He glanced at my bandage.

“Something always spills.”

Dad passed me the vegetables.

“Car has fuel?”

“Full tank.”

“Good.”

Nobody told me not to go.

Honest Work had hired a red carpet.

It ran from the curb through the gym doors and stopped beneath a wooden arch covered in gold flowers. Saint stared at it when we arrived.

“He stole my concept.”

“You were selling shirts,” I said.

“It's a developing concept.”

Hậu wore a dark suit that strained at the shoulders. Voss came behind him, carrying himself carefully but refusing the chair I'd offered him in the car. Trinh walked on my right. Shawna had stayed with Mom to finish the orders from her show; she'd told me that if I came home wearing a crown, she'd charge me for storing it.

Inside, the boxing ring had become a stage.

The ropes were gone. A large carved chair stood at one end, surrounded by white lilies. Bảo sat in it with his injured arm hidden beneath a dark jacket. Baojun stood behind him. Phương occupied a perfectly ordinary chair beside the stage and looked much more comfortable.

The room rose when I entered.

Applause rolled toward us. Men called my name. A woman near the bar held up her phone and asked me to turn so she could get the good side of my jacket.

Bảo clapped too, slowly, smiling through it.

Saint leaned toward me.

“This feels like a wedding where both men hate the cake.”

Trinh took her place near the front. Hậu and Voss stayed by the steps. I went up onto the stage alone.

Bảo stood.

“Aiden Trần,” he announced. “A son of a great family. A brave man. A generous man.”

“Depends what you're asking for,” I said.

The room laughed. Bảo waited for it to stop.

He took a ring of oversized ceremonial keys from Baojun. They were gold-plated and heavy enough to become an argument if thrown.

“The Pearl,” he said. “A reward for loyalty.”

I held out my hand.

He kept the keys.

“First, respect.”

The room quieted.

Bảo pointed at a cushion placed before the chair.

It was red velvet with gold fringe.

I looked at the cushion, then at him.

“Your knees hurt?”

A few people laughed. Bảo didn't.

“You understand.”

“I understand the building's already transferred.”

He stepped closer, lowering his voice.

“And I can make that very difficult.”

I took the original hundred-thousand-dollar check out of my inside pocket. It still had a faint broth stain at one corner. I folded it once, tore it in half and put the pieces on the arm of his chair.

“Refund.”

Baojun moved before his father did.

He came around the chair with a pistol in his hand, pointing it at my stomach.

I caught his wrist, turned the muzzle toward the ceiling and squeezed until he let go. The pistol fell into my other hand. I set it on the chair beside the torn check.

Baojun dropped to his knees, clutching his wrist.

I looked down at the red cushion under him.

“There. Somebody's using it.”

The room erupted in laughter so sudden that several people tried to hide it after it had already escaped.

Bảo's face went dark.

“Enough.”

Three men came up the steps behind me.

Hậu intercepted the first by wrapping both arms around his waist and lifting him backward off the stage. They landed on a table. The table collapsed. Hậu got up holding the man's belt and deposited him on the floor beside the broken legs.

Voss caught the second man's punching arm, ducked under it and drove him shoulder-first into the stage rail. His own injured jaw tightened with pain. He kept hold until the man stopped struggling.

The third man reached me with a knife low against his thigh.

I stepped onto his leading foot and punched him in the nose. He jerked backward but couldn't move the trapped foot. I caught his knife wrist and slammed it against the carved arm of Bảo's chair.

The wood split.

The knife fell between the cushions.

I hit him in the ribs with my good elbow. He doubled over. I turned him toward the stairs and sent him down them face-first.

My stitched arm burned. I kept it close to my side.

Bảo reached for the pistol I'd put on the chair.

I put my hand over his before he could lift it.

For a second we stood almost shoulder to shoulder, his good hand trapped beneath mine, his son kneeling at our feet.

“You could have handed me the keys,” I said.

He strained against my grip. I pressed his hand harder against the carved wood. One of his rings bent.

He stopped.

“Let go.”

“Drop the gun.”

His fingers opened.

I took the pistol and slid it across the stage to Trinh. She picked it up by the grip and kept it pointed at the floor.

I turned toward the room.

The men who had come to watch me kneel were standing. Some held drinks. Some held phones. Most looked at Bảo before looking back at me.

“Anyone else?” I asked.

Nobody moved.

Near the bar, the jeweler raised one cautious hand.

I looked at him.

“Photograph?” he asked.

The room broke again.

Bảo sat heavily in the damaged chair. Baojun crawled to his side. Phương crossed the stage, took her son's arm and helped him stand.

She looked at her husband.

“We're leaving.”

“Phương—”

“You paid for flowers. Use the evening.”

She guided Baojun down the steps. Bảo watched them go. Then he looked around the room at the phones, the broken table and the men who had failed to stand between us.

He took the ceremonial keys off the chair and put them in my hand.

The applause began at the back and spread forward.

It grew louder as he walked down the steps.

Trinh stood beside me. Hậu climbed back onto the stage, brushing splinters from his suit. Voss followed more slowly.

Saint appeared with the microphone.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” he said, “please give the previous management a respectful amount of room to leave.”

Bảo stopped at the door and looked back.

I held his gaze.

He left.

Money began arriving before the applause ended.

Men came up the steps with envelopes, checks, business cards folded around cash. One offered me the use of a yacht. Another offered a racehorse. I refused the horse on my wife's behalf.

Hậu stared at the growing pile on the chair.

“How much is that?”

Trinh looked once.

“Enough to replace the table.”

Saint put the plastic crown from the apartment on my head.

I took it off.

He put it on again.

“For the picture, nigga.”

I let the jeweler take one photograph.

Then I handed the crown to Hậu, pocketed the actual keys and looked toward the doors through which Bảo had gone.

My phone rang.

Unknown number.

I answered.

Sunday Mercer's voice was warm and amused.

“Congratulations,” he said. “I hear you found a chair.”

Behind me, the crowd was still cheering.

“It's a little damaged,” I said.

“They always are by the time you get them.”

“What do you want, Sunday?”

“Breakfast. Just you and me.”

I looked at the crown on Hậu's head.

He had already bent one of its plastic points.

“Pick somewhere with good plates,” I said.

## Chapter 13: Gifts for a Bastard

The racehorse arrived anyway.

It stood outside the atelier at eight on Monday morning wearing a blue ribbon and chewing part of my welcome-home banner.

Shawna looked down from the apartment window.

“Aiden.”

I came to stand beside her.

The horse looked up at us with a mouthful of painted bedsheet.

“I refused that.”

“It hasn't accepted your refusal.”

A man in riding boots stood beside a trailer holding a clipboard. Saint was talking to him with both hands moving. From above, it looked like a negotiation between someone who understood horses and someone who understood deposits.

I opened the window.

“Saint!”

He looked up.

“Good morning, Your Greatness.”

“Send it back.”

“The owner says it likes you.”

“We've never met.”

“It's seen the video.”

Shawna shut the window.

“Nigga, I am not learning to clean up after a horse because you won an argument at a boxing gym.”

I called the owner. He sounded genuinely hurt. I thanked him, complimented the horse and explained that my wife had opened a tailoring business rather than a stable.

He offered to buy us a stable.

It took another ten minutes.

When I finally went downstairs, the horse was leaving and a refrigerator was arriving.

I pointed at Saint.

“Stop accepting appliances.”

“This one's for the Pearl.”

“Why is it here?”

“The driver wanted a picture.”

I stood beside the refrigerator. The driver took the picture, thanked me and handed me an envelope.

I didn't open it until he'd gone.

Five hundred dollars.

Shawna looked over my shoulder.

“You should have let him take a video.”

By noon, the apartment contained enough flowers to interfere with breathing. The hallway held three televisions, a marble side table and a painting of me riding a tiger. The painter had made my jaw wider than my shoulders.

“That's how he sees your aura,” Saint said.

“That's how he avoids painting a neck.”

Hậu carried the painting upstairs. He had already found a place for the plastic crown on top of our kitchen cabinet. He insisted he hadn't put it there. Nobody believed him.

Trinh arrived with the first week's cash from the Pearl and two of the Circle's smaller gaming rooms. She put the bag on the counter and opened it.

Saint stopped examining the tiger painting.

“That's a healthy animal.”

I looked at the bundled money. It smelled faintly of cigarette smoke and someone's perfume. These rooms had paid Bảo for years. Now the managers wanted me to know they understood the change.

“They all come willingly?” I asked.

Trinh gave me a dry look.

“Some came enthusiastically. Some came because they watched you take apart the stage.”

“Which ones are useful?”

She separated three envelopes from the rest.

“These want to expand. These two want a dispute settled. This one wants you to frighten his wife's boyfriend.”

I pushed the last envelope back.

“Tell him to buy flowers.”

Saint looked at the apartment.

“We can supply those.”

There was another knock at the door.

The visitor introduced himself as Benny Châu. He was small, neatly dressed and perspiring despite the cool morning. He owned a private card room near the marina and had spent the previous evening applauding me with both hands above his head.

He held a wooden presentation box.

Shawna saw it and pointed toward the stairs.

“If there's something alive in there, leave.”

“A key,” Benny said quickly.

“One?”

“One main key. There are others.”

He opened the box.

Inside was a brass key attached to a silver tag reading ORCHARD HOUSE.

I looked at him.

“What is Orchard House?”

“A house.”

Saint folded his arms.

“Strong opening, Benny. Keep going.”

The house stood on a low rise overlooking the river, fifteen minutes from Bell Street. Benny had bought it as a place to entertain clients. His wife hated it. His clients had begun preferring the Pearl. He wanted to give me the use of it, including the staff, for as long as my games made his games fashionable.

“The staff work for themselves,” Shawna said.

“Of course. I mean I pay their wages.”

“Then say that.”

Benny nodded rapidly.

I picked up the key.

“What do you want in return?”

“You come to my room once a month. Sit at a table. Be seen.”

“Play?”

“Please don't.”

I laughed.

Benny looked at the black equipment case beneath the table.

“I heard about the computer.”

“Everybody did,” Saint said proudly.

“You told everybody,” Trinh said.

“Again. Publicist.”

We went to see the house after lunch.

It had seven bedrooms, a terrace above the river and a pool shaped like somebody had described an oval to an architect during an argument. A woman named Valerie Banks met us at the door with a tablet and the expression of a person who had already survived wealthy people attempting to explain what they wanted.

“Mr. Trần. Mrs. Nguyễn. I manage the house.”

“Aiden,” I said.

“For emergencies or generally?”

“Generally.”

“Good. Mr. Châu had four preferred titles depending on who was visiting.”

She showed us the rooms. Shawna walked through the largest bedroom, inspected the adjoining dressing room and stood very still.

I waited by the door.

“Is it enough?”

She opened a second cupboard.

“For now.”

Valerie handed her a key of her own.

“That locks the workroom downstairs. I was told you might need one.”

Shawna looked at me.

“You thought of that?”

“I'm occasionally useful.”

She kissed me in front of Valerie, who studied her tablet with professional discretion.

Saint was already on the terrace taking photographs.

“We should do the official portrait here,” he called.

“There's no official portrait,” I said.

“Then this place lacks leadership.”

Hậu stood beside the pool, looking down into the water.

“Can I use this?”

“Yes.”

“Whenever?”

“Within reason.”

He looked at the width of the pool.

“That's a lot of reason.”

My phone rang before we'd finished the tour.

Auntie Loan didn't bother greeting me.

“Two men downstairs wearing your shirts. They say they're collecting for you.”

I looked toward Saint on the terrace.

He stopped taking pictures when he saw my face.

“What are they collecting?” I asked.

“Money. And one of them keeps touching my scissors.”

“Don't let them leave.”

“Nigga, I'm doing his eyebrows. He's not going anywhere.”

We drove back to Bell Street.

The two men sat in Auntie Loan's chairs when we entered. Both wore BELL STREET AIRLINES shirts. One had a towel around his neck. The other had white wax painted across both eyebrows and the terrified eyes of a man who had agreed to something he didn't understand.

Loan stood behind him holding a strip of cloth.

“There he is,” she said. “Your employer.”

The man with the towel started to stand.

Hậu put a hand on his shoulder and kept him seated.

I looked at the other man's shirt.

“Where did you buy that?”

“Outside.”

Saint leaned close to inspect the print.

“That's counterfeit.”

“That isn't the important part,” I said.

“The wings are backwards.”

I held out my hand to the man in the chair.

“What did you collect?”

He looked at Loan's strip of cloth.

“Nothing from here.”

“Elsewhere.”

He reached into his pocket and took out a folded stack of money. I waited. He took out another stack from the other pocket.

His companion sighed and produced an envelope.

“We thought you wouldn't mind,” the first man said.

“You put my face on a robbery.”

“It's just a shirt.”

Loan pulled the wax strip.

He screamed.

“It's just an eyebrow,” she said.

I took the money and put it on the counter.

“Hậu will go with you. Every place you visited gets its money back. Then you take off the shirts.”

Saint looked hopeful.

“We could sell them the real ones.”

I looked at him until he became interested in the floor.

The man with one bare eyebrow nodded repeatedly.

“We understand.”

“You don't work for me.”

“We understand.”

“Say it.”

He said it. His companion said it. Loan removed the other eyebrow because she'd already started and didn't like uneven work.

Outside, people had gathered again. The men from the gaming rooms had sent more flowers. Somebody had parked a new motorcycle beside the bakery with a card tied to its handlebar.

I looked at it.

Saint looked at me.

“You can't send everything back.”

“I'm starting with the shirts.”

My phone buzzed.

A message from Sunday.

*Breakfast ran late. Bowling tomorrow. Noon. I'll bring the plates.*

Beneath it was a photograph of Orchard House taken from across the river.

Shawna stood on the terrace in the picture.

I put the phone away before Saint could see my face.

Then I called Sunday.

He answered warmly.

“Enjoying the house?”

“Tomorrow,” I said. “Bring yourself.”

He laughed.

“I wouldn't miss it.”

## Chapter 14: Sunday Bowling

Sunday had rented every lane at Crown Bowl except lane seven.

An elderly couple occupied lane seven. The woman wore a purple bowling shirt with her name stitched across the back. Her husband stood beside her holding a ball and looking disappointed in the laws of motion.

“Why are they here?” Saint whispered as we entered.

Sunday heard him.

“Mrs. Whitcomb has had Tuesdays at noon for thirty-one years. I offered to pay for another time.”

“And?”

“She offered to outlive me.”

Mrs. Whitcomb released her ball. It rolled straight down the lane and knocked over nine pins.

“Again,” her husband said.

“I can count, Frank.”

Sunday smiled and held out his hand to me.

I looked at it.

“You sent men to my father's shop.”

“Did I?”

“One of them said your name while holding an engine.”

Sunday lowered his hand.

“People use my name when they want to get out of things.”

“Then they should choose lighter things.”

Rhett King stood two lanes away beside the ball return. He wore a green polo shirt, dark trousers and rented bowling shoes. Seeing those little red-and-blue shoes beneath the rest of him made Saint stop midstep.

King looked at him.

Saint found something fascinating on the ceiling.

Sunday gestured toward a table set with plates of fried chicken, sandwiches and a large glass pitcher of lemonade.

“I said I'd bring plates.”

“You also sent somebody a picture of my wife.”

His expression remained pleasant.

“A beautiful house should be admired.”

I stepped closer.

“Look somewhere else.”

For the first time, his smile faded completely.

Then Mrs. Whitcomb shouted at her husband, and he glanced toward lane seven.

“Let's bowl,” he said.

I took off my jacket. The bandage showed beneath my rolled sleeve. Sunday looked at it without commenting. King looked at it and smiled.

Hậu stayed near the table. He'd brought his own water. Saint accepted a sandwich, inspected it for half a second and ate it anyway.

Sunday picked a black ball from the rack.

“My uncle knew your great-grandfather.”

“A lot of people did.”

“Duke Mercer.”

Hậu glanced at me. I kept my eyes on Sunday.

“I've heard the name.”

“I'm sure the stories are flattering.”

“Depends who's telling them.”

Sunday rolled his ball. It curved across the lane and struck the pocket cleanly. Ten pins fell.

He turned with both hands open.

“Your turn.”

I picked a ball, stepped onto the approach and sent it down the lane. It struck a little high. The pins scattered. The last one rocked twice and stayed standing.

King chuckled.

Saint pointed at it.

“That's defective.”

I picked up the second ball and knocked it down.

Sunday sat beside the table.

“Your family has always understood spectacle. Your great-grandfather put half this city on the river for a party and made the other half pay to look at it.”

“You weren't born.”

“I was four.”

“Then you had a very early business interest.”

He smiled.

“I grew into it.”

He took a folded brochure from his jacket and laid it beside the chicken. On the cover was a large white ferry with dark windows and a gold stripe along its side.

THE SUNDAY BEST.

Saint leaned over it.

“You named a boat after yourself?”

“People remember.”

“I respect that part.”

Sunday opened the brochure. Restaurants, private rooms, a performance deck, an upper lounge overlooking the water. The photographs made the ferry look like a hotel somebody had pushed into the harbor.

“The city likes tourism,” he said. “Visitors like feeling they've discovered something. My guests like games the city doesn't need to know about.”

“And you need the Circle's guests.”

“I need you.”

I looked up from the brochure.

“That's an expensive sentence.”

“I can afford it.”

He put a second envelope on the table.

Saint made a quiet, involuntary noise.

I didn't touch it.

“Appearances?” I asked.

“An opening night. A few private dinners. Your name attached to the upper room. You sit, people come, everybody gets richer.”

“And the men with guns?”

“Security.”

“At my wife's show?”

He held my eyes.

“Vinh was ambitious.”

“Vinh was paid.”

Sunday turned the envelope slightly with one finger.

“So are most people.”

King picked up a bowling ball with one hand, his fingers wrapped around it instead of in the holes. He squeezed.

A crack opened across the ball's surface.

Hậu stopped chewing.

King squeezed again. A chunk broke free and hit the floor beside his shoe.

Sunday sighed.

“Rhett. They charge for those.”

King looked at me.

“Just checking the equipment.”

I took the broken ball from his hand.

The surface was rough where the shell had split. I turned it once, set it on the lane and nudged it forward with my foot.

It rolled crookedly, wobbling toward the gutter. Halfway down the lane it caught the edge, bounced back inward and struck the far-right pin. That pin hit the next one. The line collapsed across the rack until the head pin fell last.

Ten.

Mrs. Whitcomb put down her own ball.

“Do that again.”

I looked at the broken ball disappearing into the return.

“I'd rather not test my luck.”

She pointed at her husband.

“See? Some men know when to stop.”

Saint clapped loudly enough for the whole building.

King took a step toward me.

Sunday put a hand on his chest.

“We're having lunch.”

I sat down across from Sunday and pushed the envelope back.

“No.”

He looked at it.

“You haven't counted.”

“I'm very good at counting.”

“Then name a number.”

“One. You get one more chance to stop sending people near my family.”

Sunday leaned back in his chair. For a while he watched the lane instead of me.

“Bảo is still alive,” he said eventually.

“Yes.”

“His son has friends. His managers have habits. A room can applaud you and still call somebody else afterward.”

“Then I should stay busy.”

“You should stay employed.”

I stood.

King moved between me and the exit.

Hậu put down his water and rose beside the table. Saint stopped chewing.

Mrs. Whitcomb looked over.

“Move away from the approach,” she said. “People are playing.”

King ignored her.

She picked up her ball.

Sunday watched her face and said, “Rhett. Let him pass.”

King stepped half a pace to the side.

There was room for me to squeeze past him. I didn't squeeze.

I walked directly forward. My shoulder met his chest. He planted his feet. I kept walking.

The rubber soles of his rented shoes squealed across the polished floor.

One inch. Then another.

He caught my upper arm, right where the bandage covered the stitches.

Pain flashed white behind my eyes.

I caught his thumb with my good hand and bent it backward.

His grip loosened.

I drove my forehead into his face.

His nose flattened with a blunt crack. He staggered backward into the ball rack. The rack tipped and spilled six balls across the floor.

Sunday stood abruptly.

King roared and came off the rack toward me.

I kicked one of the loose balls under his leading foot.

His shoe rolled. He caught himself on the table, driving one huge hand through its top. Plates jumped. The lemonade pitcher overturned into his lap.

Hậu took Saint by the back of the collar and pulled him clear of the falling food.

I stepped away from King and picked up my jacket.

Behind us, Mrs. Whitcomb bowled her spare.

The last pin fell.

“Finally,” she said.

We left Sunday standing beside his broken lunch.

Outside, Saint bent over with both hands on his knees and laughed until he couldn't breathe.

Hậu held up half a sandwich.

“You dropped this.”

Saint took it gratefully.

I looked at my bandage. A thin red line had begun spreading through it.

“Fuck.”

Hậu saw it.

“We should get that checked.”

“I know.”

He looked back at the bowling alley.

“He didn't use the other hand.”

“Who?” Saint asked.

“King.”

I had noticed too. He'd squeezed the ball, grabbed my arm and caught the table with his right hand. His left had stayed close to his body the whole time.

The chain at the truck. The fall in the yard. Something had hurt him.

I put on my jacket carefully.

“We'll remember.”

We drove back to Bell Street. Trinh was waiting outside the Pearl with a man who owned three card rooms and wanted to move all three beneath my name by the weekend. He'd brought the keys in a jewelry box. I told him to talk to Trinh and went upstairs to call Shawna.

She listened without interrupting.

Then she said, “You reopened the stitches.”

“A little.”

“The doctor said a week.”

“It felt longer at the bowling alley.”

“Come home.”

I promised I would.

Hậu left to get food from Bishop's. Saint went with him, still explaining how the broken-ball strike could become a commercial.

I was packing the black machine into its case when I heard tires shriek outside.

Then Saint shouted my name.

I reached the window in two strides.

A gray van stood sideways in the street. Its sliding door was open. Three men were dragging Hậu inside. He had one foot planted on the curb and both hands locked around the doorframe.

King stood behind him.

He hit Hậu in the back of the head with a short black club.

Hậu's hands opened.

The men pulled him into the van.

I went through the window.

The stained glass broke around me. I landed on the roof of a parked car, crushed it beneath both feet and jumped to the street.

The van's door slammed.

I caught the rear handle as it accelerated.

The handle tore out in my hand.

I stood in the road holding the broken metal while the van disappeared around the corner.

Saint staggered toward me with blood on his lip and a torn sleeve.

“They took him,” he said.

I looked down at the handle.

Then I threw it through the empty space where the Pearl's window had been.

## Chapter 15: The Brother in the Van

Saint's hands wouldn't stop shaking.

He tried to wipe the blood from his lip with the back of one wrist and missed twice. I took the tissue from him and pressed it where he needed it.

“Look at me.”

He did.

“Which way?”

“Alder. Then east.”

“How many?”

“King. Three in the van. One driving.”

“You see a plate?”

He shook his head, angry with himself.

“I was trying to pull him out.”

“I know.”

“I had his hand.”

I held the tissue against his lip until he stopped trying to talk around it.

Rafa arrived in the tow truck with Voss beside him. Trinh came downstairs carrying my equipment case and the red box. She put both in the cab without asking what I intended to do.

My phone rang.

Sunday didn't bother pretending this time.

“Your friend is comfortable.”

“Put him on.”

“First—”

“Put him on.”

There was a scrape, then Hậu's breathing.

“Aiden.”

“You hurt?”

“They hit me in the head.”

“I saw.”

“Then why ask?”

I closed my eyes for half a second.

“I'm coming.”

Sunday took the phone back.

“The old Morrow Mall. East entrance. Bring the machine.”

“You want the computer now?”

“I want you to understand that we can still make an arrangement.”

“You've made one.”

He hung up.

Saint reached for the truck's door.

I stopped him.

“You can stay.”

His face tightened.

“That's my friend too.”

I looked at his shaking hands. He clenched them into fists and held my gaze until I moved aside.

Morrow Mall had closed three years earlier. The anchor store's sign had been removed, leaving pale letters on the wall where the sun hadn't reached the concrete. Weeds grew through the parking lot. A giant plastic rabbit from the mall's final Easter promotion lay on its side near a locked service gate.

The gray van stood by the east entrance.

King leaned against it with a fresh strip of tape across his nose.

“You've had a busy afternoon,” I called as I got out.

He looked at the equipment case in my hand.

“Leave your friends.”

“They don't like waiting.”

“Then they can learn.”

I walked toward him. Saint, Rafa and Voss stayed by the truck. King pushed open the glass door and let me pass.

Inside, the mall was dim and hot. Empty storefronts lined a long central walkway. A dry fountain stood beneath the skylight, full of dust and a few coins nobody had bothered to steal. Artificial palm trees leaned over benches with torn cushions.

Hậu sat in a wheelchair in the middle of the walkway.

His wrists were tied to its arms. Blood had dried along the back of his neck. A man with a pistol stood behind him, one hand on the chair's handles.

Sunday stood beside a shuttered jewelry store.

He'd changed his shirt since bowling.

“You came quickly.”

I looked at Hậu.

“Why the wheelchair?”

“They couldn't find a chair with wheels that fit,” he said.

“That is a chair with wheels.”

“I made that point.”

Sunday held out his hand toward the case.

“Set it down.”

I put it on a bench.

“Untie him.”

“After we see it work.”

“You've heard what it does.”

“I've heard a man jumped over a boxer. I still prefer demonstrations.”

He nodded toward the jewelry store. A small safe sat on a handcart behind its half-raised shutter. Its electronic display glowed red.

“Open it.”

I looked at the safe, then at him.

“With the machine?”

“That would be the point.”

I walked to the handcart, put my good hand beneath the safe's front edge and tipped it forward. It fell off the cart with a crash that echoed through the empty mall.

Sunday flinched despite himself.

I put my foot on its side and pulled the handle.

The latch tore out through the door.

I dropped the handle beside the safe.

“Open.”

King laughed once behind me. Sunday looked at him until he stopped.

“The computer, Aiden.”

I returned to the bench and opened the case.

“Then untie him. He's bleeding on your chair.”

Sunday watched my hands for a moment. Then he nodded to the gunman.

The man behind Hậu lowered the pistol slightly and reached toward the knot at Hậu's right wrist.

Hậu moved.

He drove both feet against the floor and threw his weight backward. The wheelchair tipped into the gunman's knees. The man's hand flew up to keep his balance.

I threw the equipment case.

It hit the gunman's chest. The pistol went off into the skylight. Glass rained onto the dry fountain.

Hậu hit the floor still tied to the overturned chair.

King lunged at me from the entrance.

I jumped onto the bench, kicked off its back and caught the lower branch of an artificial palm. The plastic branch tore free in my hand. I swung the trunk itself sideways by its steel core.

The heavy planter skidded across the tiles and struck King's shins.

He stumbled. I let go, landed on the fountain rim and jumped to Hậu.

Sunday drew a pistol.

I grabbed the overturned wheelchair by its frame and pulled it, with Hậu attached, behind the fountain wall.

The first bullet struck the tiles where his head had been.

“You could've untied me first,” he said.

“Busy.”

I snapped the cord at his right wrist, then the left. He rolled free of the chair and took one deep breath.

King hit the fountain wall.

The concrete cracked inward. Hậu and I scrambled in opposite directions as King climbed over it. His foot crushed the wheelchair's wheel against the fountain floor.

I picked up the metal wheel rim and swung it into the side of his head.

He caught the second swing with his right hand.

His left stayed close to his ribs.

I let go of the rim and drove my fist into that side of his body.

He grunted and turned away. I hit the same place again. His elbow dropped to cover it.

Hậu came up behind him with both hands locked around a length of fountain pipe. He drove the pipe across the backs of King's knees and pulled.

King fell backward into the dry basin.

We climbed out.

Sunday was running toward the escalators. Two more men appeared from a side corridor with guns raised.

A car horn blasted inside the mall.

Rafa's tow truck came through the glass entrance in a glittering shower.

Saint leaned out of the passenger window.

“Customer pickup!”

The men with guns jumped behind a bench as the truck bore down on them. Rafa braked hard beside the fountain. The rear wheels slid across the polished tiles.

Voss pushed open the rear door.

“Get in!”

Hậu climbed first. I grabbed the equipment case from the floor, threw it after him and jumped onto the running board.

King rose out of the fountain behind me.

He caught the back of my jacket.

The truck accelerated.

For a moment I hung between the moving cab and King's grip. The jacket tore across the shoulders. I slipped one arm free, twisted out of the other sleeve and fell against the open rear door.

Voss caught my belt and hauled me inside.

King was left holding the jacket.

“I liked that one too,” I said through my teeth.

Rafa drove straight down the central walkway. Storefronts flashed past on both sides. Saint shouted directions based on a mall layout he remembered from buying sneakers there at sixteen.

“Left after the pretzel place!”

“Which one's the pretzel place?” Rafa shouted.

“The one with the—fuck, they took the sign!”

Sunday appeared ahead of us at the top of a short service ramp. He aimed down at the windshield.

I grabbed the back of Rafa's seat.

“Right.”

Rafa turned hard. The truck smashed through the half-open shutter of an empty department store. Metal screamed along the cab roof. We burst into a wide room full of dusty display stands and abandoned mannequins.

The rear of the truck swung sideways and knocked down a row of them.

Saint looked back.

“Shawna could use those.”

“Later,” I said.

Rafa drove through the stockroom doors and out onto the loading dock. The truck dropped off the dock's low edge, landed hard on its suspension and rolled into the service lane behind the mall.

No one spoke for several seconds.

Then Hậu leaned forward between the seats.

“Who brought food?”

Saint began laughing. It came out shaky and too loud, but he kept going until Hậu put a hand on the back of his neck and pulled him close.

“You came through a building for me,” Hậu said.

Saint wiped his face with his sleeve.

“Rafa was driving.”

“You still came.”

I looked down at the equipment case. Its outer shell was dented. The machine inside had survived, though the screen had a crack across one corner.

Hậu saw me checking it.

“Sorry.”

I closed the lid.

“It opens folders. You eat sandwiches. I made a choice.”

He looked away toward the window, smiling despite the blood on his collar.

We took him to the clinic. The doctor who had stitched my arm after the cinema looked at all five of us in the waiting room and stopped walking.

“Fashion?” he asked.

“Retail,” Shawna said from the doorway behind him.

I turned.

She stood beside my mother, carrying a clean shirt and an expression I had no interest in arguing with.

“Saint called,” she said.

“He does that.”

“Good.”

Hậu went in with the doctor. Mom followed him because she'd decided he was family sometime between the sandwiches and the gunfire. Saint sat down beside Voss and finally let himself stop smiling.

Shawna handed me the shirt.

“Your jacket?”

“King has it.”

She closed her eyes.

“I'm billing the whole fucking city.”

I put my forehead against hers.

“Start with me.”

Across the waiting room, my phone lit up.

Detective Pike.

*We need to discuss the mall. Come alone this evening. I can keep this from becoming much worse.*

I looked at the message until the screen went dark.

## Chapter 16: Trunk Full of Applause

Detective Pike chose the parking garage beneath the Eastbridge Civic Center.

Upstairs, a local business association was giving out awards. I knew because three people stopped me on the way to the elevator and tried to give me theirs.
