“For what you did at the cinema,” one woman said, pressing a glass triangle into my hand.

I looked at the inscription.

OUTSTANDING CONTRIBUTION TO COMMERCIAL REFRIGERATION.

“I think this belongs to you.”

“We can get another engraved.”

She insisted on a photograph. I held the award while she stood beside me and gave a thumbs-up. Her husband offered me their parking pass. The man behind him offered a discount on restaurant seating, which was the first gift in days that seemed immediately useful.

By the time I reached the garage, I carried a gift bag, two plaques and a bowl of wrapped chocolates shaped like tiny hands.

The packet called them A ROUND OF APPLAUSE.

I put them in Dad's trunk and went to meet Pike.

She stood beside a gray unmarked sedan near the far wall. Another officer waited by the passenger door, younger, broad-faced, with his uniform shirt buttoned to the throat despite the heat. His nameplate read WALKER.

Pike looked at the bandage under my sleeve.

“You heal slowly for a celebrity.”

“You call quickly for a detective.”

“The mall owner called faster.”

“Did he mention the kidnapping?”

“He mentioned his doors.”

I stopped a few feet from her.

“Then he's going to enjoy the rest of the story.”

Walker looked at me, then at Pike. She didn't look back at him.

“Where's Hậu Phạm?” she asked.

“Recovering.”

“From what?”

“Being kidnapped.”

“By whom?”

“You want the name I already told you, or a new one for variety?”

She held out her hand.

“Your phone.”

I kept it in my pocket.

“Show me why.”

Pike took a folded sheet from her jacket. Before she could open it, Walker cleared his throat.

“Detective, dispatch asked whether we're still at the garage.”

“Tell them yes.”

He touched the radio at his shoulder.

Pike watched me while he spoke.

“You were seen taking Vinh Đào into a car Saturday night.”

“He was having trouble walking.”

“You were also seen delivering him to Bảo Lâm's house.”

“Then you're having a good week for witnesses.”

“Vinh is missing.”

I looked at her face.

“Ask Bảo.”

“I did.”

“And?”

“He says you took Vinh away again.”

I said nothing for a moment.

Pike smiled slightly.

“That's inconvenient.”

Walker had stopped talking into his radio. He looked between us with a crease forming above his nose.

“There are cameras at the house,” I said.

“I'm told they weren't working.”

“They were working when his son was filming.”

That made her pause.

I saw it and kept my eyes on hers.

“You should ask for his phone.”

She folded the paper again without showing it to me.

“Come with us.”

“Am I under arrest?”

“I'm asking you to cooperate.”

“Then ask a question.”

She stepped closer.

“You have something people want. You're making this harder than it needs to be.”

Walker looked at her sharply.

From somewhere behind us, an engine started.

I turned my head.

A black utility vehicle rolled out from behind a concrete pillar. Its windows were dark. It stopped beside Dad's sedan, blocking the lane to the ramp.

Two men got out.

Neither wore a uniform.

Pike didn't turn around.

“Put your hands on the car,” she said.

Walker took a step backward.

“Detective?”

One of the men opened the rear of the utility vehicle. The other pointed at me.

I recognized him from Bảo's garage.

He'd been holding the electrical cord.

I looked back at Pike.

“There he is,” I said. “Your next witness.”

She drew her pistol.

Walker drew his a fraction of a second later, but he didn't point it at me. He aimed toward the men by the utility vehicle.

“Hands!” he shouted.

The man with the open trunk raised both hands. The other stepped behind the vehicle.

Pike swung her gun toward Walker.

I hit her wrist with the back of my good hand.

The pistol struck the sedan's roof and went off. The bullet punched into the concrete above us. Walker ducked behind the passenger door.

I caught Pike's elbow, turned her against the hood and took the gun from her hand.

“Stay down,” I told Walker.

The man behind the utility vehicle fired at me.

I dropped beside Pike's sedan. A bullet shattered its rear window. Another hit the pillar behind my head.

Pike tried to reach the radio beneath her jacket.

I shoved her under the car by the shoulder and hip. She slid across the concrete, swearing at me. A round struck the pavement where she'd been kneeling.

Walker fired twice toward the utility vehicle. The gunman ducked.

I put Pike's pistol beneath the front tire, stepped on the roof of the sedan and jumped across the gap to the black vehicle.

I landed on its hood.

The metal folded under my feet. The gunman looked up. I kicked his pistol hand against the windshield frame. His gun flew across the garage. I caught his collar and drove him face-first into the hood beside my shoe.

The other man ran toward the stairwell.

I tore the hood free of its bent hinge and threw it low across his path.

It struck his legs from behind. He went down hard and slid into the stairwell door.

The alarm on the utility vehicle began shrieking.

For a moment, all I could hear was that alarm and Walker shouting into his radio.

I climbed down.

Pike crawled out from under her sedan. She had a scrape along one cheek and a black second pistol in her hand.

I stepped behind the utility vehicle's open rear door.

She fired through it.

The bullet punched past my shoulder. I caught the door's edge and slammed it outward. It hit her gun arm and knocked her sideways against the concrete pillar.

Walker came around the sedan with his pistol held steady.

“Drop it!”

Pike looked at him.

“Ben—”

“Drop the fucking gun!”

She let it fall.

I stepped away from the utility vehicle with both hands visible. Walker looked at me once, then back at Pike. He kept his gun on her until the first responding officers came down the ramp.

They made all of us lie on the floor.

I obeyed. My injured arm hurt enough that the concrete felt almost cool against it.

Beside me, the man I'd hit with the hood groaned.

“You broke my leg.”

“You've got another one.”

An officer told me to stop talking.

I stopped.

When they opened the utility vehicle's rear compartment, the garage grew quiet in a different way.

Vinh lay inside beneath a gray blanket.

He was dead.

There was a dark hole in the front of his shirt and a plastic bag around one hand. His face still showed the bruises from Crown Billiards. Someone had placed a pistol beside his knee.

I looked at Pike.

She looked at the floor.

Walker stood beside the open trunk, breathing through his mouth.

The officers took photographs. They took statements. They took Pike's guns and the gun beside Vinh. They took the men from the utility vehicle away on stretchers.

They put me in the back of a patrol car.

I spent the next several hours in rooms that had been designed to make a chair feel like an accusation.

Shawna arrived with a lawyer whose suit cost more than the clinic's entire waiting room. Estelle had sent him. He introduced himself, asked me three questions and then told everybody else to stop asking theirs until he'd finished reading what they had.

I liked him immediately.

Saint waited outside with my mother. Dad arrived after closing the shop. Great-Grandpa called three times. The first time he asked whether I'd eaten. The second time he asked whether the police station had good chairs. The third time Mom answered and told him to stop offering to come down there.

By the time I left, it was after two in the morning.

Walker stood near the station entrance.

He looked exhausted.

“They're keeping Pike,” he said.

“Good.”

“I didn't know.”

I looked at his face.

“You aimed at the right person.”

He nodded once, then looked away.

Shawna put her arm around my waist as we walked to the car. Dad had retrieved the blue sedan. Its rear window was intact, which surprised me until I remembered most of the shooting had hit Pike's car instead.

“Fuel?” he asked.

I looked at him.

He opened the driver's door.

“I'm making conversation.”

Saint opened the trunk to put in the bag of my returned belongings.

The awards were still there.

So were the little chocolates shaped like clapping hands.

He picked up the glass triangle and read the inscription.

“Commercial refrigeration?”

“It was a long evening.”

He turned toward the station with the award held high.

“They got the right nigga in the end.”

Mom took it out of his hand.

“Get in the car, Darius.”

As we drove away, I watched the station disappear in the rear window.

My phone had one new message.

No name. No photograph.

*Bảo is leaving town. Ask him why before he does.*

I showed it to Shawna.

She read it, handed the phone back and laid her head against my good shoulder.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

I put the phone away.

For once, I let tomorrow keep it.

## Chapter 17: No Flash Photography

Valerie banned photographs in the house after a man tried to take one while I was brushing my teeth.

He'd come to deliver curtains.

“My son won't believe I'm here,” he explained from the bathroom doorway.

I stood over the sink with toothpaste in my mouth.

“Your son can survive disappointment.”

He apologized, backed into the hall and offered to waive the installation charge.

Shawna appeared behind him in a robe.

“Full price,” she said. “Then leave.”

Valerie posted the rule by the front door before lunch.

NO PHOTOGRAPHS WITHOUT ASKING.

Saint added a smaller note beneath it.

ASK SAINT.

Valerie removed the smaller note and handed it to him folded into a very sharp square.

The next ten days passed without anybody successfully setting fire to a room I occupied. I took that as progress. My arm stayed wrapped for most of them. The doctor removed the stitches, told me the same things he'd told me before and made Shawna promise to continue being the sensible person in our household.

She asked whether that came with a reduced bill.

It did not.

The lawyer dealt with the police. Walker's account and the garage cameras had made Pike's story difficult to maintain. That didn't erase the mall, the fights or the questions about Vinh. It did mean the people asking those questions now had to ask some of them of her.

Bảo left town three days after the garage.

Before he left, Phương called Shawna and asked to meet.

They chose Bishop's. I arrived late and found them already drinking coffee, with Baojun sitting at the counter trying not to look like a boy whose mother had brought him to apologize.

His wrist was in a brace.

He looked at me as I sat down.

“You didn't have to do that.”

“You pointed a gun at me.”

“I wasn't going to—”

Phương set down her cup.

“Finish that sentence in your head.”

Baojun closed his mouth.

She took a phone from her bag and slid it across the table to me.

“His recording. From the garage. Original file.”

I looked at her.

“Why give it to me?”

“Because my husband has decided that losing his rooms wasn't enough. He wanted to lose his family next.”

Baojun stared at the counter.

“Vinh was alive when you left,” Phương said. “The video shows that. Bảo called someone afterward. I don't know whom. I didn't stay to listen.”

“Sunday,” I said.

She said nothing.

Shawna took the phone and put it in her bag for the lawyer.

Phương watched her do it.

“You were good at the cinema.”

“So were you at the gym.”

Phương smiled faintly.

“I've had more practice removing him from rooms.”

Baojun turned on his stool.

“Dad says you're taking everything.”

I looked at him for a moment.

“Your mother just saved you more than I took.”

He looked toward her. She lifted her cup and kept drinking.

They left Eastbridge the next morning. I didn't ask where they were going. Phương sent Shawna a message saying the plane had good legroom and no speeches. Shawna showed it to me while we were unpacking the last boxes at Orchard House.

“She should've left earlier,” I said.

“People usually know that afterward.”

She put the phone away and held up the painting of me on the tiger.

“Where?”

“Guest bathroom.”

“That's cruel to guests.”

“They'll leave faster.”

She considered it, then carried it upstairs.

Saint announced the housewarming without consulting either of us.

By the time I learned about it, seventy people had confirmed, a caterer had offered to work for a photograph and somebody had promised a live band.

Valerie looked at the guest list.

“This house holds forty comfortably.”

“We don't want them comfortable,” Saint said. “We want them impressed.”

She looked at me.

I pointed toward the terrace.

“Outside. And he cleans.”

Saint nodded quickly.

He hired three people to clean before I could clarify what I'd meant.

The party began at seven and escaped him by eight.

People came up the drive carrying gifts large enough to have their own arrival schedules. Someone brought a chandelier. Someone else brought a signed basketball in a glass box. A man I had never met offered me a small percentage of a nightclub in exchange for attending its anniversary.

“What anniversary?” I asked.

“We can choose one you're free for.”

I sent him to Trinh.

She stood near the terrace doors with a drink, a notebook and the patience of a woman who had realized that half my new empire consisted of men trying to invent reasons to pay me.

Hậu arrived with a bandage at the back of his head and a new shirt that actually fit his shoulders. Denise had found a tailor who understood him as a structural problem rather than a size.

“How's the head?” I asked.

“Still mine.”

“Good.”

He looked out at the pool.

“Can I?”

“Not in that shirt.”

He nodded solemnly and went to find a place to change.

Dad and Mom came together. Dad carried a small toolbox. Mom carried a covered dish and immediately asked Valerie whether the kitchen had enough serving spoons.

“Dad,” I said, looking at the toolbox, “you don't have to fix anything.”

“I know.”

He went past me toward the terrace door, which had been sticking since the day we'd moved in.

Granddad Hòa arrived on foot.

I saw him at the gate carrying a paper bag from the pharmacy. The guard stepped out of the booth to stop him, took one look at his face and opened the gate with both hands.

Granddad thanked him and came up the drive.

“You walked?” I asked.

“The bus stopped.”

“Where?”

“Before the hill.”

He handed me the bag. Inside were bandages, antiseptic and a small packet of cough drops.

“Why cough drops?”

“Your great-grandfather said you were getting hoarse from accepting applause.”

I laughed.

Granddad touched my good shoulder and went inside.

Great-Grandpa himself arrived five minutes later in the tiny electric cart.

Saint saw him at the gate and seized the microphone from the bandleader.

“Ladies and gentlemen, the original—”

Great-Grandpa sounded the cart's horn until Saint stopped talking.

“I've been original all day,” he called. “Find me a plate.”

People parted as he drove onto the terrace. Somebody offered him a seat. He pointed at the cart.

“I brought one.”

Dad came out with the terrace door moving smoothly behind him. Great-Grandpa looked from the toolbox to the repaired hinge.

“You charging your son?”

“No.”

“Soft.”

Mom put her covered dish on the table and pointed at both of them.

“No business at dinner.”

Great-Grandpa looked around at the envelopes being handed to Trinh.

“Then what the fuck is this, Mai?”

She opened her mouth, saw the pile of gift boxes and shut it again.

Granddad Hòa smiled into his drink.

Shawna came downstairs wearing a dark blue dress she'd finished that afternoon. The band was halfway through a song. The singer saw her, missed a word and looked at me as if I'd arranged an unfair distraction.

I met her at the terrace doors.

“You did that on purpose.”

“I made the dress on purpose.”

“The rest too.”

She put a hand against my chest.

“Try to survive an evening without a window.”

I took her onto the small dance floor Saint had rented. People clapped when we passed. She raised one hand without looking at them, and they lowered their phones.

For three songs, I let her lead whenever she wanted and pretended I hadn't noticed when she stepped on my foot.

“That was deliberate,” I whispered.

“You were showing off.”

“It's my house.”

“It's my dress.”

I kissed her. The applause started again. She laughed against my mouth and told me I'd never hear the end of it.

Near ten, I found a quiet room off the hall and sat down for the first time in an hour.

The door opened a moment later.

I expected Saint.

Instead, a woman I didn't know stood there holding a tray with one glass of water.

“Mrs. Nguyễn said you were hiding.”

“Resting.”

“She used the other word.”

I took the water and thanked her.

She hesitated at the door.

“My brother saw you pull that man out from under the statue. He works with the delivery crew.”

“How's he doing?”

“Fine. He keeps telling the story.”

She put a folded note on the side table.

“He asked me to give you that.”

She left before I opened it.

Inside was a photograph of the worker with his two children, all three grinning beneath a paper version of Saint's wings. No money. Just their names and a thank-you.

I put it in my jacket pocket.

My phone buzzed.

A new message from an unknown number.

The photograph showed the Sunday Best at its berth. Workers were hanging lights along the upper deck. Beneath it was a date three weeks away.

*Opening night. Your name is on the invitation whether you come or not.*

I stared at the picture.

Outside, Hậu hit the pool with a splash that made six guests jump out of their chairs.

Saint shouted something about a tidal warning.

I put the phone away and went to see how much water was left.

## Chapter 18: Granddad's Errand

Granddad called at nine and asked whether I could drive him to the library.

I was standing in Orchard House's kitchen while Valerie explained that the pool filter had not been designed to process a silk pocket square, three cocktail napkins and a plastic crown.

“Yes,” I told him immediately.

“You sound relieved.”

“I like books.”

“Then we should have done this sooner.”

He waited outside his house with a canvas bag and his folding chair. I put the chair in the trunk. He kept the bag on his lap.

“Which library?” I asked.

“Harbor branch.”

“There are closer ones.”

“This one has my book.”

“A book you wrote?”

He looked at me.

“A book I haven't returned.”

We drove through the neighborhood with the windows down. People waved when they saw me. Granddad waved back first, which confused a few of them into waving more respectfully.

At a traffic light, a man in a delivery van leaned out of his window.

“Aiden! My nephew bought the shirt!”

“Tell him thanks.”

The man looked at Granddad in the passenger seat and suddenly sat straighter.

“Mr. Hòa.”

Granddad nodded.

“Still speeding, Paul?”

“Not now, sir.”

The light turned green. The van pulled away with exaggerated care.

“Student?” I asked.

“Two years.”

“You remember all of them?”

“The ones who think traffic lights are suggestions.”

The harbor library occupied an old customs building with high windows and a stone staircase worn smooth in the middle. Granddad went inside with his canvas bag. I followed him to the desk.

The librarian saw him and smiled.

“Mr. Lê.”

“I brought it back.”

“I was beginning to wonder.”

He took a slim blue book out of the bag and put it on the counter. The librarian checked the date slip inside its cover.

Her eyebrows rose.

“Twenty-seven years.”

I looked at him.

“Granddad.”

He looked at the book.

“I wanted to finish.”

The librarian laughed, shook her head and took it to the shelf behind her. When she returned, she asked whether he'd like to renew his card.

“I brought identification,” he said.

He took an envelope from his pocket. Inside were two old photographs, a receipt and a folded letter.

He looked through them slowly.

“Maybe I didn't.”

The librarian waved it away.

“I know who you are.”

Granddad put the envelope back in his pocket. One photograph slipped out before he could close it.

I picked it up.

It showed a much younger Hòa standing beside a collapsed railway bridge. Tín stood a few feet behind him with his shirt open at the neck. Both men were muddy. A locomotive sat across the broken span at an angle that made no sense to me until I realized the front half was resting on a pile of rails.

Something had bent those rails upward into a cradle.

On the back, someone had written two words.

*Ask Hòa.*

I turned it toward him.

“Who took this?”

He slipped it back into the envelope.

“A woman with a camera.”

“What happened?”

“The train stopped.”

“I can see that part.”

He looked at me, smiled faintly and took his renewed library card from the librarian.

“Come on. I have another stop.”

The other stop was a small repair shed at the edge of the commercial harbor.

A woman in oil-stained overalls came out when she saw the car. Her hair was tied back beneath a blue cap, and she carried a wrench long enough to be useful in an argument.

“Mr. Hòa.”

“Imani.”

She hugged him with one arm and held the wrench away from his shirt with the other.

He introduced us.

“Captain Imani Cole. She knows boats.”

“And he knows when I've forgotten my homework,” she said.

She looked at me.

“You're the grandson.”

“One of them.”

“The expensive one.”

Granddad smiled.

Imani led us into the shed. Half a boat engine sat on a stand near the door. The back wall was covered in photographs of ferries, tugboats and crews standing in front of water they looked tired of seeing.

Granddad set up his folding chair beside the workbench.

“You wanted a ferry captain,” he told me.

I looked at him.

“I didn't ask you for one.”

“You showed your mother the invitation. She showed your grandmother. By then everybody was having an opinion.”

Imani sat on a stool across from us.

“I used to command the boat Mercer bought. Before he put gold stripes on it.”

I took the brochure from my jacket and laid it on the workbench.

She looked at the cover.

“He calls it the Sunday Best?”

“Yes.”

She closed her eyes briefly.

“Of course he does.”

I told her what had happened at the mall, the garage and the cinema. I kept it short. She listened without interrupting, except to ask whether King had been the man in the green shirt.

“You know him?”

“He came to this shed and asked for the boat's old keys. I told him I'd already returned them.”

“Had you?”

“No.”

Granddad peeled an orange she'd given him and divided it neatly on a paper towel.

Imani opened a drawer and took out a bundle of photographs. She spread them beside the brochure. The same ferry appeared in them, older paint, different name, crew members smiling on a sunlit deck.

“He keeps changing things,” she said. “Walls where people used to move. Furniture where crew used to work. He thinks money improves a boat the way it improves a room.”

“Does it?”

“Depends whether the room floats.”

She tapped one photograph with a blunt fingernail.

“If he fills it the way he's advertising, somebody sober needs to be aboard.”

“Would you?”

She looked at Granddad.

He offered her an orange segment.

“He can pay,” he said.

She took the segment and looked back at me.

“Then yes. And I choose my crew.”

“Done.”

We were looking at a photograph of the lower vehicle deck when a van stopped outside.

Imani glanced toward the door and put down the photograph.

“That's not a customer.”

Three men came into the shed. The first wore a blue jacket with a marina logo. The second had one hand beneath his shirt. The third stayed by the door, looking at the machinery as if measuring what could be broken quickly.

The man in the blue jacket saw me and hesitated.

Granddad kept peeling the last strip of orange skin.

“We're closed,” Imani said.

“Mr. Mercer needs the old crew list.”

“He can call me.”

“He sent us.”

I stood.

The second man drew his pistol.

Granddad flicked the orange peel at his face.

The man blinked.

Hòa was beside him before the peel reached the floor.

He caught the gun by its slide, turned his wrist and took it out of the man's hand. Metal squealed softly. He set the pistol on the workbench.

Its barrel pointed upward at an angle the rest of it hadn't agreed to.

The man stared at his empty hand.

Granddad adjusted the man's shirt collar with two fingers.

“You should ask before bringing things into a workplace.”

The third man grabbed a length of chain from beside the door and swung it toward Hòa's head.

I started forward.

Granddad reached back without turning around.

The chain stopped in his hand.

He pulled once.

The man holding the other end flew across the shed, struck the side of the engine stand and folded over it. The stand slid six feet across the concrete. Imani caught a mug before it fell from the workbench.

Granddad let the chain drop.

The man in the blue jacket raised both hands.

“We didn't know you were here.”

“You should have been polite anyway,” Granddad said.

He walked back to his chair and sat down.

The three men left, one supporting the man who'd hit the stand. Nobody tried to retrieve the bent pistol.

Imani watched the van pull away.

Then she turned toward Hòa.

“You still do that.”

He looked at the orange segments.

“Only when people interrupt.”

I picked up the bent pistol with a cloth and put it aside. Granddad had moved faster than I had. I replayed the first step in my head and couldn't find the moment when his weight had left the chair.

He looked at me watching him.

“What?”

“Could you do that to Great-Grandpa?”

Imani became very interested in her mug.

Hòa held out the last orange segment.

“He would complain about the peel.”

“That's not what I asked.”

He smiled.

“I know, nigga.”

On the drive home, he sat with the empty canvas bag folded on his lap. Imani had agreed to bring two crew members she trusted. She'd also given me a number for the boat's former chief engineer, who apparently owed her money and would therefore answer carefully.

Granddad watched the harbor pass beyond the window.

“You could tell me,” I said.

“About the train?”

“About any of it.”

He looked at me for a long moment.

Then he took the envelope from his pocket and handed me the photograph again.

“Keep that one.”

I glanced at the words on the back.

*Ask Hòa.*

“Who wrote this?”

“Your great-grandfather.”

I looked at him.

He pointed through the windshield.

“Light's green.”

## Chapter 19: The Price Goes Up

Sunday put my face on a bus.

Not a photograph of the boat. Not a small endorsement beneath the window. My entire face, twelve feet wide, smiling above the words COME ABOARD WITH THE KING.

The bus stopped outside Bishop's while I was eating lunch.

Denise looked through the window, looked back at me and put another bowl in front of me.

“You eating for two now?”

Saint went outside to take a photograph. I caught him by the back of his jacket before he reached the curb.

“Do not admire the problem.”

“I'm documenting unauthorized usage.”

“You're smiling.”

“I can do both.”

The driver opened the door when he saw me.

“You want a ride?”

“Who gave you that advertisement?”

He pointed at the depot number on his shirt.

“They give me keys. I don't choose the people on the side.”

I nodded. He looked relieved.

Then he leaned closer.

“Can you sign it?”

Saint produced a marker so quickly I suspected he'd been carrying it for this exact emergency.

I took the marker, went around the side of the bus and wrote across my own enormous forehead.

I DIDN'T AGREE TO THIS.

The passengers watched through the windows. One of them applauded. The driver got out, read it and looked worried.

“Am I supposed to wash that off?”

“Ask the people who gave you the keys.”

He considered that, nodded and drove away.

Saint stood beside me with the marker cap in his hand.

“You just improved the advertisement.”

“Then let's improve the competition.”

By evening, Trinh had booked the Pearl for the night of the ferry opening. Three other Circle rooms agreed to host their own parties. Shawna offered to bring the remaining pieces from her collection to the Pearl. Saint called every person who had paid to photograph me and told them exactly where I intended to be.

“No boat,” he said repeatedly. “Dry land. Reliable floor. A man with a face that belongs to him.”

People paid deposits before he finished the calls.

He kept a tally on a napkin until Trinh took it away and gave him an actual notebook.

“You've entered civilization,” she said.

“It lacks romance.”

“It has page numbers.”

The next morning, Benny Châu came to the Pearl with a worried expression and two men carrying a safe.

The safe was small enough to fit behind the bar but heavy enough that the men needed to stop twice before they reached it.

“For the house,” Benny said.

I looked at him.

“You're already lending me a house.”

“For the money in the house.”

“You could have brought a shelf.”

He swallowed.

“Mercer came to my room last night.”

I let him finish.

Sunday had asked about Orchard House. About the staff. About the terrace and the river side of the property. Benny had answered some questions before he understood what kind they were.

“I told him I wasn't involved,” Benny said.

“And?”

“He said everybody who profits is involved.”

Saint looked up from his notebook.

“I hate when a dangerous nigga discovers a slogan.”

I went around the bar and stood beside Benny.

“Did you give him keys?”

“No.”

“Did anyone who works for you?”

“No.”

“Then keep coming to the Pearl.”

He looked at the safe.

“You don't want it?”

“I want you to stop apologizing with furniture.”

He laughed nervously, then put a thick envelope on the counter.

“This isn't furniture.”

I let him leave it.

We were making more money than we had space to count. Some came from games. Some came from appearances. Some arrived from men who understood that if Sunday lost, they wanted to be standing close to whoever remained.

I took my share. I paid Trinh hers. I gave Hậu and Rafa enough to stop pretending their cars and bodies were being offered as unpaid favors.

Hậu looked at the transfer on his phone for a long time.

“That's too much.”

“You went through a mall in a wheelchair.”

“You did most of the steering.”

“Buy something that fits.”

He looked down at his shirt.

“This fits.”

“Something with a roof.”

His eyes came back to mine.

“You mean that?”

I nodded.

He went quiet in a way I'd never seen before. Then he took a sandwich from the plate between us and handed me half.

“Thank you.”

“Hank the Thank.”

He laughed and shook his head.

“Don't let Saint print it.”

Across the room, Saint was already writing it down.

Imani brought her former chief engineer to Orchard House that afternoon. Edwin Marsh was a narrow man with silver hair, permanently blackened fingernails and a voice that sounded as if it had spent forty years arguing with engines.

He stopped in the doorway when he saw Dad sitting at the kitchen table.

“Minh.”

Dad looked up from the broken toaster he'd brought from our old apartment.

“Ed.”

“You still making everybody else look unemployed?”

“Only on Thursdays.”

Edwin laughed and shook his hand. Imani looked between them.

“Everybody knows everybody,” she said.

“Usually after something breaks,” Dad said.

We went out to the terrace. Edwin spread photographs of the ferry on the table. He kept the technical talk short because Imani interrupted whenever he began describing something she already knew.

“Can it run safely?” I asked.

“With a crew that knows it,” he said. “And without some idiot locking people out of places they need to reach.”

“Mercer's doing that?”

He tapped a photograph of a new steel door.

“He calls it privacy.”

“Can you undo it?”

Edwin looked at Imani.

She looked at me.

“We can get people off a boat,” she said. “We won't help you fill it with more people to prove a point.”

“I don't want them on it.”

“Good. Then we understand each other.”

I paid them before they left. Edwin tried to refuse part of it because Dad was watching. Dad told him to take it and stop wasting everybody's afternoon.

After they were gone, I sat beside him in the kitchen.

The toaster lay open between his hands. A small spring rested on the table beside a screwdriver.

“How do you know Ed?” I asked.

“A truck.”

“That's not much of a story.”

“It was a big truck.”

He put the spring back in place and closed the toaster.

“Your great-grandfather asked whether you're trying to buy the river.”

“No.”

“Good.”

“Why?”

Dad plugged in the toaster and lowered the lever.

“He says he still has some of the paperwork.”

I stared at him.

The toast popped up.

Dad caught it before it landed on the table and handed me one piece.

“Ask him after dinner. He likes an audience.”

Two nights later, Sunday's men came to one of the smaller Circle rooms on Ash Street.

They didn't bring guns. They brought six large men, a van full of folding tables and a new sign with Sunday's name on it. Their plan appeared to be replacing the owner in front of his own customers and seeing whether anyone objected.

The owner called Trinh.

Trinh called me.

I arrived to find a man on a ladder unscrewing the old sign above the entrance.

“Leave that,” I said.

He looked down, saw me and climbed off the ladder immediately.

Inside, two men were emptying the till. Four others stood around the room, blocking the customers from leaving. A woman at the nearest table clutched her handbag against her chest.

I stopped in the doorway.

“Who wants to explain?”

The taller man at the till turned around with a handful of cash.

“New management.”

“Again? Busy month.”

He set the money down and came toward me.

I picked up the nearest folding chair, closed it and handed it to him.

He took it automatically.

I drove the chair back into his chest with both hands.

He flew across the room and struck the edge of a table. The chair bent around his shoulders. He landed on the floor with it still in his hands.

The other man at the till reached for a bottle.

Hậu took it away from him and tried to drink before realizing the cap was still on. He lowered it, annoyed with himself, and used his free hand to pin the man against the bar.

Two of the men by the tables headed for the rear exit. Rafa stood there with a wrench. They stopped and raised their hands.

The last two looked at each other.

I pointed at the new sign leaning against the wall.

“Take your furniture.”

They took it.

The man wrapped in the folding chair needed help getting through the door. His companions turned him sideways and carried him out while the customers watched.

Then the applause began.

The owner came from behind the bar holding the recovered cash.

“For you.”

I took half and pushed the rest back.

“Open tomorrow.”

“Of course.”

Outside, Saint waited beside the car.

He looked at the departing van, the bent chair and the customers crowding the doorway behind me.

“Do we need to update your appearance fee?”

I got into the car.

“Double it.”

## Chapter 20: A Brother's Name

Hậu bought the old firehouse gym with a handshake, a transfer from his phone and a promise to leave the previous owner's photograph above the water fountain.

Then he asked me to help move the photograph.

“You promised.”

“I promised above the fountain. I didn't say how far.”

We stood in the gym's entrance beneath a picture of a man with an enormous mustache holding a championship belt upside down. The frame was five feet wide. A painted eagle spread its wings behind him.

“That's a lot of photograph,” I said.

“He had a lot of confidence.”

Milo Voss came out of the back room carrying a box of old gloves.

“That's Sal. He never won that belt.”

Hậu looked at him.

“What?”

“He rented it.”

I looked at the picture again.

“Saint's going to love this place.”

Hậu had hired Voss to teach boxing and help with the gym. Voss had accepted before Hậu finished explaining the hours. His sister came by that afternoon to see it. Her right hand still didn't close properly. She shook mine with her left and told me Milo had been talking about the gym in his sleep.

He tried to deny it.

She looked at him.

“You shouted about floor mats at two in the morning.”

“They were a good price.”

She hugged him and stayed to help clean the office.

The old firehouse had high ceilings, thick brick walls and a wide garage door opening onto the street. Hậu planned to put weights at one end, mats at the other and the wrestling ring in the center. He wanted a place where people could learn without having to lose first to someone who enjoyed it too much.

He said that once, while we were carrying the ring posts.

Then Saint arrived with a banner reading HANK THE THANK'S HOUSE OF PAIN AND GRATITUDE, and the conversation became less dignified.

“No,” Hậu said.

Saint held it higher.

“You haven't seen it from the street.”

“I can read from here.”

“That's why the lettering is good.”

We compromised on BELL STREET FIGHT CLUB, with Hậu's actual name printed beneath it. Saint put THE THANK in smaller letters on the flyers when Hậu wasn't looking.

The opening was the Friday before the ferry's launch week. By then my arm had closed cleanly, though a hard pull still reminded me of the knife. King had apparently stopped guarding his left ribs too. A video from one of Sunday's rooms showed him lifting a barbell overhead with both hands while three men applauded from a safe distance.

I watched it once and put the phone away.

Voss saw my expression.

“You were hoping he stayed hurt.”

“I was hoping he'd take up painting.”

“He'd break the brushes.”

The gym filled before six.

Denise brought trays of food. Loan brought a cash box and claimed she was handling donations, though Hậu hadn't asked for any. Mom printed membership cards with his name in raised black letters. Dad brought two heavy bags, hung them himself and told Hậu the ceiling bolts were now the building's problem.

Great-Grandpa sent a wooden bench.

Attached to it was a note.

*For when you stop running around.*

Hậu read it twice.

“Is that a threat?”

“He likes multipurpose gifts,” I said.

Shawna had made Hậu a jacket for the opening. It fit properly across the shoulders and closed without asking anything unreasonable of the buttons. He stood in front of the mirror for a long time after putting it on.

“You like it?” she asked.

He nodded.

“Then stop looking surprised. You have shoulders. I measured them.”

He laughed and touched the sleeve with one finger.

Saint climbed into the ring with the microphone.

“Ladies and gentlemen, tonight we celebrate a man who has eaten at every restaurant on Bell Street and tipped with his whole heart.”

Hậu put both hands over his face.

“Please stop him.”

“He wrote notes,” I said. “That means it can get worse.”

Saint continued.

“A man who once broke a folding chair by sitting down politely. A man who went into a hostile meeting and negotiated dental. A man who has finally bought a roof high enough for all his ambitions.”

The laughter softened into applause.

Hậu looked up.

Saint held out the microphone.

“Come on, nigga. Say your name.”

Hậu climbed through the ropes. He took the microphone in both hands, looked around the room and swallowed.

“Hậu Phạm,” he said.

People cheered.

“Some of you know me from work. Some of you know me from buying too much food. Some of you know me because I owe you money.”

Loan raised one hand.

He pointed at her.

“That was a sandwich.”

“It was two,” she said.

He smiled and looked down at the microphone.

“I want this place open early. I want people to come here because they like coming here. If you need to learn something, we'll teach you. If you already know everything, there's a mirror in the back. Go argue with it.”

The room applauded again.

He handed the microphone back before Saint could make him say more.

Voss climbed into the ring for a short exhibition. He and Hậu circled each other while Saint offered commentary that neither had requested. Voss landed two clean taps against Hậu's guard. Hậu caught his next arm, stepped across him and tossed him onto the mat with enough care to make the throw look almost friendly.

Voss rolled, got up and pointed at him.

“You're paying for the next floor.”

“I own this one,” Hậu said.

They touched gloves.

Near the entrance, a man in a white tracksuit began clapping slowly.

He had a shaved head, a narrow mustache and three friends who stood behind him with their hands in their pockets. None looked interested in joining a gym.

Hậu saw them and stopped smiling.

“Tucker,” he said.

The man raised both hands.

“Just supporting local business.”

Voss stepped toward the ropes.

“Support it from outside.”

Tucker looked at me, then back at Hậu.

“I heard the Thank got a place. Thought I'd see whether he still falls down when people mean it.”

The room quieted.

Hậu took off his gloves.

“You can pay for a class.”

“I'm offering one.”

I moved toward the ring.

Hậu looked at me and shook his head once.

I stopped.

Tucker climbed between the ropes. His friends spread out along the edge of the room. Rafa put down the plate he was holding. Dad stood near the heavy bags with his hands in his pockets. Mom took Shawna's sleeve and drew her a little farther from the ring.

Tucker bounced on his toes.

“No gloves?”

Hậu handed his to Voss.

“You didn't bring any.”

Tucker threw the first punch before his last word had finished.

Hậu took it on his left forearm and stepped into him. Tucker twisted away, kicked the inside of Hậu's knee and drove a second punch into his cheek.

Hậu's head moved. His feet stayed planted.

Tucker hit him again, faster, then tried to step out of reach.

Hậu caught the back of his tracksuit.

He pulled Tucker back, wrapped both arms around his waist and lifted him straight off the mat.

Tucker kicked behind him. One heel struck Hậu's shin. Hậu adjusted his grip and carried him three steps toward the center of the ring.

Then he turned and drove Tucker down onto the canvas.

The ring shook.

Tucker rolled onto one elbow, gasping.

Hậu stepped back and waited.

“You done?”

Tucker reached into his waistband.

I saw the flash of metal.

Hậu saw it too.

He stamped on Tucker's wrist before the knife cleared the cloth. The blade dropped onto the mat. Hậu kicked it under the bottom rope, caught Tucker by the front of his shirt and hauled him upright.

Tucker swung wildly with his free hand.

Hậu ducked beneath it, lifted him again and threw him over the top rope.

I caught Tucker before he hit the first row of chairs.

He stared at me, upside down in my arms.

“Wrong address,” I said.

I carried him to the door and put him outside beside his friends, who had suddenly become very interested in leaving with him.

Behind me, the gym exploded into cheers.

Saint was shouting Hậu's name into the microphone. Loan had both hands in the air. Voss climbed into the ring and raised Hậu's arm. Hậu looked bewildered, then delighted, then embarrassed by how delighted he was.

I stood in the doorway and watched him accept it.

Tucker spat on the pavement beside me.

“Mercer says your boat ride's still booked.”

I looked down at him.

“Tell him to keep a seat warm.”

His friends helped him away.

When I went back inside, Hậu had been given a bouquet, three envelopes and a pair of expensive boxing gloves he didn't need.

He looked at the gifts, then at me.

“Is this how it starts?”

“Wait until they bring the horse.”

He laughed so hard he had to lean against the ropes.

Later, after the guests had gone, we sat on Great-Grandpa's bench eating the last of Denise's food. Saint had fallen asleep in a chair with the microphone still in his lap. Voss's sister helped Shawna fold the unused tablecloths. Dad had found something else to fix.

Hậu turned one of the new membership cards over in his hands.

“My name,” he said quietly.

“It's been yours the whole time.”

He nodded, still looking at it.

Then he put the card in his jacket pocket and handed me another sandwich.

“Eat. You look skinny.”

## Chapter 21: The Best Dressed Man at a Robbery

Eight days after Hậu opened the gym, Sunday launched his boat.

He did it with fireworks, a red carpet and an advertisement calling me the evening's guest of honor.

I stood at the Pearl beneath a replacement stained-glass window and watched the announcement on Saint's phone.

“He used the tiger painting,” Saint said.

On the screen, my enormous painted jaw smiled above the words THE KING TAKES THE RIVER.

“I should have drowned the painter.”

“He takes criticism badly.”

The Pearl was full. So were the other rooms Trinh had booked. Shawna's clothes hung along the little stage, and the women who'd ordered at the cinema were arriving to collect them. Denise had sent food. Loan had sent a bill for the food she'd helped carry. The band played loudly enough that the glasses behind the bar hummed against each other.

People came to shake my hand every few minutes. Some brought envelopes. Others brought nothing but a story about where they'd seen me last. I stayed long enough to hear each one and gave Saint a look whenever he tried to turn a conversation into an invoice.

At seven, Imani called.

I stepped into the small office behind the bar.

“How many?” I asked.

“About a hundred and forty guests. Thirty crew and service staff. Fewer guests than Mercer expected.”

“Good.”

“He doesn't think so.”

I heard voices behind her, then a door closing.

“He dismissed two of my crew. Brought his own people into the bridge. Ed's below, but they've locked the access from the lounge.”

“Can you get off?”

“I can. The kitchen staff can't. They think they're working a normal party.”

“Tell them.”

“I'm trying.”

The call ended abruptly.

I stared at the phone.

A message arrived a few seconds later.

*Don't call back yet.*

I went out into the room and found Trinh.

She read the message, looked toward the stage and lowered her voice.

“I'll keep things here moving.”

“You have the copies?”

“The drive. The garage recording. Everything you gave me.”

“If I don't call—”

“Don't make a speech. Tell me what to send and whom to call.”

I told her. She wrote it down, tore the page from the notebook and folded it into her pocket.

Hậu came over before I called his name.

He wore the jacket Shawna had made for his opening. Voss stood behind him in a black shirt. Rafa waited by the stairs, keys in hand.

Saint looked at all four of us.

“We're going to the boat.”

“You can stay here,” I said.

He looked offended.

“I already explained this at the mall.”

Shawna came off the stage carrying an empty garment bag.

She stopped when she saw our faces.

“What happened?”

I told her about the crew, the locked doors and Imani's call. She listened, then put the garment bag on a chair.

“Come upstairs.”

I followed her to the small dressing room.

She took a white dinner jacket from a hook and held it up.

“Arms.”

“Shawna.”

“If he's put your face on every advertisement in the city, you're going to look like you chose to arrive.”

I put my arms through the sleeves. The jacket settled across my shoulders without pulling at the scar on my left arm. She smoothed the lapels and fastened the button.

“Better,” she said.

I looked at us in the mirror.

“You're charging me for this?”

“For repairs.”

I turned toward her.

She took my face in both hands and kissed me. When she stepped back, her fingers stayed at the edge of my collar for a moment.

“Come home in it.”

“I'll try.”

“Come home, Aiden.”

I nodded.

She let go and opened the door.

We drove to the harbor in two cars. Rafa had arranged a small launch with a man he knew from the repair yards. He refused to explain how the man knew him, except to say that favors traveled farther than tow trucks.

The Sunday Best glowed at its berth beneath strings of gold lights. Music carried across the water. A crowd gathered behind barriers on the quay, watching guests climb the gangway.

The billboard beside the entrance showed me standing in front of the ferry with one hand raised. He'd hung a second copy on a banner along the ferry's upper-deck rail.

Saint looked at it through the windshield.

“That's a good photograph.”

I looked at him.

“Still unauthorized,” he added quickly.

We got out.

The crowd recognized me before we reached the barrier.

“Aiden!”

Phones rose. Somebody started clapping. A man in a tuxedo hurried toward me carrying a velvet rope as if the rope had personally requested the honor of being moved.

“Mr. Trần. We didn't know whether—”

“I'm here.”

“Of course. Of course.”

He lifted the rope. The crowd cheered as we passed.

Saint walked beside me with his face arranged into professional satisfaction. Hậu kept his eyes on the men near the gangway. Voss watched the upper deck. Rafa peeled away toward the side pier where the launch waited.

At the foot of the gangway, a woman with a clipboard held out a small envelope.

“Your appearance payment.”

I looked at it.

“He paid in advance?”

“Half.”

I took the envelope and handed it to Saint.

“For the boat repairs.”

He put it inside his jacket.

“I'm keeping the receipt.”

We climbed aboard.

The main lounge glittered with glass, brass and people trying to look as if they spent every Saturday on a private ferry. Waiters carried trays between tables. A singer stood on a raised platform near the windows. Beyond her, dark water moved against the hull.

The applause began before the singer finished her song.

She looked toward the entrance, saw me and held the last note until the band caught up with the change in the room.

Sunday stood near the center table in a dark blue dinner jacket.

He applauded with everyone else.

“The king,” he said when I reached him.

“The man with my face.”

He held out his hand.

I shook it because every camera in the room was pointed at us.

His grip tightened.

Mine tightened more.

His smile stayed in place, but the skin around his eyes pinched.

“Let go,” he said softly.

“Where's Imani?”

“Working.”

“Where's King?”

“Also working.”

I released his hand.

He lowered it carefully and turned toward the room.

“Ladies and gentlemen, our guest of honor.”

The applause rose again.

Saint leaned toward me.

“I hate how good he is at this part.”

Sunday gestured toward a chair at the head of the nearest table. It was larger than the others, upholstered in white leather and positioned beneath a spotlight that made it look ready to forgive a small country.

I looked at him.

“You people keep buying the same furniture.”

He smiled.

“Sit. Enjoy something.”

I sat.

Hậu took the chair on my left. Saint sat on my right. Voss stayed standing behind us, his eyes moving between the doors.

A waiter poured champagne. Another brought a platter of food. A third put a small black box in front of me and left before I could stop him.

Inside the box was the broken handle from the van that had taken Hậu.

Sunday watched my face.

Hậu saw it and went very still.

I closed the lid.

“You saved it.”

“A reminder,” Sunday said.

“Of what?”

“You can't hold everything.”

I picked up the box, stood and walked to the window.

The nearest guests turned to watch. I opened the window latch, dropped the box into the water and closed it again.

“Neither can you,” I said.

Sunday's smile disappeared.

The ferry's horn sounded.

I felt the deck shift beneath my feet.

Through the window, the quay began sliding slowly backward.

We were moving.

My phone vibrated in my pocket.

Imani.

*Lower deck. Ed hurt. They have the crew together. Get them up.*

I looked toward the doors at the far end of the lounge.

Two men had taken positions in front of them.

King came down the staircase from the upper level, fastening the cuffs of his shirt.

Both hands moved freely.

He saw me and smiled through his newly straightened nose.

I put the phone away.

“Hậu,” I said quietly.

He stood before I finished saying his name.

## Chapter 22: No One Leaves the Party

Sunday caught my sleeve as I passed his chair.

“The program hasn't begun.”

I looked down at his hand.

He removed it.

“Where are you going?”

“To see the part of the boat you didn't put in the brochure.”

King stopped at the foot of the stairs.

He rolled his shoulders once. The green shirt from the bowling alley had been replaced by white linen, open at the neck. His hands hung loose at his sides.

“We can do this after dinner,” he said.

“You get tired after meals?”

He smiled.

“Only when they're small.”

Hậu stepped beside me. Voss moved to my other side. Saint remained at the table, watching the doors and looking for something useful to become.

The singer finished her song. A few guests applauded uncertainly. Most had noticed the line of men near the staircase.

Sunday rose and lifted his glass.

“Ladies and gentlemen. A small private matter. Please enjoy yourselves.”

I picked up the microphone from the singer's stand.

“The crew downstairs need the exits opened,” I said. “If you work on this boat, find Captain Cole. If you're a guest, keep away from the stairs until we clear them.”

Sunday's glass stopped halfway to his mouth.

The room became very quiet.

Saint took the microphone from me.

“And put down the champagne, niggas. You can carry your own feet.”

King moved first.

He drove his right hand toward my chest. I stepped left and caught his forearm with both hands. The punch carried us halfway across the polished floor before I could turn it past me.

Hậu hit him low at the waist. Voss struck his left knee from the side.

King staggered one step.

Then he seized Hậu by the back of the jacket and threw him into the nearest empty table.

The table broke beneath him.

Voss came up with a short punch to King's jaw. King turned with it, caught his shoulder and shoved him backward into the stair rail. Voss stayed on his feet, but the rail bent around his back.

I grabbed a champagne bottle from a passing tray and smashed it across King's temple.

Glass burst against his head.

He blinked. Blood ran down the side of his face.

I drove the broken neck toward his eye.

He caught my wrist.

I let go of the glass and punched him in the throat with my free hand.

His grip loosened. I pulled away, kicked his knee again and shouted Hậu's name.

Hậu rolled off the broken table, caught the edge of another and shoved it into King's legs.

I jumped onto the table and over King's shoulder, landed by the stairs and went down two steps at a time.

Voss followed. Hậu stayed above to keep King off us.

Behind me, Saint's amplified voice told the guests which way to move. Chairs scraped. A woman shouted for her husband. The bandleader kept playing for three confused bars before someone told him to stop.

The lower passage smelled of warm metal and cooking oil. A steel door blocked the way to the vehicle deck. Two men stood in front of it, one with a pistol, one holding a heavy key ring.

The gunman raised his arm.

I slid the last few feet on the smooth floor and kicked both his legs out from under him.

He fired as he fell. The shot struck the ceiling behind me.

Voss stepped over my shoulder, caught the key man's wrist and drove his fist into the man's stomach. The keys fell. Voss caught them before they reached the floor.

I took the pistol from the fallen gunman and shoved him face-first against the wall.

“Stay there.”

He stayed.

Voss tried three keys before the lock turned. We pulled the door open together.

Thirty people crowded the space beyond it: cooks in white jackets, servers, two musicians and several deckhands. Edwin sat on an overturned crate with a cloth pressed to his forehead. Imani knelt beside him.

She stood when she saw me.

“Upper lounge?”

“Saint is moving people.”

“Then we get these people to the open deck.”

She took the key ring from Voss and began giving orders. The crew moved when she spoke. The frightened servers watched the deckhands and followed their lead.

I crouched beside Edwin.

“Can you walk?”

“I can complain standing up.”

I helped him rise. He swayed once, found his balance and pointed toward the far end of the deck.

“They've got somebody who thinks throttle is a personality.”

The deck shifted under my feet.

We were turning sharply.

Imani looked up at the overhead lights as they swung.

“Get them out now.”

I went back up the stairs.

Hậu was on one knee near the lounge entrance. Blood ran from a split in his eyebrow. King stood over him, gripping the back of his collar.

I hit King from behind with both feet.

The impact drove him forward across the lounge. He let go of Hậu and crashed into the bar. Bottles fell around his shoulders.

I landed badly on my left foot, caught the edge of a table and stayed upright.

Hậu tried to stand.

“Help Imani,” I told him.

He shook his head.

“I can—”

“She needs someone who can carry Ed if he stops complaining.”

He looked at me, then toward the stairs.

“Don't let that nigga keep another jacket.”

He went down.

Saint had cleared most of the guests from the lounge. A few remained near the windows, frozen by indecision or still filming. He moved from group to group, using the microphone less like an entertainer and more like a man who wanted to get everyone somewhere he could count them.

“You in the purple tie. Put the phone down. Your wife is already outside. Follow your good fortune.”

The man lowered the phone and moved.

Sunday stood near the upper stairwell with two guards.

He looked at the emptying room and the broken furniture.

“You could have sat down,” he said.

I picked up a chair and threw it at him.

He ducked behind the stair rail. The chair burst against the wall above his head. His guards pulled him up the stairs and out of sight.

King rose from behind the bar.

He took a broken bottle out of his shoulder, dropped it and looked at me.

“Just us.”

My phone rang.

Shawna.

I answered without taking my eyes off King.

“Are you safe?”

“Your father is making a parking decision.”

I heard an engine roar, then a heavy metallic crash.

“Shawna?”

“I'm inside. We're all inside. Two trucks came to the printshop.”

King took a step toward me.

I moved around the nearest table, keeping it between us.

“Put Dad on.”

The sound changed. A scrape, a grunt, then my father's voice.

“Busy.”

“Mercer's men?”

“They haven't introduced themselves.”

A man shouted in the background. Metal tore with a long, shrill noise.

Dad spoke away from the phone.

“Take your foot off the pedal, nigga. You're wasting fuel.”

I heard Great-Grandpa laughing.

Then Mom's voice, sharp and furious.

“Minh! Not against my window!”

Dad came back on the line.

“Handle your boat.”

He hung up.

King overturned the table between us.

I jumped backward as it struck the floor. He came through the space it had occupied with both fists moving.

I slipped the first punch. The second hit my guard hard enough to drive my forearms into my chest. I stumbled back two steps.

Behind him, Saint reached the last pair of guests.

“Out,” I shouted.

He looked at me.

I nodded toward the deck doors.

He took the guests with him.

The lounge emptied.

King rolled his neck. Something popped.

I took off the white jacket, folded it once and laid it on the back of an unbroken chair.

He watched me do it.

“You think you're coming back for that?”

I loosened my collar.

“My wife made it.”

He grinned.

“Then I'll try not to bleed on it.”

The ferry hit a wake hard enough to make the chandelier swing above us.

I planted my feet as the floor tilted.

King came forward.

## Chapter 23: King Takes King

King hit me before the floor leveled.

I saw the shoulder move and got my right arm across my body. His fist struck the guard, drove it into my ribs and lifted me off my heels. I landed against the edge of the bar. Glass crunched beneath my shoes.

He came after me without hurrying.

I picked up a metal ice bucket and threw it at his head. He knocked it aside. Ice scattered across the floor between us. I stepped into the space behind the bucket and punched him under the chin.

His head went back.

I hit him again before it came down.

The second punch opened his lower lip. He caught my wrist on the third, pulled me toward him and drove his knee into my stomach.

Air left me in a hard grunt.

He did it again.

I hooked my heel behind his standing ankle and dropped my weight. His knee struck my thigh instead of my stomach. I twisted my trapped wrist toward his thumb, pulled free and headbutted him across the bridge of his nose.

The fresh tape across his straightened nose came loose against my forehead.

He roared and swung both arms around me.

I went sideways between them, slipped on the spilled ice and hit the floor on my back. His foot came down beside my head. I rolled under the nearest table as he stamped again.

The floorboard split where my shoulder had been.

I grabbed the table's center pedestal and shoved upward. The tabletop caught him under the jaw. He staggered half a step. I came out on the other side and drove the table into his chest.

He caught its edge with both hands.

We stood on opposite sides of it, bent forward, the polished wood trembling between us.

His arms straightened.

Mine bent.

The table moved toward me across the floor.

I let go.

He stumbled into the space I'd stopped occupying. I jumped onto the tabletop as it tipped, planted one foot near its center and kicked him in the side of the head with the other.

He fell against the bar.

I landed on the floor and reached for his collar.

He caught my hand, squeezed and twisted.

Pain flashed through my fingers. I drove my left fist into his ribs, the place that had hurt him at the mall.

He smiled at me.

Then he punched me in the chest with his left hand.

I flew backward over the broken table and struck the wall beside the stage.

The frame of a decorative mirror cracked against my shoulder blades. I dropped to one knee with a mouthful of blood.

King drew a deep breath without favoring his ribs.

“Better now.”

I spat onto the floor.

“I noticed.”

He picked up the heavy end of the broken table and hurled it at me.

I jumped aside. The wood smashed through the mirror and lodged halfway into the wall. A strip of gold trim fell around my feet.

I grabbed the trim, whipped it across his eyes and moved left as he reached for his face.

My first punch hit his ear. The second caught the hinge of his jaw. I drove my knee into the outside of his thigh and pulled his head down toward the rising edge of the stage.

His forehead struck the wood.

The stage board cracked.

He caught my belt with one hand and threw me over his shoulder.

I went through the singer's empty music stand, struck the base of the piano and rolled onto my side. The piano lurched backward on its wheels. Two keys sounded together, a ridiculous bright little complaint in the middle of everything.

King came up the step.

I kicked the piano's front leg.

The leg broke. The piano tilted toward him. He put both hands against its side and held it there.

I drove my shoulder into it.

Its weight carried him backward off the stage. His heel caught the step. The piano fell across his thighs and slammed him to the floor.

The strings rang inside the broken case.

I took two breaths, both shallow, and went around its side.

King put his hands beneath the piano.

The whole thing rose.

He shoved it away from him and stood with a long strip of black wood hanging from one trouser leg.

I stared for half a second.

“That's rented,” I said.

He kicked the broken panel free.

“So are the shoes.”

He charged.

I jumped for the low balcony above the stage. My hands caught the rail. I pulled upward as his shoulder hit the wall beneath me.

The wall shook. One of my hands slipped on blood.

I swung my knees over the rail and rolled onto the narrow balcony floor. King looked up. I stood, stepped onto the rail and jumped toward the open stairwell on the opposite side.

For a moment I could see the whole ruined lounge beneath me: broken tables, glass, the white jacket still hanging from its chair, the dark water moving beyond the windows.

I caught the far rail with one hand.

My shoulder nearly came out of its socket.

I hauled myself over and landed on the upper landing.

King took the stairs after me.

I picked up a small service cabinet and threw it down at him. It broke across his shoulders. He pushed through it without stopping.

At the top of the stairs, I hit him with a fire door.

I slammed it against his face, pulled it back and slammed it again. On the third swing he caught the edge and tore it off its closer.

I stepped through the doorway as the door came loose.

He followed me into the narrow service passage.

The passage gave him less room to swing. It gave me less room to leave.

He drove his right fist down the center. I slipped it by turning my shoulders and punched his stomach twice. He lowered an elbow onto my back. My knees buckled. I caught the handrail along the wall and stayed off the floor.

He grabbed my collar.

I let the collar tear and ducked under his arm. His fingers scraped the back of my neck. I kicked the service trolley parked behind him, sending it into the backs of his knees.

He stumbled over it.

I went past him and down the metal staircase at the end of the passage. It doubled back below the lounge in two tight flights.

The lower vehicle deck opened beneath me.

Most of the old loading space had been turned into storage for the party. Cases of liquor stood beside folded tables. A black luxury car occupied the center of the deck, polished so brightly it reflected the overhead lights in straight white lines. Beyond it, a chain hoist hung from a beam above an open maintenance bay.

Water slapped against the hull somewhere close.

I looked back up the stairs.

King stood at the top, breathing hard through his mouth.

Blood covered one side of his face. His shirt hung open at the shoulder where the piano had torn it. He looked at the car, then at me.

“You keep finding things to hide behind.”

I put a hand on the car's roof.

“You keep finding them with your face.”

He came down the stairs.

I moved around the car, keeping it between us. He went the other way. For a few seconds we circled, both watching the other's feet beneath the body.

Then he caught the car beneath the front fender and lifted.

The front wheels rose off the deck.

He shoved the car toward me on its rear tires.

I jumped onto the trunk, ran two steps up the rear window and kicked off the roof as the car slammed into the storage racks behind me.

Bottles burst beneath it. Liquor spread across the deck.

I landed near the maintenance bay. My left ankle turned under me. I caught a hanging chain before I fell.

King watched the ankle.

I knew he had seen it.

He came faster.

I pulled the chain sideways and swung the heavy hook at its end into his shoulder. He grunted and kept coming. I swung it back across his chest, let go and ducked as he grabbed for it.

His fist struck the beam beside my head.

The metal rang.

I drove both hands into his face, thumbs pressing against his brow to keep his eyes away from mine, and pushed him backward toward the slick floor.

He caught my wrists.

His shoe slid in the spilled liquor.

I kicked his other ankle.

We fell together.

He landed on top of me.

The weight drove the air out of my lungs. His forearm pressed across my throat. I shoved at his elbow with both hands, but he lowered himself farther and pinned my shoulders to the deck.

I couldn't get a full breath.

Above his shoulder, the overhead lights swung in a slow arc.

The ferry was rolling.

King pressed harder.

I drew one knee up between us, planted my foot against the underside of the wrecked car's bumper and pushed with everything I had left in that leg.

The car moved.

Only a few inches, but enough.

Its broken fender caught King's hip. He shifted to avoid the sharp metal. I turned my head into the gap beneath his forearm, dragged in half a breath and drove my forehead into his mouth.

His lip split against his teeth.

I did it again.

He lifted his head. I brought my knee into his stomach, pushed him sideways and rolled out from beneath him.

We both came up on our knees.

I hit him first.

Right hand to the cheek. Left to the throat. Right again, shorter, into the broken place beside his mouth.

He hit me in the ribs.

Something gave beneath the impact.

I went sideways, caught the hanging chain and used it to keep from falling into the maintenance bay.

King stood.

I pulled myself up too.

Every breath now had a sharp edge. Blood ran from my nose onto my shirt. My right hand had begun to swell. I opened and closed it once, making sure the fingers still answered.

King came toward me with his head lowered.

I watched the chain moving beside my shoulder.

The ferry rolled left.

The hook swung away from me.

King stepped over a broken bottle.

The ferry rolled back.

I jumped.

Both feet left the deck. I caught the overhead beam, swung my legs forward and drove both heels into King's chest.

He flew backward into the wrecked car.

The car slid across the spilled liquor and struck the side barrier of the maintenance bay. Metal buckled. The rear wheels dropped through the gap.

King grabbed the roof to keep himself from falling with it.

I dropped from the beam, caught the hanging hook and pulled it across the deck toward him.

He saw it coming and reached for my wrist.

I let the hook go past his hand, caught the chain with my other hand and pulled it tight across his chest.

The hook caught beneath the car's torn front pillar.

King stood between the chain and the car.

I planted both feet, leaned backward and pulled.

The car tilted farther into the maintenance bay. Its weight dragged the chain against his chest. He pushed outward with both arms, holding it away from his throat.

I took one step backward.

Then another.

My injured ankle shook beneath me. I moved my good foot back and kept pulling.

The car dropped another six inches.

King's heels left the deck.

He roared, twisted and caught the chain in both hands. The muscles in his neck stood out. A link near my right hand stretched visibly.

I pulled harder.

The link snapped.

The released chain whipped past my face. King stumbled forward, suddenly free of the car's weight.

I stepped into him.

My fist struck his jaw from below.

His feet left the deck.

I followed him with a second punch before he landed.

He hit the side of the maintenance bay shoulder-first, bounced against the rail and fell onto his back. His head struck the deck with a sound I felt through my shoes.

I stood over him, breathing in small, painful pieces.

He moved one hand.

I stepped on the sleeve beside his wrist.

“Stay.”

His eyes found mine.

For a moment I thought he'd try again.

Then his hand opened.

I took my foot off the sleeve.

He lay still, chest rising and falling, blood bright against the white cloth beneath his face.

The car groaned in the maintenance bay. I caught the loose chain, looped it over the remaining rail and pulled the car far enough back that it stopped dragging at the edge. I didn't try to lift it clear. My ribs had begun objecting to the continued existence of my lungs.

King watched me through one half-open eye.

“Your father,” he said thickly.

I looked down at him.

“What about him?”

He swallowed blood and tried to finish.

I shook my head.

“Meet him when you can stand.”

Footsteps rang on the stairs.

Hậu came down with Voss behind him. Hậu's eyebrow had been wrapped with a strip of cloth. Voss carried a length of rope and an expression that changed when he saw King on the floor.

He stopped beside him.

For several seconds, he said nothing.

Then he crouched, took King's empty hand and looked at it.

“My sister,” he said.

King closed his eyes.

Voss held the hand a moment longer, then let it fall and began tying King's wrists.

Hậu came to me.

“You look terrible.”

“How do you look?”

“I'm standing behind you. You don't get to review.”

He put a hand against my side. I flinched before I could stop myself.

“Ribs?”

“Probably.”

“You should sit.”

The ferry lurched.

The overhead lights swung hard toward the wall. Somewhere above us, an alarm began sounding.

Imani's voice came over the speaker system, sharp and clear.

“Everybody away from the forward rail. Hold something fixed.”

I looked at Hậu.

He looked back.

Then Saint's voice came through my phone.

“Aiden. Sunday took the bridge. He's aiming us at the old terminal.”

I wiped my mouth with the back of my hand and headed for the stairs.

Hậu caught my arm.

“Your jacket,” he said.

He'd carried it down over his shoulder.

I stared at the white cloth.

Then I let him help me put it on.

## Chapter 24: The Last Fare

The old terminal appeared through the forward windows as I reached the lounge.

Its roof had partly collapsed years earlier. Concrete pillars stood in the water beneath a long loading platform, dark with river slime. Beyond them, a service crane leaned over the abandoned berth.

We were going toward it too quickly.

The lounge floor tilted under my feet. I caught a chair, waited for the roll to settle and kept moving. My left ankle had stiffened. Each breath scraped against the broken place in my side.

Saint stood by the deck doors with a life jacket over his suit and another one in his hands.

“Put this on.”

“Where's Imani?”

“Trying to get into the bridge.”

“The guests?”

“Aft deck. Crew with them. Rafa's bringing the launch around.”

He held the life jacket against my chest until I put my arms through it. The strap pressed against my ribs. I swallowed a curse and tightened it anyway.

Saint looked at my face.

“How bad?”

“Ask me when the floor stops moving.”

I went up the stairs.

Imani stood outside the bridge with one hand against the locked door. A deckhand beside her had a bleeding scalp and a useless ring of keys.

“He's inside,” she said. “One guard with him.”

I knocked.

Sunday's voice came through the door.

“Where's Rhett?”

“Lying down.”

Silence.

I took a step back.

Imani moved the deckhand out of the way.

I kicked beside the lock.

The frame cracked, but the door held. Pain shot from my ankle to my knee. I shifted onto my other foot and hit it with my shoulder.

The frame broke away from the wall.

I went through with the door falling beneath me.

The guard fired.

I hit the floor on my side. The bullet passed over my head and shattered a window behind Imani. I grabbed the fallen door by its upper edge and shoved it upright between us.

The guard fired again into the wood.

I drove the door forward, pinning him against the chart table. His gun hand stuck out beyond the edge. I caught it, bent it down and knocked the pistol against the table until he let go.

Imani came past me and went straight to the controls.

Sunday stood on the far side of the bridge, holding a black bag against his chest. His other hand gripped a pistol.

“Nobody touches that,” he said.

Imani didn't look at him.

She moved the controls, glanced through the windows and swore softly.

Sunday raised the gun toward her.

I threw the guard into him.

Both men hit the bridge wall. Sunday's shot went through the ceiling. I caught his gun wrist before he could aim again and slammed it against the metal window frame.

He cried out.

The black bag fell between his feet.

Bundles of cash spilled across the floor.

Sunday drove his knee into my injured side.

My grip loosened. He pulled free and ran through the side door onto the narrow outer walkway.

I took one breath that didn't go far enough and followed.

Wind hit me in the face. The terminal loomed ahead, closer now. I could hear people shouting on the deck below and Imani speaking into the bridge radio behind me.

Sunday ran toward the forward observation platform.

I caught him at the end of the walkway.

He turned and fired from the hip.

The shot tore through the loose side of my life jacket. I felt the heat of it against my shirt.

I hit his gun hand with both of mine and drove him against the rail.

The pistol fell into the water.

He grabbed my collar, pulling me close enough that I could smell the champagne on his breath.

“You ruined everything.”

I drove my forehead into his face.

His hands opened.

I hit him in the stomach, then caught his jacket before he fell over the rail.

He hung there, bent backward over the metal, one shoe scraping the deck.

Below us, the river rushed along the hull.

“You put them on the boat,” I said.

He looked up at me through blood running from his nose.

“They paid to see you.”

He reached into his jacket.

I caught the wrist as the little knife came out.

For a moment we stood locked together at the rail, his knife hand between us, my ribs burning, the terminal growing larger behind his head.

Then the ferry struck the outer fender.

The impact threw us sideways.

Sunday's back hit the rail post. The post tore loose at its base. I caught the remaining rail with my free hand as the deck lurched beneath me.

He slashed at my fingers.

The blade cut across two knuckles. My grip slipped.

I let go of his wrist, caught the front of his jacket with both hands and lifted him clear of the broken rail.

His eyes widened.

I threw him away from me.

He struck the concrete edge of the loading platform, folded against it and dropped into the water between the pillars.

I grabbed the broken post and pulled myself back onto the walkway.

For several seconds I couldn't stand.

The ferry scraped along the terminal fender with a roar of tearing wood. Above me, the service crane's hanging cable swung toward the windows. Imani was shouting from inside the bridge.

I got to my feet and staggered through the side door.

She had both hands on the controls. The deckhand stood beside her, bleeding into a cloth while relaying her orders into the radio.

“Can you stop it?” I asked.

“I'm keeping the people end away from the concrete.”

Another impact shuddered through the hull.

She looked at me.

“Get them off.”

I went down the stairs.

The lounge had become a tilted room full of loose furniture. Chairs slid across the floor. A table struck the bar and broke its last intact mirror. Money from Sunday's fallen bag had blown down the staircase and scattered beneath the tables.

Saint stood near the deck doors, trying to keep a man from going back for a dropped wallet.

“There are literally dollars on the floor,” he told him. “Choose a new wallet later.”

I caught the man's sleeve and turned him toward the exit.

“Go.”

He went.

On the aft deck, the guests crowded along the sheltered rail. The crew had put life jackets on everyone they could reach. Rafa's launch rose and fell beside the ferry, separated from it by a narrow strip of dark water.

Hậu stood at the boarding gate with a crew member. Voss waited behind him, holding King upright with another man. King was conscious, barely, his wrists tied in front of him.

Rafa looked up when he saw me.

“You look like shit.”

“Everybody keeps getting more specific.”

He brought the launch closer. A crew member secured it long enough for the first group to climb down. People moved slowly at first, then faster when the ferry shuddered again.

Hậu lifted a woman who couldn't manage the step and passed her into the arms of the man waiting below. Then a child. Then an elderly man who apologized for his knees.

“You brought all of yourself,” Hậu told him. “That's enough.”

The man squeezed his shoulder as he went down.

A harbor rescue boat approached from farther out. Its lights flashed across the water. Imani's radio calls had reached someone who knew how to arrive without applause.

I looked toward the lower gate.

Water was coming through the gap beneath it.

The gate had bent in its frame during the impact. Each roll drove another wash onto the deck. The crew had tried to brace it with a length of timber, but the timber had split.

I went over and put both hands against the gate.

The next surge hit from outside.

It drove me backward six inches.
