I planted my good foot against the base of the rail and pushed the gate toward its frame. Metal grated. Water forced itself through the narrowing gap around my hands.

“Aiden,” Hậu called.

“Keep moving them.”

The launch pulled away with its first load. The rescue boat came in behind it. More people climbed down.

I held the gate while the ferry rolled against me.

My ribs hurt with every shove. The torn skin on my knuckles burned in the water. I shifted my grip, set my shoulder against the steel and used both legs to drive it another inch into the frame.

Someone behind me began praying.

Someone else said my name.

“Get on the boat,” I told them.

The pressure eased for a moment. I looked back.

The deck was nearly clear.

King stood by the boarding point between Voss and a crew member. He watched me hold the gate.

For a second his eyes met mine.

Then he lowered his head and let them help him onto the rescue boat. Voss settled him beside a medic, then stepped back onto the ferry to help with the remaining crew.

Saint came to stand beside me.

“I'm not leaving you.”

“Go help Hậu.”

“He told me to help you.”

“Everybody's very generous tonight.”

He put both hands against the gate beside mine. His shoes slid immediately. He braced them against a deck fitting and pushed again.

Hậu joined him on the other side.

Together they took enough of the pressure for me to move my shoulder. I sucked in a breath and looked toward the stairs.

Imani appeared with Edwin and the last two deckhands.

“We're clear below,” she called.

Rafa brought the launch back alongside.

The remaining crew climbed down. Edwin needed help, but he complained the whole way, which Hậu seemed to find reassuring.

Imani looked at the gate, then at me.

“Leave it.”

“It'll open.”

“Then let the boat have the water. We've got the people.”

I nodded.

Hậu and Saint moved first. I held the gate for one more roll, waited for the pressure to ease and stepped away.

It burst inward.

Water rushed across the deck behind me.

I limped toward the boarding point as the ferry listed. My bad ankle gave way on the last step.

Hậu caught me under one arm. Voss, who had climbed down ahead of the last group to help them aboard the launch, caught the other from below.

They dragged me over the rail and dropped me into the launch between two benches.

Pain went through my ribs so sharply that I couldn't make a sound.

Saint landed beside me. Imani came down last, stepped over my legs and told Rafa to move.

The launch pulled away.

I lay on my back looking up at the underside of the ferry's lights. The Sunday Best leaned against the old terminal, its gold stripe vanishing beneath the dark water along one side.

Somewhere above it, the banner on the upper rail still showed my enormous painted face.

Saint saw me looking.

“We're getting that down,” he said.

I tried to laugh and regretted it immediately.

At the rescue quay, people were waiting beneath floodlights. Medics moved among the passengers. Blankets passed from hand to hand. Somebody had brought boxes of bottled water and was refusing payment with the sternness of a man who understood the occasion.

Hậu and Voss helped me off the launch.

The first person to recognize me was the woman we'd passed down to Rafa at the gate.

She stood.

Then the man with the bad knees stood beside her.

People began clapping.

The sound spread along the quay until even the men carrying blankets stopped for a moment and joined it.

I tried to wave. My arm didn't get very high.

Saint lifted it for me.

“Careful,” I said.

“I'm managing the image.”

A medic pushed between us and pointed at a stretcher.

“Lie down.”

I lay down.

As they wheeled me toward the ambulance, an old man pressed a folded twenty-dollar bill into my good hand.

“For getting us off.”

I looked at the money.

Then at the ambulance.

“That's probably not going to cover it,” I said.

He laughed and put another twenty on top.

## Chapter 25: Long Live Whoever Pays

The hospital put me in a room with a view of the harbor.

I asked whether they had anything facing a wall.

The nurse looked at the water, then at the bruises across my chest.

“Bad evening?”

“I'm developing a preference for land.”

She closed the curtain halfway and told me the doctor would be in soon. I lay back against the pillows and tried to find a position that didn't involve owning ribs.

Two were cracked. My ankle had swollen to a size that made the hospital sock look personally offended. There were cuts across my knuckles, a split inside my mouth and a dark bruise spreading beneath my left eye.

The doctor read the list aloud while Shawna stood at the foot of the bed.

“Could have been worse,” I said.

He looked at me over the chart.

“I'm sure you'll keep trying.”

Shawna made a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob. He softened a little, finished explaining what came next and left us alone.

She came around the bed and sat beside me.

For a while she just held my good hand.

“The jacket?” I asked eventually.

She looked at me.

“That's your opening?”

“I came home in it.”

“You came to a hospital in it.”

“The direction was correct.”

She covered her face with her free hand, laughed once and shook her head. When she lowered her hand again, her eyes were wet.

“I hate watching the phone when you're out there.”

I tightened my fingers around hers.

“I know.”

“No, you know I don't like it. That's different from sitting with it.”

I didn't try to fix the sentence. I let her say what she needed to say. She told me about the first message from Saint, then the sound of the trucks outside the printshop, then the long stretch when nobody answered because everyone was busy surviving.

Her thumb moved over the uninjured side of my hand while she talked.

When she finished, I pulled her closer with the arm that still worked properly.

She leaned against me carefully.

“You're not getting out of hemming those trousers,” she said into my shoulder.

“I don't know how.”

“You'll be sitting down for a while. Learn.”

I kissed the top of her head.

The door opened.

My mother came in carrying food. Dad followed with a paper bag. Great-Grandpa Tín came behind them in a wheelchair he'd apparently borrowed from the entrance. He was propelling it backward with his feet while arguing with the attendant walking beside him.

“I can turn it around myself,” he said.

“Sir, it's easier if—”

“I'm a hundred and four. I've tried easier.”

He turned the chair, rolled into the room and looked at me.

“You look like the other man got some opinions in.”

“He had several.”

“Good. You needed the conversation.”

Mom put the food on the side table and came to the bed. She touched my hair, looked at my face and kissed my forehead without making a joke.

Then she pointed at the hospital breakfast tray.

“Don't eat that.”

“I already did.”

“Then we're dealing with two emergencies.”

Dad set the paper bag beside my feet. Inside were clean clothes, a phone charger and the little mug with my baby picture on it.

I looked at the mug.

“You brought Master Chigga.”

“Hospital cups leak,” he said.

Great-Grandpa peered at the gold lettering.

“That's a very small master.”

Dad took the mug back out of the bag and put it on the table where it could be seen properly.

I looked at his hands. There was a scrape across one knuckle. Otherwise he looked exactly as he had at dinner before the boat: blue shirt, dark trousers, no visible interest in making an occasion of himself.

“What happened at the printshop?” I asked.

Mom took out her phone.

“These two idiots happened.”

She held the screen where Shawna and I could see it.

The printshop's security camera showed the street at night. Two heavy trucks had come around the corner together, one behind the other. The first mounted the curb in front of the shop. People ran from the doorway.

Dad stepped off the curb to meet it.

He put both hands against the front grille.

The truck kept coming for another foot.

Dad's shoes scraped two pale lines across the pavement.

Then the truck stopped.

Its rear tires spun. Smoke rose around them. The driver leaned on the horn. Dad shifted one foot back, straightened his arms and pushed the front of the truck away from the shop.

The tires dragged sideways across the curb.

Behind it, the second truck turned toward the alley entrance.

Great-Grandpa walked into its path carrying a grocery bag.

He set the bag on top of a parking meter, reached beneath the truck's front bumper and lifted.

The front wheels rose off the ground.

The driver kept pressing the accelerator. The rear tires bounced and spun against the street. Great-Grandpa walked the raised front of the truck sideways until its cab faced the first truck instead of the alley.

Then he set it down.

Dad still had both hands on the first truck's grille.

Great-Grandpa went behind that truck, crouched slightly and caught the frame beneath its rear bed.

He stood up.

The whole truck came off the road.

Dad's feet left the pavement with it. He remained attached to the grille for one startled second before letting go and dropping back to the street.

On the hospital screen, my father turned slowly toward the old man holding the truck.

Great-Grandpa rotated it across the empty lane and set all its wheels down between two parked cars.

The grocery bag was still on the parking meter.

The camera had sound. I heard Mom from the doorway.

“You blocked the delivery entrance!”

Great-Grandpa pointed at Dad.

“He chose the parking.”

Dad said something too quiet for the camera to catch.

Mom stopped the video.

I looked at him.

He looked at the hospital television.

“You could have put it down first,” he said to Tín.

“You were holding on.”

“I was stopping it.”

“And I finished.”

Shawna pressed a hand over her mouth.

I laughed and immediately regretted it. Pain cut through my side. Mom told everybody to stop being funny until I could breathe properly.

Great-Grandpa looked at her.

“Then why'd you marry him?”

She pointed at the door.

He took a piece of fruit from the tray and stayed exactly where he was.

Granddad Hòa arrived later with flowers and a crossword book. He looked at the flowers already crowding the windowsill and put his in the bathroom, where he said they would have less competition.

“You see the video?” I asked.

He sat beside the bed.

“I was there.”

“Where?”

“Inside. Holding the soup.”

Great-Grandpa snorted from his wheelchair.

Hòa looked at him.

For a moment neither spoke.

Then Hòa opened the crossword book and put it on my lap.

“Seven letters. A person who insists on doing things twice.”

“Aiden?”

“You need more letters.”

“Aiden Trần.”

He took the pencil out of my hand.

“We'll come back to this when you're less pleased with yourself.”

By afternoon, the corridor outside my room had become a reception line.

The hospital staff allowed two visitors at a time. Saint tried to interpret this as two parties at a time and was told that a party of eleven still counted as eleven people.

He sat beside the door with a notebook and began organizing appointments until a nurse asked whether he worked there.

“Spiritually,” he said.

She handed him a stack of empty water cups to throw away.

Denise came first, carrying enough food for the staff as well as me. Loan brought a pillow she'd embroidered with DON'T JUMP YET. Benny brought a check. Trinh brought news from the rooms and made Benny put the check away until she'd finished talking.

“The Pearl had its best night,” she said.

I looked at her.

“While I was on the boat?”

“People stayed to wait for news. Then they stayed to celebrate. Then several lost enough money to wish they'd gone home earlier.”

“How much?”

She showed me the number.

I stared.

Saint leaned in from the doorway.

“You should almost die less often, but charge more when you do.”

Shawna looked at him.

He withdrew from the doorway.

Imani and Edwin came together. Edwin had stitches above one eyebrow and a fresh complaint about the hospital coffee. Imani handed me a folded list of names.

“Everyone off,” she said.

I read the first few names, then looked up.

“Everyone?”

“Guests. Crew. Your people. Even the large bastard who broke the piano.”

I leaned back against the pillows.

For the first time all day, I took a breath without trying to hide what it cost.

“Good.”

She squeezed my shoulder.

“You paid for a crew. You got a crew.”

Later, Walker came with another detective and the lawyer. They asked about the bridge, the knife and the fall. I told them what I remembered. The lawyer stopped them when the questions began circling the same point for the third time.

Sunday's body had been recovered near the terminal pillars that morning.

I listened to that without speaking.

Walker watched my face, wrote something down and closed his notebook.

There would be more questions. There were recordings, witnesses and a ferry full of damage. The lawyer said we'd deal with them in the order they arrived.

After they left, Hậu came in with Voss and Rafa.

All three had been cleaned, bandaged and told to rest. None looked interested in doing it anywhere apart from my room.

Rafa carried a black bag.

I recognized it from the bridge.

“You kept that?”

“Found it in the lounge,” Saint said, appearing behind them. “I was moving people. It was in the way.”

“So you moved it too.”

“I'm thorough.”

Inside were the remaining bundles from Sunday's escape money. Some were damp. Most were intact. Saint had added the appearance-payment envelope on top.

Shawna looked into the bag.

Then she looked at me.

“The jacket repairs are covered.”

I smiled.

Hậu put the bag beneath the chair, out of the way of the next nurse, and sat down beside me.

“King asked about you,” Voss said.

“What did he ask?”

“Whether you lived.”

“What did you tell him?”

Voss looked toward the corridor full of flowers, food and people waiting to hand me things.

“That he was about the only person in Eastbridge who hadn't sent a gift yet.”

Rafa laughed. Hậu laughed. Saint laughed from the doorway.

I tried not to.

I failed.

## Chapter 26: How They Spent It

The first person to ask me for money after I left the hospital was a man who sold pictures of me asking other people for money.

He had a table outside the Pearl.

The pictures cost twenty dollars. For thirty, he would write an inspirational quotation beneath my face. His best seller showed me coming down the ferry's stairs beneath the words NEVER LEAVE THE GRIND.

In the photograph, I was fleeing a man with a piano.

“You got a permit for that table?” I asked.

The man looked up. He was wearing my face on his chest, which complicated his attempt to pretend he didn't recognize me.

“Saint said the pavement was a common resource.”

“Saint charges people to use common resources.”

“He charged me.”

I held out my hand.

The man sighed and reached into his cash box.

“For a picture,” I said.

“Oh.”

“The one with the stairs.”

He gave it to me. I turned it over, wrote PLEASE LEAVE THE GRIND IF THE GRIND HAS A PIANO, signed it, and handed it back.

“That's the accurate one.”

He looked from the writing to me.

“Can I sell this?”

“You can sell anything Saint hasn't already sold.”

He put it on a little easel and changed the price to eighty dollars before I reached the door.

Inside, everyone stood.

“Sit down,” I said.

They sat.

It remained an excellent trick.

Trinh had put my chair at the end of the long cardroom, where I could see the entrance without turning my sore body. Beside it stood a side table with water, a clean ashtray and a little brass bell.

I looked at the bell.

“What does that do?”

“You ring it,” she said, “and Saint stops whatever he's doing until somebody explains why you're unhappy.”

I rang it.

From upstairs came a sudden silence.

Trinh folded her arms.

“Worth every penny.”

The Pearl had acquired new curtains, two card dealers, a pianist who had been specifically instructed to remain near his instrument, and an unreasonable number of people who wanted to give me presents. A cigar importer offered a cabinet. A jeweler sent cuff links. Three brothers who ran a wrecking yard brought a black truck and told me the doors were reinforced.

“Against what?” I asked.

The oldest brother glanced at my bandaged fingers.

“We were hoping you could tell us.”

I accepted the cuff links. The cabinet went to the lounge. I let Rafa inspect the truck, which he did with the solemn attention other people gave newborn children.

“Suspension's good,” he said after crawling underneath. “Engine's clean. They put an alarm on it.”

“Useful.”

“For other people, yeah.”

He caught the keys I tossed him.

Then he stopped smiling.

“What?”

“Your tow truck's fucked.”

“It's still a truck.”

“It currently has a shopping-mall directory in the radiator.”

“That's information.”

“Keep this one.”

He turned the keys in his hand. He looked at the three brothers, then at the vehicle, then back at me.

“You sure?”

“You drove through a wall for me.”

“It was mostly glass.”

“You want a smaller truck?”

He closed his fist around the keys.

“Nigga, I love this truck.”

Hậu emerged from the kitchen holding an entire plate of small sandwiches. He watched Rafa climb into the cab and sounded the horn for him by leaning through the passenger window.

“Do I get a truck?” he asked.

“You got a gym.”

“Gym doesn't have a horn.”

“We'll work on that.”

Upstairs, Saint had arranged four chairs around a table. The black bag sat in the middle. Sunday's last attempt to leave Eastbridge now smelled faintly of river water and hotel soap.

We'd spread the damp notes across spare towels at Orchard House. Valerie had discovered them when she came to discuss a leaking tap.

She'd looked over the drying racks, moved a bundle away from a dripping windowsill, and said, “I prefer advance notice when the laundry becomes a bank.”

There was enough to pay the house staff their promised bonuses, replace what we'd wrecked, and make everybody in the room sit more quietly than usual.

I named the shares.

Saint began an argument about the spiritual value of finding the bag.

Hậu reached across and covered Saint's mouth with a sandwich.

“You found us on the boat too. You getting paid for everybody?”

Saint ate the sandwich.

“Depends if we're counting King.”

Voss sat with both hands around his cup. He'd come from the gym, where his sister had been painting the office wall with her good hand while insulting his color choices. They'd finally agreed on blue because every other color had become personal.

I slid his share over.

He didn't touch it immediately.

“He asked to see me,” he said.

We knew who he meant.

“You going?” I asked.

“Already went.”

Hậu put his plate down.

“And?”

“He looked like shit.”

“That part was Aiden.”

Voss smiled briefly.

“They've got him watched. Lawyer outside. Cop by the door. He asked if my sister was working again.”

“What did you say?”

“That he didn't get to ask her anything.”

Voss pulled the envelope toward him.

“Then I left.”

Nobody tried to improve that with a speech.

Saint counted his share twice. Hậu counted his once, lost his place, and asked Trinh to do it. Rafa stared at the number on his envelope until I threw a paper ball at his head.

“Buy something,” I said.

“I just got a truck.”

“Something that doesn't need oil.”

“You are closing a lot of doors.”

He bought a boat that afternoon.

It needed oil.

***

A partner from my lawyer's firm met me at Shawna's atelier a week later because she had decided the Pearl's waiting room made people feel as though they were about to lose either money or a finger.

“Usually money,” I told her.

“I'm delighted by your restraint.”

Shawna put us at her cutting table. She was fitting a jacket to a customer in the next room and had made both of us wipe our shoes.

There were questions about Sunday. There would continue to be questions about Sunday. I answered them with the firm's partner beside me. We went through where I'd stood, what he'd held, where the boat had struck the terminal. She stopped me whenever I tried to replace a location with the phrase right fucking there.

The surviving crew had given their accounts. So had Imani. Pike's own recordings and the garage video had made her explanation of Vinh's death increasingly difficult to maintain. Kenny Vale had supplied dates and names through a lawyer of his own, then left town.

“He asked whether your mechanic still wanted payment for the damaged truck,” my lawyer said.

“Which damaged truck?”

She consulted a note.

“That was his exact question.”

Rafa sent three photographs and an invoice. Kenny paid before dinner.

Shawna came through carrying a sleeve turned inside out.

“Are you two finished?”

“For today,” the lawyer said.

“Good. He's booked.”

“I am?”

My wife pointed toward the fitting platform.

I climbed up carefully. The ankle had improved. The ribs still objected to sudden turns, laughter, and Hậu's habit of greeting me as though I'd been missing for seven years.

Shawna draped a length of dark cloth across my shoulder.

“Arms out.”

“What am I modeling?”

“A husband who stays where he's put.”

“Limited edition.”

“Extremely.”

She pinned the cloth. In the mirror, I could see the front window, the new display, the woman at the counter collecting a finished dress. There were proper shelves now. Her assistant had labeled the garment bags. A newspaper photograph from the Alder Cinema show hung beside the doorway; Shawna stood at its center while the models lined the stage behind her.

My picture was nowhere on that wall.

I liked hers better.

“Estelle paid the balance?” I asked.

“And ordered another dress.”

“How is she?”

Shawna smoothed the cloth beneath my collar.

“Tired. Angry. She wants a dress with pockets.”

“Reasonable.”

“She said her brother spent his whole life making entrances and left her to find all the exits.”

The pin stopped moving for a moment.

I looked at my wife in the mirror.

“What did you say?”

“That she could pick the lining herself.”

Then she put the pin where she wanted it and told me to stop lifting my shoulder.

I stood while she worked. Her phone rang twice. She answered one call, rejected a delivery substitution on the other, and made me hold a measuring tape against my chest while she found a missing spool. At some point the woman collecting the dress recognized me.

Her eyes widened.

“Oh my God.”

I prepared a modest smile.

“You're blocking the good mirror,” she said.

Shawna turned me six inches to the left.

***

The statue returned to the Pearl on a Monday.

Rafa brought it upright in his new truck, secured with straps he had chosen specifically to withstand the judgment of my father. Saint had hired two men to unveil it. Loan arrived with a chair because she said anyone reopening a business with a statue of himself deserved supervision.

The bronze face still resembled Bảo if you knew what had happened beneath the repainting. Saint had corrected the hair, which now looked as if a bird had won a fight with a helmet. The fish at its feet had survived everything with its mouth open.

“We can replace the head,” Rafa offered.

“Leave it,” I said.

“Why?”

“Reminds me what happens when you pay somebody before checking their work.”

Loan leaned forward.

“Finally. A statue teaches something.”

We put it beside the stairs. Saint removed the old plaque and unveiled the new one.

THE MAN WHO CAME BACK.

Underneath, in smaller letters:

PLEASE DO NOT RUB THE FISH.

“Why would anyone rub the fish?” I asked.

“They will now,” Saint said.

They did. Within an hour, somebody claimed the fish had helped him win at cards. By evening, its nose shone brighter than the rest of the statue. Saint proposed selling commemorative fish cloths.

I rang the brass bell.

He stopped talking.

The first truck arrived at seven. Three crates came through the service entrance with paperwork that said kitchen equipment and contents that would have disappointed a cook. Trinh checked the seals. I met the buyer in the back room. He'd known Sunday, knew exactly whose chair I occupied, and tried to use both facts to negotiate a better price.

I let him finish.

Then I put the price back where it had started.

He paid.

I took my share upstairs and put it in the safe. Down below, the cardroom filled. A singer tested the microphone. Somebody kissed the fish. At the front door, a man removed his hat before asking whether I might be available for a very expensive favor.

Trinh looked up at me from the landing.

“Working tonight?”

I straightened the new cuffs Shawna had fitted to my shirt.

“Send him up.”

## Chapter 27: Places We Could Go

By the autumn of 2027, there were six places on Bell Street where I could eat for free and one where I was charged extra because Denise said I had become irritating to feed.

“You bring people,” she explained.

“They're customers.”

“They bring problems.”

She pointed through the window.

Hậu stood on the pavement beside a man wearing a foam boxing glove on each hand. The man was advertising the gym. He had discovered that he could neither drink his coffee nor remove the gloves without help.

Hậu was holding the cup to his mouth while giving what appeared to be a motivational speech.

“That one's employed,” I said.

“Aiden, employment isn't the same as an improvement.”

She put another plate beside mine anyway.

Shawna arrived seven minutes late, wearing a coat she'd made herself and carrying a folder that she set on the table before she kissed me. The folder landed with the deliberate weight of something that had already won an argument elsewhere.

“I got it,” she said.

“The gallery?”

She nodded.

I stood too quickly. My chair hit the floor behind me. Two men near the door stood as well, because people had started assuming that any sudden movement I made required assistance.

“My wife got the gallery,” I told them.

One of them began to clap.

The other joined him without knowing what a gallery had done to deserve it.

Shawna closed her eyes.

“Sit down.”

Denise appeared with two clean cups.

“Let them clap. Some people actually work for a living.”

Shawna's winter collection would open in a former electrical showroom downtown, a beautiful long room with pale brick walls and tall windows. She'd wanted it for months. The owner had wanted an established brand, a deposit large enough to hurt, and evidence that the ceiling would survive whatever happened around her husband.

“I showed her the cinema photographs,” Shawna said.

“The ceiling ones?”

“The clothes.”

“Good choice.”

She opened the folder. There were drawings, fabric samples, names, dates. I leaned closer. She explained where the audience would enter and how the models would pass between them before reaching the far windows. The afternoon light would catch the moving panels in the dresses. She had arranged for a photographer who understood cloth instead of treating every dark surface like a hole in the universe.

“And this,” she said, tapping a line near the bottom, “is the part where you don't buy every seat.”

I looked offended on principle.

“I've never bought every seat.”

“You tried to buy the seats on a flight because you didn't like a man's suitcase.”

“It was leaking.”

“It was a plant.”

“Plants have responsibilities.”

She moved my cup away from the drawings.

“I want people who will buy clothes, Aiden. People who'll wear them somewhere I haven't already been.”

I studied the room on the page again.

“Can I get a seat?”

“You can get two.”

“Generous.”

“And you can carry boxes on Friday.”

“There's the love.”

***

On Friday, I carried boxes.

Marisol, who had become Shawna's assistant after surviving an interview that involved repairing a cuff while answering questions about delivery schedules, met me at the gallery door. She held a clipboard and looked entirely unmoved by the man behind me trying to hand me a bottle of expensive liquor.

“Liquor in the kitchen,” she told him. “Boxes at the back.”

“It's for Mr. Trần.”

“Then he can carry it after the boxes.”

I took six garment cartons upstairs. On the second trip, a builder asked whether I could shift a display pedestal three feet to the left. I moved it. He asked for another foot. I moved it again.

Then Shawna entered and told him it had been correct before he touched it.

He looked at me.

I carried it back.

“You afraid of her?” he whispered.

“I'm married to her.”

He considered this and stepped aside.

There were lights to hang and a rack to assemble. I had just finished the rack when the security shutter over the side entrance jammed halfway up. A delivery driver crouched beneath it with a carton balanced on his shoulder.

The motor made a noise like an animal reconsidering its profession.

Then the shutter dropped.

I caught its bottom rail above the driver's back. His carton struck the floor. He stayed crouched, eyes closed, while the motor continued to pull the steel downward against my hands.

“Move,” I told him.

He moved.

The builder ran for the switch. I held the shutter at shoulder height, my feet skidding a little on the polished floor. When the power stopped, I lifted it until the rail reached the upper frame and folded the corner of the runner inward to hold it there.

The room had gone quiet.

The driver straightened.

“Jesus Christ.”

Marisol looked at the carton on the floor.

“Is that the steamer?”

“Yes.”

“Check it.”

Shawna came over, examined my palms, and kissed one.

Then she pointed at the bent runner.

“You're fixing that.”

The driver began applauding.

“After,” she told him. “We open in four hours.”

Dad arrived with tools before I had finished calling him. He'd been two streets away repairing a refrigeration unit for a man who insisted the problem was spiritual because it stopped working whenever rent was due.

He inspected the shutter, checked the motor, and looked at the builder.

“You installed this?”

The builder shook his head so vigorously I worried about his neck.

Dad disconnected the drive and straightened the bent guide with the heel of his hand. Then he lowered the shutter, lifted it, and lowered it again while the builder watched his own future employment become uncertain.

“New runner,” Dad said. “New limit switch. Nobody uses it until both are here.”

“What do I owe you?” Shawna asked.

“A good seat.”

She smiled.

“Already yours.”

Dad nodded at me.

“You can stand.”

***

I did get a chair. It was close enough to the runway to see the tiny fastening at the throat of the first coat and far enough from the entrance that Saint couldn't drag every visitor over to greet me.

He tried anyway.

Loan intercepted him with a program folded into a narrow strip.

“She working,” Loan said. “You sit.”

“I'm helping.”

She hit his wrist with the program.

He sat.

The room filled with people I mostly didn't know. Buyers, stylists, women carrying bags that cost more than cars I'd stolen, men who examined a seam with the concentration I normally associated with a concealed weapon. Estelle arrived in a dark suit and brought two friends. She greeted me politely, then went straight to Shawna.

Denise came with Mom. Hậu wore the jacket Shawna had made him and held his arms slightly away from his body, afraid that ordinary movement might damage it. Voss's sister helped him sit without catching the hem. Rafa had washed his hands so thoroughly that the absence of engine oil seemed medically significant.

My family occupied the second row.

Great-Grandpa was one hundred and five. He had brought peppermints, his own reading glasses, and the conviction that any event requiring a printed schedule had probably been planned badly.

“Where's the food?” he asked.

Mom pointed to the program.

“Reception afterward.”

“Ambitious.”

Grandpa Hòa unfolded his glasses and examined the room. He glanced at the repaired shutter, then at Dad. Dad gave him a small nod. Whatever that meant, neither of them explained it to me.

The lights changed.

Music began.

The first model stepped between the chairs wearing the dark coat I'd seen in pieces on our breakfast table. The panels moved as she walked. They caught the light, opened, settled again. A woman in front of me leaned forward. Another lifted her phone, then lowered it so she could look directly.

I found Shawna beside the far doorway.

She wasn't watching me. She watched the hem, the turn, the distance between the first model and the second. Her fingers moved once, a small adjustment nobody else could see. Marisol touched her elbow and said something. Shawna nodded.

I kept my hands folded and stayed exactly where she'd put me.

At the end, when she stepped out, I stood.

This time everyone stood for her.

The applause filled the long room. Shawna looked startled for half a second, then smiled and bowed her head. Mom was crying. Denise handed her a tissue and pretended she only needed one herself because the room was dusty.

Great-Grandpa leaned toward Hòa.

“That's the good one.”

“They're all hers,” Grandpa said.

“I meant the wife.”

Afterward, I watched three people wait for Shawna while she spoke to a fourth. Somebody asked me to photograph them with her. I held the phone and made sure everyone's face was in the frame.

It felt remarkably good.

***

The gallery owner gave Shawna a list of people who wanted appointments. She also gave her a prospectus for an upcoming exhibition at Aster House.

I found it on our kitchen counter the next morning, beneath a spoon and an unpaid invoice for display lighting. The cover showed an old house with too many windows to clean without developing a grudge.

Inside were photographs of a recent restoration. A staircase curved beneath a chandelier. Doors opened into rooms the color of money trying to look tasteful. There were drawings of a new wing, credited to An Vân and an architect named Đặng Minh Khải.

“You know this place?” I asked.

Shawna looked up from her breakfast.

“By reputation.”

“Good reputation?”

“Expensive reputation.”

I turned a page. One section of the plan was marked PRIVATE. Another showed a room beyond the public galleries with no photograph beside it.

“They forgot one.”

“Maybe you don't get every room for the price of a brochure.”

“What's that one?”

She leaned over.

“Ninth Room, apparently.”

“What happens in it?”

“If I knew, I wouldn't be reading the brochure with you.”

I closed it and put it beside her folder.

She took my hand across the table.

“Thank you for yesterday.”

“I moved a pedestal five times.”

“You also stayed in your chair.”

“My greatest feat.”

“One of my favorites.”

We had no appointments for the next hour. Nobody stood outside with a present. Valerie had the morning off. Saint's phone went directly to silence because Loan had confiscated it after he tried to sell an unauthorized recording of the show to a man who was already its photographer.

Shawna pulled her chair closer to mine. I kissed her. She tasted of coffee and the jam she'd said she wasn't going to eat.

Later, she fell asleep against my shoulder on the sofa while I looked through the photographs from her show. I stopped at one of her laughing with Mom, the two of them bent over a sleeve, everyone else blurred behind them.

I sent it to the printer.

Then I put the phone away and stayed there until she woke.

## Chapter 28: Standing at Home

Mom asked us to come over on Sunday and bring nothing.

Shawna brought flowers. I brought dessert. Saint brought an antique clock he had purchased from a man who insisted it had belonged to a king.

“Which king?” Dad asked at the door.

Saint glanced at me.

“A different one.”

Dad turned the clock over. A battery fell out.

“Progressive kingdom.”

He handed it back and let us in.

The house smelled of garlic, hot oil and the sweet sauce Mom only made when she intended to accuse everyone of eating too much. Shawna took her flowers into the kitchen. Saint followed the food. I set the dessert on the table and found my father in the hallway with a little step stool beneath the smoke alarm.

“Battery?” I asked.

“Saint brought one.”

He tested the alarm. It squealed. From the kitchen, Great-Grandpa shouted that if dinner was on fire, somebody should tell the rice.

Dad smiled and climbed down.

I bowed.

He put his palm behind my neck, as he had when I was small, and pulled me close enough to feel his kiss against my temple.

“You late?” he asked.

“I'm early.”

“Good. Your mother needs chairs.”

“How many?”

“More than she said.”

The chairs were in the garage. So were a dismantled lawn mower, two engines, a shelf of tools and a wooden crate with a shipping label so old that the ink had nearly vanished. Dad moved the lawn mower with his foot and pointed at a stack beneath the window.

I took four chairs in each hand.

“Careful of the paint,” he said.

“On the chairs?”

“House. Chairs will survive you.”

Behind him, the garage door began to descend. Saint had found the wall switch and pressed it under the mistaken impression that every button in a room existed to improve the lighting.

Dad put one hand up without turning. The lower edge of the door struck his palm and stopped. The motor continued humming. The hinges along the upper panels trembled.

“Other button,” Dad said.

Saint pressed another one.

The outside sprinkler came on.

“Nigga, how many kinds of darkness does this house have?”

Dad reached back with his free hand, pressed the correct switch, and lowered his arm as the door rose.

I carried the chairs inside before Saint discovered the gas.

Grandpa Hòa sat in his familiar folding chair near the kitchen doorway, tying a fresh piece of blue cord around the bent leg. There were better chairs in the house. There were chairs in our house that cost more than the car I'd owned at seventeen. He continued to bring this one.

“You could let me fix that,” I said.

“It is fixed.”

“It has a knot.”

“Good knot.”

He tugged it once. The frame settled level beneath him.

“Where did it get bent?” I asked.

Great-Grandpa looked over from the counter.

Grandpa kept working on the cord.

“Chair had a difficult afternoon.”

“Was it near a railway bridge?”

The old man's fingers paused.

Only for a moment.

Then he tucked the loose end beneath the knot and looked up at me.

“Your father needs help with the table.”

Great-Grandpa bit into a slice of fruit. He was smiling around it.

I pointed at him.

“You wrote on that photograph.”

“I can write on several things.”

“You wrote Ask Hòa.”

“And you asked him. Excellent system.”

He handed me a piece of fruit and walked away before I could improve the question.

***

The table had acquired an extra leaf and an argument.

Mom wanted it moved closer to the kitchen. Dad said it was already close to the kitchen. Mom demonstrated that it could be closer by pushing the nearest chair into his shin.

“There,” she said. “Space.”

We moved it.

She examined the distance.

“Too close.”

Dad looked at me across the tabletop.

I kept my face still.

“You laughing?” he asked.

“No.”

“Good.”

We moved it back three inches.

Hậu arrived carrying two bags of fruit and a box containing a horn.

He set the horn on the counter.

I stared at it.

“You bought one.”

“You promised.”

“For the gym.”

“I'm demonstrating.”

He squeezed it. The blast rattled a spoon in a cup. Everyone in the kitchen stopped moving.

Great-Grandpa took the horn from him, examined it, and carried it to the back door.

He opened the door.

We heard a short, astonished honk from somewhere beyond the fence.

He came back empty-handed.

“Demonstration finished.”

Hậu looked at me.

I spread my hands.

“You want it back, you ask him.”

Hậu picked up the fruit bags.

“I brought oranges.”

Rafa arrived with his girlfriend and an immaculate shirt she had apparently selected under protest. Voss came with his sister. Loan appeared with a dish Mom claimed she didn't need and immediately made room for. Denise entered without knocking, kissed Mom's cheek, and ordered Saint away from the food with the precision of someone moving furniture she'd moved before.

The room filled. Chairs scraped. People reached around each other for plates. My grandmother Hương arrived from the backyard, where she'd been cutting herbs, and put a hand on Hòa's shoulder as she passed. He caught her fingers and held them until she bent down to hear whatever he wanted to say.

She laughed, struck his shoulder with the herbs, and continued to the kitchen.

“What did you say?” I asked.

“Private lesson.”

“You teach a lot of those.”

“Excellent students.”

At the other end of the room, Dad was attempting to carry a full tray through a gap Saint had filled with his entire body. Saint stepped left. Dad stepped left. Saint stepped right. Dad remained where he was and waited until Saint understood that only one of them needed to continue making choices.

We sat.

Hậu had the seat nearest the rice. He looked at it, then at Mom, with the tenderness of a man discovering he had been remembered in a will.

Great-Grandpa watched Dad serve Mom before filling his own plate.

“Look at this,” he said. “Manners.”

Mom lifted an eyebrow.

“He's always had manners.”

The old man laughed so hard he had to put down his chopsticks.

Dad continued serving rice.

“Careful,” Mom told her grandfather.

“He came to my house wearing a jacket that still had another man's tooth in the pocket.”

“It wasn't his jacket,” she said.

Great-Grandpa pointed at her.

“Listen to the defense.”

“It was a borrowed jacket.”

“I didn't ask who owned the tooth.”

Saint folded his hands beneath his chin.

“Please continue.”

Mom handed him a bowl.

“Please eat.”

Dad's ears had gone a little red. I had seen him bend steel. I had seen him stop machinery large enough to flatten our street. Watching my mother inspect him over the rim of her glass remained one of the few things I couldn't do to him myself.

“What happened to the jacket?” Shawna asked.

“Cleaned it,” Dad said.

“What happened to the tooth?”

Great-Grandpa leaned forward.

“Your mother-in-law made him put it in an envelope.”

Mom covered her eyes.

“It was disgusting.”

“She wrote Lost Property.”

Denise put her fork down and laughed into her napkin.

Dad looked at Mom. She looked back. For a moment their faces changed in the same way at the same time, and I could see the two people they had been before any of us had begun watching them.

Then Mom took another spoonful of rice and said, “He also forgot the soap.”

“I got the soap.”

“The next day. It was after midnight.”

“On the way home.”

“On a different day.”

“It was a large soap.”

Great-Grandpa slapped the table.

“A romantic!”

***

After dinner, we cleared the plates while the people who claimed to have cooked enough in their lives supervised us from their chairs.

Dad asked me to bring a box down from the cupboard above the hall closet. It contained old photographs, a packet of cards, and a cream envelope with his name written across the front.

The envelope slipped free when I put the box on the table.

Dad had written an address on the back, beneath a name I recognized.

“Calvin Rook?”

Dad looked over.

“Long time ago.”

“You knew him?”

“He paid me.”

Saint appeared beside my shoulder so quickly that I wondered whether he'd been hiding in the cupboard too.

“For what?”

Dad dried his hands.

“Standing by a door.”

Saint looked at the envelope, then at the doorway, then at his own shoes.

“I do that every day.”

“You talk too much.”

“How much did he pay?” I asked.

“A hundred thousand.”

I looked up again.

Mom came from the kitchen with tea.

“He wanted your father to make people feel safe.”

Great-Grandpa made a thoughtful noise from his chair.

“How did that work out?”

Dad took the envelope from me and set it beside the box.

“For some people.”

Hậu pulled a chair closer.

Dad glanced at him.

“What are you doing?”

“Getting safe.”

Shawna sat beside me, tucked one leg beneath herself, and took the cup Mom offered. Rafa closed the back door. Voss's sister asked whether this was the story about the motorcycle, and Mom told her that depended which motorcycle.

I looked at the people arranging themselves around my father.

Then at the cream envelope.

“You never told me about this.”

Dad shrugged.

“You were busy.”

“I wasn't born.”

“Busy elsewhere.”

Great-Grandpa laughed. Hòa leaned back in the chair with the blue cord, hands folded across his stomach. There was a small mark on the back of one hand that I hadn't noticed before, a pale straight line cutting across two knuckles.

He saw me looking and covered it with his other hand.

“One story at a time,” he said.

“Yours next?”

He smiled.

“Tea first.”

Mom refilled his cup. Then she sat beside Dad and took the envelope between two fingers, examining the paper as though she might still have an opinion about its price.

“This was terrible stock,” she said.

“Cost him a hundred thousand,” Saint murmured.

“Then your father could have bought better paper.”

Dad began to answer, but Great-Grandpa raised one finger.

“Before you start making yourself handsome, remember who was there.”

“I am handsome.”

“Your wife is in charge of that rumor.”

Mom straightened Dad's collar.

“And I run it very well.”

I leaned back. Shawna's hand found mine under the table. Outside, a car slowed near the house, then continued when its driver saw the rooms were full. My phone vibrated once with a message from Trinh. I checked it, saw that the Pearl was open and making money, and put it facedown.

Dad took the envelope from Mom and turned the address toward himself. A shopping list followed it in her younger handwriting.

He smiled at the last item.

“All right,” he said.

Saint reached for his phone.

Loan caught his wrist without looking.

Dad waited until we were all settled. His cup stood beside the old envelope. Mom's knee touched his. The man who had held a truck in the street, who had stopped a garage door without turning around, who had hugged me each time I came home, looked down at a list that included scallions and began to laugh.

Then he told us what happened when he agreed to stand by that door.

---

# Book II: The Man at the Door

## Chapter 1: Door Money

Calvin Rook offered Minh a hundred thousand dollars to attend a party.

Minh asked whether he had to clap.

“You have to stand by the door,” Rook said.

“For how long?”

“Until midnight.”

“Which side?”

There was a pause on the telephone. In the shop, Mai held up two paper samples. Minh pointed at the cream one. She shook her head, turned both over, and showed him the prices.

He pointed at the cream one again.

Rook cleared his throat. “The inside.”

“Open or closed?”

“Open.”

“You can buy something for that. Little rubber thing. Goes under it.”

Mai covered her mouth with the samples.

“I know what a doorstop is, Minh.”

“You offered me a hundred thousand dollars. I wanted to make sure.”

“People are nervous. There will be substantial money in the room. Your presence will reassure them.”

“And the people outside?”

“You'll reassure them too.”

Minh looked at the carburetor on his bench. Three screws lay beside it. He had found the fourth inside a customer's air filter and charged the man for an hour he had spent looking for a problem the man had created with his own screwdriver.

“Cash,” Minh said.

“Naturally.”

“When I arrive.”

“Naturally.”

“My friend comes.”

“Which friend?”

“The one driving me home with a hundred thousand dollars.”

“Fine.”

“He eats.”

“It's a banquet.”

“You haven't seen him eat.”

Rook gave him an address in the harbor district. Minh wrote it on the back of an envelope. When he hung up, Mai took the envelope and added milk, laundry soap, and scallions beneath the address.

“We have scallions.”

“We have a jar of water where scallions used to live.”

“A hundred thousand.”

“Congratulations. Get the large soap.”

He caught her around the waist. She put one hand on his chest to keep the grease off her blouse, then allowed him to pull her closer.

“Cream paper,” he said.

“I already ordered it.”

“You asked me.”

“I enjoy our conversations.”

He kissed her. She kissed him back, then held his chin between two fingers.

“Eighteen days.”

“I know when I'm getting married.”

“You thought the rehearsal was the wedding last week.”

“Your father wore a tie.”

“He had a meeting.”

“Your father wears a tie when somebody is about to lose something.”

Mai smiled. “Then come home with the money.”

***

Leon Price arrived in a white suit and a borrowed stretch limousine.

The limousine occupied the space in front of Minh's garage and part of the bakery next door. Its rear tire rested on the curb. Leon leaned out of the driver's window wearing sunglasses despite the sun having disappeared behind the warehouse roofs.

“Get in, nigga. We employed.”

Minh looked at the car.

“Who died?”

“Nobody yet. Why you making this negative?”

“You said you'd bring a car.”

“And I brought enough for both of us.”

Mai came outside carrying Minh's jacket. She stopped at the limousine and looked through its open window. Leon's white trousers matched the seats. A little gold chain crossed the front of his vest.

“Leon.”

“Miss Mai.”

“Does the owner know you have this?”

“He knows somebody has it.”

She waited.

“I'm bringing it back before his daughter's breakfast.”

“Why does she need a limousine for breakfast?”

“She's marrying a dentist. We all suffering.”

Minh took the jacket. It was the dark one Mai liked, with a tear in the lining he had promised to repair. Under it he wore his cleanest work shirt. His trousers had a pale mark where a customer had knocked a can of primer against him. He had scrubbed it twice. The mark remained.

Leon watched him approach.

“You wearing that?”

“Rook hired me to stand.”

“You can stand handsome.”

Minh put his toolbox in the back.

Leon lowered his sunglasses. “Why the tools?”

“Door might stick.”

Mai laughed and shut the car door on both of them.

As Leon pulled away, two boys outside the bakery stopped arguing over a bicycle and stared at the limousine. A woman from the apartments raised a camera. Leon slowed enough to give her his good side.

“You going to the party?” she called.

“We the party,” Leon said.

Minh opened the envelope again.

“We also need scallions.”

***

Rook had rented the entire Hotel Meridian and placed a red carpet over the service entrance.

The hotel's main entrance faced the bay. Limousines stood along it beneath hanging lights. Men in black suits collected car keys and pretended not to see the guns some of their customers wore badly. A woman in a silver dress directed traffic with two fingers and an expression that made the drivers hurry.

Leon drove past all of them.

“Service entrance?” he said.

“That's the address.”

“Nigga, we got a limousine. Service can come outside.”

The silver dress saw them. She lifted one hand, started toward the car, and recognized Minh through the glass.

Her hand went higher.

“Mr. Trần!”

Three valets turned. A man beside the front steps looked over, stopped lighting his cigarette, and let it fall from his mouth.

Leon smiled at the windshield.

“There he is. They found the correct entrance.”

The woman opened Minh's door herself. Behind her, a valet rolled a luggage cart toward the toolbox.

“Should I take that up?”

“It has oil on the bottom.”

The valet took his own jacket off and laid it across the cart.

Leon got out slowly. “Damn. I should've brought something dirty.”

The man who had dropped the cigarette came forward with both hands visible. Minh remembered him from a pool hall on Carson Avenue. He had once tried to collect money from a bartender using a crowbar. Minh had bent the crowbar around a parking meter while the man still held it. They had stood together for eleven minutes waiting for someone to bring a saw.

“Good to see you,” the man said.

“You get the meter fixed?”

“Yes.”

“City charge you?”

“Yes.”

Leon leaned closer. “He asking whether you learned, nigga.”

“I learned.”

Minh patted his shoulder and went inside.

The hotel had covered its lobby fountain with a glass platform. A white sports car stood on top, its hood raised to display an engine plated in gold. Beside it, a sign announced that the car belonged to the evening's prize convoy. Six women in matching black dresses held trays of champagne. A seventh held a tray with a single cigar.

Leon took the cigar.

“Sir, that's for—”

He pointed at Minh.

“His friend.”

The woman looked at Minh, then at the empty tray.

“Of course.”

“Don't light it in here,” Minh said.

“I wasn't going to.”

Leon put away the lighter he had already opened.

Rook waited by the elevators with a silver briefcase between his shoes. He was sixty, broad across the shoulders, with his white hair combed straight back. His dinner jacket fitted so precisely that Minh wondered whether somebody followed him around making adjustments.

Rook smiled without opening his mouth.

“You're early.”

“You said cash on arrival.”

The smile opened by a fraction.

He lifted the briefcase and handed it over. Minh set it on the reception counter and opened it. Bundles of hundred-dollar bills filled both sides.

Leon took his sunglasses off.

“We should arrive more often.”

Minh ran one thumb over the exposed edges, lifted two bundles, and put them back.

“A hundred thousand,” he said.

“You counted that?” Rook asked.

“You short?”

“No.”

“Then we agree.”

He closed the case and gave it to Leon.

Rook glanced at the toolbox arriving behind them. “Expecting trouble?”

“You hired me.”

“I hired a reassurance.”

Leon held up the briefcase. “Nigga, you purchased the deluxe package.”

Rook stared at him.

Leon stared back, chewing the unlit cigar.

The elevator opened.

***

The ballroom occupied the hotel's second floor. Its wide entrance faced a row of windows overlooking the loading court. Two steel fire doors had been concealed inside ornamental wooden frames. Minh noticed the fresh bolts in the tracks before he noticed the orchestra.

Then the orchestra stopped.

A trumpet held one embarrassed note after the rest of the band had gone quiet. The player lowered it. Two hundred people turned toward the entrance.

At the nearest table, a man swept a pile of betting slips into his jacket.

Across the room, another man stood so quickly that his chair fell backward.

“No,” he said. “Close it. Close the fucking line.”

His companion had a telephone against one ear. “He's here.”

The man beside the entrance began applauding. Three others joined him. A woman on the far side lifted her glass and shouted Minh's name. The applause spread through the tables until Rook's orchestra began playing again, louder than before.

Leon looked at Minh.

“What you do in here?”

“First visit.”

“Nigga, they having memories in advance.”

Rook raised his hands for quiet. It took longer than he liked.

“Ladies and gentlemen. As promised, our door will remain open throughout the evening. No purchaser will be detained. No disagreement will interfere with your departure.”

He put a hand toward Minh's shoulder, thought better of completing the gesture, and pointed instead.

“Mr. Trần will make certain of it.”

A woman near the stage called, “Can he make certain of the shrimp?”

Leon answered before Rook could.

“I got that department.”

The room laughed. Rook's mouth tightened.

Minh set his toolbox beside the right door and looked at the left. A small green light shone above its track. The light belonged to something newer than the hotel.

“Don't touch that,” a voice said.

The man approaching wore a sleeveless black shirt, leather trousers, and a championship belt over one shoulder. His arms were covered with tattoos of flames. A camera crew followed him. On a low platform behind the crew stood a custom motorcycle with an enormous front wheel and polished silver pipes.

A poster above the motorcycle showed the same man smashing a concrete block.

SƠN THE UNBROKEN.

Minh looked from the poster to the man.

“You bring your own?”

Sơn stopped. “My own what?”

“Compliment.”

Leon turned away with the cigar between his teeth.

Sơn looked at the mark on Minh's trousers.

“Workers use the rear stairs.”

“Then use them.”

The nearest table went silent.

Sơn shifted the championship belt higher. “You know who I am?”

Minh pointed at the poster.

“You prepared that question.”

The cameraman made a small sound behind his equipment.

Rook stepped forward. “Sơn. Mr. Trần is my guest.”

“Your guest brought a fucking toolbox.”

“You brought a motorcycle,” Minh said. “You having trouble getting home?”

Leon bent over the back of a chair. The woman beside him moved her champagne out of the way.

Sơn handed his belt to a member of the camera crew. He unrolled his shoulders. The people around the entrance began moving their chairs, creating a clear space without being asked.

“I don't want to embarrass you,” Sơn said.

Minh took off the jacket Mai had brought him. He folded it and set it on the toolbox.

“Then help yourself out.”

Sơn hit him in the chest.

The sound cut through the orchestra. A button flew from Minh's shirt, crossed the space between them, and struck Sơn's cameraman in the forehead.

Minh looked down at the open collar.

The cameraman lowered his equipment with one hand pressed above his eyebrow.

Sơn pulled his fist back. His knuckles had already begun to swell.

“Again?” Minh asked.

Sơn kicked.

His right foot rose toward Minh's face. Minh caught the ankle with one hand, stepped sideways, and lifted. Sơn's left foot left the carpet. His arms swung out. Minh turned once, carrying him horizontally at waist height, and walked the three steps to the display platform.

“That's a hundred and forty thousand dollars!” somebody shouted.

Minh sat Sơn on the motorcycle.

The seat went through the frame. Both wheels jumped off the platform. The front fork folded backward until the tire pressed against Sơn's chest. The rear wheel rose behind his head. Minh pushed the handlebars down over his shoulders and let go.

Sơn sat inside the motorcycle with his knees near his ears.

One silver pipe detached, rolled across the platform, and fell onto the carpet.

The orchestra's drummer hit a cymbal by mistake.

Leon pointed at him. “Keep that nigga. He understands the assignment.”

People stood. Somebody began clapping again. Sơn's cameraman raised the camera with his good hand and moved three feet closer.

“Turn that off,” Sơn said.

“You're under contract,” the cameraman answered.

Minh picked up the championship belt and hung it on the folded front wheel.

“There. Complete set.”

He returned to the doorway. Rook stood beside the toolbox, watching the men at the nearest table tear up their betting slips.

“Was that necessary?” Rook asked.

Minh held the two sides of his shirt together.

“You got a sewing kit?”

A woman pushed past Rook carrying one from her handbag. She had gray hair, diamond earrings, and a grin she made no attempt to hide.

“Sit down, baby. I got you.”

“He's working,” Rook said.

She pulled up a chair beside the door.

“Then his job got a chair.”

Minh sat. Across the ballroom, Leon opened the silver briefcase just far enough to look inside again. He closed it, patted the lid, and asked a waiter where the large plates were.

Rook's son appeared on the stage beneath the auction lights. Dante wore a red jacket and a headset. He watched the doorway while his father spoke to him through a small radio.

Minh lifted one arm so the woman could thread her needle through his shirt.

The green light above the door turned red.

Steel moved inside the frame.

Minh put one foot beneath the descending door.

It stopped against his shoe with a hard clang.

Onstage, Dante pressed his headset.

Minh smiled at him.

“I think your father paid for open.”

## Chapter 2: Open Until Midnight

The door tried Minh's shoe twice.

Each time, the motor above it whined, the steel panel shuddered, and the toe of his right shoe remained on the carpet. The woman sewing his shirt glanced down.

“You want to move that?”

“It's fine.”

“I mean your arm. You're pulling my thread.”

He lowered his elbow.

Across the entrance, the second steel panel struck the floor. Its bottom edge cut through the carpet and left a white stripe in the marble beneath. A man holding a champagne glass jumped back. Champagne went into the pocket of the man behind him.

“Motherfucker,” the second man said.

“I was pushed.”

“By a building?”

Leon came back from the buffet carrying two plates. He had balanced the silver briefcase beneath his left arm. A tail of lobster meat hung over one plate's edge.

“We leaving?”

“Apparently we're staying,” Minh said.

Leon looked at the doors, then at the buffet.

“I can work with that for twenty minutes.”

Rook had reached the stage. Dante stepped backward before his father touched him. Minh saw the red jacket turn, the headset come off, the two men leaning close enough to speak through their teeth.

The woman bit her thread.

“There.”

Minh looked down. She had replaced his lost button with a black one, slightly larger than the rest.

“Thank you.”

“Don't let that fool hit this one. It came off my husband's good coat.”

“Where's your husband?”

She pointed at the man whose pocket was full of champagne.

“Still talking about a coat he doesn't wear.”

Minh stood. The steel panel rose on his foot. He lifted it another six inches, slid his fingers beneath the edge, and took the weight in his right hand.

The woman carried her chair out of the way.

“I knew you was going to do something with that.”

The motor gave a long grinding cough. Two bolts fell from the housing and bounced down the panel. Minh lifted until the bottom cleared his head, then pushed harder. The top of the panel drove through its cover. A length of broken track came loose and struck the floor beside him.

People began applauding.

He looked over his shoulder.

“Anybody leaving?”

Six hands rose. Then fifteen. A woman in blue took her husband's wrist and began pulling him toward the gap.

“We haven't bid,” he protested.

“We haven't been buried either. Keep moving.”

A guard came down the near aisle with one hand beneath his jacket.

“Everyone remains in the room until Mr. Rook—”

Minh pulled the steel panel out of its track.

The last bolts tore free in a short burst. The panel tilted toward the guard. Minh caught its top edge, turned it flat, and set it against the closed half of the entrance. The guard had stopped speaking. His hand remained beneath his jacket.

Leon set one plate on a table.

“You want to complete that sentence, nigga?”

The guard took his hand out.

“I was instructed—”

“We all been instructed. My doctor said vegetables. Look at my plate.”

The woman in blue passed between Minh and the guard. Her husband followed with his auction paddle still in his hand. She took it from him and dropped it into a champagne bucket on the way out.

More guests came. Minh stood beside the gap, nodding to the people who thanked him and accepting a napkin from one who mistook the grease on his hand for blood.

At the back of the ballroom, somebody shouted that the money was gone.

The departing line stopped.

“Which money?” Leon asked.

He moved the briefcase from beneath his arm to between his feet.

Three men pushed through the stage curtains. One had a bleeding nose. Another carried the lid of a wooden display box. The third wore a security vest with the front unfastened.

“The convoy,” the man in the vest said.

Rook looked at his son.

Dante's face had gone pale beneath the auction lights.

The man with the display-box lid held it up. A red velvet cushion was fixed inside it. The cushion had the outline of a necklace and nothing else.

“The prize lots. The cars. Everything staged downstairs.”

The man whose pocket had been filled with champagne began emptying it onto the carpet.

“I bought the necklace.”

“You haven't paid,” his wife said.

“I was going to.”

“Then enjoy being early for once.”

Two guards went to the service door behind the stage. It opened inward before either reached it. A man in a hotel vest came through backward, shoved hard enough to knock both guards into the curtain.

Behind him stood another man carrying a shotgun.

“Everybody down.”

Leon picked up his second plate.

“Now we leaving.”

The shotgun fired into the ceiling. Plaster rained across the tables. A light fitting dropped on a platter of fruit and rolled into a woman's lap. She threw it at her husband, who threw it at the floor.

Minh moved before the gunman brought the barrel level again.

The nearest table stood between him and the stage. Eight people sat around it. He put both hands on the back of an empty chair, jumped, and carried it over the table. His feet cleared a man's head by a foot. The man ducked afterward, taking his wig off with both hands.

Minh landed on the stage steps with the chair in front of him.

The gunman fired.

The shot broke the chair's back. Minh drove the remaining frame over the barrel, twisted it downward, and kicked the gunman in the stomach.

The man went through the curtain. A drum crashed behind it. The band stopped again, this time all at once.

Minh pulled the shotgun out of the chair, bent its barrel against the metal stair rail, and dropped it.

The drummer emerged with one stick in his hand.

“That's my bass drum.”

Minh pointed at Rook.

“He hired the room.”

“I hired music,” Rook snapped.

“You got percussion.”

Two more men were coming up the service stairs. Minh could see them through the open doorway: black jackets, gloves, one shotgun and one heavy pistol. The lower man raised his weapon around his partner's shoulder.

Minh caught the top of the service door and pulled it toward himself.

Its hinges came out of the wall. He turned the door on its long edge and drove it into the stairwell like a shovel.

The top man struck it chest-first. His gun went off into the concrete ceiling. The door hit the man behind him, knocked his pistol against the rail, and carried both down five steps. Their legs tangled beneath the wooden panel.

Minh went after them.

The man with the shotgun tried to lift the door. Minh put one foot on it. The bottom man screamed something muffled into his partner's jacket.

“Drop the guns.”

The pistol fell first. The shotgun followed.

Minh picked them up and set them on the landing behind him. He bent the stair rail across the door, pinning it over both men. Then he went back into the ballroom.

Leon stood in the entrance with the briefcase in one hand and Minh's jacket in the other.

“Time?” he asked.

Minh looked at the ballroom clock.

“Ten twelve.”

“Contract?”

“Midnight.”

Leon looked at the gap where the steel panel had been.

“Nigga, that motherfucker staying open until Christmas. Come on.”

***

Rook caught them in the corridor.

He had brought six men. None came closer than the length of the steel panel leaning against the wall.

“My son says your people were downstairs.”

Minh looked at Leon.

Leon lifted the plate he had retrieved.

“My people was at the butter.”

“He means other people,” Rook said.

“Then he needs another description.”

Dante came through the ballroom behind his father. He had taken off the red jacket. Sweat darkened the collar of his shirt.

“They said they came with you,” he told Minh.

“Who?”

“The loading crew.”

“Names.”

“They didn't give names.”

Minh looked at Rook. “You let men take your prize convoy because they said my name?”

Rook's jaw moved.

Leon put the plate down.

“How many times can a nigga use that? Asking for employment.”

Dante stepped toward him. Minh put one finger against Dante's chest. The young man stopped with his weight still coming forward, looked down at the finger, and moved backward again.

“I asked you who,” Minh said.

“A driver. Short hair. Brown jacket.”

“There's a city outside.”

“He knew you.”

“Apparently so do you. You're doing a terrible job with it.”

The corridor windows overlooked the loading court. Minh went to the nearest one. Below, hotel workers stood around three empty parking spaces. An armored truck waited at the far end with its rear doors open. Two guards sat on the ground beside it, their hands tied behind them.

At the court's exit, a dark sedan turned into the street.

The driver looked back through his open window.

Duy.

Minh put his palm against the glass.

The sedan disappeared around the corner.

Rook joined him. “What?”

“Your loading court needs a gate.”

“Don't make jokes.”

Minh turned toward him.

“You paid me to keep your ballroom door open. It's open. Those people tried to close it. I stopped them. You have a missing convoy and a son who hired men without asking their names.”

Dante opened his mouth.

Minh pointed at him without looking.

“Finish breathing first.”

The young man shut his mouth.

Rook moved closer to Minh. He lowered his voice.

“Twelve million dollars in cash, diamonds, and vehicles.”

Leon picked up the plate again.

“Damn. You should've hired him for outside too.”

Rook ignored him with effort.

“I want it back.”

“Then get it.”

“I'm asking you.”

“You were accusing me.”

“I'm revising my request.”

A small man in a cream dinner jacket came out of the ballroom carrying two auction paddles. Minh recognized Bách Vũ before he saw the diamond pinkie ring. Everybody on Bell Street called him Uncle Dollar. Bách had started the name himself and recently begun correcting people who forgot the second word.

He looked at the torn door, the six guards, and Rook's face.

Then he smiled at Minh.

“I had money on the motorcycle.”

“You lost.”

“I switched when I saw your shoes.”

Leon nodded. “Educated investor.”

Bách tapped one auction paddle against his palm.

“Calvin, how much are you offering?”

“This is private.”

Bách looked behind him. Half the ballroom had followed the conversation into the corridor.

“Then your privacy has witnesses.”

Rook looked at Minh.

“Two hundred thousand.”

“For twelve million?” Bách said.

“For recovery.”

“And the man who stole it gets what? Eleven point eight? I want the other job.”

Somebody laughed behind him. The man in the wet dinner jacket raised his empty champagne glass.

“Pay him a million.”

“It's not your money,” Rook said.

“That was my necklace.”

His wife touched his arm. “You still haven't paid.”

“I'm participating.”

Bách raised one auction paddle.

“A million.”

Rook stared at him.

Bách raised the second paddle. “A million from this side of the room too. Very strong demand.”

Minh watched Rook decide which humiliation he could afford.

“One million,” Rook said. “On return of the convoy.”

“Everything you listed,” Minh said.

“Yes.”

“And nobody follows Mai.”

Rook's expression changed.

“I haven't mentioned your fiancée.”

“Now you don't have to.”

Minh held out his hand. Rook took it carefully.

Bách began applauding. The corridor joined him. Leon put the plate beneath one arm and applauded with the briefcase against his palm.

Minh let go before Rook's fingers started to make noise.

“I'll call you.”

***

Downstairs, three valets were waiting with the limousine. One had polished the toolbox. Another held Minh's jacket as if it belonged in a museum.

Leon slid into the driver's seat and waited until Minh shut the rear door.

“You saw somebody.”

Minh looked up at the ballroom windows.

“Duy.”

“Shit.”

“Driving out.”

“He see you?”

“Yes.”

Leon put the car in gear. For the first block, he said nothing. The limousine rolled past the harbor gates, its white body reflected in the dark shop windows.

Then he glanced into the mirror.

“We still getting groceries?”

Minh took out the envelope.

“Large soap.”

“Nigga, we got a hundred thousand dollars.”

“Then we can afford it.”

At the all-night market, Leon parked across three spaces and guarded the briefcase while Minh went inside. The cashier looked at the soap, the scallions, the milk, and the hundred-dollar bill.

“Got anything smaller?”

Minh opened his wallet. Nothing.

He looked back through the window at Leon, who was pretending not to see him.

“No.”

The cashier pressed the intercom button.

“Manager to register two. Again.”

Minh stood beside the groceries and waited.

## Chapter 3: The House Has Rules

Mai opened the apartment door wearing one of Minh's shirts and holding a hammer.

He looked at the hammer.

“You heard?”

“The cupboard came loose.”

“Oh.”

“What should I have heard?”

Leon appeared behind him with the briefcase and the grocery bags.

“Your fiancé got promoted.”

“From what?”

“Standing.”

Mai moved aside. Leon went straight to the kitchen and put the milk in the refrigerator. He arranged the scallions in the empty jar, set the soap beside the sink, and placed the briefcase on the table with a flourish.

“All departments complete.”

Mai opened the case.

She looked at the money for several seconds. Then she took the hammer out of her hand and laid it carefully on the counter.

“That much standing?”

“I sat for some of it,” Minh said.

Leon pointed at the new shirt button. “Medical break.”

Mai touched the button. “Who sewed this?”

“A married woman.”

“That answers a question I hadn't asked yet.”

“Her husband was there.”

“Was he sewing too?”

Leon opened a cupboard and took down three cups. “I'm going to let y'all finish the investigation while I make tea.”

Minh sat. Mai remained standing over the money, one knee against his. He described the ballroom, the door, the motorcycle. Leon interrupted twice to improve the sound of the motorcycle and once to demonstrate the expression on Rook's face.

Mai laughed at that. She stopped laughing when Minh said Duy's name.

“Driving?”

“Leaving the court.”

“Maybe he was hired.”

“He looked back.”

“People look back.”

“He saw me and went faster.”

Leon put a cup in front of her.

“Duy owes people. Last week he tried selling me a watch he was still making payments on.”

“You bought it?” Mai asked.

Leon looked offended.

She looked at his wrist.

He pulled his sleeve down.

“I got a very good price.”

Minh took out his telephone and called Duy. It rang until a recorded voice offered to take a message.

He called again.

Mai sat beside him. “Don't leave a threat.”

“I wasn't.”

The recorded voice returned.

Minh waited for the tone.

“Duy. Call me.”

He hung up.

Leon nodded. “Terrifying.”

Mai closed the briefcase and slid it farther from the tea.

“Nobody comes upstairs with a gun,” she said.

“They'd have to come through the shop.”

“Then put that in your advertisement. Seventeen days until our wedding. Ground floor available for stupidity.”

Leon raised his cup.

“I want the table near the food.”

“You have a table near the food.”

“How near?”

“Leon.”

“I'm bringing a gift. Distance should reflect commitment.”

***

At eight the next morning, somebody delivered a refrigerator.

Minh heard the truck backing toward the garage and looked down from the apartment window. Two men were lowering a large silver refrigerator onto the sidewalk. A red bow covered most of its top door.

“Wrong address,” he called.

One man checked a card.

“Trần?”

“Yes.”

“Correct address.”

“We have one.”

“Now you have options.”

Mai came to the window. Behind the refrigerator truck, another vehicle stopped. Its driver climbed out carrying a basket of fruit large enough to hide a person. A third vehicle followed with a washing machine strapped into its open bed.

Mai watched the washing machine arrive.

“I should have written more on the grocery list.”

Minh went downstairs barefoot. The man beside the refrigerator handed him a cream envelope embossed with a dollar sign.

INSURANCE AGAINST WARM CHAMPAGNE.

UNCLE DOLLAR.

The washing machine had come from the woman who sewed his button. Her husband had written the card.

PLEASE STOP ACCEPTING BUTTONS FROM MY COAT.

The fruit basket contained a business card from an auction guest Minh did not recognize and three thousand dollars in an envelope labeled TRAVEL EXPENSES.

Mai lifted the envelope.

“Where did he want you to travel?”

“Away from him, probably.”

Reggie Mills arrived carrying a video camera and wearing a jacket with EASTBRIDGE COMMUNITY ACCESS sewn across the back. The final S had come loose and hung by one thread.

“Don't move,” he said.

Minh looked at the refrigerator blocking his shop entrance.

“That part's easy.”

Reggie framed the shot through his camera.

“Local man receives congratulations from business community.”

“Put that down,” Mai said.

“Local woman rejects free publicity.”

She walked toward him.

The camera lowered.

“I'm documenting prosperity, Mai.”

“Document the men scratching my doorframe.”

Reggie turned immediately.

“Sir. On camera. Was the damage intentional?”

The refrigerator deliveryman stopped pulling.

“Man, get that thing out my face.”

Minh lifted the refrigerator off the dolly. The red bow brushed his cheek. He turned sideways, carried the appliance through the garage, and set it by the rear wall. The two deliverymen stared at the empty dolly.

Reggie swung his camera back too late.

“Do that again.”

“Pay me.”

“Nigga, you just got a refrigerator.”

“Then film it.”

The first deliveryman put his hands on the dolly's handles. The second took the clipboard from beneath his arm, crossed out a line, and held it toward Minh.

“Sign here.”

Minh read the amended line.

CUSTOMER ASSISTED.

He signed.

***

Hòa arrived while the fruit was being redistributed.

He parked his plain blue sedan behind the washing machine truck, got out, and looked at the sidewalk. A neighbor offered him an orange. He accepted it, peeled one strip of skin, and waited until Minh noticed him.

“Breakfast,” he said.

“We ate.”

“Your mother didn't cook for the refrigerator.”

Mai came out with two bags of fruit.

“He means lunch,” she told Minh. “She began breakfast four hours ago and kept finding more people.”

Hòa took one bag. It contained most of the basket. He held it by the thin paper handle without supporting the bottom.

“Bring Leon.”

“He's returning the car,” Minh said.

Hòa nodded. “Then he can bring the owner.”

He put the bag in the sedan, got back in, and drove away.

Reggie looked after him.

“Your father-in-law scares me.”

“We aren't married yet.”

“Nigga, that man already got jurisdiction.”

***

The Lê house stood three blocks from the garage, behind a short brick wall and a gate Tín had replaced twice because visitors kept reversing into it. Minh had offered to move the driveway. Tín had suggested improving the visitors.

By noon, seven cars occupied the curb. Leon's borrowed limousine was among them. Its owner sat on the porch beside him, eating from a bowl and wearing the expression of a man who had begun the morning angry and encountered food.

“He had a wedding,” Minh said.

Leon pointed at the owner.

“It got delayed.”

The man swallowed. “Dentist's mother locked herself in the bathroom.”

“Why?”

“She wanted a different photographer.”

Leon leaned closer to Minh.

“I told him you charge for doors now.”

Minh went inside before the owner could ask.

Hương stood at the stove with Mai beside her. Bích sat at the kitchen table sorting herbs into a basket. She looked up when Minh entered and beckoned him close enough to inspect the new button.

“Who did this?”

“A woman at the party.”

Bích turned toward Mai.

“Good stitch.”

“Everybody has inspected it,” Minh said.

“Then somebody should have told you it doesn't match.”

She returned to the herbs.

Tín sat in the living room with one slipper off and a newspaper folded on his knee. At seventy-eight, he had retained a back so straight that Minh sometimes found himself sitting straighter before the old man looked at him.

Today he was watching a delivery crew maneuver a safe through the front door.

“Mine?” Minh asked.

“Unless you've started sending me presents with your name on them.”

The safe was black, waist-high, and topped with another red bow. A card hung from its handle.

FOR YOUR NEW RESPONSIBILITIES.
