Minh picked it up. No signature.

The deliverymen had caught one wheel of their dolly against the sill. Minh took the safe off it and held the weight against his chest. He turned toward the living room.

Tín extended one finger.

“There.”

“Where?”

The old man's finger touched the safe's underside.

Minh's arms rose.

The safe rose with them. Tín lifted it six inches, then another foot. Minh let go before his shoulders followed it any higher.

The old man held the safe on one finger while examining the scuff it had left on the doorframe.

“They charge for delivery?”

One deliveryman shook his head.

“Good.”

Tín lowered the safe onto the rug beside his chair. He did not get up. The floor gave a short creak.

Leon came in from the porch, saw Minh standing over the safe, and looked at Tín.

“You did it again?”

Tín put his slipper back on.

“Nigga brought it into my house.”

Leon laughed so hard the limousine owner appeared behind him to see what had happened.

Minh rubbed his palms together and looked toward the kitchen. Mai stood in the doorway with both hands over her smile.

“Don't,” he said.

“I'm being very quiet.”

“Your whole face is loud.”

***

Lunch covered the dining table, the counter, and the top of a cabinet nobody was supposed to put hot things on. Hương moved a dish from the cabinet herself and warned everyone else against doing it.

Tín took the chair at the end of the table. Bích sat beside him. Hòa waited until Mai had a seat, then pulled out the remaining chair with his foot and sat without looking behind him.

Minh told them about Rook.

Tín continued eating until he heard the name.

“Calvin?”

“Yes.”

“He still wearing those shiny shoes?”

“Yes.”

“Must have dried.”

Leon stopped with his spoon halfway to his mouth.

“Eight years, Uncle.”

“Some men take longer.”

Hòa reached for the rice. His sleeve touched the glass of water beside Minh's elbow. Minh moved to catch it as it tipped. Hòa's other hand was already beneath the glass, two fingers holding its base level.

No water reached the table.

He set it down and continued serving himself.

Tín looked at his son. Hòa looked back.

Mai nudged Minh's ankle beneath the table before he could ask anything.

“Eat.”

He ate.

Hương asked whether the wedding band had been paid. Mai said yes. Bích asked whether the photographer was reliable. Leon's guest made a strained sound and became interested in his bowl.

Tín asked Minh how much Rook had paid him.

“A hundred thousand.”

“For what?”

“Keeping a door open.”

The old man put his spoon down.

“Hòa.”

“I heard.”

“We've been doing that for free.”

Bích tapped Tín's wrist with her spoon.

“You charge people enough for coming in.”

The table broke into laughter. Minh leaned back beside Mai and let himself laugh too. Under the table, she found his hand and squeezed it.

Somebody knocked at the front door.

Leon looked toward the hall.

“That cost anything?”

“Depends what they want,” Tín said.

Reggie came in holding a stack of flyers.

He had one taped across the front of his camera. In thick black letters, it announced a celebration the following morning on Bell Street.

WELCOME YOUR NEW KING.

Below that was a photograph of Minh lifting an engine, cropped so his expression looked furious rather than bothered by sun in his eyes.

Hòa took one flyer. Mai took another.

Minh read the bottom line.

ALL DEBTS, DISPUTES, AND DONATIONS ACCEPTED.

Leon leaned over his shoulder.

“Nigga, you got office hours.”

## Chapter 4: Congratulations, You Owe Everybody

The red carpet outside Minh's garage ended at the liquor store.

Somebody had run it across the sidewalk without moving the trash cans. Two cans stood on it with their lids polished. A third had a bow. At the shop entrance, a man from a party-rental company was inflating gold balloons beside a banner that read LONG MAY HE REPAIR.

Mai stood beneath the banner with a cup of coffee.

“That one I like,” she said.

Minh looked down the carpet. “Who paid?”

“Everybody claims somebody else.”

Leon appeared from the liquor store carrying a crate of sparkling cider.

“Nine in the morning,” Minh said.

“Coronation got hours?”

“You put this together?”

“I improved an existing situation.”

Behind Leon, Reggie walked backward with his camera trained on a group of women arriving from the bakery. Each carried a tray. A man in a paper crown followed them with a portable keyboard tucked beneath one arm.

Minh recognized the keyboard before the man.

“That's Duy's.”

The man stopped.

“He sold it.”

“When?”

“Yesterday.”

“To you?”

“To my cousin. I borrowed it.”

Leon took the crate into the garage. “This street got more cousins than people.”

Minh went to the keyboard player. The man's paper crown advertised a hamburger special. He had folded the restaurant's name inward, leaving a printed picture of fries above his ear.

“What did your cousin pay?”

“Two hundred.”

“Did Duy need cash?”

“He didn't ask for a piano in exchange.”

Mai laughed into her coffee.

Minh took out his telephone and called Duy again. Straight to the recorded voice. He closed the phone and returned it to his pocket.

The keyboard player set up beneath the banner. His first chord came out much louder than he expected. A dog barked from an upstairs window.

“Sound check,” the player said.

The dog barked again.

“Everybody a critic.”

***

By ten, the sidewalk held forty people and six gifts Minh had not found room for inside.

A furniture dealer sent a leather sofa long enough to block both motorcycle bays. A barber sent a year's free haircuts and a framed photograph of himself holding the scissors. The woman who ran the corner market brought the change Minh had left waiting for the previous night.

“Manager didn't come?” he asked.

“Manager came. You went to the soap aisle and picked up the whole box.”

“It was faster.”

“My cashier thinks you're opening a laundromat.”

Mai accepted the envelope of change. “We have the machine.”

The woman looked at the washing machine by the back wall.

“Congratulations.”

Then Bách arrived in a pale yellow Rolls-Royce.

Two men got out before he did. One carried flowers. The other carried a cake shaped like a garage. The cake's tiny front door stood open. A sugar figure of Minh occupied the doorway wearing a gold crown and holding what appeared to be a wrench the size of a tree.

Leon studied it.

“They got the shoulders.”

Mai leaned closer. “They made you taller.”

“How much taller?” Minh asked.

“Tasteful amount.”

Bách handed Minh the Rolls-Royce keys.

The conversation around them stopped.

Minh looked at the car, then at the keys.

“For me?”

“For the wedding.”

“To keep?”

“You plan to get married temporarily?”

Leon made a small reverent noise.

Mai held out her hand. Minh passed her the keys. She went straight to the driver's door.

Bách watched her sit behind the wheel.

“She drives?”

Minh smiled at him.

“You about to find out.”

The engine started. Mai adjusted the mirror, lifted one hand through the window, and drove the car twenty feet forward into an empty space before somebody else's gift truck took it.

She got out and locked it.

“Thank you,” she told Bách. “The seat needs fixing.”

“I can have someone—”

She pointed at Minh.

“I have someone.”

Bách laughed and clapped Minh on the back. His hand stung. He concealed the sting by reaching immediately for a slice of cake.

“Now,” he said, “about the flyers.”

“You printed them?” Mai asked.

“No.”

“You distributed them?”

Bách considered his cake.

“Some.”

“How many?”

“Enough to support the occasion.”

She stepped closer.

“Bách.”

“Two thousand.”

Leon whistled. “Strong occasion.”

Minh took a flyer off the stack Reggie had placed by the entrance.

“Who printed them?”

“They arrived at my restaurant before sunrise. I assumed you had made an announcement.”

Mai folded the flyer once. She rubbed the ink with her thumb and smelled the paper.

“Not mine.”

“We know,” Leon said. “Yours would've spelled donations correctly.”

Minh looked down.

DONATIONS had become DONATONS.

“That sounds like a large animal,” Reggie said.

“Put the camera down,” Mai told him.

He lowered it six inches.

“It's still recording,” she said.

“History keeps happening.”

***

A man with a shaved head approached Minh carrying a folded envelope. He wore a mechanic's shirt from a garage across town.

“Mr. Trần.”

“Minh.”

“I need a favor.”

Leon appeared beside them with a fresh slice of cake.

“We open.”

The mechanic looked at him.

“You work here?”

“Emotionally.”

The man turned back to Minh. “There's a crew on Foster taking money from my drivers. I pay once. They come twice. I pay twice, now they asking about my wife's salon.”

He held out the envelope.

Minh did not take it yet.

“Who's asking?”

“A man called Al.”

“Big Al or Little Al?”

“Big.”

“He's little.”

The mechanic hesitated.

“The one with the dog.”

“That's Little Al. He's big.”

Leon pointed his fork at the man. “This why we need names on paper.”

Minh took out his telephone. He dialed a number from memory and waited.

“Al. You at Foster?”

A voice answered loudly enough for Leon to lean away.

“Stop charging the garage.”

The voice became quieter.

“Because I'm asking.”

Minh listened.

“No. You can keep the dog. I didn't mention the dog.”

He hung up and took the envelope. Inside lay five thousand dollars.

The mechanic looked astonished.

“That's it?”

“He'll call you.”

“And if he comes back?”

“Then I come with you.”

The man shook his hand with both of his. He left so quickly that he almost collided with the cake table.

Leon watched him go.

“You fixing cars and men now?”

Minh put the envelope in his jacket.

“Men keep bringing money.”

Bách raised his cup. “A diversified business.”

Mai folded her arms beneath the banner.

“The cars have appointments.”

“Then make appointments for the men.”

“Do I look like your receptionist?”

Minh held up the envelope.

She glanced at it.

“I charge separately.”

***

The flower van arrived while Leon was explaining why the cake figure should remain intact for future generations.

It was a dark green delivery van with white lettering and a sliding side door. The driver stopped beyond the Rolls-Royce. A man in a florist's apron got out carrying a tall rectangular arrangement of lilies.

Minh saw the stems move without the flowers moving.

He put his cake plate in Leon's hand.

“Down.”

The florist's right hand came out of the flowers holding a compact gun.

Minh threw the cake table at him.

The folding legs struck the man's chest. The cake went over his shoulder and burst against the van's windshield. He fell backward, firing through the tabletop as it landed across him.

People dropped behind the parked cars. Leon shoved Reggie beneath the Rolls-Royce's front bumper and lay across his legs.

Minh crossed the sidewalk in two steps. The gunman pushed the table up. Minh stamped it down and caught the gun barrel as it poked past the edge. He twisted it until the man's wrist turned with it.

The gun fell.

Minh pulled the table away, grabbed the man by his apron, and threw him into the van's open side door.

Another gunman had been kneeling inside. The florist hit him across the shoulders. Both went backward into a rack of buckets. Water and white petals spilled into the street.

The van's driver hit the accelerator.

Minh caught the rear bumper.

The van moved two feet. The bumper began to peel from its mounts. Minh stepped closer, slid his hands beneath the rear frame, and lifted.

Both rear wheels rose off the street.

The driver kept accelerating. Tires spun above Minh's head. The van's nose scraped the pavement, throwing sparks from beneath the front bumper. In the open side door, the gunmen slid forward through the water and struck the backs of the seats.

Minh held the van tilted on its front wheels.

“Turn it off.”

The engine screamed.

He lifted another foot.

The windshield cracked across the cake frosting.

“Turn it off.”

The engine stopped.

For a second the only sound was the keyboard, still holding a note because its player had fallen against it.

Leon raised his head from behind the Rolls-Royce.

“Let go of the music, nigga. We heard you.”

The note ended.

Minh lowered the van until its rear wheels touched the road. He opened the driver's door and took the keys. The driver stared at him with his mouth open.

“Who sent flowers?”

“I don't know.”

Minh looked at the cake across the windshield.

“You know something.”

“I was paid to drive.”

“By who?”

The man looked toward the open side door.

The florist tried to climb out. Mai stood beside the door holding a tire iron from the garage. She struck the metal step in front of his hand.

He pulled his hand back.

“There's a door charge,” she said.

He stayed inside.

Minh leaned closer to the driver.

“You see my fiancée?”

The driver nodded.

“She's having a good morning. Help her keep it.”

“Benny,” the driver said. “Benny at Crown Arcade. He paid me. That's all.”

Minh took the man's wallet, looked at the identification, and handed it back.

“Sit.”

The man gripped the steering wheel with both hands.

Reggie crawled out from beneath the Rolls-Royce.

His camera remained on his shoulder.

Leon stared at him.

“You got all that?”

“Most.”

“You got me pushing you to safety?”

“Your elbow covered the lens.”

Leon shut his eyes.

“Nigga, I risked my suit for a close-up of skin.”

***

Sergeant Ray Carter arrived without a siren. He parked behind the flower van, got out, and looked at its broken nose.

Then he looked at Minh.

“I was told shots fired.”

Minh pointed at the florist.

Carter looked at the table full of bullet holes.

“And a traffic accident.”

Leon brushed dirt from his trousers.

“Separate department.”

Carter had known Leon long enough to ignore him on the first attempt. He asked Mai whether anyone had been hurt. She showed him a small cut on Reggie's cheek. Reggie moved his camera so Carter could see the better side.

“I have footage.”

“Good.”

“Station can buy a copy.”

Carter turned toward him slowly.

Reggie nodded. “Public service discount.”

While the officers collected the guns, Minh walked to the Rolls-Royce. Mai joined him. Cake frosting covered its hood and half the windshield. The little sugar figure of Minh lay on its side beside the wiper.

Its crown had survived.

Mai picked it up and handed it to him.

“Long may you repair.”

He bit the crown off.

She stared at him, then began laughing.

Across the sidewalk, Leon found the mechanic from Foster waiting beside the garage. The man held another envelope.

“What's that?” Leon asked.

“Al called. Said to give him this too.”

Minh accepted the second envelope. Ten thousand dollars.

From behind him, Carter said, “I don't want to know.”

“Then stop looking over my shoulder,” Minh said.

Carter stepped beside him instead.

“I want a statement.”

Minh looked at the flower van, then at the clock above his workbench.

“You want it now?”

“Yes.”

He put the envelope away.

“Leon. Call Crown Arcade. Tell Benny I'll be late.”

Leon took out his phone.

“How late?”

Minh glanced at Carter's notebook.

“Depends how fast he writes.”

## Chapter 5: The Arcade King

Benny had put a sign on Crown Arcade's front door.

CLOSED FOR PRIVATE MAINTENANCE.

Minh read it through the windshield of Leon's own car, a brown sedan with a blue passenger door.

“He got your message,” he said.

Leon switched off the engine.

“Told him you were coming. He said he wasn't there.”

“On his own telephone?”

“Nigga answered enthusiastic. Had to become absent halfway through.”

Minh opened his door. Before he could get out, a young man appeared beside the car wearing red trainers, loose black trousers, and a shirt that read MASTER CHIGGA in gold letters.

The young man leaned down to the window.

“You Minh?”

“Depends what your shirt wants.”

The man looked down at himself.

“It's a brand.”

Leon got out on the other side and came around the hood.

“Brand of what?”

“Me.”

“How sales?”

“Building.”

Minh looked at the arcade. Through the darkened glass, a shape moved away from the door.

“You work here?”

“I play pool here.”

“Name?”

The young man tapped the shirt.

“Before the shirt,” Minh said.

“Tú.”

“Tú. Move.”

Tú stepped aside so quickly he nearly tripped over the curb. Leon caught his elbow.

“Mastering sidewalks next?”

“Those shoes new?” Tú asked.

Leon looked down at the scuffed white shoes he had refused to change after the flower attack.

“They were.”

Tú nodded sympathetically. “Hard launch.”

Minh knocked on the arcade door.

Somebody inside held up a handwritten note.

READ THE SIGN.

Minh put his hand on the door handle and pulled.

The lock broke out of the frame. He caught the piece before it hit the sidewalk and handed it to the man with the note.

“Maintenance.”

***

The arcade smelled of fried food, warm electronics, and the carpet cleaner somebody had poured over a much older smell. Rows of machines flashed in the half-dark. Beyond them, a rope divided the games from a pool room lit by green-shaded lamps.

A woman behind the change counter looked up from a magazine.

“Benny isn't here.”

“Where is he?”

She turned a page.

“Ask the sign.”

Leon put both hands on the counter and smiled.

“Veronica.”

She looked at him over the magazine.

“You still owe me thirty dollars.”

Leon stopped smiling.

“Different conversation.”

“Same mouth.”

Minh placed thirty dollars on the counter.

Veronica picked it up.

“Office. Back left. He'll tell you he left.”

Leon followed Minh toward the rope.

“You didn't have to do that.”

“You didn't have to borrow it.”

“It was for a gift.”

“For her?”

Leon said nothing.

Minh looked at him.

“You borrowed money from her to buy her a gift?”

“She liked the earrings.”

Behind them, Tú made a noise that became a cough when Leon turned.

The pool room held three tables and eight men. On the nearest table, a triangle of balls waited at the far end. A man in a gold waistcoat stood beside it holding a cue. Minh recognized Benny from the driver's description of an enormous watch and a small, irritated head.

Benny smiled.

“Didn't think you'd come yourself.”

“You sent flowers.”

“That wasn't me.”

Minh took the cue from his hand.

Benny let it go after a moment in which both of them watched his fingers.

“I want the man who hired your driver.”

“People hire drivers every day.”

Minh looked at the racked balls. He placed the white ball at the near end, leaned over the table, and struck it.

The break cracked through the room.

Balls scattered into six pockets. One striped ball hit the side cushion, jumped onto the neighboring table, struck its white ball, and sent that into the corner pocket. The last red ball circled the first table, tapped the eight, and followed it into the side.

The felt went still.

Tú stared.

“Nigga.”

Leon nodded without looking away.

“That's the correct technical term.”

Minh laid the cue down.

“Your table leans left.”

Benny's smile had become much smaller.

“You could make money doing that.”

“I'm trying to make money doing this.”

He stepped closer.

“Who hired the driver?”

Benny looked at the men around the room.

Three moved. The first came from behind Minh holding a pool cue by its narrow end. The second lifted a bar stool. The third took a knife from his waistband.

Minh caught the first cue under his arm without turning. He stepped backward into the man holding it. The man's breath left him. Minh lifted him by the belt and laid him across the pool table, face-down, hard enough to bounce the cue ball out of the return tray.

The stool came at Minh's head.

He ducked beneath it, put one palm against the attacker's stomach, and pushed.

The man flew backward through the rope and hit a racing machine. Its plastic steering wheel broke across his back. The screen flashed GAME OVER while he slid into the seat.

Leon looked at the machine.

“Nigga got there on one quarter.”

The knife man stopped.

Minh turned toward him.

“You can keep it in your hand if you stay over there.”

The man looked at Benny.

Benny opened his mouth.

“Answer him yourself,” Minh said.

The man put the knife on a table.

Benny backed toward the office.

Tú moved to block him. Benny shoved him into a chair. Tú fell over the chair and came up holding it by both legs.

“Nigga, I was trying to keep this professional.”

Leon took the chair from him.

“You need a license for the first part.”

Benny ran.

Minh picked up the pool table.

He lifted its near end until the legs left the floor, turned it sideways, and pushed it through the gap between the other tables. The far edge struck the office door as Benny reached it. The door slammed shut in his face.

Benny bounced off it, staggered backward, and found the pool table across his path.

Minh stepped onto the raised edge and looked down at him.

“That's private maintenance.”

Veronica called from the change counter.

“You breaking the pool tables?”

“Moving them.”

“Benny owns those.”

“Good.”

“Don't touch my machines.”

The man sitting in the broken racing game groaned.

Leon pointed at him. “That one bought a ride.”

***

Benny's office contained a desk, two filing cabinets, and a photograph of Benny beside a boxer who clearly had not wanted the photograph taken. Minh put Benny in the chair beneath it.

Leon stood in the doorway. Tú hovered behind him, trying to see around his shoulder.

Minh put the driver's description back into the conversation.

“Green van. Flowers. Men with guns.”

Benny rubbed his nose.

“It was supposed to scare you.”

“It scared the cake.”

“I wasn't there.”

“You're here.”

Benny looked toward the window. It had bars on the outside. Minh waited until he finished evaluating them.

“Dante,” Benny said.

“Rook's son?”

“He said you took something.”

“What?”

“A car. Money. I don't know. He paid for a message.”

Minh took the telephone off Benny's desk and held it out.

“Call him.”

“He's not answering.”

“Then he'll disappoint us together.”

Benny dialed. Minh listened to the ringing. After six rings, a voice answered.

Benny's face changed before he said a word.

“Dante. It's Benny.”

The voice at the other end spoke sharply.

“No. No, he's—”

Minh took the receiver.

“Hello.”

Silence.

“I got your flowers.”

The line clicked.

Minh put the receiver down.

Leon folded his arms.

“Young man got manners problems.”

Minh opened the top drawer. Benny reached toward it, stopped halfway, and put his hand back in his lap.

Inside lay cash, three watches, a packet of photographs, and a key ring bearing a brass tag.

LOT 7.

Minh picked up the keys.

Benny swallowed.

“That's mine.”

“Which car?”

“A Cadillac.”

“Color?”

“White.”

Leon looked toward the street. “White Cadillac out back.”

“I won it,” Benny said.

“From who?”

“Duy.”

Minh put the keys on the desk.

“When?”

“This morning.”

“How?”

Benny looked toward the pool room.

Tú pushed past Leon.

“That's bullshit. You made him play on the short table.”

Benny turned on him. “You don't work here.”

“I lose here. I got standing.”

Minh looked at Tú.

“Duy was here?”

“Six in the morning. Sweating. Had keys for three cars and a bag he wouldn't put down. Benny offered him a game.”

“And he played?” Leon asked.

Tú nodded.

Leon looked at Minh.

“That nigga could fall into a bank vault and come out owing the hinges.”

Minh picked up the photographs. They showed prize cars parked in the hotel's loading court. The white Cadillac appeared in the first image. Beside it stood Dante, one arm around Duy's shoulders.

Minh stared at the arm.

Benny began speaking quickly.

“I don't know anything about a robbery. I won a car. That's it.”

“Where did Duy go?”

“He asked for a phone.”

“Who did he call?”

“I didn't listen.”

Minh raised his eyes.

Benny put both hands flat on the desk.

“Blue Palm Car Wash. I heard Blue Palm. That's all.”

Leon took a pen from the desk and wrote the name on his palm.

“Car wash,” he said. “Appropriate. Nigga needs cleansing.”

***

The white Cadillac waited beneath a canvas awning behind the arcade. Its paint had a pearl finish. Chrome covered its wheels. A little plaque on the dashboard identified it as the seventh lot in Rook's auction.

Minh opened the door.

Tú leaned over his shoulder.

“You taking it?”

“It was stolen.”

“From you?”

“From the man paying me.”

“So professionally stolen back.”

Leon opened the passenger door and sat down.

“Master got comprehension.”

Minh lifted the driver's seat cushion. Beneath it lay a brown envelope held shut with a rubber band. He opened it.

Thirty thousand dollars.

Leon looked across the car.

“I would like to register a complaint about my vehicle.”

Minh put the envelope back beneath the seat.

“Duy didn't know that was there.”

“You sure?”

“He sold his keyboard for two hundred dollars.”

Tú whistled.

From the arcade doorway, Veronica called Minh's name.

She held a grocery bag in one hand and the broken lock in the other.

“Take Benny's cameras too,” she said. “He keeps footage in his office. He'll erase it after you leave.”

Minh looked back at the open door.

Benny had appeared behind her. He disappeared again.

Minh smiled.

“Leon.”

Leon got out of the Cadillac.

“I heard her.”

Tú followed him.

“Can I help?”

“You can carry the tapes.”

“What do I get?”

Leon turned at the doorway.

“A chance to be Master Outside.”

Tú looked back at Minh. Minh nodded toward the office.

The young man grinned and went after Leon.

## Chapter 6: The Bride's Driver

Mai's fitting was at one.

At twelve fifty-eight, Minh drove the yellow Rolls-Royce through a puddle and arrived outside Felicia Jackson's dress shop with one clean side.

Mai came out onto the sidewalk before he switched off the engine.

“You're early.”

“Two minutes.”

“I was preparing a speech.”

He opened her door from inside.

“Save it. I'll disappoint you later.”

“You better not. I have a second appointment.”

She leaned through the window and kissed him. Then she looked at the back seat.

“Why is there a bag marked EVIDENCE?”

“Tú wrote that.”

“Who is Tú?”

“A man branding himself.”

“As police?”

Minh took the bag out and put it in the trunk. The videotapes inside belonged to Benny. Leon had found six more than they needed and insisted on taking all of them because Benny became nervous every time he reached another shelf.

Mai watched the trunk close.

“You found Duy?”

“Found one of the cars. Leon's checking the car wash.”

“Without you?”

“He can look.”

Minh's telephone rang.

Leon spoke before Minh said hello.

“Nigga, they got a man outside washing the same tire for twelve minutes.”

“Then stop watching him.”

“I'm being subtle.”

“What car are you in?”

“The white Cadillac.”

Minh closed his eyes.

“The stolen prize car?”

“It's got better seats.”

“Leave.”

“We just got here.”

“Leon.”

Mai took the phone from Minh.

“Go buy lunch. Park where nobody is washing a tire. We will call you.”

Leon said something she declined to repeat.

“No. Lunch doesn't count toward your gift.”

She ended the call and returned the phone.

“Your department,” Minh said.

“Apparently.”

***

Felicia had pinned a sign above her sewing table.

IF YOU CAN MAKE IT YOURSELF, GO HOME.

Below it, she stood on a low platform adjusting the shoulder of a jacket worn by a man who looked frightened to breathe.

“I'm just saying my cousin paid less,” the man said.

“Then your cousin can marry you.”

Minh stopped in the doorway.

Felicia looked up, smiled at Mai, and pointed one pair of scissors at him.

“You. Sit.”

“I haven't done anything.”

“That's the behavior I'm preserving.”

He sat in a chair by the window. The man on the platform looked at Minh and recognized him.

“You were at Rook's.”

“Yes.”

“My uncle saw the motorcycle.”

Felicia pressed a finger against the man's chin and turned his head forward.

“Your uncle can look at your suit when I'm done.”

Mai disappeared behind a curtain. Minh watched the curtain for a moment, then looked at a display of buttons beside his chair. He found one that matched the black button on his shirt and held it up.

Felicia glanced at it.

“Twenty dollars.”

“For a button?”

“For asking while I'm working.”

He put it down.

The man on the platform gave him a tiny, grateful smile. Minh smiled back. Felicia caught both expressions in the mirror.

“You two forming a support group?”

“I need his uncle to testify,” Minh said.

She snorted and returned to the jacket.

Mai came out wearing the unfinished wedding dress.

Minh stood.

Felicia looked up, saw his face, and stopped telling him where to sit.

The dress had a narrow waist and a skirt that moved around Mai's legs when she stepped onto the platform. Its sleeves were still pinned. One side of the hem had been turned under and the other remained loose. Mai looked at herself in the long mirror, then at Minh behind her.

“Don't step on anything.”

He went closer.

“I won't.”

“You say that like the floor belongs to you.”

He stopped beside the platform. She held out one hand and let him take it.

For several seconds he forgot the bag in the trunk, the missing cars, and the number Rook had offered him. Mai watched him forget and smiled slowly.

“Well?”

“Yes.”

Felicia made a pleased sound.

“I haven't asked you anything,” Mai said.

“Save time.”

She laughed. He lifted her hand and kissed the place below her ring.

The man waiting in his half-finished suit looked away with an expression that suggested he had suddenly remembered somebody he ought to telephone.

Felicia knelt beside the hem.

“Turn a little.”

Mai turned.

“Other way. Your man taking up the whole mirror.”

Minh moved back. His knee hit the little chair behind him. The chair slid across the floor and bumped the wall.

Felicia looked at it.

“Romance is expensive in my shop.”

Minh sat down carefully.

***

The first visitor brought roses.

Minh stood before the deliveryman reached the counter.

The man stopped with the bouquet between them.

“Flowers,” he said.

“I can see.”

“For Miss Mai.”

“From who?”

The man looked at the card.

“From you.”

Minh remembered ordering them three days earlier.

Behind the fitting curtain, Mai began laughing.

Felicia took the roses from the deliveryman.

“He gets confused when the romance goes according to plan.”

Minh tipped the man enough to make him check the bill twice.

“Thank you,” the deliveryman said.

“Use the front door.”

“I was going to.”

The second visitor did not bring anything.

He wore a dark suit and stood outside the window pretending to read the sale notice. The notice concerned bridesmaid alterations. He read it for almost a minute without moving his eyes.

Minh watched him in the mirror.

A black sport-utility vehicle stopped across the street. Its engine remained running. Another rolled slowly past, continued to the corner, and stopped where it could see both ends of the block.

Mai came out in her own clothes carrying the shoes she would wear with the dress.

She saw Minh's face and looked toward the window.

“How many?”

“Enough to lose two cars.”

Felicia came around the counter.

“No.”

Minh looked at her.

She pointed at the dresses hanging along the wall.

“Whatever your face is doing, take it outside.”

He took Mai's shoes.

“Back room. Both of you.”

Mai did not move.

“Where are you going?”

“To ask what they want.”

“You know what they want.”

He glanced at the man reading the notice.

“Bridesmaid alterations.”

“Then charge them.”

She kissed him quickly and followed Felicia behind the curtain.

***

The man outside turned as Minh opened the door.

“Mr. Trần.”

“You need a fitting?”

“We'd like you to come with us.”

“Who's we?”

The man glanced at the vehicle across the street.

“Mr. Rook wants to discuss the reward.”

“He has my number.”

“He prefers privacy.”

Minh stepped onto the sidewalk and shut the shop door behind him.

“Then stop looking through the window.”

The man's right hand moved toward the inside of his jacket.

Minh caught his wrist through the cloth, pulled him close, and took the pistol before it cleared the pocket. He folded the man's hand around the empty lining and pushed him against the wall.

Across the street, the sport-utility vehicle's doors opened.

Minh lifted the man by his jacket and carried him into the road.

“Close them,” he called.

One of the men getting out raised a gun.

Minh threw the pistol he had taken.

It hit the raised weapon and the hand holding it. The man cried out and dropped both. Minh crossed the remaining distance with the suited man held in front of him, then drove the man's shoulder into the open rear door.

The door folded backward against its hinges. The man slid down it onto the seat.

The driver put the vehicle in reverse.

Minh reached through the open front window, caught the steering wheel at the top, and pulled.

The column tore free of the dashboard. The driver clung to the bottom of the wheel until it hit his chest. Minh took it away and dropped it on the sidewalk.

The vehicle rolled backward into a parking meter and stopped.

At the corner, the second vehicle accelerated toward him.

Minh stepped out of its path, caught the edge of the front wheel arch with both hands, and lifted as it passed.

The left side rose. Its right tires remained on the road for half a turn, then lifted too. Minh turned with the moving weight and shoved upward.

The vehicle went onto its side across the first one's hood.

Metal buckled. Both horns began sounding. Glass poured into the street around Minh's shoes.

The men inside the overturned vehicle hung from their belts. One tried to climb toward the upper door. Minh opened it for him, took him by the back of the collar, and lowered him headfirst through the first vehicle's broken windshield.

“Ask your driver for a ride.”

The man shouted into the empty dashboard.

Minh stepped back. Blood ran down his forearm from a strip of glass caught beneath his sleeve. He pulled it out and dropped it beside the stolen steering wheel.

The man who had lost his gun sat on the curb holding his hand. Minh crouched in front of him.

“Which Rook?”

The man stared at the two vehicles.

“Calvin or Dante?”

“Dante.”

“Where?”

“I don't know.”

Minh picked up the man's telephone from the road. Its cover had come off. He pressed the loose piece back into place and held the phone out.

“Tell him the fitting ran long.”

***

Mai came outside with a clean cloth and her shoes in a box.

She stopped at the curb and looked at the wrecked vehicles.

Felicia came out behind her.

“You stacked them?”

“Parking problem,” Minh said.

Felicia looked at the empty spaces the vehicles had left behind.

“You did open the block up.”

Mai took Minh's arm and wrapped the cloth around it. Her mouth tightened when she saw the depth of the cut.

“This needs cleaning.”

“It will close.”

“So will my shop. I still clean it.”

He let her tie the cloth.

Across the street, the man who had been having his suit fitted stood in Felicia's doorway with his telephone against his ear.

“Uncle,” he said. “The motorcycle wasn't the whole story.”

Felicia pointed at him.

“You still owe me for the sleeves.”

He covered the receiver. “I know.”

“Tell your uncle that too.”

Minh opened the Rolls-Royce for Mai. She placed the shoe box on the seat, turned, and put both hands against his chest.

“For the wedding, can we arrive normally?”

“Define normally.”

“Four wheels beneath the car. Both of us inside. No men in the windshield.”

He considered it.

“I'll put it in writing.”

She kissed him, slower this time. Felicia went back inside and deliberately shut the door.

When Mai let him go, his telephone rang.

Leon sounded as if he was chewing.

“We got lunch.”

“Good.”

“And Tú knows a pawnshop where Dante's man sold the car-watch thing.”

“What car-watch thing?”

Tú's voice came from farther away.

“The tracker, nigga!”

Leon swallowed.

“Tracker. Boy wanted me to lead with technology.”

Minh looked at the two stacked vehicles, then at the Rolls-Royce's untouched yellow paint.

“Send me the address.”

“Over the phone?”

“Say it, Leon.”

Mai sat down and closed her door. Through the window, she lifted the shoe box and mouthed, Home first.

Minh nodded.

Leon gave him the pawnshop address. Minh repeated it once and put the phone away.

He drove Mai home with both hands on the wheel.

## Chapter 7: Pawnshop Royalty

Marisol Vega had put Minh's photograph in her pawnshop window.

Under it, she had written SECURITY.

Minh stood outside and read the sign while Leon parked the Cadillac. The photograph showed him carrying a washing machine. Reggie had taken it that morning. Somebody had drawn sunglasses on his face with a black marker.

Marisol opened the door.

“You coming in or protecting the sidewalk?”

“I don't work here.”

“Neither does the alarm. People still respect it.”

He pointed at the sunglasses.

“Those aren't mine.”

“You looked too friendly.”

Leon came up beside him and inspected the photograph.

“You should've charged for the eyes separately.”

Marisol stepped back to let them enter. Glass cases filled the narrow shop. Rings lay beside watches, watches beside pocketknives, pocketknives beside a signed photograph of a singer Minh knew had died before he was born.

Tú waited by the counter with a bag of chips. He had changed into a second shirt with the same gold lettering.

Leon looked at it.

“How many of those you got?”

“Three.”

“Nigga built an empire out of laundry.”

Minh put a hand on the counter.

“The receiver.”

Marisol took a metal box from beneath the glass. It had a small screen, a carrying handle, and an aerial that folded against one side. A sticker on its lid bore Rook's crown-shaped auction logo.

“Dante's man brought it yesterday. Said it controlled a racing car.”

“What did you pay?”

“Enough.”

“How much is enough leaving?”

“More.”

Minh smiled. She smiled back.

Leon opened his mouth. Marisol pointed at him without looking.

“You still owe me for the amplifier.”

He closed his mouth.

Minh turned toward him.

“How many women on this street are financing you?”

“I'm locally supported.”

Tú nearly choked on a chip.

Marisol tapped the receiver.

“Five hundred.”

Minh took five bills from his pocket. She accepted them and pushed the box toward him.

“And the car,” she said.

He looked up.

“What car?”

Marisol pointed at the ceiling.

***

A red two-seat sports car stood on the pawnshop roof.

Its rear wheels rested on a wooden platform. Its front wheels pointed toward a banner stretched between two poles.

WIN BIG. DRIVE HOME.

Leon looked up from the alley.

“Drive home from where?”

“Promotional display,” Marisol said.

“Whose promotion?” Minh asked.

“Dante's. He paid to use the roof for a week.”

“Then he stole his father's convoy and came here with it.”

Marisol folded her arms.

“That's an unfortunate sequence for him.”

“You knew?”

“I knew he had a car. I know lots of men with cars. I don't ask every one whether his father is upset.”

Minh shaded his eyes. The car's windshield had a gold number in the corner.

LOT 11.

“How did it get up there?”

“Crane.”

“Where's the crane?”

“Finished its work. Something men do sometimes.”

Leon looked toward the street. “I can call somebody.”

Marisol pointed at Minh's photograph in the window.

“I already got somebody.”

Minh went back inside and climbed the narrow stairs behind the counter. A roof hatch opened beside the car. He lifted it and stepped out into the sun.

The roof's tar surface had softened in the heat. Tire marks led from the hatch to the platform. Someone had pushed the car into position after lowering it. The wooden planks beneath the wheels had begun to split along the grain.

Minh opened the driver's door. Keys hung from the ignition. On the passenger seat lay a pair of white gloves and a folded hotel napkin with a telephone number written on it.

He took the napkin.

Below, Leon called up.

“Nigga, don't drive it down the stairs.”

“Wasn't planning to.”

“I like my concerns heard.”

Minh put the receiver on the seat and switched it on. The screen brightened. Eleven small numbered boxes appeared. Two flashed steadily. Another blinked once, went dark, and blinked again.

He glanced at the gold eleven on the windshield, then at the white Cadillac parked below. Seven and eleven shone on the screen. Three pulsed faintly at its edge.

He pressed the button marked SEARCH.

The receiver made a high electronic chirp.

The car beneath him answered with a soft click from its dashboard.

Minh called Leon.

“Move the Cadillac farther down the street.”

“Why?”

“I want to see something.”

Leon got in and drove half a block. Seven moved across the little screen. Minh smiled and put the receiver back in its case.

He had a direction. He would need distance, and he could get that by moving.

Before he could call Leon back, the roof hatch banged shut behind him.

A voice said, “You can leave the keys.”

Minh turned.

Sơn stood beside the hatch wearing a loose tracksuit and a brace around his left wrist. Two large men flanked him. One carried a length of pipe. The other carried a folded jacket over his right hand.

Minh looked at Sơn's wrist.

“You drove?”

“I have a driver.”

“Good.”

Sơn glanced at the red car.

“Dante asked me to collect that.”

“Then you should've brought a crane.”

The man with the pipe laughed once. Sơn turned his head. The man stopped.

Minh leaned against the car.

“How's the motorcycle?”

“The company says it can't be repaired.”

“Which company?”

“The fucking motorcycle company.”

“I know a mechanic.”

Sơn stared at him. Then, very slowly, he looked at Minh's work shirt.

The man with the jacket stepped forward.

“We didn't come to talk about a motorcycle.”

He lifted the jacket.

Minh kicked the roof hatch upright.

The metal cover struck the man's gun hand. The shot went into the air above the alley. Minh crossed the space before the man could lower the weapon again, caught the back of his neck, and pushed his face through the open hatch.

The man's feet left the roof. His shoulders struck the sides of the opening. He hung upside down with his shoes kicking above the tar.

From below, Marisol shouted.

“Who the hell is in my stairs?”

“Ask him,” Minh called.

The pipe man swung.

Minh caught the pipe in his left hand. He pulled the man forward, turned him toward the car, and drove the pipe through the empty space between the car's front wheels. The pipe bent around the axle housing. The man's hands remained on it until he understood he had become attached to the vehicle.

He let go.

Minh caught his collar before he could run and lowered him into the driver's seat.

“Stay. I need weight on that side.”

Sơn stood by the hatch with both hands raised.

“I told him to keep the gun down.”

“Before or after he brought it?”

“Before.”

Minh looked at the man kicking in the hatch.

“He should listen to professionals.”

Sơn lowered his hands an inch.

“I don't want another problem.”

“Then take his shoes off. He's marking the roof.”

Sơn looked at him.

Minh waited.

The fighter bent and pulled one shoe from the trapped man's foot. The man shouted from inside the stairwell.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping,” Sơn said.

***

Minh could have called a crane.

The roof beneath the platform made a sharp cracking sound while he considered it.

He opened the car's door and pulled the pipe man back out. The man staggered toward Sơn, who caught his sleeve and pointed him at the far wall.

The rear platform collapsed.

Both back wheels dropped through the roof. The car tilted. Inside the shop, Marisol screamed a word that reached the alley and made Tú step away from the building.

Minh caught the car beneath its rear fender.

The roof continued tearing around the wheels. He bent his knees, put his other hand beneath the chassis, and lifted.

The car came out of the hole trailing wood and insulation. One rear wheel spun slowly beside his face. He carried the weight toward the roof edge, each step leaving a deep mark in the softened surface.

Leon had brought the Cadillac back. He got out and looked up.

“You need help?”

“Move the car.”

Leon looked at the Cadillac, then at the red sports car above him.

“Yes, sir.”

He drove away fast enough to chirp the tires.

Minh reached the roof edge. The alley below was clear except for a dumpster against the opposite wall. He put one foot on the low parapet and held the car out over the drop.

Sơn watched from beside the hatch.

“You're going to drop it?”

“Eventually.”

Minh stepped off the roof.

He fell with the car held across his chest. His feet struck the pavement first. The impact cracked the concrete and drove his heels through the soles of his shoes. His knees bent. He lowered the car the last three feet until its tires touched the ground.

The suspension bounced once.

The car horn sounded as the loose receiver case struck the steering wheel.

Minh stood upright and stepped out of the holes beneath his heels.

Tú held both hands on top of his head.

“Nigga.”

Leon parked around the corner and came running back.

He looked at the car, the holes, and Minh's shoes.

“We got to start buying those wholesale.”

Marisol came out of the shop carrying a piece of ceiling.

“Your photograph is paying rent.”

Minh took out his wallet.

“How much?”

She looked at the red car.

“I will prepare a number.”

***

Sơn came down the stairs carrying the gunman's shoes. Behind him, the pipe man helped the gunman walk. The latter had a strip of insulation caught in his hair and a red mark running across the bridge of his nose.

Sơn put the shoes on the counter.

“Where do you want them?”

Marisol looked at the labels inside.

“Thirty dollars.”

“They're his.”

“Then he gets thirty dollars.”

The gunman reached for them. Marisol put one hand on top.

“After he pays for the stairs.”

Minh took the napkin from the sports car and showed it to Sơn.

“Dante's number?”

Sơn nodded.

“Where is he?”

“I was supposed to call when I had the car.”

“Call.”

Sơn took out his telephone. This time he put it on the counter so Minh could hear.

Dante answered on the fourth ring.

“You got it?”

Sơn looked at Minh.

“I'm with the car.”

“Good. Bring it to Blue Palm. Back gate.”

“And Duy?” Minh asked.

Silence.

Dante breathed into the line.

“You're becoming annoying.”

“You keep giving me cars.”

“Those belong to my father.”

“Then bring him a card. Father's Day came early.”

The line went dead.

Sơn picked up his phone.

“You want me to come?”

Leon looked at him.

“Nigga, your wrist still got that party on it.”

“I can drive.”

Minh held out the sports car's keys.

Sơn took them carefully.

“Follow us. Don't turn until I turn.”

The fighter nodded.

Tú watched him walk to the car.

“He works for you now?”

“He's driving.”

“Can I drive something?”

Leon pointed at the empty dolly leaning beside Marisol's counter.

“Start with that. We working up.”

Marisol handed Minh a receipt before he left. Beneath the five-hundred-dollar receiver purchase, she had added a second line.

CEILING: DISCUSSION PENDING.

He folded it and put it in his pocket.

Outside, Sơn started the red car. The engine filled the alley with a deep, expensive sound. Leon slid into the white Cadillac and adjusted his seat until he could see his entire smile in the mirror.

Minh got in beside him.

“Blue Palm,” he said.

“Three minutes away.”

Minh looked at the receiver. The box marked three had moved closer to seven and eleven.

“Then let's not make Duy wait.”

## Chapter 8: Three Minutes at the Car Wash

The man at Blue Palm was still washing the same tire.

Leon stopped the Cadillac across the street and pointed through the windshield.

“See?”

Minh watched the man move a brush around the wheel. The wheel was already clean. Water ran over it into a drain beneath the curb.

“Maybe he likes it.”

“Forty minutes, nigga. That's a relationship.”

Behind them, Sơn parked the red sports car. He got out carefully, holding his injured wrist against his stomach. Tú climbed out of the passenger side and adjusted his shirt before looking around.

The receiver on Minh's lap showed three directly ahead. Seven and eleven sat close together beneath it.

He switched the box off and put it under the seat.

“Leon. Take the Cadillac down the block. Leave room behind the exit.”

“How much room?”

Minh looked at the wash bay.

“A car.”

Leon glanced at him.

“Normal car or one of your arrangements?”

“We'll see.”

***

The Blue Palm sign offered a three-minute wash for seven dollars.

Minh walked beneath it carrying the sports car's keys. The tire man saw him, dropped his brush, and went through a side door without saying anything.

Tú picked up the brush.

“You want me to finish?”

Minh looked at him.

Tú put it down.

“Establishing cover.”

Inside the office, a television showed a baseball game with the sound turned low. A cash drawer stood open beneath the counter. Nobody had touched the bills inside it.

Minh could hear water running behind the wall.

He went through the office into the wash bay.

A black luxury sedan sat on the conveyor halfway through the building. Blue strips of cloth hung around its roof. Its rear window was dark. Its brake lights shone red through the water.

At the far end, Dante stood beside a metal control cabinet.

Duy sat in the sedan's driver's seat.

His hands were tied to the steering wheel.

Minh stopped.

Dante lifted one hand.

“There he is.”

“Move away from the cabinet.”

“You could say hello first.”

“You sent flowers to my home.”

“I sent men to ask a question.”

Tú looked at the black sedan, then at Sơn beside him. Sơn moved the young man behind his right shoulder.

Dante noticed.

“You too?”

Sơn held up his wrapped wrist.

“I had new information.”

Dante's mouth tightened.

“I paid you.”

“You paid me to collect a car. It's outside.”

“You're standing with him.”

“Car doesn't need supervision.”

Minh went closer to the conveyor. Duy saw him through the glass and shook his head hard enough to strike the headrest.

Dante rested his hand on the control cabinet.

“Don't. I had the line modified.”

Minh looked above the sedan. The heavy horizontal brush hung from two steel arms. A chain had been added between the brush frame and a hydraulic ram used to service the machinery. The ram's base had been bolted into the overhead beam.

“That's going through the roof,” Dante said.

“I can see.”

“Then listen. You give me the two cars. You leave the receiver. You tell my father you found nothing.”

“And Duy?”

“He goes home.”

Duy shook his head again.

“He doesn't believe you,” Minh said.

“Duy has a very expensive opinion of himself.”

Dante pressed a switch.

The overhead ram moved. Its chain tightened. The brush frame lowered until the bristles pressed flat against the sedan's roof.

Duy shouted behind the glass.

Minh stepped onto the conveyor.

Dante pushed the switch farther.

The roof began to crease.

Minh put one hand beneath the brush frame and lifted.

The ram stopped. Its hydraulic line jerked against the beam. Water sprayed over Minh's face and ran down his open collar. He shifted his feet between the conveyor rollers and pushed the frame upward another inch.

Dante stared at his hand.

“Turn it off,” Minh said.

Dante took a pistol from behind the cabinet.

Minh's free hand caught the sedan's door handle. He pulled the entire door off and threw it down the bay.

It struck the control cabinet edge-first. The pistol fired into the wall. Dante fell behind the cabinet with the door across his legs.

Minh reached through the open side of the car and tore the binding from Duy's wrists.

“Out.”

Duy tried to move. His legs were tied beneath the dashboard.

Minh looked down, bent the steering column upward with one hand, and pulled Duy across the seat by his jacket. The cord broke around his ankles. Duy fell into the water beside the conveyor and crawled toward the office.

The ram's pipe burst.

Fluid sprayed across the overhead beam. Minh shoved the brush frame upward. The chain snapped and whipped into the far wall. He ducked beneath the returning length, caught the frame before it swung down again, and threw it sideways through the partition.

The entire wall of the office shook. The baseball television fell forward onto the counter.

From behind the cabinet, Dante crawled toward an open rear door.

Minh stepped off the conveyor.

A gunshot cracked from the office.

Sơn had his good arm around a man's throat. Another man lay across the change counter. Tú stood beside him holding the broken television with both hands.

“Put it down,” Sơn said.

“He getting up.”

“Then hit him again.”

Tú looked at the man.

The man lay back down.

“Negotiated,” Tú said.

Minh turned toward the rear door.

Dante was gone.

***

Outside, an engine roared.

Minh ran through the rear doorway and found Dante behind the wheel of a heavy tow truck. Its winch cable had been attached to the black sedan's rear frame. The truck pulled forward. Inside the bay, the sedan jerked against the conveyor guides.

Dante looked in the mirror and saw Minh.

He accelerated.

Minh jumped onto the tow truck's rear platform. His feet landed on either side of the winch. He caught the cable with both hands and pulled backward.

The truck slowed.

Dante drove harder. The engine filled the yard with smoke. The rear tires spun over the wet pavement.

Minh pulled again.

The black sedan came out of the wash bay sideways, tearing the conveyor's guide rail loose as it moved. Its remaining doors flapped open. The front bumper struck the edge of the building and came off in one piece.

Leon stood beyond the yard exit.

He saw the sedan coming and ran backward toward the Cadillac.

“You said a car!”

Minh let the cable slide through his hands for one turn of the winch drum, then caught it tight.

The sedan stopped sliding.

The tow truck's rear rose.

Dante hit the brakes. Minh kept pulling the cable upward. The rear wheels lifted clear. The truck's front bumper touched the ground. Its windshield caught a reflection of the sky.

Minh jumped down beside the cab with the cable still over one shoulder.

He lowered the rear until the tires touched again, then pulled the driver's door open.

Dante was climbing across the passenger seat.

Minh grabbed the back of his trousers.

The belt broke.

Dante slid through the far door in his underwear and ran.

Minh stood holding a pair of expensive trousers.

Leon looked from the trousers to the fleeing man.

“Nigga, you got collateral.”

Dante disappeared through a gap between two warehouses. Minh took one step after him, then heard Duy shout from the wash bay.

He turned back.

The front office was on fire.

***

The broken television had landed across the open cash drawer. Smoke poured from the wiring behind it. Flames climbed the paper price list pinned to the wall.

Tú stared at the screen.

“That wasn't on when I hit him.”

Sơn shoved the last conscious gunman out through the front door. Duy had dragged the other one away from the counter and was trying to reach the extinguisher mounted behind it.

Minh took the metal cash drawer in one hand, lifted it out of the counter, and carried the burning television through the doorway on top of it.

He set both beneath the outdoor hose.

Tú turned the water on.

The screen cracked. Steam rose around Minh's arm. He stepped back as the last flame died.

Leon arrived carrying the flower driver's stolen apron from somewhere in his car.

“Why do you have that?” Minh asked.

“Emergency cloth.”

He wrapped it around the injured gunman's bleeding forearm and knotted it tightly.

Sơn watched him work.

“You a medic?”

“Nigga, I been friends with him ten years.”

Duy sat on the curb with both wrists rubbed raw. His trousers had been torn from knee to ankle. He looked at Dante's abandoned trousers in Minh's hand.

“Those his?”

“Yes.”

“Can I have them?”

Minh stared at him.

Duy looked down at his own legs.

“Just temporarily.”

Leon began laughing. He tried to stop when Duy turned toward him, failed, and walked behind the Cadillac to finish.

Minh searched Dante's pockets before handing over the trousers. He found a roll of cash, a room key, and a folded invitation to a private dinner at the Harbor Crest Club.

The invitation was for the following night.

Calvin Rook's name stood above the address.

“Get dressed,” Minh said.

Duy took the trousers.

“Where are we going?”

“Somewhere with chairs.”

***

They ate at a noodle shop two blocks away while the car-wash owner arrived to discover what three minutes had become.

The owner knew Leon. This did not improve his mood.

Minh gave him Dante's name, the invitation's address, and enough money to pay for the broken office counter. He kept the room key. The owner looked at the cash and asked whether Minh intended to return.

“No.”

“Then we're starting well.”

At the noodle shop, Duy ate three mouthfuls before speaking.

“It was supposed to be an insurance job.”

Minh put down his spoon.

“Whose?”

“Rook's. Dante said his father wanted the convoy moved. Paid me to drive. Said everybody knew.”

Leon looked at him.

“Everybody except his father?”

Duy rubbed one wrist beneath the table.

“I found out after we left. They changed the route. Dante put a gun in my lap and told me to look employed.”

“Then you gambled a Cadillac,” Minh said.

“I had keys.”

“You had a stolen car.”

“I thought if I got cash, I could leave before he found me.”

Tú stopped eating.

“You could've driven away in the car.”

Duy looked at him.

“Who are you?”

Tú pointed at his shirt.

Duy read it, closed his eyes, and returned to his food.

Minh let him finish another mouthful.

“Where is the rest?”

“Cold storage yard by Pier Nine. Last place I saw the trucks. They moved the cases into a blue container.”

“Diamonds?”

“Dante took those himself. Cash went in the container.”

Leon whistled quietly.

“Twelve million reasons not to play pool.”

Duy looked at Minh across the table.

“I'm sorry I didn't call.”

“You sold your keyboard before you called.”

“I thought you were busy.”

Minh leaned back.

Leon put his spoon down. Even Tú stopped chewing.

Duy looked from one face to another.

“That sounded worse out loud.”

“You want to work?” Minh asked.

“For you?”

“You know a container. You know a yard. You know the man who tried to fold you into a car.”

Duy nodded.

“Then finish eating. You're going to show me all three.”

Sơn raised one hand slightly.

Minh looked at him.

“Am I still driving?”

“Yes.”

The fighter nodded and picked up his spoon.

Leon leaned toward Tú.

“See? That's a profession. Put Driver on the next shirt.”

## Chapter 9: Lunch With the Wrong Old Man

The following day, Calvin Rook brought a tree to the Lê house.

It stood in a glazed pot on a velvet-covered cart, twisted branches arranged above a small bed of white stones. Two men carried the cart up the path. Rook followed them with a paper bag held carefully away from his trousers.

Hương opened the door.

She looked at the tree, the cart, and the men.

“Plant outside,” she said.

Rook smiled.

“It's a gift.”

“Still a plant.”

Minh stood behind her holding a bowl of peeled garlic. He had come to the house to collect Mai and been given a job before he reached the kitchen.

Rook saw him and lifted the bag.

“I thought we should speak.”

Hương took the bag. Inside were pastries from a bakery so expensive it did not put prices in the window.

She examined one.

“You eating?”

“I hadn't planned to.”

“Then why bring six?”

Rook looked at Minh for help.

Minh peeled another clove of garlic.

***

Rook's limousine had stopped on the cross street, twenty feet short of Bell.

He pointed this out as soon as he entered the living room.

Tín sat beneath the window repairing the wooden handle of a kitchen knife. A small clamp held the two halves together. He looked toward the street, then at Rook's shoes.

“You walked.”

“The car remained outside the boundary.”

“And sent its lawyer ahead?”

Rook lowered himself into the offered chair.

“Eight years, Tín.”

“You counting because you owe me an anniversary present?”

Minh leaned against the kitchen doorway. Rook had brought one guard inside, a man with a shaved head, heavy jaw, and hands that hung open beside his thighs. The man stood behind Rook's chair and looked around the room.

His eyes stopped on the safe beside Tín.

“That's a commercial model,” he said.

Tín returned to the knife handle.

“Then it should contribute.”

The guard looked at Rook, who made a small motion telling him to stop.

Mai came downstairs with a roll of printed paper under one arm. She stopped when she saw Rook.

“You followed my fiancé home?”

“I came to see him.”

“At my parents' house.”

Rook looked at Minh again.

Minh held up the garlic bowl.

“I'm occupied.”

Mai set the paper on the table and went into the kitchen. Rook waited until she was gone before leaning forward.

“Dante called.”

“He get trousers?” Minh asked.

The guard's mouth moved before he could stop it.

Rook turned his head.

The guard studied the safe again.

“You found my son,” Rook said.

“He keeps finding me.”

“He says you attacked him.”

“He tied Duy inside a car and tried to lower a machine through the roof.”

Rook sat very still.

Tín tightened the little clamp one turn. The wooden handle creaked.

“Duy?” the old man asked.

“He's at Leon's,” Minh said.

“The one who sings too loud?”

“Yes.”

“Tell him I fixed my radio. He can stop helping.”

Rook waited for the conversation to return to him. When it didn't, he put both hands on his knees.

“I want the convoy recovered. I want Dante brought to me. Alive.”

“Then tell him to stop firing at people.”

“He's frightened.”

“He should enjoy the novelty.”

Rook's guard looked at Minh.

“You watch how you speak.”

Tín stopped turning the clamp.

The guard noticed. Rook noticed the guard noticing.

“Outside,” Rook said quickly.

The man hesitated.

“Now.”

He went toward the front door, brushed the safe with his knee, and stumbled one step. He looked back at it as if it had moved into his path.

Tín returned to the knife.

“Nice boy. House-trained.”

***

Hương put Rook to work carrying plates.

He accepted the first stack with the cautious dignity of a man who had paid other people to carry things for decades. Minh gave him a second stack. Bích pointed him toward the porch table.

“There.”

Rook went.

Mai watched him through the kitchen window.

“He brought armed men.”

Hương tasted the broth.

“They can wash after.”

“Mom.”

“Nigga, I didn't invite their guns. I asked whether they eat.”

Mai looked at Minh. He smiled into the garlic bowl.

“You started this,” she told him.

“I was offered work.”

“And now we own two refrigerators and Calvin Rook is setting our table.”

“You want him to do the other side?”

She laughed despite herself, took the bowl, and pushed him toward the porch.

Outside, Rook had arranged the plates with an inch of space between each edge. Bích came behind him and moved every one. He watched her make the changes and said nothing.

The tree sat beside the porch steps. Hòa had returned while Rook was in the kitchen. He stood next to the pot with a screwdriver in one hand, looking at the cart beneath it.

“Wheel's bent,” he said.

“I'll replace the cart,” Rook answered.

Hòa crouched and turned the wheel one full revolution. It caught at the same point each time. He put two fingers against the metal bracket and pressed. The bracket straightened. The wheel spun freely.

He stood, wiped his fingers on a cloth, and looked at Rook.

“There.”

Rook's eyes moved from the wheel to Hòa's hand.

“Thank you.”

Hòa took the screwdriver inside. On the way, he passed Minh and touched his bandaged forearm with one finger.

“Glass?”

“Yes.”

“Your mother has ointment.”

“Mai cleaned it.”

“Then stop finding new places to put it.”

He went into the house.

Minh looked toward Tín through the open doorway. The old man had watched the wheel repair. He raised one eyebrow at Minh, then returned to removing the clamp from the knife.

Minh kept his question to himself.

***

The trouble began with the limousine's horn.

It sounded once from the cross street. Rook looked up from the porch table. A second blast followed, longer than the first.

His driver stood beside the car waving one arm. The shaved-head guard had opened the rear door. Another vehicle, a battered pickup carrying a large metal drum, had stopped behind the limousine.

Three men got out of the pickup.

Minh recognized the tire washer from Blue Palm.

Rook stood.

“Sit down,” Hương called from the kitchen. “I just brought that out.”

The guard at the limousine reached into his jacket. The tire washer hit him across the wrist with a short club. The pistol fell beneath the car. The other two men went to the rear window.

Minh put down his chopsticks.

“Are those yours?” he asked Rook.

“No.”

The pickup driver rolled the drum off its bed. Liquid splashed against the pavement.

Mai stood beside Minh.

“They followed him here.”

“I can see.”

“Get them off the street.”

Minh went down the porch steps.

One of the men saw him and shouted. The tire washer turned. His face changed. He ran back toward the pickup before either of his companions understood why.

Minh reached the limousine as the first man struck a lighter.

He caught the man's wrist, pulled the flame away from the spilled fuel, and drove him chest-first across the limousine's hood. The lighter went out. Minh lifted the metal drum with his free hand and tipped it over the man's head.

The drum was nearly empty. It dropped around the man's shoulders and caught at his elbows.

He shouted inside it.

Minh pushed him gently onto his side. He rolled into the gutter and stopped against the curb.

The second man swung the club.

Minh caught it in his left hand, snapped it in half, and hit the man's right thigh with one broken piece. The leg folded. He fell to one knee.

Minh took his belt from the buckle, looped it around the man's wrist and the limousine's door handle, and pulled it tight.

“Wait for your friend.”

The pickup reversed.

Its tire washer driver looked back over one shoulder. He did not see the blue sedan pull across the far end of the street.

Hòa got out of the sedan and shut his door.

The pickup stopped with a squeal.

Its driver looked forward at Minh, then backward at Hòa. He turned the wheel hard and tried to mount the curb.

Hòa put one hand on the pickup's tailgate.

The truck stopped. Its rear wheels spun against the road.

The engine revved. The truck shuddered against his hand. A hubcap fell off and spun around Hòa's shoe.

He looked down at it, then up at the driver.

“Turn it off.”

The driver obeyed.

Minh walked to the pickup. Hòa opened its passenger door and took the keys from the ignition without climbing in.

“He has something under the seat,” Hòa said.

Minh pulled the driver out and looked beneath it. A pistol lay beside a paper bag of cash.

He took both.

The tire washer stared at Hòa's hand still resting on the tailgate.

“Who the fuck are you?”

Hòa looked toward the porch.

“Late for lunch.”

***

Rook's guard had recovered his pistol and most of his dignity. He began threatening the man inside the drum.

Minh took the pistol from him.

“We have neighbors.”

“He attacked Mr. Rook.”

“Then call a taxi for Mr. Rook.”

Rook came down the steps with a napkin still in his hand.

The tire washer saw him and began talking immediately.

“Your son said you'd be in the car. He said just scare you. He said—”

Rook hit him.

The punch drove the man's head sideways and dropped him against the pickup. Minh caught Rook's second fist before it landed.

Rook looked at him.

For a moment the old shipping boss's face contained none of the politeness he had brought to the house. His right arm strained against Minh's fingers. His left hand opened and closed beside his thigh.

Minh held the fist where it was.

“At your house,” he said.

Rook stopped straining.

Minh let go.

From the porch, Tín called, “Calvin.”

Rook turned.

The old man stood beside the tree with the repaired kitchen knife in one hand. He used it to cut the red ribbon from the pot.

“Take your boys. Leave the pastries.”

Rook folded the napkin once, handed it to Minh, and went to the limousine.

His guard helped the man in the drum to his feet. The man's arms remained trapped. They guided him toward the pickup by turning the drum from one side to the other.

Leon arrived at that moment carrying a bag of takeout containers.

He stopped at the gate.

“Nigga, why is the lunch walking?”

***

Rook waited until Minh came to the limousine window.

“My son is out of control.”

“He learned somewhere.”

The words landed. Rook looked straight ahead for several seconds.

Then he took an envelope from the inside of his jacket.

“Tomorrow's dinner. Bring Mai.”

Minh did not take it.

“She's busy.”

“Then bring whoever you trust. I want this finished. We will discuss the recovery in front of the men whose property is missing. No more questions about your involvement.”

“And Dante?”

“Bring him if you find him.”

Minh took the envelope. It matched the invitation from Dante's trousers.

Rook noticed his expression.

“What?”

“Nothing you haven't printed.”

He stepped back. The limousine pulled away, its front window cracked, its hood dented, its owner sitting rigidly in the back.

Minh returned to the porch.

Mai had kept his plate beside hers. She gave him the napkin Rook had left and looked at the new invitation.

“Dinner?”

“Tomorrow.”

“Good. Felicia finished your suit.”

“I'm taking Leon.”

Mai raised her eyebrows.

“Nigga, Leon isn't wearing my dress.”

Across the table, Hương laughed into her cup.

Minh sat down beside Mai and opened the invitation.

## Chapter 10: Very Expensive Hospitality

The Harbor Crest Club had a canal in its dining room.

Minh stopped at the entrance and looked at the little boat floating between the tables. A man in a striped shirt stood in it with an oar. He had nowhere to go except twelve feet forward and twelve feet back.

Leon came up beside Minh.

“Rich people got indoor traffic.”

Mai took Minh's arm. Her blue dress caught the light when she moved. Felicia had given her a matching jacket and instructions concerning anything red, oily, or on fire.

“Don't break the boat,” she said.

“I just saw it.”

“You have a look.”

The boatman pushed off from the little dock. A waiter handed him a tray of drinks. He traveled six feet, stopped beside a table, and offered champagne to a man who could have reached the dock without standing.

Leon watched him come back.

“Nigga needs mileage reimbursement.”

Behind them, Sơn gave their names to the hostess. He wore a black suit over his wrist brace and held the Rolls-Royce keys in his good hand.

The hostess looked from him to Minh.

“You're driving for Mr. Trần?”

Sơn nodded.

She smiled. “My husband owes me fifty dollars.”

He put the keys in his pocket.

“Your husband bets too much.”

“Apparently.”

***

Rook had placed Minh at the center table.

Bách sat on his right. On his left waited a heavy man in a green velvet jacket who introduced himself as Eugene Moss and immediately offered Minh the use of a fishing boat.

“How big?” Leon asked.

Moss looked at him.

“Forty-two feet.”

Leon nodded gravely. “We could experience that.”

Mai sat beside Minh. Rook's hostess had put her place card at another table. Mai brought it with her, moved an empty chair, and set it down beside Minh's plate.

The hostess opened her mouth.

Mai looked up.

“Somebody sitting here?”

The woman looked toward Rook. He shook his head almost imperceptibly.

“No, ma'am.”

“Perfect.”

Bách leaned across Minh.

“You like the car?”

“Very much,” Mai said. “He fixed the seat.”

“Already?”

“I asked nicely.”

Minh looked at her.

She took a sip of water.

“The second time.”

Moss offered Minh a cigar case. Another guest sent over a bottle with a handwritten card. A waiter brought a small velvet box containing cuff links shaped like door handles.

Leon held one up.

“Nigga, your occupation got jewelry.”

Minh put the cuff link back and opened the card.

FROM THE PEOPLE WHO LEFT EARLY.

He smiled.

Rook arrived with two men behind him and a red mark across the knuckles of his right hand. He shook hands around the table, stopping at Mai last.

“You look lovely.”

“I know. Your invitation was expensive to answer.”

“I hope the evening will justify it.”

“So do I. Felicia charges for repairs.”

Rook sat.

***

Dinner began with soup and a man arguing about the stolen necklace.

He had brought his wife, who listened to three sentences before putting her spoon down.

“You did not buy it.”

“I intended to.”

“Then grieve your intention quietly.”

Bách covered his mouth with his napkin. Leon did not bother.

Rook waited for the laughter to end.

“Three vehicles have been located.”

“Two you can drive,” Minh said. “One requires optimism.”

“The black sedan was damaged by my son's poor judgment.”

“And a machine.”

Rook's fingers tightened around his spoon.

Moss leaned forward.

“What about the cash?”

Minh looked at the two men behind Rook. One stood near the kitchen door. The other watched the stairs leading to a private balcony above the dining room.

“I'm looking.”

“Looking where?”

“Places with cash.”

Leon nodded. “Targeted approach.”

Moss sat back. Bách raised his glass.

“To our recovery specialist.”

The table drank. Rook took one measured swallow and set his glass down without a sound.

From the next table, a young woman called Bách's name.

“Dad.”

Bách turned.

“You promised not to do that thing.”

“Which thing?”

“The thing where you offer people access to my life because they impress you.”

Minh glanced at Mai. She looked delighted.

Bách spread his hands.

“I haven't offered anything.”

“You asked whether he had cousins.”

“For conversation.”

“I have a husband.”

The man beside her raised one hand.

“Still here.”

Leon leaned toward Minh.

“Family networking.”

Mai touched Bách's arm.

“You can offer your restaurant. It doesn't already have a husband.”

Bách laughed, turned red, and ordered another bottle.

***

The large man by the staircase began the next problem by taking Sơn's chair.

Sơn had stood to let a server pass. The man pulled the chair away and sat in it, spreading his knees so the injured fighter had to step around him.

“Didn't know drivers ate upstairs,” he said.

Sơn looked at the chair.

“You sitting on something.”

The man looked down.

“Your future embarrassment,” Leon said.

Sơn smiled at that. The large man did not.

He stood. His jacket opened over a chest so broad that the shirt buttons had begun to turn sideways. A pale scar ran along his jaw. He took Sơn's wrapped wrist and lifted it.

“What happened?”

Minh set down his glass.

Sơn moved first.

His good hand caught the man's thumb. He stepped inside the reach, struck the man's knee with his own, and drove his forehead into the broad nose above him.

The man stumbled backward. Sơn followed with a short kick to the stomach that lifted both his feet off the carpet.

He landed across the empty chair. It broke beneath him.

The room went quiet.

Leon nodded toward the wreckage.

“He told you.”

Another guard came down from the stairs with a knife held low beside his thigh. Sơn saw him but could not turn his injured wrist quickly enough to take the grip he wanted.

Minh caught the guard's knife hand as it passed behind his chair.

He kept eating with his other hand.

The guard stopped moving.

Minh looked at him.

“You need something?”

The man tried to pull free. Minh's fingers closed. The knife fell onto the table beside the bread basket.

Mai picked up the basket and moved it.

“That was clean.”

Minh stood, still holding the wrist. He turned the man toward the canal and placed one hand between his shoulders.

The guard tried to brace.

Minh pushed.

The man crossed the narrow strip of carpet, stepped once onto the little dock, and flew into the boat. He landed on his back across both seats. The boat rocked violently. Its oarsman jumped to the dock without letting go of his oar.

Water spilled over the polished floor.

The guard sat up, reached for the gun at his ankle, and stopped when Minh picked up a heavy brass ice bucket.

Minh threw it underhand.

The bucket struck the bottom of the boat between the guard's feet and drove through it.

Water rose around his shoes.

Leon stood to see.

“You got time to rethink that ankle, nigga.”

The guard took his hand away.

Rook had gone pale.

“This is a private club.”

Minh looked at the sinking boat.

“They should keep people out.”

***

The shot came from the balcony.

Minh heard the scrape of a shoe above him and saw the barrel tip pass beneath the rail. It pointed past his shoulder, toward the kitchen door.

Duy stood there wearing a waiter's jacket.

Minh caught the back of Mai's chair and pulled it toward himself. With his other hand, he lifted the table's heavy serving tray.

The shot struck the tray at an angle and punched through it, tearing a line across the tablecloth before burying itself in the empty chair beyond.

Mai dropped beneath the table.

Minh threw the tray upward.

It struck the balcony rail and folded around the gunman's forearm. The pistol spun over the edge. Minh jumped, caught the rail with both hands, and pulled himself onto the balcony before the gun hit the floor.

The gunman swung his free hand at Minh's face.

Minh caught him by the waistband and lifted him over the rail.

The man hung above the dining room.

Every table beneath him cleared.

“Who?” Minh asked.

The man kicked. One shoe fell into a bowl of soup.

“Who?”

His eyes moved toward Rook.

Minh saw it.

So did Mai, looking up from beside her chair.

Rook stood very still at the center table.

Minh pulled the gunman back over the rail and drove him face-first into a padded bench. He stayed there.

Downstairs, Leon had Duy behind a pillar. Sơn stood beside them with the fallen pistol in his good hand.

Minh came down the stairs.

Rook stepped into his path.

“This wasn't arranged by me.”

Minh looked past him at Mai. She was standing. Her dress had a wet patch along one side from the overturned water glass. She touched her own ribs, checking, then shook her head: no injury.

Minh looked back at Rook.

“Then your hospitality needs supervision.”

He took Rook by the front of his jacket and moved him aside.

Rook's shoes left the floor. Minh set him on top of the table between the soup bowls, still upright, then let go.

The table sagged beneath him.

Nobody offered to help him down.

***

Duy had come to identify a face.

He explained this in the parking court while Sơn brought the Rolls-Royce around.

“The man who paid me before the convoy. He works in Rook's office. I wanted to see whether he was here.”

“And?” Minh asked.

“He was at the kitchen door.”

“The shooter aimed at you.”

Duy nodded.

Mai put a hand on Minh's arm.

“We all saw where the shooter looked.”

Leon stood beside the Cadillac holding the bread basket he had taken on the way out.

“I saw that too.”

Minh looked at him.

“What?” Leon said. “We paid with an evening.”

Bách came out of the club with Moss behind him. The restaurant owner had a wet cuff and a broad smile.

“You need a boat?”

Moss looked at him. “I offered a boat.”

“You offered forty-two feet. I have sixty.”

“Fishing equipment?”

“A bar.”

Leon raised one hand.

“We should inspect both.”

Minh looked from Bách to Moss.

“I need trucks.”

Both men stopped smiling for a moment.

“How many?” Bách asked.

“Enough for a container.”

Moss took out his telephone.

“I can do that.”

“And a place to open it,” Minh said.

Bách lifted his chin. “My old packaging yard.”

Mai opened the Rolls-Royce's door.

“Give him the keys. You can compete over the champagne after he comes home.”
