Bách took a key ring from his pocket. Moss began talking into his phone. Leon stood between them with the bread basket and the satisfied expression of a man watching other people cater.

Minh took Mai's hand and helped her into the car.

“You all right?”

She looked down at the water stain on her dress.

“I'm billing him.”

“Rook?”

“Everybody.”

He kissed her forehead and shut the door.

Behind him, the club's front doors opened. Rook appeared between two guards. He had a soup stain on one trouser leg.

Minh waited until the old man saw him.

Then he got into the Rolls-Royce and drove away.

## Chapter 11: A Man Named on the Cake

Gordon Peel celebrated his birthday twice a year.

“Actual birthday in March,” Duy said. “Company birthday in June. He says people work harder when they know their employer's interests.”

Leon looked at him across the garage.

“Nigga interested in presents.”

“That's what I said.”

“To him?”

“That's why I stopped getting the afternoon routes.”

Minh sat on a low stool replacing the soles of his work shoes. One of the shoes from the pawnshop roof rested between his knees. Its heel had gone through the leather and left a round hole. He pushed a thick needle through the new patch and pulled the thread tight.

“He controls the yard?”

“He has the container key. He had it around his neck at the dinner.”

“You saw?”

Duy nodded. “Red cord. Little silver key. He wears it because he doesn't trust his pockets.”

Tú stood beside the white Cadillac practicing the gesture of catching a man's wrist. He practiced it on himself, which gave the exercise an uncertain appearance.

Leon watched him.

“You win yet?”

“Working on technique.”

“Nigga, somebody has to lose. You holding both jobs.”

Mai came in carrying a flat cardboard box. She set it on Minh's bench and opened it.

Inside lay a printed portrait of Gordon Peel large enough to cover a dining table.

Peel wore a sailor's cap and smiled above the words CAPTAIN OF OUR HEARTS.

Minh looked up from his shoe.

“He ordered that?”

“Five copies. Pickup this morning.”

Duy leaned closer.

“That's his company birthday.”

“I gathered.”

Mai took out a second sheet. It showed the same face surrounded by cartoon anchors.

Leon closed his eyes.

“Nigga sponsored his own humiliation.”

Minh put the shoe down.

“Where's pickup?”

Mai smiled.

“He changed it to delivery.”

***

The party occupied the upstairs room of the Lucky Star Lounge, a karaoke bar between a tire shop and a store selling fishing equipment nobody on Bell Street had ever seen near water.

Peel had hired a cake on wheels.

It was six feet long, shaped like a cargo ship, with a sugar bridge, chocolate containers, and a small portrait of Peel fixed where the ship's name should have been. The caterer stood beside it on the sidewalk, refusing to push it up the stairs.

“You said elevator,” she told the lounge manager.

“There is an elevator.”

“For dishes.”

“It elevates.”

Minh arrived carrying the printed portraits. Mai walked beside him with the delivery receipt. Leon followed in a white kitchen jacket he had borrowed from someone who would eventually notice.

The caterer saw Minh.

“You work here?”

“Today.”

“Then solve that.”

She pointed at the cake.

Minh put the portraits in Leon's hands. He caught the two ends of the cake's steel cart, lifted it level, and carried it toward the stairs.

The caterer followed with both hands raised beneath a ship she could not reach.

“Slowly. Slowly. Those rails are sugar.”

Minh turned the cart sideways to clear the landing. Its front wheels passed within an inch of the wall. One paper flag trembled on the sugar bridge.

He kept the cart level and climbed the remaining steps.

At the top, two guards watched him emerge carrying the entire ship.

One stepped back.

The other said, “You can put it there.”

“I was hoping to,” Minh said.

He lowered the cart onto the carpet.

The caterer inspected the flag, the rails, and Peel's portrait. Then she took twenty dollars from her pocket and pressed it into Minh's hand.

“For you.”

He looked at the bill.

Mai smiled beside him.

“Good work gets recognized.”

Leon leaned toward the caterer.

“I carried the captain.”

She looked at the rolled paper under his arm.

“Then unroll him.”

***

Peel stood beneath a balloon arch wearing a real sailor's cap and a jacket covered in little brass buttons. He was short, thick through the middle, and pleased by almost everything he could see.

Minh positioned himself behind the cake while Mai handed Peel the delivery receipt.

Peel looked at her dress, then at her face.

“You were at the club.”

“You ordered the portraits.”

“You're his fiancée.”

“And a printer. We fit two things into a person now.”

Peel took the receipt.

The silver key hung on a red cord beneath his collar. Minh saw it when the man leaned forward to sign.

At the far side of the room, Duy entered carrying a microphone stand. He had slicked his hair back and borrowed a pair of glasses from Reggie. The glasses had plain lenses. They made him look like himself with confidence in reading.

Reggie followed with the camera.

“Birthday message package,” he announced.

Peel turned immediately.

“Who paid for that?”

“Friends of the captain.”

“Which friends?”

Reggie lifted the camera.

“You want names or a good angle?”

Peel adjusted his cap.

“This side.”

He turned away from Mai and faced the lens. Duy set up the microphone beside him. Leon unrolled the enormous portrait across the wall behind them.

The room applauded.

Peel smiled at the camera.

“I wasn't expecting all this.”

Mai looked at the receipt in her hand.

Minh smiled at her from behind the cake. She folded the receipt and put it away.

Duy handed Peel the microphone.

“A few words, Captain.”

Peel took it.

Then he looked at Duy.

His smile vanished.

Duy smiled harder.

“Surprise.”

***

Peel dropped the microphone and reached for the key beneath his collar.

Duy caught the red cord.

For a moment both men stood pulling opposite ends while the microphone rolled beneath a table and squealed through the speakers.

Leon winced.

“Nigga, use your indoor kidnapping voice.”

The first guard reached Duy from the side. He caught the back of Duy's jacket and pulled him away from Peel. The cord broke. The key flew across the room and landed on the cake's sugar bridge.

Peel ran toward it.

Minh stepped from behind the cart.

Peel stopped so suddenly that the guard behind him collided with his back.

“You,” Peel said.

“Happy birthday.”

Minh picked up the key.

The second guard drew a pistol.

Mai hit the fire alarm beside the door.

Bells rang through the lounge. The karaoke screen went dark. Downstairs, someone shouted that they had only just paid for the room.

The guard looked toward the door for half a second.

Minh pushed the cake cart into him.

The steel edge struck his thighs. He went over the cake's bow and landed face-first in the sugar bridge. The pistol skidded under the cart. Frosting spread across his ears.

The caterer screamed.

“I told you the rails were sugar!”

Minh caught Peel by the front of his sailor jacket and lifted him onto the cake's empty stern. Chocolate containers collapsed beneath him. He sank to his waist in sponge and cream.

Leon took a photograph with Reggie's still camera.

Peel tried to stand.

Minh pushed his shoulder down with one finger.

“Stay in character, Captain.”

***

Duy fought the first guard beside the microphone stand.

He ducked a punch, stepped behind the man's leg, and pulled him backward over the stand's heavy base. Both went down. The guard landed first. Duy rolled away with the man's jacket sleeve still in his fist.

Tú came through the doorway carrying a tray of empty glasses.

He saw the guard getting up and threw the tray.

It struck the man's forehead flat. Glasses flew in six directions. The man sat back down.

Tú looked at Duy.

“Technique.”

Leon pointed at the broken glasses.

“Inventory.”

Two more men came from the rear room. Sơn met them at the doorway. He drove the first into the wall with his shoulder, caught the second man's arm, and threw him across the first. The men tangled in the balloon arch.

Balloons burst above their heads.

The party guests began leaving in a line that became much more orderly when they saw Sơn standing beside the door.

One elderly man stopped at the cake.

“Can I get a piece?”

Minh looked at Peel embedded in the stern.

“From the other end.”

The man found a clean plate and helped himself.

***

Minh wheeled Peel into the rear room while the fire alarm continued ringing.

The room contained a couch, a drinks cabinet, and another large photograph of Peel. Minh shut the door. Mai remained outside with the caterer, who had begun naming figures in a tone that suggested each one included a personal insult.

Duy stood beside the cake. Leon blocked the door. Reggie placed his camera on a cabinet and aimed it at the man in the sailor cap.

“Turn that off,” Peel said.

Reggie checked the little red light.

“Birthday wishes should be preserved.”

Minh held up the key.

“Which container?”

“I don't know what you're talking about.”

Duy took Peel's cap off.

Peel grabbed for it.

“Don't touch that.”

“Which container?” Duy asked.

Peel looked at him with naked dislike.

“You were paid to drive.”

“And you were paid to shoot me?”

Peel shut his mouth.

Minh leaned against the drinks cabinet.

“He remembers the yard. I have the key. You're going to save me some walking.”

Peel looked at the door, then at Leon.

Leon smiled.

“I can stand too. Don't know what I charge yet.”

Peel wiped cream from his chin.

“Blue container. North stack. White patch on the right corner. Number ends in forty-six.”

“What's inside?”

“Cash cases. Three vehicles. Some equipment.”

“Diamonds?”

“Dante took those.”

“Who knows the container's there?”

Peel stared at Minh.

Minh waited.

“Rook,” Peel said.

“He knows where his missing money is?”

Peel pressed his lips together.

Duy looked away, then back.

“He paid for the move,” Duy said. “You told me that before I drove. It wasn't just Dante.”

Peel took a breath.

“The boy changed things.”

“Which things?” Minh asked.

“The diamonds. The men he hired. He was supposed to follow the arrangement.”

“And the arrangement for me?”

Peel's eyes moved to the camera.

Reggie waved one finger beside it.

Minh pushed the cake cart six inches closer.

Peel swallowed.

“You were supposed to be seen letting the loading crew through. People would ask questions. Calvin would answer them. He'd offer you help. He wanted you dependent.”

Leon looked at Minh.

“Nigga spent a hundred thousand on an invitation to get his ass kicked.”

Minh picked up Peel's cap from Duy's hand and put it back on the man's head.

“Thank you.”

Peel blinked.

“You're leaving?”

“You have a birthday.”

“The cake—”

Minh opened the door.

The caterer stood outside with both hands on her hips.

“You,” she said to Peel.

Leon stepped aside.

“Captain's available.”

***

They left through the service exit as the first fire engine turned into the block.

Mai gave Minh the paid delivery receipt. She had collected the balance from the cash box beneath Peel's gift table with the caterer watching and counting.

“Work complete,” she said.

Minh looked at the number.

“You charged him for delivery?”

“He changed the address twice.”

“I carried the cake.”

“You got twenty dollars.”

He laughed.

Reggie came out behind them carrying the camera beneath his jacket. Duy followed with Peel's sailor cap in one hand.

Minh looked at it.

Duy put it on.

“He wasn't wearing it when I left.”

Leon opened the Cadillac's trunk.

“Everybody put the evidence where it belongs.”

Tú lifted his empty tray.

“This count?”

“That's your career. Keep it close.”

Minh got into the Rolls-Royce beside Mai. She sat with the delivery envelope on her lap, her hair loosened around her face, and the little silver container key between two fingers.

“What now?” she asked.

He started the engine.

“We collect our wedding present.”

She turned the key once in the light.

“Get the large one.”

## Chapter 12: No Respectable Man Keeps a Tank

Moss's truck was armored.

Bách's truck had a bar.

Leon walked between them with the serious expression of a man choosing where to receive medical treatment.

“We can combine the features,” he said.

Minh stood in Bách's old packaging yard and looked at the two vehicles. Moss had sent a six-wheeled recovery truck with steel plates around its cab, an extending load deck built for containers, and a towing assembly heavy enough to lift an armored car. Bách had sent a long black hospitality vehicle with smoked windows, a refrigerator, and leather seats facing one another.

“I asked for something to move a container,” Minh said.

Bách opened the hospitality vehicle's rear door.

“You can put your men inside.”

“And the container?”

“Behind it.”

Moss laughed.

Bách shut the door harder than he needed to.

The packaging yard occupied a block of warehouses near the old rail spur. It had a covered loading area, two forklifts, and a corrugated shed large enough to hide several bad ideas.

Minh looked at the shed.

“What's in there?”

Bách looked away too quickly.

Leon saw it.

“Open the big present.”

***

The vehicle in the shed had tracks.

Its front blade rose almost to Minh's shoulder. A low armored cab sat behind the blade, with a circular hatch on top and a short, thick tube mounted above the windshield. Someone had painted the whole thing dark green and added a gold dollar sign to each side.

Tú walked around it once.

“Uncle got a tank.”

“It's a modified demolition tractor,” Bách said.

Leon put one hand on the blade.

“Nigga, that's a tank with employment history.”

Moss stared at Bách.

“Why do you own this?”

“A client couldn't pay.”

“What did the client do?”

“Apparently not pay.”

Minh climbed onto the track and looked through the cab window. The controls had been altered badly. Three wires hung loose below the dash. A cracked pressure gauge had been taped in place where a clock should have been.

“Does it run?”

Bách smiled.

“That's why you're here.”

Minh looked down at him.

Leon began laughing before either man spoke.

“Nigga thought he was receiving tribute. Uncle brought a repair bill.”

Bách spread his hands.

“We can both benefit.”

Minh opened the cab and climbed in.

The seat collapsed beneath him.

He sat several inches lower than expected, looking at the steering controls through the space where his knees should have been.

Outside, Tú put a hand over his mouth.

Minh looked at him through the window.

Tú turned away.

“Check the tracks,” Minh said.

“Yes, Master.”

Leon looked at the gold letters on Tú's shirt.

“Brand acquisition.”

***

Minh spent twenty minutes inside the tractor.

He removed a handful of unnecessary wiring, replaced a broken linkage with a straight piece from the tool tray, and got out to turn the engine by hand through an access panel. The great fan moved once, twice, then continued under its own power.

Black smoke climbed toward the shed roof.

Bách applauded.

Moss stepped away from the exhaust.

“You going to use that in the city?”

“Only the part where people stand in the way,” Leon said.

Minh climbed back into the cab. The track on the left moved. The right remained still. He stopped, looked through the side window, and pointed at a shipping brace bolted across the rear wheel.

Tú stared at it.

“I thought that belonged.”

“It belongs off.”

The young man found a spanner. Sơn joined him, held the brace with his good hand, and helped pull it clear when the last nut came loose.

Minh pressed the control again.

Both tracks moved.

The tractor came out of the shed with a deep grinding sound. Its blade cleared the doorway by two inches on either side. Leon walked backward in front of it, smiling like a child who had discovered that adults were allowed bigger mistakes.

“Nigga, I want to go to school in this.”

“You don't go to school,” Moss said.

“I will enroll.”

Minh stopped the tractor in the yard and got out.

“The tube?” he asked Bách.

“Foam cannon. Fire-suppression demonstration. The client showed me photographs.”

Leon looked at the tube.

“What kind of photographs?”

Bách ignored him.

Minh opened the side compartment. A large tank occupied most of it. The gauge showed pressure. He looked at the hose, followed it with his eyes, and closed the panel.

“We'll test it away from people.”

Tú lifted his hand.

“Can I sit on top?”

“Away from Tú too,” Leon said.

***

The first vehicle through the yard gate was a police car.

Carter got out, shut his door, and looked at the tractor.

Nobody spoke.

He walked across the yard slowly. His eyes moved from the tracks to the blade, from the blade to the gold dollar sign, and finally to Bách.

“Yours?”

Bách looked at Minh.

Minh looked back.

Leon leaned against the recovery truck.

“Family discussion.”

Carter stopped in front of the tractor.

“Why is it running?”

“Because it wasn't,” Minh said.

“That answer always costs me paperwork.”

He took a folded piece of paper from his pocket and held it out. It was one of the coronation flyers.

“My lieutenant got this.”

“He's welcome to donate,” Leon said.

Carter did not look at him.

“Somebody used your name to recruit men for a job at Pier Nine.”

Minh's expression changed.

“When?”

“Tonight.”

“Who told you?”

“A man who wanted to know whether the police would be there before he agreed to carry a gun.”

Moss took one step back from the truck he had supplied.

Bách watched Minh closely.

“What job?” Minh asked.

“Moving stolen property.”

“Then somebody's confusing my schedule.”

Carter folded the flyer again.

“If you go there tonight, men are expecting you.”

“Men often are.”

“Some of them will be mine.”

Minh nodded once.

Carter looked toward the tractor.

“And this stays off public streets.”

Leon raised one hand.

“What if the street becomes private while we're using it?”

Carter turned toward him.

Leon lowered his hand.

“Academic.”

***

After Carter left, Moss began walking toward his car.

Minh watched him go.

“You want the truck back?”

Moss stopped.

Bách leaned against the tractor's blade with an expression of bright encouragement.

“It's a dangerous moment, Eugene.”

Moss turned.

“My name is on the registration.”

“Then spell it clearly,” Bách said. “People will want to know who contributed.”

Minh walked to the recovery truck and put one hand on its front bumper.

“I can take the container without it. The truck keeps me from dragging it through five blocks.”

Moss looked at the hand, then at the truck.

“You really can do that?”

Minh lifted the front of the truck until both wheels cleared the ground.

He held it there while Moss watched.

Leon took out his telephone.

“Don't move. I need a witness for my mechanic.”

Minh lowered the truck.

Moss took the keys from his pocket and put them in Minh's hand.

“Keep the truck.”

Bách's smile faded.

“Keep?”

Moss straightened his jacket.

“Wedding present.”

Leon looked at Bách.

“Your tank just became shy.”

Bách took a breath.

“The tractor is yours too.”

Minh looked between them.

“Thank you.”

Tú grinned.

“We should show people broken things more often.”

***

Minh returned to the apartment after dark with oil under his nails and two sets of keys he had not owned that morning.

Mai sat on the bed sorting envelopes. She looked up as he entered.

“You smell like a bridge.”

“Bách gave us a tractor.”

She stared at him.

“A small one?”

“No.”

“For the wedding?”

“Apparently.”

Mai put the envelopes down.

“We have to stop inviting people.”

He went to the washbasin and scrubbed his hands. She watched him through the open doorway. When he finished, she came close enough to inspect the cut on his forearm.

It had closed along most of its length. A narrow red line remained near the elbow.

She touched the unbroken skin beside it.

“Does that hurt?”

“When you press it.”

She pressed it again, lightly.

He caught her hand.

“You enjoying the experiment?”

“I like proof you're still in there.”

He kissed her wrist and drew her close. She put both hands against his shoulders, leaned back to look at him, and smiled.

“You like this,” she said.

“You?”

“The cars. The gifts. Leon acting like he has a royal appointment.”

“He does. He invented it.”

“Minh.”

He looked toward the open door. Downstairs, the garage held the white Cadillac, the red sports car, a refrigerator, and more envelopes of money than he had made repairing engines in the past year.

“Yes,” he said.

Mai nodded.

“Good. I don't want to marry a man who takes all that and acts like somebody forced the keys into his hand.”

He laughed softly.

“You want the car back?”

“I have the car. I'm deciding what else I want.”

“Tell me.”

“Felicia wants the empty storefront beside mine. Bigger fitting room. Proper windows. I want the rear space for another press.”

“Then take it.”

“I was going to. I wanted you to know where some of this is going.”

He put his forehead against hers.

“And the rest?”

She pulled him toward the bedroom.

“We can discuss the rest after you stop smelling like the harbor.”

“I washed.”

“I noticed. You have more than hands.”

She closed the door with her foot.

***

Later, when Mai slept, Minh sat beside the open window and called Duy.

Leon answered.

“He asleep.”

“Wake him.”

“Nigga just stopped describing his birthday cap.”

“Carter says the yard is waiting for us tonight.”

Leon went quiet.

In the background, Minh heard a television turn down.

“We still going?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“Tell Duy to show me the roads in the morning. We're taking the container while they move it.”

Leon was silent for two seconds.

Then he said, “I'm putting my other shoes on.”

## Chapter 13: Bell Street Eats First

Duy knew four ways out of Pier Nine.

He showed Minh all four before breakfast and tried to buy breakfast with a twenty-dollar bill from Dante's trousers.

Minh looked at the bill.

“You still got his money?”

“He tried to kill me. I thought the pockets were fair.”

They sat in a diner booth overlooking the harbor road. Trucks passed beyond the window in a steady line. Duy pointed at a junction, a low bridge, and the fenced entrance to an old refrigeration plant.

“The heavy loads go through there. Other road has a weight limit.”

“Rook respects signs now?”

“Rook respects replacing an axle.”

Minh watched a truck make the turn. Its rear wheels climbed the curb by a few inches. The driver corrected, slowed, and pulled the trailer straight before continuing beneath the bridge.

“There,” Minh said.

Duy looked at him.

“That's where we take it.”

“On the turn?”

“After.”

“With cars behind it?”

“We'll be the cars behind it.”

Duy put his cup down.

“You're smiling.”

Minh looked at the truck disappearing beyond the bridge.

“It's a nice road.”

***

By the time they returned to Bell Street, somebody had put a grill across Minh's first motorcycle bay.

Leon stood behind it wearing an apron that read KISS THE MANAGEMENT. Smoke rose around his face. He held a pair of tongs in one hand and a telephone in the other.

“No, I can't come help you move,” he said into the phone. “Nigga, I have responsibilities.”

Minh looked at the grill.

Leon hung up.

“Community meal.”

“In my shop.”

“You got shade.”

“I also got gasoline.”

Leon pointed to the far wall. Every can had been carried outside and lined up beside the back door. Mai had put a handwritten NO SMOKING sign above them.

“We professional,” Leon said.

From upstairs, Mai called, “Move the grill farther out.”

Leon lowered his voice.

“Under supervision.”

Minh took the grill by both side handles and carried it onto the sidewalk. Leon walked beside it with a piece of meat still held in the tongs.

“Don't tilt, nigga. This one's nearly ready.”

Minh set it down.

Leon turned the meat.

“Perfect.”

***

The food arrived in stages.

Hương brought rice, pickled vegetables, and a pot she ordered everyone to stop opening. Bích brought herbs wrapped in damp towels and corrected the position of every bowl. Felicia brought two folding tables and a tray of cornbread she said was payment for the emotional damage Minh had done outside her shop.

“That's backwards,” Leon said. “We should be feeding you.”

“I tasted your marinade. I'm protecting myself.”

Reggie set up his camera on the furniture dealer's donated sofa. A neighborhood barber arrived carrying a portable mirror and offered Minh a free trim for the broadcast.

“It's lunch,” Minh said.

“It's public lunch. Your head has obligations.”

Mai came downstairs with a stack of plates and a grin she had been saving for the occasion.

“Sit. Let him fix it.”

“What's wrong with it?”

“You look like you cut it yourself.”

“I did.”

“We solved the mystery.”

Minh sat on the sofa. The barber tucked a towel around his collar and began working while people filled plates around him.

A young man from the basketball court stopped beside the camera.

“That's him?”

Reggie tilted the lens toward Minh.

“That's the angle.”

“I heard he picked up a van.”

Leon turned from the grill.

“You heard late.”

The young man laughed. He leaned closer to Minh.

“You the one called Little Al and told him keep his dog?”

“Al brought the dog up.”

“My cousin heard it. Said Al started saying yes before you finished.”

Minh kept his head still for the barber.

“Al can be efficient.”

The young man looked at Leon.

“Who taught this nigga to talk like that?”

Leon lifted his tongs.

“Me. Ten-year warranty.”

“You gave him a pass?”

“I gave him keys to my house. The vocabulary came with the couch.”

Minh looked at the young man through the mirror.

“You need a pass to eat, or you just standing there?”

The young man laughed hard enough to bend at the waist.

“Nah, you good, my nigga.”

Leon pointed him toward the plates.

“He was good before you got hungry. Go eat.”

***

Tú arrived with his mother.

She wore a plain green blouse and carried a covered dish. He walked half a step behind her wearing his third branded shirt.

Mai greeted the woman warmly. Tú tried to pass them and disappear near the grill.

His mother caught his sleeve.

“Tell her what you told me.”

Tú looked at the sky.

“Mom.”

“Tell her.”

Mai waited.

“I told her I had found work.”

“And who employs you?” his mother asked.

Tú pointed at Minh, who sat trapped beneath the barber's towel.

Minh met his eyes in the mirror.

Tú silently begged.

“He carried some things,” Minh said.

The mother looked at her son.

“You told me management.”

Leon came over with the tongs.

“He manages to arrive.”

“Does he get paid?”

Minh reached into his pocket and handed Tú two hundred dollars.

The young man's eyes widened.

His mother took the money before he could fold it.

“Good. He owes me for the shirts.”

She went toward the food.

Tú watched her leave with his wages.

Leon patted his shoulder.

“First day in business, Master.”

***

Tín and Hòa arrived together on foot.

Tín carried a small wooden box. Hòa carried nothing. The old man put the box in Minh's lap just as the barber finished the back of his head.

“For the wedding.”

Minh opened it. Inside lay a pair of cuff links, simple gold squares with a dark stone in each center.

“They were mine,” Tín said.

Minh took one out carefully.

“You sure?”

“I wore them. I remember.”

Mai came to look. She touched the edge of the box and kissed her grandfather's cheek.

“Thank you.”

Tín patted her hand.

The barber removed the towel from Minh's shoulders.

Minh stood and bent his head toward the old man. Tín placed one hand on the back of his neck. The pressure took him lower than he had intended, until his forehead nearly touched the cuff-link box.

Minh tried to straighten.

Tín's hand remained there.

The old man leaned closer.

“Don't lose them.”

He let go.

Minh straightened slowly. Across the sidewalk, Leon had turned away to laugh into his apron. Mai's shoulders shook beside him.

Hòa looked at his father, then at Minh.

“Put them upstairs. Then eat.”

Minh took the box upstairs.

Nobody asked for an explanation.

***

The shooting started when Leon lifted the grill lid.

A sharp crack came from the roof above the liquor store. The lid jumped in Leon's hand. He dropped it. A red line opened along his upper arm.

Minh caught him before he fell against the grill.

“Down!”

People dropped behind cars and tables. Mai pulled Tú's mother through the garage entrance. Hòa stepped in front of Bích and guided her behind the refrigerator. Tín took the pot from Hương's hands so she could move faster, then carried it inside with him.

The second shot struck the wall above the garage.

Minh lowered Leon behind the engine stand.

“Stay.”

Leon gripped his bleeding arm.

“Nigga, I wasn't going jogging.”

Minh crossed the sidewalk beneath the line of parked cars. He reached the delivery truck at the corner, put one hand on its roof, and jumped.

His feet struck the truck roof. He sprang again before the metal stopped flexing.

He cleared the alley and caught the edge of the liquor-store roof with both hands. The gunman tried to turn his rifle toward him.

Minh pulled himself over the parapet.

The rifle fired past his hip.

He caught the barrel and drove it upward through the gunman's hands. The stock struck the man's jaw. Teeth hit the roof. Minh took the rifle, broke it across the raised concrete edge, and dropped both pieces.

The gunman reached inside his jacket.

Minh drove his fist into the man's chest.

He flew backward, struck the rooftop water tank, and fell beneath it. The tank rang once and rocked on its metal supports.

Minh caught the nearest support before it buckled. He pushed the tank upright, set the bent leg against the concrete block beneath it, and turned toward a second man running for the roof stairs.

The man stopped when Minh stepped into his path.

“Who?” Minh said.

“Rook.”

No hesitation. No performance.

Minh took him by the jacket and carried him down the stairs.

***

Leon refused to leave the grill until somebody promised to turn the meat.

Hương promised. He allowed Mai and Felicia to sit him in the garage. Blood had soaked the sleeve of his white shirt. The wound ran along the outside of his upper arm.

“Does it look bad?” he asked.

Felicia examined the ruined shirt.

“On several levels.”

“I mean the arm.”

“The arm can stay. The shirt's finished.”

Mai pressed a folded towel against the wound. Leon hissed through his teeth.

“Sorry,” she said.

“No, you ain't. You been wanting me to sit down all morning.”

She smiled without easing the pressure.

Minh brought the captured man through the shop door and put him on the floor beside the motorcycle lift.

Leon looked at him.

“That the nigga?”

“He came with him.”

The man tried to speak. Minh put a hand on his shoulder. He stopped.

Outside, a siren approached.

Reggie stood at the entrance with his camera lowered. A thin cut marked one cheek where something had struck the glass beside him. His hands shook around the camera handle.

“You got him?” he asked.

Minh nodded.

Reggie looked toward Leon.

“He all right?”

“I'm fucking hungry,” Leon said.

The camera rose an inch, then lowered again.

“Okay,” Reggie said.

***

Carter arrived before the ambulance.

He took one look at the man on the floor and called for another unit. Then he crouched beside Leon.

“You always this difficult?”

Leon looked at the towel around his arm.

“I was cooking.”

“I smelled it three blocks away.”

“That's quality.”

Carter stood and went outside to speak to the witnesses. There were many. Several tried to speak at once. The barber held up a pair of scissors and complained that his client had left before he finished the front.

Minh stood beside Mai as the ambulance crew examined Leon.

Her hand found his.

“Rook?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the bullet hole above the garage.

“Then stop waiting for his money.”

Minh watched the medics wrap Leon's arm.

“I am.”

“Good.”

Across the street, a man in borrowed trousers stood half-hidden behind the phone booth.

Dante.

He lifted both hands when Minh saw him.

Minh crossed the road. Dante did not run.

“He put men at the yard,” Dante said quickly. “They're moving the container tomorrow morning. I know the truck.”

“You sent men to my home.”

“I know.”

“You tried to kill Duy.”

Dante swallowed.

“My father wants me dead too.”

“Where are the diamonds?”

Dante looked toward the men beside the ambulance.

“He sent people to my apartment. They took the case. I got out through the bathroom window.”

“You hid stolen jewelry from your father in an apartment he pays for?”

“I moved the furniture.”

Minh stared at him.

Dante lowered his eyes.

“It sounded better before I said it.”

Minh looked back toward the garage. Leon was arguing with the medics about walking to the ambulance under his own power. Mai stood beside him holding his clean jacket. Tín had returned the pot to the table and begun serving the people who remained.

Minh turned back to Dante.

“You're going to tell me about the truck.”

Dante nodded.

“Then you're going to ask Leon whether you can eat.”

## Chapter 14: The Prize Convoy

Leon arrived for the robbery wearing a sling over his best black shirt.

Mai looked at him from the hospitality vehicle's driver's seat.

“You're not driving.”

“I didn't ask.”

“You're looking at the keys.”

“Nigga can appreciate equipment.”

She opened the passenger door. Leon climbed in, settled his injured arm against his chest, and inspected the little refrigerator between the seats.

“Bách stocked it.”

“Water.”

“I was identifying options.”

Across the packaging yard, Duy sat behind the recovery truck's wheel while Dante climbed into the passenger seat. Neither looked pleased.

“You put me in a car the other day,” Duy said.

“Five days ago.”

“You improving the crime with a calendar?”

Minh opened the truck's rear compartment and took out a length of chain. He checked each end, laid it across the towing platform, and shut the lid.

Tú watched him.

“Do we have code names?”

“You have names.”

“For the operation.”

Leon leaned out of the hospitality vehicle.

“Your operation is lifting when somebody says lift. Call yourself Ready.”

Tú nodded thoughtfully.

“Ready Chigga.”

Mai covered her face for a moment.

Reggie checked his camera battery. Sơn stood beside the white Cadillac with his hands in his pockets. The wrist brace remained. He had taken the gold championship belt out of the car and left it on a workbench.

Minh noticed.

Sơn shrugged.

“It gets caught.”

Minh handed him the first radio.

“Stay in front. If they stop, keep moving until I call.”

Sơn nodded.

Minh looked at the others.

“We take the container. Nobody goes hunting for Rook.”

Dante looked down at his hands.

“He's not coming.”

“Then he won't be difficult to avoid.”

***

The convoy left Pier Nine at eight thirteen.

Dante saw the lead vehicle through the recovery truck's windshield and pointed.

“That one.”

It was a dark van with a white roof. Behind it came the container truck. Two sport-utility vehicles followed, one black and one silver. A second van brought up the rear.

The blue container had a white patch on its front corner.

Its number ended in forty-six.

Minh stood on the recovery truck's rear platform holding the rail beside the cab. The chain lay coiled at his feet. He watched the container pass the yard gate, then lifted his radio.

“Sơn.”

The white Cadillac moved into traffic ahead of the lead van.

Duy pulled the recovery truck out two vehicles behind the convoy. Mai followed at a greater distance, the black hospitality vehicle blending with the traffic until its gold dollar sign caught the sun.

Minh heard Leon over the open radio channel.

“Subtle uncle.”

Through the hospitality vehicle's window, Reggie's camera pointed toward the convoy.

The convoy reached the low bridge. Sơn slowed before the bend. The lead van's driver sounded his horn.

Sơn raised one hand through his window and continued at the same speed.

The horn sounded again.

“You can play music too,” Sơn muttered over the radio.

Behind the container truck, the black sport-utility vehicle moved outward, looking for a way around. Duy put the recovery truck into the gap before it could take it.

The vehicle's passenger looked up and saw Minh on the towing platform.

He stopped talking.

Minh nodded.

Then he jumped.

***

He landed on the container's rear locking bar with both feet together.

The bar bent beneath him. He caught the upper hinge with his right hand and brought his left foot higher until he could stand beside the door. The truck was still moving. Beneath him, the road passed in gray strips divided by the white lane markings.

The passenger in the escort vehicle raised a pistol through his window.

Minh tore the lower locking bar free and dropped it.

The steel bar struck the escort's hood, bounced through its windshield, and lodged across the front seats. The driver swerved. The vehicle hit the curb and stopped with its wheels turned inward.

Minh took the silver key from his pocket.

The lock opened on the first turn.

He pulled the right door out.

A man inside fired a shotgun.

Minh swung behind the steel door. The shot struck its inner face. He kicked the door inward before the man could fire again.

The edge hit the gunman's shoulder and drove him across the container floor. His shotgun slid beneath a parked car.

Minh stepped inside.

Two vehicles stood nose to tail on the container floor. A third occupied a steel rack above the farther car. Cash cases had been stacked and strapped around them. Four guards occupied the narrow spaces beside the lower cars. One was still trying to stand after the door hit him.

The nearest guard drew a knife.

Minh caught the man's wrist, turned him toward the rear opening, and pushed his head between the doors. He tore the remaining locking bar from its lower bracket and bent it around the man's waist and the door handle, leaving him hanging sideways against the steel.

The second guard climbed onto a car hood and raised a pistol.

Minh drove one hand through the car's side window, caught the steering wheel, and pulled the front of the car sideways.

Its tires squealed across the container floor.

The guard fell off the hood into the gap beside it. His pistol fired into the ceiling. Minh stepped onto the hood, caught the man's gun hand, and pressed it flat against the roof until the weapon fell.

The third guard looked toward the rear opening.

The road still moved beneath it.

He put his gun down.

“Good choice,” Minh said.

The man nodded rapidly.

“I got a daughter.”

“Then lie down.”

He did.

***

The truck driver had begun to understand that somebody was inside his container.

He accelerated out of the bend.

Minh felt the load shift beneath his feet. A cash case broke loose from its strap and slid toward the rear opening. He caught its handle with one hand and set it beneath the nearest car.

The case had opened an inch.

Hundred-dollar bills showed through the gap.

He closed it with his heel.

Outside, the silver escort vehicle pulled alongside the container. A man stood through its open roof holding a long gun.

Minh picked up the surrendered guard's pistol and emptied it into the container floor, away from the men. The sharp reports made the man in the escort duck instinctively.

Minh threw the empty pistol.

It hit the roof gunman's forehead. He fell back through the opening. His long gun bounced against the roof and dropped into the street.

Mai swerved around it in the hospitality vehicle.

Leon's voice came through the radio.

“He littering.”

Reggie answered from somewhere behind him.

“You want to collect it?”

“I'm retired from bending today.”

Minh climbed onto the container roof.

Wind struck his face. Ahead, the driver swung wide around a delivery van, trying to reach the open road beyond the refrigeration plant. Sơn's Cadillac remained in front of the lead escort, moving exactly slowly enough to make the driver furious.

Minh ran along the container roof and jumped down onto the truck's cab.

The roof dented beneath his feet.

The driver looked up.

Minh put his head through the open passenger window.

“Pull over.”

The driver reached for something beneath his seat.

Minh pulled the passenger door off.

He held it outside the window and looked at the driver again.

“You need a clearer view?”

The driver took his hand away from the seat.

“Brakes,” Minh said.

The truck slowed.

***

From the truck's cab, Minh saw the final van come up behind the hospitality vehicle.

Its side door opened. Leon's voice sharpened over the radio.

“Mai.”

The barrel rose toward their rear window.

Mai braked hard.

The hospitality vehicle slowed beneath the gunman's aim. Reggie swore over the open channel. The van passed on their left, its passenger staring down into Mai's side window.

She turned the wheel.

The hospitality vehicle's armored running board struck the van's rear wheel. The van swung sideways. Its gunman fell back inside as the open door slammed against his arm.

Mai straightened, accelerated, and pushed the van into the empty entrance of a tire yard.

It hit a stack of old tires and buried its nose.

“Nigga, I love weddings.”

Mai kept her eyes on the road.

“Tell him about this when he complains about my parking.”

***

The container truck stopped beside the refrigeration plant.

Duy brought the recovery truck behind it. Tú jumped down carrying the chain, tripped over its last loop, recovered, and arrived at the trailer breathing as though he had completed the hard part.

Minh took the chain.

“Driver stays in the cab,” he told Duy.

Duy pointed at Dante.

“Which one?”

“Both, if they can manage it.”

Dante folded his arms.

“I'm helping.”

“Then help quietly.”

Minh climbed beneath the trailer's rear edge. He wrapped the chain around the container's corner fitting and attached its other end to the recovery truck's towing assembly. Duy lowered the heavy boom until the chain took tension.

The container's rear rose an inch.

Minh walked to its front end, put both hands beneath the steel edge, and lifted.

The container came free of the trailer.

Inside, one guard began shouting. A car alarm sounded. The man tied to the rear door closed his eyes and held very still.

Minh stood with the container's front end across his palms while the recovery truck supported the rear.

“Move the tractor unit,” he called.

The original truck driver stared at him through the missing passenger door.

Dante climbed down, opened the driver's door, and pulled him out by the sleeve.

“He means this part, idiot.”

He got behind the wheel and drove the truck and its empty trailer forward.

For a moment the blue container hung between Minh and the recovery truck, clear of everything beneath it.

Tú stood with his mouth open.

“Stop standing there,” Minh said.

The young man snapped his mouth shut and ran to extend the recovery truck's load deck.

Minh ducked beneath the container and moved his hands inward along its underside. He reached the center, planted his feet wide, and stood. The entire container rose onto his shoulders. The towing chain went slack.

“Unhook it.”

Tú hurried to obey. Duy moved the recovery truck clear, swung it around, and backed its extended deck beneath the suspended load. Minh walked sideways until the container lined up with the platform's edges, then bent his knees and lowered it.

Steel struck steel. The entire truck settled on its suspension.

The car alarm inside stopped.

Leon arrived beside them in the hospitality vehicle.

He looked out at the container.

“That's a generous wedding registry.”

***

The lead escort returned while Minh was closing the container doors.

Sơn came around the corner behind it in the Cadillac, horn sounding continuously. The escort's driver had finally escaped him by driving over a curb and through an empty parking lot.

The van accelerated toward the recovery truck.

Minh stepped into its path.

The driver saw him and swerved toward the refrigeration plant.

Minh caught the open side-door rail as the van passed. He pulled sideways with one hand.

The van turned around him, its rear wheels sliding across the road. It struck the curb broadside and tipped onto its side.

Minh let go before it finished falling.

The roof hit the pavement. Glass burst beneath it. The horn began sounding inside the crushed front end.

Sơn stopped the Cadillac twenty feet away.

He looked at the overturned van, then at Minh.

“I kept moving.”

“I saw.”

The fighter smiled despite himself.

In the distance, sirens began.

Mai leaned out of her window.

“Minh.”

He untied the guard from the container door and lowered him to the pavement. The other three came out when he called them. He put all four beside the overturned van, away from the road.

“Your help is coming,” he said.

Then he climbed onto the recovery truck's rear step.

Duy drove.

***

At Bách's yard, the container doors opened in front of eleven people who had found reasons to be present.

Moss stood closest. Bách stood half a step behind him, then corrected the arrangement. Leon sat on a folding chair with his arm in the sling. Mai stood beside Minh holding the silver key.

Duy opened the first case.

Nobody spoke.

Bands of hundred-dollar bills filled it from edge to edge.

He opened another. Then another.

Leon slowly removed his sunglasses.

“Nigga.”

Tú nodded.

“Technical term.”

Minh counted the cases, lifted two bundles from the nearest one, checked the depth beneath them, and looked at the cars strapped farther inside.

“Eight million in cash,” he said.

Bách made a soft sound through his nose.

Moss put both hands in his pockets, took them out again, and looked at his recovery truck with visible affection.

Mai closed the nearest case.

“The doors,” she said.

Every man looked at her.

She pointed at the yard gate.

“Close them before the whole city comes shopping.”

Tú ran to the gate.

Minh looked at Mai. She looked back at him with the silver key held between two fingers.

“Large enough?” he asked.

She smiled.

“We're getting another press.”

## Chapter 15: Everybody Has a Cousin

Leon looked inside the case Minh gave him and closed it immediately.

Then he opened it again.

“Same money,” Minh said.

“I'm making sure it likes me.”

They stood in the packaging yard while Moss supervised the removal of the first car from the container. Bách had brought champagne. Mai had brought a padlock large enough to discourage casual optimism.

Leon ran one finger over the top bundle.

“How much?”

“Two hundred and fifty thousand.”

Leon put his good hand over his mouth.

Minh waited.

“Nigga,” Leon said quietly.

“You can buy your own limousine.”

“I can buy the dentist.”

Mai came over carrying another case.

“Pay Veronica first.”

Leon looked at her.

“Minh paid Veronica.”

“Then pay him.”

Minh held out his hand.

Leon took thirty dollars from his wallet and placed it in Minh's palm with great ceremony.

“My final debt.”

From the yard entrance, Marisol called, “Excuse me?”

Leon closed his eyes.

***

News of the money reached Bell Street before the cars did.

By the time Minh drove home, a line had formed outside his garage. Some people held envelopes. Some held photographs. One man carried a framed portrait of Minh that Reggie had never taken.

Minh stopped beside him.

“That's not my head.”

“Artist's interpretation.”

“That's not my body either.”

“We expanded the concept.”

The portrait showed Minh standing beside a lion in front of a building with gold windows. His left hand had six fingers. The lion wore a necklace.

Mai got out of the car and took the portrait.

“How much?”

“For you? A gift.”

She smiled.

Minh looked at her.

“You're keeping that?”

“Of course. I'm marrying a man with a spare finger.”

She carried it upstairs.

The next man in line held out a business card.

“I'm your cousin.”

Minh read the card.

The man's surname was Henderson.

“Which side?”

“Leon.”

“Leon isn't my cousin.”

“Then we early.”

Leon came up behind Minh carrying the closed money case against his uninjured side. He saw the man and stopped.

“Curtis.”

“Cousin.”

“We went to school together.”

“Shared childhood.”

“You stole my bicycle.”

“Shared transportation.”

Minh began laughing.

Curtis held his business card higher.

“I sell tires.”

“Then bring me prices,” Minh said. “Leave the family tree.”

Curtis nodded and went away smiling.

Leon watched him leave.

“Nigga gonna put our photograph on the card.”

***

Mai put a table across the garage entrance.

On it she placed three signs.

REPAIRS.

WEDDING.

WHATEVER THIS IS.

The third line became the longest.

Felicia joined her with a chair and a cup of coffee. Within ten minutes they had redirected two men looking for loans, collected the deposit on a real printing job, and informed a self-appointed wedding singer that six minutes of his voice was an audition, not an engagement.

Minh stood beside the workbench while Tú tried to explain his own payment to his mother over the telephone.

“Yes, it's work.”

A pause.

“No, I can't describe it like that.”

Another pause.

“I carried things.”

Leon went past him holding a plate.

“We paying by the thing now.”

Tú covered the receiver.

“She wants to know if it's dangerous.”

Minh looked at him.

“Tell her yes.”

Tú hesitated, then did.

The answer at the other end was long enough for Leon to finish half his food.

Tú lowered the telephone.

“She wants to talk to you.”

Minh took it.

The woman spoke for nearly a minute. He listened. He answered two questions and refused to promise something he could not do. When she finished, he looked at Tú.

“You told her you were working in a bank?”

Tú stared at the floor.

Leon put his plate down.

“Nigga has been near money. That's the curriculum.”

Minh returned the telephone.

“She's coming.”

Tú swallowed.

“Why?”

“To discuss your uniform.”

The young man looked down at the gold letters on his shirt.

***

The basketball challenge came from a man called Stretch who was not especially tall.

“My jump is tall,” he explained.

He wore red shorts, a white jersey, and a chain thick enough to strike his chin when he ran. Three friends followed him into the garage carrying a basketball and a portable radio.

“Five thousand,” Stretch said.

Minh looked up from the motorcycle on the lift.

“For what?”

“One dunk. From the line.”

“Which line?”

“Free throw.”

Leon leaned against the doorway.

“Nigga, why?”

Stretch spread his arms.

“People saying he can do anything. I'm offering recreation.”

Minh lowered the motorcycle.

“You have five thousand?”

Stretch looked at his friends. They produced envelopes, a wallet, and a folded sock.

Mai appeared at the front table.

“No sock money on my paperwork.”

Leon collected the wager in a clean plate.

“We walk to the court. Nobody films until I look ready.”

Reggie was already filming.

***

The court stood behind the community center, enclosed by a chain-link fence. Afternoon sun lay across the painted free-throw line. A group of players moved aside when they saw the crowd coming.

Stretch bounced the ball twice and handed it to Minh.

Minh wore work trousers and the shoes he had repaired the previous night.

“You want to change?” Stretch asked.

“You want more time?”

The men beside the fence laughed.

Stretch took a step back.

“From behind the line.”

Minh put one foot at the line, looked at the basket, and stepped back another pace.

Mai stood beside Leon with her arms folded.

“Don't break the court.”

Minh bounced the ball once.

He jumped.

His feet left the ground without a running start. He rose past the height of the backboard, still holding the ball in one hand. For a moment he could see over the community center's roof to the harbor cranes beyond it.

Then he came down toward the basket.

He put the ball through the rim and caught the top of the backboard with his other hand to slow himself.

The steel support bent forward.

Minh's shoes touched the ground beneath the basket. He kept hold of the backboard, pushed it upright, and straightened the support with a short movement of his shoulder.

The ball bounced behind him.

Nobody spoke.

Stretch looked at the line, then at the basket.

Leon picked up the plate of money.

“Healthy activity.”

The silence broke into shouting.

Minh walked back across the court. Reggie followed him with the camera held high. A man at the fence held out his shoes and asked whether Minh would sign them.

Mai looked at the straightened backboard.

“You nearly broke it.”

“Nearly is free.”

She laughed and took his hand.

Stretch came over with his friends behind him.

“Can I get that on tape?”

Reggie smiled.

“Separate purchase.”

***

Dante waited at the garage with Duy standing between him and the street.

He had changed into clothes Mai bought from a store down the block. The receipt remained pinned to his shirt because she had not yet decided whether he deserved to keep them.

Minh noticed the receipt.

Dante looked down at it.

“She said not to remove it.”

“Then don't.”

Duy handed Minh the telephone.

“Your number. Somebody called.”

Minh took it.

Rook's voice came through immediately.

“You have my money.”

“Some of it.”

“Eight million dollars.”

“You found it.”

“You and I had an agreement.”

Minh looked at Leon's sling.

“You shot my cook.”

Leon raised a finger.

“Executive cook.”

Rook continued as if he had not heard.

“Bring the money to me, and the misunderstanding ends.”

“You can come collect it.”

There was a pause.

“Where?”

“Bell Street.”

The line went quiet for several seconds.

Dante watched Minh's face. Duy stood with his arms crossed beside the workbench. Mai had come inside from the table and stopped where she could see the telephone.

Rook said, “You think that address protects you.”

Minh looked toward the open garage door. Outside, people were still arguing over the height of his jump. Stretch had returned to collect his portable radio and found three neighbors asking him to describe the moment from his own angle.

“You have the address,” Minh said.

He hung up.

***

That evening, the portrait with the lion went above the apartment's small dining table.

Minh stood on a chair while Mai told him which way to move it.

“Left.”

He moved it left.

“Your other left.”

“That's right.”

“Good. We're communicating.”

He fixed the hook and stepped down.

The six-fingered version of him stared proudly over the room.

Mai came to stand beside him.

“I love it.”

“You enjoy mocking your future husband.”

“I'm investing in longevity.”

He put one arm around her waist. She leaned against him and looked up at the ridiculous painting.

Downstairs, the telephone began ringing again. Minh let it ring. Mai turned toward him, caught the front of his shirt, and pulled him away from the doorway.

“Dinner first,” she said.

He followed her to the table.

## Chapter 16: The Party Is on Television

Rook bought an hour of local television and used the first six minutes to describe himself as a concerned parent.

Minh watched from the garage while Mai printed wedding place cards beside him. Leon sat on the donated sofa with his arm in the sling and a bowl balanced on his stomach.

On the screen, Rook wore a dark suit and a small ribbon supporting a harbor charity nobody in the room had heard of.

“My son has become involved with dangerous men,” he said.

Dante looked up from the sandwich Mai had allowed him to make.

“He bought me my first gun.”

Leon pointed his spoon at the television.

“Nigga, tell the host.”

The host, Joyce Dean, nodded with professional sympathy. Behind her, an enormous photograph showed Rook standing beside a fishing boat. The boat's name had been painted out of the picture.

Mai noticed first.

“That's Bách's boat.”

Minh leaned closer.

The little dollar sign on the cabin door remained visible beneath the retouching.

Leon sat up.

“Man stole the background.”

Rook folded his hands.

“A man calling himself the king of Bell Street has taken property belonging to several families.”

The phone began ringing.

Minh answered without taking his eyes off the screen.

Bách's voice came through so loudly that Mai heard every word.

“That is my fucking boat.”

***

Reggie arrived six minutes later carrying a padded bag full of tapes.

“We can answer him.”

Minh looked at the television.

“He's there now?”

“Live. Channel Six. Studio by the old post office.”

Mai took the telephone from Minh and called Felicia.

“Your clothes getting publicity,” she said. “Turn on six.”

Reggie opened the bag.

He had the ballroom footage somebody from Sơn's camera crew sold him, the flower-van attack, the cake confession, and his own recording from the convoy. He put the last tape aside.

“Maybe we keep that one at home.”

Leon looked at it.

“Excellent editorial judgment.”

Minh picked up his jacket.

Mai ended the call.

“I'm coming.”

“I know.”

“Good. I hate wasting the sentence.”

Dante stood.

Nobody looked at him for a moment.

Then Minh took the receipt off his shirt.

“You can keep that one.”

***

The station's receptionist recognized Minh before he reached the desk.

She looked at the television mounted above the waiting chairs, where Rook was still talking, then back at the man coming through her door.

“Oh,” she said.

Minh stopped at the desk.

“He's expecting me.”

On the television, Rook said, “I have made repeated attempts to speak privately with this individual.”

The receptionist looked up at the screen.

“Apparently.”

Reggie held up his community-access badge.

She stared at it.

“That expired.”

“The work didn't.”

“Last year.”

“Time is affecting all of us.”

Mai leaned on the counter.

“Calvin Rook is using footage he didn't own. The boat owner is on his way. We can either explain that here or in front of your cameras.”

The receptionist looked at Dante.

He lifted one hand.

“Concerned son.”

She picked up the telephone.

***

Joyce Dean had reached the part of the interview involving civic responsibility when the studio door opened.

Minh walked in first. Mai came beside him. Dante followed, then Reggie carrying the bag of tapes. Leon remained in the corridor arguing with a vending machine that had accepted his dollar without delivering anything.

Rook stopped speaking.

Joyce looked from him to Minh.

Her expression changed in a way that made the producer behind the glass sit forward.

“Mr. Trần,” she said. “Would you join us?”

Rook put one hand on the edge of his chair.

“This is a scheduled interview.”

“And you were discussing him.”

Joyce turned toward the empty chair beside the set.

“Please.”

Minh sat. Mai took the chair behind the camera rather than leaving the room. Dante stood where his father could see him.

Joyce folded her notes.

“You have heard Mr. Rook's concerns.”

“Some of them.”

“He says you are holding property belonging to him.”

“He paid me a hundred thousand dollars to keep a door open. His son tried to close it. Then his men shot at my home.”

Rook leaned forward.

“Those are accusations.”

Reggie lifted the bag.

“They come with pictures.”

The producer behind the glass began pointing at people. A technician came through the side door and took the first tape.

Rook watched it leave Reggie's hand.

“I will not participate in an ambush.”

Minh looked at him.

“You purchased the hour.”

***

They played the flower-van footage first.

On the studio monitor, the deliveryman's gun came out of the flowers. Mai pulled a neighbor behind the garage doorway. The cake table crossed the frame. The van's rear rose above Minh's head.

Joyce watched without looking at her notes.

When the tape ended, she turned toward Rook.

“Do you recognize these men?”

“No.”

Dante laughed once.

Rook turned toward him.

“You should be at home.”

“Which one? The one you sent men to, or the one you're telling everybody I can't leave?”

Joyce looked at Dante.

“Have you been detained by Mr. Trần?”

Dante glanced at Minh.

“He's mostly been feeding me.”

Mai held up the delivery receipt she had removed from his shirt.

“Clothing too.”

The cameraman nearest her made a small choking sound.

Rook stood.

His guard came through the studio door.

Minh remained seated.

“Sit down, Calvin.”

The guard put a hand beneath his jacket.

Minh took the empty chair beside him and slid it across the floor with one foot.

It struck the guard at the knees. The man fell into the chair involuntarily and continued backward until the chair hit the wall.

His gun dropped into his lap.

Every camera turned toward him.

Joyce looked directly at the nearest lens.

“We are going to remain with this.”

The producer behind the glass nodded so hard his headset slipped.

***

Rook's second guard reached the control room from the corridor.

Reggie saw him through the glass.

The man pushed the technician aside and reached toward the console. The picture on the studio monitor jumped, then went black.

Leon appeared behind him holding an unopened bag of chips.

He hit the man across the head with the vending machine's removable coin box.

The guard folded over the console.

Leon looked at Reggie through the glass.

“Machine owed me money.”

The technician pulled the guard's arm away from the controls. The monitor lit again.

In the studio, Rook had moved toward the exit. Dante stood in his path.

“You had Peel hire me,” Dante said.

“Move.”

“You said we'd share the business.”

“We will speak about this elsewhere.”

Dante did not move.

Rook hit him.

The slap drove Dante's head sideways. He caught himself against the wall. Before Rook could raise his hand again, Minh stood between them.

He caught Rook's wrist and turned him toward the nearest camera.

“Concerned parent,” Minh said.

Rook looked into the lens.

The little red light shone above it.

Minh let go.

Rook straightened his jacket, looked at his son once, and walked out of the studio.

Nobody followed him until his guards had recovered enough to stand.

***

Joyce stayed in her chair.

She looked at Minh, then at the empty place where Rook had been sitting.

“We still have twenty-two minutes.”

Leon came into the studio carrying the bag of chips and the coin box.

“You got food sponsors?”

Mai began laughing.

The producer opened the control-room door.

“Mr. Trần, would you stay?”

Minh looked at Reggie.

Reggie already had another tape in his hand.

They played Gordon Peel's birthday confession. Joyce asked three short questions afterward. Minh answered two. When she asked where the recovered cash was, he smiled and said Rook had already shown what happened when he knew an address.

She accepted the limit and turned to Dante.

He told the camera about the false loading order, the diamonds, and his father's plan to make Minh appear responsible. He did not make himself sound helpful. He had stolen from his father, hired men, and hurt people. The words came out unevenly. Mai watched him from beside the camera without nodding for him.

When he finished, Joyce let the silence last a second.

Then she asked whether he had spoken to police.

“Not yet,” Dante said.

Minh looked toward the studio entrance. Carter stood there with two officers behind him.

“He can now,” Minh said.

***

Bách arrived during the last commercial break.

He carried a framed photograph of his boat with its name plainly visible.

“I want a correction.”

The receptionist pointed him toward the studio.

Moss came in behind him carrying a second photograph.

“That's not the biggest boat available to Mr. Trần.”

Mai looked at both men and sat down on the waiting-room sofa.

“This is going to take a while.”

Minh sat beside her.

Through the open studio door, Bách explained the ownership of the vessel, its length, and the quality of its bar. Moss interrupted twice. Joyce allowed them to finish just enough of their argument to make both appear ridiculous and neither feel certain of it.

Leon watched on the waiting-room television.

“Excellent programming.”

Reggie stood beside the reception desk counting the tapes back into his bag.

The receptionist handed him a form.

“New badge application.”

He looked at it.

“Promotion?”

“Current year.”

He accepted the form with both hands.

***

Outside, Carter spoke to Dante beside the police car.

The young man looked at Minh over the roof. Minh nodded once. Dante turned back to the officer and continued speaking.

Mai leaned against the Rolls-Royce beside Minh.

“That won't make Rook quiet.”

“No.”

“Good. I want to hear him coming.”

Minh opened the passenger door for her.

Leon stopped beside the car with his telephone against one ear.

His face brightened.

“For that price?”

He listened, looked at his sling, and smiled.

“Nigga, I'll bring the money myself.”

Minh held out his hand.

Leon covered the receiver.

“Car. Convertible. Guy saw me on television.”

“Which guy?”

“He knows my cousin.”

Mai closed her eyes.

Minh kept his hand out until Leon gave him the telephone.

## Chapter 17: The Brother With the Keys

The man selling the convertible said he knew Curtis.

Minh asked which Curtis.

“Henderson.”

“The tire man?”

“That's him.”

Minh looked at Leon.

Leon spread his good hand.

“He expanded.”

On the telephone, the seller described a silver convertible with a black leather interior, low mileage, and a price low enough to make Leon keep leaning toward the receiver.

“Where?” Minh asked.

The man named a parking garage near the waterfront.

“Top level. Better light.”

Minh ended the call.

Leon looked at him hopefully.

“We know it's a trap,” Minh said.

“I know the price is unusual.”

“Top floor.”

“Better light.”

Mai looked at both of them from the car.

“You two are going anyway.”

Minh handed Leon back his telephone.

“I want to see who answers the door.”

Leon smiled.

“And the interior.”

***

They went the following afternoon.

Minh drove Leon's brown sedan. The blue passenger door rattled every time they crossed a patched section of road. Leon sat beside him with his sling pushed back enough to use the hand beneath it.

“Doctor said gentle movement.”

“Did he mention buying a car from men who want to kill you?”

“He was very busy.”

At the garage entrance, a ticket machine lowered its barrier in front of them.

Leon reached into his pocket.

Minh put one hand out of the window, lifted the barrier over the hood, and drove through.

Leon looked back.

“You paying when we leave?”

“Depends how the service goes.”

They climbed four levels. Each was nearly empty. On the top floor, sunlight lay across rows of painted parking spaces and a low concrete wall.

The silver convertible waited in the center.

Leon sat forward.

“Oh, that motherfucker pretty.”

Minh parked three spaces away and got out.

A man in a tan jacket came from behind the convertible carrying the keys.

“Leon?”

Leon shut his door.

“That depends whether the roof works.”

The seller smiled and pressed a button. The convertible's roof began folding backward. Its frame settled neatly beneath a cover behind the rear seat.

Leon looked at Minh.

“Even the ceiling knows when to leave.”

Minh walked around the car once. He checked the tires, looked beneath the front bumper, and opened the driver's door.

The seller watched his hands.

“You a mechanic?”

“Sometimes.”

“You can start it.”

Minh took the keys and started the engine. It settled into a smooth idle.

Leon stood beside the open passenger door with one hand on his chest.

“Nigga.”

Minh turned the engine off.

“Good car.”

The seller smiled more broadly.

Then Minh looked at the concrete stairwell behind him.

“How many men did it come with?”

***

The seller's smile vanished.

Minh caught his right wrist before the man reached his jacket. He turned him toward the convertible and pushed his hand through the open steering wheel.

“Stay close to the product.”

The stairwell door opened.

Three men came out. The first carried a shotgun. The second held a pistol at his side. The third had a short length of chain wrapped around one fist.

Leon looked at them, then at the silver car.

“You could've sold me this honestly.”

The shotgun rose.

Minh pulled the seller across the car's hood and threw him into the gunman.

Both men fell backward through the stairwell doorway. The shotgun fired into the concrete ceiling. Dust poured over them.

Leon caught the pistol man's arm as he tried to pass the convertible. He drove the man's wrist against the doorframe with his good hand, took the pistol, and hit him across the nose with it.

The man fell onto the passenger seat.

Leon looked at the blood on the leather.

“Nigga, I haven't even negotiated.”

The chain man swung at Minh.

Minh caught the chain, pulled the man forward, and lifted him by the front of his jacket. He turned once and set him on top of the brown sedan with enough force to flatten the roof to the seat backs.

The blue passenger door popped open.

Leon stared at his old car.

“That's sentimental.”

“It rattled,” Minh said.

“Because it knew me.”

The helicopter rose above the edge of the garage.

***

Its rotors drove dust and paper across the rooftop. The pilot held it just beyond the concrete wall, skids level with Minh's shoulders. A man in the open side door braced one foot against the frame and aimed a rifle toward Leon.

Minh shoved the convertible sideways.

Its tires slid across the painted surface. It struck Leon at hip height and carried him behind the stairwell wall as the first shots hit the pavement where he had been standing.

“Stay there!” Minh shouted.

The helicopter moved toward the garage.

Minh ran straight at it.

The gunman lowered his aim.

Minh jumped from the concrete wall and caught the near skid with both hands. His weight dragged the helicopter down a foot. The pilot increased power. Rotor wash flattened Minh's shirt against his back.

The gunman leaned out to aim beneath the door.

Minh swung his legs up, hooked one heel over the skid, and pulled himself high enough to catch the man's ankle.

He took the gunman out of the helicopter.

The man fell toward the rooftop. Minh held him by one leg until his shoulders were above the concrete, then let him drop the last three feet.

The rifle struck the roof beside him.

The pilot tried to pull away.

Minh put both feet on the parking wall, held the skid, and pulled.

The helicopter moved toward him despite the pilot's efforts. Its near skid struck the wall and bent around the concrete edge.

Minh stepped backward onto the roof, dragging the aircraft with him.

The pilot's mouth was open. Both his hands worked the controls. The rotors roared. Minh's shoes slid across the concrete, leaving two dark streaks.

He bent his knees and pulled again.

Both skids struck the rooftop.

The helicopter bounced. Minh caught the upper doorframe with one hand and forced it back down. The skids flattened beneath the weight. One rotor tip struck a light pole and threw a shower of sparks across the roof.

The pilot cut power.

The blades slowed through the air above Minh's head.

He opened the pilot's door.

“Stay parked.”

The pilot nodded so quickly his headset fell over one eye.

***

Leon came out from behind the stairwell carrying the pistol by its barrel.

He looked at the helicopter, then at the flattened brown sedan.

“You couldn't trade him?”

Minh wiped dust from his face.

“You want to learn to fly?”

Leon considered the helicopter.

“I want doors that stay on.”

The seller had crawled back onto the roof. He held his right wrist against his stomach and watched Minh approach.

“Who called you?” Minh asked.

“I don't know his name.”

Minh took the seller's telephone from his jacket.

The man closed his eyes.

“Rook's office,” he said.

“Which man?”

“I don't know. White hair. The owner.”

Leon walked to the convertible and opened its trunk. Inside lay a paper bag containing cash and a white envelope.

He took out the envelope.

“This got your name.”

Minh opened it.

The card inside showed a large white passenger vessel tied beside the harbor's outer piers.

THE BELL STREET APPRECIATION CRUISE.

Rook had written a message beneath the printed invitation.

YOU HAVE MONEY BELONGING TO MY FRIENDS. I HAVE A BOAT FULL OF YOURS.

Minh looked at the date.

Tomorrow evening.

Leon read over his shoulder.

The smile left his face.

“That's the free cruise.”

“What free cruise?”

“Flyers went out yesterday. Businesses got tickets. People thought Bách paid.”

Minh took out his own phone.

***

Mai answered from the printshop.

“You bought a car?”

“Later. The cruise tickets. Have you seen them?”

“A woman brought a box this morning. I told her I didn't print them.”

“Who's going?”

Mai went quiet. He heard her move away from the press.

“Some customers. The barber and his wife. Felicia's assistant. Curtis has been selling extra tickets.”

Leon closed his eyes when he heard the name.

Minh looked toward the harbor beyond the parking wall.

“Call everyone you can reach. Tell them it's cancelled.”

“What did he do?”

“He sent an invitation with a helicopter.”

“Minh.”

“We're all right. Call them.”

“I will.”

He hung up.

The seller began saying he had not known anything about a cruise. Minh ignored him and called Bách.

The restaurant owner answered on the third ring.

“Is the money comfortable?”

“Who owns the white passenger ship at the outer piers?”

Bách's voice changed.

“Rook. Through a company.”

“Then find out who he invited.”

“Why?”

Minh read the message from the card.

For once, Bách had nothing amusing to add.

***

They left the roof in the silver convertible.

Leon drove with his injured arm resting carefully on the door and his good hand on the wheel. Minh sat beside him holding Rook's invitation.

At the exit, the barrier came down.

The attendant looked at the convertible, then at the ticket Minh handed him.

“Different car.”

Leon leaned toward the window.

“Improvement.”

The attendant looked up at the top of the garage, where the bent light pole remained visible above the wall.

“What happened?”

Minh put two hundred dollars on the counter.

“Call police. Start with the helicopter.”

The attendant stared at the money.

Leon waited until the barrier rose.

“This roof works,” he said, pressing the convertible's button.

The black top unfolded smoothly above them.

For the first time since they arrived, neither man smiled.

## Chapter 18: The Wrong Suit

Felicia refused to let Minh take his wedding suit to a hostage negotiation.

“Absolutely not.”

“I'm not negotiating.”

“That made the answer stronger.”

He stood in her shop the morning after the parking garage, with Mai beside him and Leon outside admiring the convertible he had acquired without finishing the sale.

Felicia took the garment bag from Minh's hand and hung it behind the counter.

“You get married in that. You threaten people in something else.”

Mai pointed at a dark gray suit on the rack.

“That one.”

Felicia looked at it.

“That's expensive too.”

“Charge him.”

Minh turned toward Mai.

She smiled.

“Dangerous men should support local business.”

***

The cancellation calls had reached most of the neighborhood.

The barber and his wife had stayed home. Curtis had stopped selling extra tickets after Mai asked how he intended to return the money. Bách had sent his people through the restaurants and shops with a simple message: the cruise was false, the ship was Rook's, and nobody should board it.

But thirty-one people were already aboard.

They had gone the previous afternoon to prepare tables, unload food, tune instruments, arrange flowers, and clean cabins promised to the guests. Some worked for companies Rook hired. Some lived on Bell Street. Felicia's assistant, Denise, had brought table runners in the back of her brother's van and stayed to help.

Felicia had reached her once.

Then the telephone on the ship stopped answering.

Now she fitted Minh's gray jacket with more force than the cloth required.

“She said they were being told to remain below. Somebody said a security inspection. She thought it was stupid.”

“It is,” Mai said.

“Denise doesn't like boats.”

Minh looked at Felicia in the mirror.

“I'll bring her to the shop.”

Felicia held his eyes for a second. Then she looked down and smoothed the jacket's shoulder.

“Bring the jacket too. I like both.”

***

Carter met them at the packaging yard.

He came in an unmarked car and brought a younger officer who kept looking at the demolition tractor. The gold dollar signs had been covered with brown paper at Mai's request. The tracks remained difficult to disguise.

“The harbor unit knows about the ship,” Carter said. “We're trying to reach the people aboard.”

“They're answering Rook,” Minh said.

“They're not answering us.”

“That sounds like his preference.”

Carter looked at the recovery truck, the hospitality vehicle, and the row of prize cars beneath the awning.

“You planning to put on a parade?”

Leon stood beside the convertible.

“Depends how the evening goes.”

The younger officer looked at his sling.

“You were shot.”

“I remember. Ruined lunch.”

Carter stepped closer to Minh.

“Dante is cooperating.”

“Good.”

“He says his father has a second crew aboard. Men who weren't at the hotel or the yard.”

“The jewelry?”

“On the ship. Dante saw his father put the steel case in the bridge safe before they stopped speaking politely.”

Minh nodded.

“He also says Rook has told them you can't be hurt.”

Mai came up beside Minh.

“Then they should have a relaxing evening.”

Carter looked at her, then at Minh.

“He told them to shoot everyone else.”

The yard went quiet.

Leon lowered the hand he had been using to polish the convertible's mirror.

Minh put the gray jacket over his shoulder.

“Where is Dante?”

“With his lawyer. He gave us the ship's layout.”

Carter held out a folded sheet. Minh took it and opened it against the recovery truck's hood.

Three decks. Main dining saloon above. Vehicle space below. Narrow stairs between them. At the bow, a wide loading ramp lowered to the dock.

Minh looked at the lines for less than a minute and folded the sheet again.

“I need the names of the people aboard.”

Carter gave him a second page.

Minh read every name.

***

They went to the Lê house before leaving for the harbor.

Bích was ironing a tablecloth. Hương stood beside her, arguing about how much of the wedding food could be prepared early. Tín sat near the window with a bowl on his knee. Hòa had taken the doorbell apart and laid its pieces on newspaper.

Minh stopped inside the entrance.

Tín looked at the gray suit.

“Wrong day.”

“Wrong suit,” Mai said. “Wedding one is safe.”

“Good.”

Hương put down the dish in her hands.

“How many people?”

“Thirty-one,” Minh said.

Nobody asked him to explain what he meant. Mai had called ahead.

Hòa stood from the little table and went to the cupboard. He took out a small canvas bag and placed it in Mai's hands.

“Flashlights. Spare batteries. Clean cloths.”

She opened it and looked inside.

“Dad.”

“You always need something after everybody else leaves.”

She closed the bag and hugged him. He put one hand against the back of her head, held it there briefly, and let her go.

Tín set his bowl down.

“Calvin still thinks this is about money?”

Minh looked at him.

“He wants it back.”

“He can ask.”

“He sent men with guns.”

The old man stood.

For a moment nobody moved.

Then he picked up his empty bowl and took it to the kitchen.

“Finish it before the wedding,” he said as he passed Minh. “Bích already paid for flowers.”

Minh smiled despite the tightness in his chest.

“I will.”

Hương caught his sleeve and turned the cuff back to inspect the healing cut.

“New shirt?”

“Yes.”

“Then try not to bleed through it immediately.”

Mai took his hand and led him toward the door.

Behind them, Hòa tested the repaired bell. It rang once.

Tín called from the kitchen.

“That's too loud.”
