“It announces people,” Hòa answered.

“I can hear people.”

“Then ignore the bell.”

Mai laughed softly as she and Minh went down the steps.

***

At the yard, Reggie had written PRESS across a strip of tape and fixed it to his camera bag.

Leon looked at it.

“You hoping bullets read?”

“I'm hoping somebody in charge does.”

“Minh in charge.”

“Then tell him to stop walking out of frame.”

Sơn arrived with two men from his old training gym. Both looked at Minh, then at the demolition tractor, then at Sơn's wrist brace.

“You're sure?” one asked.

Sơn nodded.

“Stay with the people. Help them move. Don't chase anything.”

The man looked surprised by the instruction.

Sơn touched his brace.

“I've chased enough for the month.”

Duy checked the recovery truck's fuel. Tú counted the flashlights Mai gave him twice, then put them in the hospitality vehicle. Bách and Moss stood by the gate arguing over which of their boats could reach the outer piers faster.

“Yours has a kitchen,” Moss said.

“People get hungry on water.”

“Mine has two engines.”

“Then it gets hungry faster.”

Minh went between them.

“Both.”

They stopped.

“Bring both boats. Keep them outside the pier until I call.”

Bách nodded first. Moss nodded harder.

Leon watched them leave.

“I love a competitive donor.”

***

Rook called as the sun began lowering behind the warehouses.

Minh answered beside the gray suit hanging from the truck's open door.

“You're coming,” Rook said.

“Yes.”

“With my money.”

“With a million.”

“Eight.”

“One gets you to the deck. Thirty-one people walk down the ramp. Then we discuss your disappointment.”

Rook breathed into the line.

“You don't set conditions.”

Minh looked at the cash case on the seat beside him. Mai had packed it herself. A million dollars filled it tightly enough that the lid needed both hands to close.

“Then enjoy your evening without me.”

He began lowering the phone.

“Minh.”

He raised it again.

“The million comes aboard first.”

“And the people leave.”

“We'll see.”

Minh hung up.

Mai came around the truck and handed him the case.

“He's not letting them leave.”

“I know.”

She opened her canvas bag, checked the flashlights one last time, and shut it.

“Then keep the receipt.”

Minh put on the gray jacket.

Leon gave a low whistle.

“Nigga, that's a very expensive bad decision.”

Mai straightened Minh's collar.

“That's why we're bringing it home.”

## Chapter 19: Dinner on Moving Water

The Monarch had been decorated for a party nobody wanted to attend.

Strings of lights hung between its upper railings. White cloth covered the dining tables visible through the windows. A banner above the loading ramp welcomed Bell Street in letters large enough to read from the shore.

Minh stood at the foot of the ramp carrying the million-dollar case.

Mai stood beside him with the canvas bag over her shoulder.

A guard came down the ramp holding a radio.

He looked at Minh, then at Mai.

“Only him.”

Mai looked past the guard at the banner.

“You invited the street. I'm on it.”

“Mr. Rook said—”

“Mr. Rook keeps saying things,” Minh told him. “Move.”

The guard looked toward the ship.

Rook stood behind the glass of the main dining saloon. He lifted one hand.

The guard stepped aside.

Minh and Mai walked up the ramp together.

***

The ship's vehicle deck smelled of diesel, paint, and the food being kept warm above it. A line of wheeled laundry carts stood against one wall. At the far end, two steel doors led to the lower service rooms.

Men with radios stood beside both doors.

Minh counted six visible guns before he reached the stairs.

The guard behind him noticed where he was looking.

“Nobody wants trouble.”

Minh looked at the man's pistol.

“You packed for it.”

Mai went up the stairs first. At the top, another guard tried to take her bag. She opened it herself and showed him the flashlights, cloths, and spare batteries.

He looked disappointed.

“What did you hope for?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Then enjoy your surprise.”

She closed the bag and continued into the dining saloon.

Rook waited beside a table set for two.

Minh looked at the two chairs.

Mai pulled over a third.

Rook watched her place it.

“You take liberties.”

“You keep buying the wrong number of chairs.”

Minh set the cash case on the table.

Rook's eyes went to it immediately.

“Open it.”

“The people first.”

“You came onto my ship.”

Minh clicked the case open just enough for the money to show.

Rook stopped speaking.

Minh shut it again.

“Thirty-one.”

Rook looked at Mai, then at the guard by the stairs.

“Bring them up.”

***

They came into the saloon in small groups.

The first woman wore an apron with food stains down the front. A man behind her carried his shoes in one hand. Two musicians followed with instrument cases held against their chests. The woman from Felicia's shop, Denise, came next, one sleeve torn where somebody had grabbed it.

She saw Mai and stopped.

“Felicia?”

“Waiting at the shop.”

Denise began to cry, caught herself, and wiped her face angrily.

“I told her I could do this delivery by myself.”

“She knows.”

“She's going to say it.”

Mai took her hand.

“Several times. You'll have opportunities to answer.”

Minh stood beside the table and watched the groups arrive. He matched faces to the names Carter had given him as Mai asked each person who they were. Some answered quickly. Others needed the question twice.

Rook grew impatient.

“They're all here.”

Minh looked at the line.

“Thirty.”

“Thirty-one.”

“Count again.”

Rook's guard counted with his finger. He stopped at the last man and looked toward his employer.

Rook turned away from him.

“One is part of the marine crew.”

“Gus Navarro,” Minh said.

The guard's eyes moved.

“Where?”

“Below,” Rook said. “Keeping the ship ready.”

“Bring him.”

“We can't leave the machinery unattended.”

Minh took the case handle.

Rook reached for it.

Minh looked at his hand.

The hand stopped above the table.

For several seconds the saloon was quiet except for the engines beneath the floor.

Then Rook said, “Let these people leave. We'll bring Navarro up when his replacement is ready.”

Mai looked at Minh.

He nodded toward the stairs.

“Take them to Carter.”

She hesitated only long enough to press her hand against his wrist.

“Thirty,” she said.

“I know.”

She led the line out of the saloon.

***

The first ten reached the pier without trouble.

Sơn met them at the foot of the ramp with two of his gym friends. Duy stood beside the hospitality vehicle helping people into seats. Reggie filmed from beside the rail, keeping the camera low enough that the arriving workers did not have to speak to it.

Leon waited with water bottles in a crate.

“Take two,” he told the first woman.

“I only need one.”

“Then surprise yourself later.”

Upstairs, Minh watched through the saloon window.

Rook stood beside him.

“Your friends are safe.”

“Twenty still on the stairs.”

“You make everything laborious.”

Minh looked at the cash case.

“You could've bought a rubber doorstop.”

Rook's mouth tightened.

On the pier, Mai helped Denise down the last section of ramp. A musician nearly dropped his case. Sơn caught it and passed it back without opening it.

Twenty people ashore.

Rook walked away from the window and picked up a telephone mounted on the wall.

Minh watched his reflection in the glass.

“Keep it at idle,” Rook said.

The engine note changed beneath Minh's feet.

He put the cash case on the table, opened it, and took out a single bundle.

Rook turned.

Minh placed the bundle beside the case.

“That gets your attention faster.”

Rook came back toward the table.

The last ten workers went down the ramp.

Mai remained at the bottom until the final man stepped onto the pier. Then she looked up toward the saloon window and held up three fingers, followed by a closed fist.

Thirty.

Minh nodded.

Rook's guard shut the door to the stairs.

***

“Now,” Rook said, “we finish.”

Minh looked at the closed door.

“Where's Navarro?”

“You have a million dollars on my table and seven million elsewhere. Let's discuss that.”

“You have one man downstairs.”

Rook picked up the loose bundle. He weighed it in his hand, then placed it neatly on top of the others.

“I gave you an opportunity.”

Minh took the bundle back and put it in his jacket pocket.

Rook stared at him.

“Deposit,” Minh said. “For my time.”

The guard by the stairs drew his pistol.

Minh kicked the table toward him.

The table struck the man's hips and pinned him against the wall. His pistol went off into the ceiling. Plates fell across the carpet. The cash case slid toward the edge.

Rook caught it.

Minh crossed the room in two strides, took the guard's gun, and bent it against the door handle. He struck the man once beneath the ribs. The guard folded over the table and stayed there.

Behind Minh, a second guard came through the service door.

Rook shouted, “The money!”

The guard looked toward the case instead of Minh.

Minh picked up a chair and threw it across the room. It caught the man across the chest and drove him back through the service doorway. Wood cracked against the frame.

Minh turned toward Rook.

The old man had gone through a narrow door behind the bar with the case in his hands.

Minh reached it as a steel panel dropped across the opening.

The panel struck the floor.

From the other side, Rook's voice came through a speaker.

“You should have accepted a place.”

Minh put both hands beneath the panel's lower edge.

“I keep getting offered furniture.”

He lifted.

***

The panel rose six inches, then jammed in its track.

Minh changed his grip and pulled outward. The lower edge bowed toward him. Bolts tore loose from the floor. He lifted again and drove one shoulder beneath the gap.

The steel folded around his back.

He stood upright with the panel across his shoulders and pushed until the top came out of the wall. The whole barrier fell behind him into the saloon.

The passage beyond was empty.

A stairway led down toward the engine spaces. Another led up to the bridge.

Minh heard a man shout below.

He went down.

***

Navarro was locked inside a maintenance room beside the engine compartment.

Minh found him by the sound of a wrench striking the door from the other side. The man was short, broad through the shoulders, and furious enough that he continued swinging after Minh pulled the door open.

The wrench stopped an inch from Minh's face.

Navarro stared.

“You the guy?”

“Which guy?”

“The one they keep saying can't be killed.”

“Not testing that today. Come on.”

Navarro stepped out. One of his ankles was swollen above his shoe. He leaned against the wall before taking another step.

“They wanted me to disable the ramp controls.”

“Did you?”

“I took a fuse. Told them the whole thing was broken.”

Minh looked at him.

Navarro took a small object from his pocket.

“I do repairs. I can make a convincing problem.”

Minh smiled and took his arm.

“You're going to enjoy meeting my fiancée.”

***

Above them, the engines rose to a deeper note.

Minh felt the deck shift beneath his shoes. Through a small round window at the end of the passage, the pier began moving backward.

The Monarch was leaving.

He brought Navarro up the service stairs and onto the vehicle deck. The bow ramp had risen halfway. Beyond its narrowing opening, Mai stood on the pier with one hand against the rail.

She saw him.

“Gus?”

Minh held Navarro higher so she could see his face.

“Thirty-one.”

The gap between ship and pier widened.

Behind Minh, footsteps struck the stairs.

He looked back.

Six armed men came down toward the vehicle deck.

Minh put Navarro behind a laundry cart.

Then he took off Felicia's gray jacket and laid it over the man's lap.

“Hold that.”

## Chapter 20: The Groom's Side

The six men stopped at the foot of the stairs.

They had helmets, body armor, and the uncomfortable expressions of people discovering that expensive equipment had not changed the person waiting for them.

Minh rolled his shirtsleeves above his elbows.

Navarro sat behind the laundry cart with the gray jacket across his lap.

“Should I cover my head?” he asked.

“Keep the jacket clean.”

“That's the priority?”

Minh looked at him.

Navarro folded the jacket once and put it beneath his own shirt.

“Understood.”

The nearest guard raised his rifle.

Minh kicked the laundry cart.

It rolled across the vehicle deck and struck the guard before he could finish aiming. He fell backward into the man behind him. Both went down beneath a rain of clean towels.

The second pair spread out.

Minh lifted another cart by its frame and threw it sideways. It hit both men across the waist and drove them into a parked baggage tractor. One helmet struck the tractor's steering column with a sound like a dropped pan.

The last two fired.

Minh was already beneath their line of aim. He slid across the wet deck on one knee, caught the first man's rifle, and pulled him into the second. The gun went off between them. Both men tried to retreat in different directions.

Minh stood with the rifle held crosswise across their throats.

He drove them backward into the wall and lifted.

Their boots left the deck.

“Drop them.”

Two guns struck the floor.

Minh lowered the men, took one by each collar, and put them inside an open laundry cage. He pulled its steel mesh door across them and bent the latch through the handle.

The first guard beneath the towels began crawling toward his rifle.

Minh stepped on it.

The guard looked up.

“I would like to stop,” he said.

“You're doing well.”

***

The ship had moved far enough from the pier that Minh could no longer hear the people ashore.

He could see them through the opening above the raised ramp. Mai stood beside Carter at the rail. Sơn and Duy were moving toward the little dock where Moss's boat had arrived.

Minh found the side access hatch Navarro pointed out and pulled it open.

Water slid past beneath them. The hatch stood twelve feet above the surface. A narrow service platform ran along the hull below it.

“That ladder folds down,” Navarro said.

Minh looked at the ladder.

Its upper hinge had been secured with a padlock.

He broke the lock in his fist and dropped the ladder.

Moss's fishing boat came around the Monarch's stern, its twin engines throwing white water behind it. Bách's larger vessel followed with lights burning along its upper deck.

Leon stood on Moss's bow wearing the sling over a black life jacket.

He looked up at Minh.

“Nigga, we came from the groom's side.”

“Get closer.”

Moss shouted toward his helmsman. The boat rose on a wave and fell beside the ship's hull. Its bow came within three feet of the ladder, then dropped away again.

Minh took Navarro beneath the arms and lowered him toward the service platform.

Navarro gripped the ladder with both hands.

“My ankle won't hold.”

“You don't need it.”

Minh climbed down behind him and held his belt. He waited for the fishing boat to rise again.

Sơn stood beside Leon, arms ready.

The bow came up.

Minh let Navarro swing outward, guided his weight across the gap, and placed him in Sơn's hands.

The fighter caught him against his chest. Leon steadied them both with his good arm.

The boat dropped away.

Navarro sat hard on the deck, still holding the gray jacket beneath his shirt.

Leon looked at the bulge.

“You stole something?”

“Apparently I'm transporting a national treasure.”

He handed over the jacket.

Leon took it with great care.

“Felicia's. Correct.”

***

Minh started down the ladder.

Gunfire struck the hull beside his head.

He pulled himself back through the hatch as metal sparked around the opening. Above, on the upper deck, a man leaned over the rail with a gun braced against his shoulder.

Minh looked toward the fishing boat.

Leon had dragged Navarro behind the cabin. Sơn stood in the doorway holding the injured man steady. Moss was shouting at the helmsman to move out.

Minh took the hatch cover in both hands and tore it away from its hinges.

He stepped onto the service platform and threw it upward.

The steel cover rose past the railing and struck the gunman from below. His weapon flew into the air. He fell backward out of sight.

Minh caught the upper rail and pulled himself onto the deck.

The gunman lay beside a row of stacked chairs. Another man came around the corner carrying a short weapon with both hands.

Minh seized the stack of chairs and pushed it into him.

The chairs slid across the deck, struck the man at knee height, and carried him toward the stern. He fell on top of them. Minh followed, took his gun, and threw it overboard.

The ship's horn sounded.

Minh looked toward the bridge.

Rook stood behind its front window holding the million-dollar case. He lifted it so Minh could see.

Then he pointed toward the shore.

***

At first Minh saw only the harbor lights.

Then a line of headlights appeared on the road leading toward Bell Street.

Four vehicles. A truck. More lights behind them.

His telephone rang.

Mai's voice came through, fast and clear.

“They're moving toward the shop. Carter got a call. Men at both ends of the street.”

“Where are you?”

“With him. I'm going back.”

“Stay with Carter.”

“He's going back too.”

Minh looked at Rook through the bridge window.

The old man smiled.

Minh put the telephone away.

Rook tapped the case once with his fingers.

Minh walked toward the bridge.

The door beside it opened. Four more guards came out, spreading across the narrow upper deck.

Minh picked up the nearest deck chair and broke it across the first man's arms. He drove the chair's remaining frame over the second man's head and shoved him into the third.

The fourth fired into the pile.

Minh caught the gunman's wrist, turned the weapon toward the sky, and drove his elbow into the man's face. The nose collapsed. The man fell against the bridge wall.

Minh reached for the door.

Inside, Rook turned a wheel beside the helm.

The Monarch heeled sharply.

Minh's feet slid across the deck. A loose chair struck his ankle. Below, the fishing boat had to turn hard to avoid the ship's swinging stern.

He looked down and saw Leon and Sơn struggling to keep Navarro behind the cabin as the smaller boat rolled through the wake.

Minh let go of the bridge door.

He ran to the rail and jumped.

***

The gap between the ships was wider than the parking garage's roof.

Minh crossed it with his arms held forward and his eyes on the fishing boat's bow. The boat rose beneath him. He landed on its foredeck, knees bending, and caught the rail before his momentum carried him through it.

The bow plunged.

Water came over the front and struck Leon in the chest. He grabbed the cabin door with his good hand and swore until the boat rose again.

Moss stared at Minh through the windshield.

“You could have waited.”

“For what?”

Moss looked at the churned water behind them and reconsidered.

Minh took the radio from the bracket beside the helm.

“Bách. Follow the Monarch. Stay far enough away that his men can't use you for practice.”

Bách answered at once.

“Where are you going?”

“Home.”

Leon pushed wet hair out of his eyes.

“That nigga just went to everybody's house.”

Minh looked toward Bell Street.

“Then we're going to make him regret the route.”

***

At the dock, Navarro tried to give the gray jacket back.

Minh took it and laid it over Leon's shoulders instead. The injured man had begun shivering as the evening wind moved through his wet shirt.

“Put that on.”

“Felicia will kill me.”

“Tell her I said.”

“Nigga, she knows you.”

Sơn helped Navarro onto the dock. Two medics came forward with a chair. Navarro sat, looked back at Minh, and lifted one hand.

“You got thirty-one.”

Minh nodded.

Then he turned toward the parked hospitality vehicle.

Duy stood beside it with the engine running.

“Mai took the Rolls,” he said.

“Carter?”

“Ahead of her.”

“Drive.”

Duy got behind the wheel. Leon climbed in beside him. Sơn and Tú took the rear seats. Reggie remained at the dock long enough to hand one tape to an officer, then ran to the vehicle with his camera under his jacket.

Minh stood beside the open door and looked once more toward the water.

The Monarch had turned toward the industrial yards beyond the old freight terminal.

Rook still had the diamonds.

He had the million-dollar case.

He had a ship full of men who kept accepting work.

Minh got in.

“Bell Street,” he said.

Duy drove hard.

## Chapter 21: A Street Full of Presents

Rook's men blocked Bell Street with three trucks and discovered that the residents considered parking a personal issue.

The first driver stopped across the bakery entrance. Its owner came outside holding a broom and began shouting before the man had finished getting out.

The second truck blocked Marisol's loading space. She took a photograph of its number plate, then another of the driver when he told her to stop.

The third truck reached the Lê house.

By the time Minh arrived, Hòa was standing beside it with the driver's door in his hand.

The driver remained in his seat.

Minh stopped the hospitality vehicle at the corner and got out.

Hòa looked toward him.

“He parked across the gate.”

Minh looked at the detached door.

“Did you ask him to move?”

“We had a conversation.”

The driver stared straight ahead.

Hòa set the door against the wall and went back into the courtyard.

Minh continued toward the garage.

***

Mai had brought the Rolls-Royce across the shop entrance at an angle. Behind it, Felicia and Hương were taking people through the rear passage into the next building. Carter's car stood sideways at the intersection with its lights flashing.

Six armed men occupied the sidewalk opposite.

Their leader wore a tan coat and held a radio. He saw Minh and took one step back before remembering his audience.

“Where's the money?”

Minh looked at the trucks.

“You bring receipts?”

“Rook wants what's his.”

“Then he should come ask for it.”

The man raised the radio.

Minh crossed the street before the man's thumb reached the button.

He caught the radio hand, turned it outward, and pressed the man's own knuckles against his cheek.

“You can tell him that.”

The other men raised their guns.

Minh lifted their leader by the back of his coat and held him between them.

“You first?” he asked the man on the left.

The man lowered his barrel an inch.

The leader struggled.

“Shoot him!”

“He's holding you,” the man said.

“I can see that!”

Leon leaned out of the hospitality vehicle.

“Strong briefing, nigga.”

The gunman nearest the bakery fired.

Minh turned. The bullet struck the wall beside his shoulder. He threw the leader into the shooter, caught the nearest parked motorbike by its handlebars, and swung its rear wheel into the next man's legs.

The man fell flat. Minh set the bike on its stand before going after the others.

The bakery owner stared at her motorbike.

“You scratched it.”

“Later,” Minh said.

“I am keeping track.”

***

Two men ran toward the garage.

Mai stood behind the Rolls-Royce with a flashlight in one hand and the tire iron in the other. She shone the light into the first man's eyes as he came around the car. He raised a hand. She struck his gun wrist with the tire iron and kicked him backward into his companion.

The pistol fell beneath the Rolls.

Minh reached them before they recovered.

He caught the first man by the front of his shirt and put him headfirst into the laundry machine standing beside the garage door. The man's shoulders stuck in the opening. His legs kicked against the polished front.

The second man looked at the machine, then at Minh.

“I quit.”

“Put it down.”

He placed his weapon on the sidewalk.

Mai took the keys from his pocket and pointed him toward Carter.

“That man wants to talk.”

The man went quickly.

Carter looked at him, looked at Mai, and took out his handcuffs.

From inside the washing machine, the trapped man shouted that he couldn't breathe.

Minh pulled him out by his belt and sat him beside it.

“Then stop shouting.”

The man took several large breaths.

Leon came up carrying a bottle of water.

“You want to rinse?”

Mai turned toward him.

“Go sit down.”

He went.

***

The remaining truck accelerated toward the intersection.

Its driver had turned the vehicle so its steel front guard pointed at Carter's car. The officer moved two arrested men behind the nearest building and reached for his radio.

Minh ran toward the truck.

Before he reached it, the demolition tractor came around the corner.

Tú stood in its hatch wearing a life jacket over his gold-lettered shirt.

Sơn drove.

The tractor's blade met the truck's front guard with a crash that shook the shop windows. The truck stopped. Its cab pitched forward. The driver hit his air bag and disappeared in a puff of white fabric.

Tú looked down through the hatch.

“Was that the brake?”

Sơn said something Minh could not hear.

The foam cannon fired.

A thick white stream crossed the street and struck the truck's windshield. It spread across the cab, poured over the hood, and covered the driver as he tried to open his door.

Tú vanished into the hatch.

The stream stopped.

For a moment everyone stared at the white mound where the truck had been.

Then Leon called from the garage.

“Nigga ordered the wedding package.”

Minh reached the truck and pulled its door open. Foam slid around his shoes. He took the coughing driver out and put him on the sidewalk.

Carter came over with his radio still in one hand.

He looked at the tractor.

“I told you to keep that off the street.”

Minh pointed at Sơn in the cab.

“Different driver.”

Carter looked at Sơn.

The fighter lifted his wrapped wrist.

“I was following instructions.”

Tú's voice came from inside the hatch.

“Not mine!”

Carter closed his eyes briefly.

***

The gunmen at the far end of the block decided to leave together.

They had a van and a narrow space between the parked cars. The driver reversed toward the cross street while three men climbed through the side door.

Tín stood beside the curb holding a covered dish.

The van's rear corner came toward him.

Minh saw it from the intersection.

“Grandfather!”

Tín turned his head.

He put his free hand on the van's rear panel.

The metal folded inward around his palm. The van stopped so abruptly that all three men in the back fell toward the driver's seats. Its rear tires spun against the pavement.

Tín looked at the covered dish in his other hand.

He set it on a parked car's roof, took the van's bumper in both hands, and lifted the rear until the wheels hung at the height of his chest.

The driver took his foot off the accelerator.

The old man tipped the van gently toward the open side door.

Three guns slid out onto the road.

One man followed them and landed on his hands and knees.

Tín lowered the van.

He picked up the covered dish and looked toward Minh.

“They can wait,” he said. “This gets cold.”

Minh stopped running.

Across the street, Hòa leaned against the courtyard gate and watched his father carry the dish toward the garage.

He caught Minh looking and shrugged once.

Then he went to help Carter collect the men from the van.

***

The street smelled of foam, exhaust, and the food Hương insisted on reheating once the shooting stopped.

More police cars arrived. The surrendered men sat along the curb with their hands behind them. Several kept looking toward Minh as if he might be persuaded to change their location.

He stood beside the Rolls-Royce while Mai examined a scratch running along its front wing.

“That's deep,” she said.

“I can fix it.”

“I know. I'm deciding what you owe me while you do.”

He put one hand at her waist and pulled her close.

She looked up at him.

For a moment the police radios and shouting neighbors became less important than whether her breathing was steady.

It was.

He kissed her.

Leon looked away with exaggerated politeness.

“Public affection. I support it.”

“Then stop narrating,” Mai said without letting go of Minh.

***

Bách called from the water.

The Monarch had reached the old freight terminal and tied up beside a loading pier. Men were moving equipment from the shore onto its lower deck. Rook had brought another truck to the ramp.

“What's he loading?” Minh asked.

“I can't see from here. Crates. Steel cages. He has the lights on the pier turned toward us.”

“Keep watching.”

“Minh.”

“What?”

“My boat has several bullet holes.”

Minh looked toward the tractor.

“I'll bring you something with thicker sides.”

He ended the call.

Mai watched him put the telephone away.

“You going back?”

“He keeps sending people here.”

She looked at the men along the curb, then at the family gathered inside the garage.

“Finish it.”

Minh nodded.

He went to the tractor and climbed onto the track. Sơn opened the hatch for him.

“Can you drive the recovery truck?” Minh asked.

Sơn nodded.

“Then put this on it.”

Tú leaned out of the hatch.

“We taking the tank?”

Minh looked at the gold dollar sign showing through the torn brown paper.

“We're returning a call.”

## Chapter 22: Rook's Last Bid

The demolition tractor reached the freight terminal on the back of Moss's recovery truck.

Its foam cannon pointed at the sky. Its blade hung over the rear edge. Tú sat in the hatch wearing a bicycle helmet somebody had found in the garage.

Leon looked up at him from the hospitality vehicle.

“That helping?”

Tú tapped the helmet.

“Safety.”

“Nigga, we appreciate the gesture.”

Minh stood on the recovery truck's rear platform as they rolled toward the terminal gate. Beyond it, the Monarch lay beside the loading pier with its upper decks lit white. Men moved along the railings. A line of trucks blocked the approach to the bow.

Bách's boat waited farther out, its cabin lights turned low. Moss had taken his fishing boat to the opposite side. Carter's harbor officers kept their vessels beyond both, watching the ship's windows and the armed men behind them.

Minh's telephone rang.

Rook.

He answered.

“You brought a tractor,” Rook said.

“Wedding present.”

“You think this is a joke.”

Minh looked at the burned sleeve hanging from the bakery owner's arm as she stood safely behind Carter's line farther down the road. She had come to identify the men who fired through her window. Mai stood beside her, holding a bottle of water against a small burn.

“No.”

Rook was silent for a second.

“Seven million. Additional. You return what you took, and I pay you seven.”

“You shot Leon.”

“He is alive.”

“He had a clean shirt.”

Rook breathed hard into the telephone.

“Ten million.”

Minh looked toward the ship.

“You should have started with the shirt.”

He hung up.

***

The first gate opened before the tractor reached it.

A guard came out holding both hands at shoulder height. He wore a radio on his belt and had removed the gun from the holster beside it.

“I'm leaving,” he said.

Minh nodded toward the road behind them.

The guard went past the recovery truck. He stopped beside Leon.

“You hiring?”

Leon looked at him.

“Can you drive?”

“Yes.”

“Can you avoid shooting the employer?”

“Yes.”

Leon took a card from his pocket.

“Promising start.”

Mai watched the guard leave with the card.

“You have cards?”

“Curtis printed them.”

She held out her hand.

Leon gave her one.

LEON PRICE. LUXURY TRANSPORTATION. FAMILY-ADJACENT.

Mai stared at the last line.

“He charged you for that?”

“It's a very specific service.”

Minh stepped off the recovery truck and walked through the gate.

The laughter behind him stopped as the first shot struck the road at his feet.

***

The gunman stood behind the windshield of a parked truck.

Minh moved toward the truck's left side. The gunman leaned across the cab to follow him. Minh caught the driver's door handle, pulled the door open, and put his other hand through the windshield.

Glass broke around his forearm.

He caught the rifle just ahead of the trigger guard and pulled it through the glass. The gunman came with it until his chest hit the steering wheel.

Minh bent the rifle across the doorframe and dropped it.

“Get out.”

The man got out.

Minh turned him toward the open gate and pushed once between his shoulders.

“Keep going.”

Behind the first truck, three more engines started.

The trucks had been parked nose to tail across the pier. Their drivers began moving them into the gaps, closing the approach to the Monarch's ramp. Men with guns climbed onto the roofs.

Minh lifted his radio.

“Sơn.”

The recovery truck lowered its rear platform.

The tractor rolled down.

***

Minh climbed into the tractor's cab while Tú scrambled out of the hatch and onto the pier.

“I thought I was operating.”

“You operated the helmet,” Leon called. “Come here.”

Minh put the tractor in motion.

Its tracks bit into the old pier surface. The blade met the first truck below its bumper and lifted. Metal folded. The truck's front wheels rose off the ground.

The men on its roof jumped down.

Minh turned the tractor and pushed the truck sideways into the second vehicle. Both slid across the pier until their wheels hit the raised edge beside a stack of pallets.

The driver of the third truck tried to reverse.

Minh caught its rear with the blade and shoved it forward into the space the first two had left. The truck climbed the edge of an empty loading platform and stopped with its front wheels hanging over it.

The driver opened his door and jumped.

The foam cannon fired once.

White foam struck the men running between the trucks. One fell. Another tried to climb over him and went down too. Their guns disappeared beneath the spreading mound.

From the hospitality vehicle, Leon watched through the open window.

“He better not bring that to the reception.”

Mai looked at the white-covered pier.

“The photographs would be spectacular.”

***

The Monarch's loading ramp stood open.

It was wide enough for two vehicles, with steel rails on either side and heavy hinge housings where it joined the ship. A truck carrying stacked steel plates had been parked halfway up it. Another load of dense machinery sat near the upper end, secured by chains to the ramp's structure.

Minh stopped the tractor before the lower lip.

He could see the added weight.

He could also see Rook watching from the bridge.

The machinery had been chained directly to the ramp. Its outer lip rested on the pier; its inner edge joined the ship at two enormous hinge housings. Heavy hydraulic arms ran along both sides. Men stood beside their control cabinets.

Minh got out of the tractor.

He looked back at Mai, Leon, Duy, Sơn, Tú, and Reggie. The six had come through the cleared approach and stood behind the last truck.

“Stay on the pier,” he said.

Mai looked at the ramp, then at the ship's open lower deck.

“You need someone outside the door.”

“I have several.”

“Then stop choosing for all of them.”

He held her gaze for a second.

Then he nodded toward the rail.

“Keep the radio. If that ramp moves, everybody off it.”

She took the radio from his hand.

***

Rook's voice came over the ship's loudspeaker.

“You could own a place in this city.”

Minh walked up the ramp.

“I have a garage.”

“I mean power.”

Minh stopped beside the truck full of steel plates and looked toward the bridge.

Behind him, the terminal gate stood open. The trucks blocking the pier had been pushed aside. Rook's men were surrendering to officers at the road or hiding beneath foam.

Minh lifted one hand.

“You mean permission.”

Rook did not answer.

Minh continued up the ramp.

Three men waited inside the vehicle deck with long steel poles. They had chosen weapons that kept them farther from him than a fist would.

The first thrust his pole toward Minh's chest.

Minh caught it, pulled the man forward, and used the far end to strike the second man's knee. The second man fell. Minh turned the pole in both hands and swept the third man's feet out from under him.

The first tried to let go and run.

Minh caught his jacket.

“Too late for the first half. Still time for the second.”

He shoved the man toward the open ramp.

The man ran.

***

Inside the vehicle deck, Rook had stacked crates in two rows with a narrow passage between them.

Minh moved through the passage. A gunman stepped from behind the left row. Minh pushed the nearest crate into him. The crate burst against the opposite stack, spilling coils of rope across the deck.

A second man fired from farther back.

Minh dropped, caught one rope coil, and threw it around the gunman's legs. He pulled. The man fell forward and struck his chin on the deck. Minh reached him, took the gun, and drove it into the gap beneath a steel support until its grip broke off.

Behind him, Mai came through the opening with Sơn beside her.

Minh turned.

She held up the radio.

“Carter has men on the pier. Nobody is leaving that way with a weapon. I'm watching this side.”

Sơn stood at the entrance to the crate passage. His good hand closed around a loose pole.

“I can do doors,” he said.

Minh looked at the brace on his other wrist.

“You already do driving.”

“Expanding.”

Mai smiled at him.

From above, a motor began turning.

The loading ramp lurched sideways.

***

Duy shouted from the pier.

“The support's going!”

Minh turned toward the opening.

The ramp's shipward edge dropped. The two hinge housings were tearing away from the bow. Its outer lip still rested on the pier, but the truck and the chained machinery were pulling the inner end toward the water.

Leon stood halfway down the ramp with Reggie beside him. They had been helping a wounded guard onto the pier. The steel tilted beneath their feet.

Mai ran toward them.

“Off! Now!”

Duy and Tú caught the wounded guard from below. Leon pushed Reggie toward their reaching hands.

The broken inner edge dropped another foot.

Minh ran past Mai and planted his shoes against the ship's fixed threshold. He bent, caught the ramp's torn edge with both hands, and lifted.

The ramp stopped falling.

The truck's chocks split.

Its load began rolling toward Minh.

## Chapter 23: A Door Wide Enough

The truck rolled toward Minh with its load of steel plates.

He had both hands beneath the ramp's broken edge. His feet rested on the ship's fixed threshold. Behind him, the vehicle deck remained level. In front of him, the ramp sagged between his hands and the pier.

The truck's front tires came within a foot of his fingers.

Minh lifted his right knee and put it against the bumper.

The truck stopped.

Its grille folded around his knee. The steel plates struck the front of the load bed with a crash. A chain snapped and whipped across the ramp.

Leon ducked beneath it. Reggie fell flat beside him, one arm over the camera.

Mai grabbed the back of Reggie's shirt and pulled him toward the pier.

“Leave the camera!”

“It's attached!”

“Then bring it faster!”

Minh pushed with his knee. The truck moved uphill six inches. He pushed again. Its tires rolled over the broken chocks and stopped against a twisted section of railing.

Below the load bed, labels named the weights of the steel bundles. Minh read them, added the machinery chained beside the truck, and glanced at the ramp builder's plate near his hand.

Ninety tonnes on the span.

The torn steel edge cut through his palms.

He bent lower and put his left shoulder beneath it.

***

Sơn came beside him carrying a length of steel from the broken guardrail.

“Under it?”

“Against the fixed deck. There.”

Sơn pushed the steel brace into the space between the ramp and the ship's threshold. He set its lower end against a raised support.

Minh let the weight touch it.

The brace bent in the middle.

Sơn jumped back as it snapped out of place and struck the wall behind him.

Minh took the weight again.

“Off the ramp,” he said.

“I can help.”

“Then help them walk.”

Sơn looked at the men still on the span. Two of Rook's guards lay near the truck's rear wheels. One had a wounded leg. The other had frozen with both hands gripping the side rail.

The fighter went to them.

“Up.”

The man with the wounded leg shook his head.

Sơn put his good arm around the man's waist and lifted him.

“Your employer's leaving. Mine says move.”

He began carrying him toward the pier.

The second guard followed.

***

Minh heard the engines before he saw the water move.

The Monarch pulled backward.

The ramp's outer lip scraped along the pier. Inch by inch, it approached the edge. Every movement sent the truck's load settling toward Minh again.

He looked up at the bridge.

Rook stood beside the helm. He had one hand on a lever and the million-dollar case at his feet.

Mai saw him too.

She took the radio from her belt.

“He's reversing. He's pulling the ramp away.”

Navarro's voice came through from Carter's boat.

“Emergency stop on the lower control panel. Beside the service stairs.”

Mai turned toward the vehicle deck.

Minh caught her eye.

“Stay behind the crates.”

She nodded and ran.

A guard appeared at the top of the service stairs. He saw her and raised his pistol.

Minh took his right hand off the ramp.

The weight drove harder into his left shoulder. The skin beneath his collar split against the torn edge. He reached down, caught a loose piece of hinge housing, and threw it across the vehicle deck.

The metal struck the guard in the chest and drove him back up two steps. His pistol went off into the stairwell wall. He fell across the landing.

Minh put his hand back beneath the ramp.

Mai reached the control panel and pulled its cover open.

Behind the wall, something clicked.

The engine note began falling.

The ship kept moving backward under its own momentum.

***

The outer lip of the ramp reached the pier's edge.

Leon was on the pier now. Duy had one arm around Reggie. Tú was helping Sơn lower the wounded guard onto a pallet. Carter's officers ran forward to take the men clear.

Minh saw the last pair of feet leave the ramp.

Then the pier disappeared from beneath it.

The entire span dropped into his hands.

His knees bent. Both feet slid backward across the threshold. He drove his heels against the raised steel strip at the edge of the deck and held.

The Monarch's bow dipped.

The truck rolled six inches toward him, struck his knee again, and stopped.

Pain ran from Minh's hands to his shoulders in one hard line. He lowered his head, drew one foot beneath his hip, and lifted the ramp's inner edge another inch.

The far end hung above the water.

Bách's boat was beneath it.

Its captain had brought the vessel around the pier to collect the last men if the span failed. Now the broken ramp covered half the boat's foredeck. Bách stood beside the cabin, looking straight up at the truck hanging above him.

For once, he had forgotten to say anything.

Minh shouted down.

“Move!”

The boat's engines roared. Its bow swung toward open water, then struck a floating timber knocked from the pier. The captain reversed, turned, and tried again.

Minh held the ramp.

***

Mai came back across the vehicle deck.

She stopped when she saw the ramp clear of the pier.

Minh's shirt had gone dark at the left shoulder. Blood moved between his fingers and dripped from the ramp's underside.

She looked down at Bách's boat.

“How long?”

“Ask him.”

Her radio crackled.

Bách's voice came through, suddenly very close and very angry.

“I'm trying!”

“Try forward,” Mai said.

“There is a timber.”

“Then stop apologizing to it.”

The boat's engines rose again. Its bow pushed the timber aside. Water broke white along both hulls as it began moving out from beneath the ramp.

Minh's right heel tore through his shoe.

He felt the steel strip beneath it begin bending away from the deck.

He moved his foot to the next welded section and held the weight steady.

Mai stood beside him, close enough that her hand could reach his face. She wiped blood from the corner of his eye with a clean cloth from Hòa's bag.

“Can you see?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I need you looking at me when I complain about this.”

He gave a short laugh that hurt his shoulder.

The boat's stern passed beneath the ramp's outer corner.

Bách waved both arms.

“Clear!”

Minh looked down once to make certain.

Then he pushed the broken span away from the ship.

***

The ramp fell flat into the harbor.

The truck and machinery went with it. Water rose above the Monarch's lower deck and struck the bow in a solid white wall. Minh turned, caught Mai around the waist, and put his back between her and the wave.

Water drove them three steps into the vehicle deck.

Loose rope, pieces of wood, and a broken wheel swept past his legs. He held Mai against him until the water began running back through the open bow.

Behind them, Bách's boat rose on the wave and fell hard into the trough. The restaurant owner disappeared behind the cabin rail and reappeared holding both hands above his head.

Leon stood on the pier, drenched again.

His voice came over the radio.

“Nigga, I am running out of dry opinions.”

Mai laughed once against Minh's chest, then stepped back and looked at his hands.

He flexed his fingers.

All ten moved.

“That enough?” she asked.

He looked toward the bridge.

“Nearly.”

***

The men remaining on the Monarch began leaving their weapons where they stood.

One put his rifle on a crate. Another laid a pistol beside the service stairs and raised both hands when Minh approached. A third stepped from the passage leading to the crew rooms with his jacket open and his empty palms visible.

“There's a way off at the stern,” he said.

Minh nodded toward it.

The man went.

Sơn came through the side access hatch from Moss's boat. His brace was wet. A new tear ran down one trouser leg.

He looked at the open bow, where the ramp had been.

Then he looked at Minh's hands.

“You want me with you?”

“Stay with Mai.”

Mai opened her mouth.

Minh looked at her.

“He needs work.”

She closed her mouth, considered that, and nodded once.

Sơn accepted the assignment with the seriousness he had once reserved for a championship belt.

Minh took the clean cloth Mai offered and wrapped it around his left hand. He used his teeth to pull the end tight.

The gray jacket had remained with Leon. His shirt hung torn across one shoulder. One shoe had no heel.

He went up the stairs.

***

Rook waited outside the bridge with a pistol in his hand.

The million-dollar case stood beside his right foot. A smaller steel case rested on top of it.

Minh recognized the red velvet caught in its clasp from the auction's necklace display.

Rook watched him reach the top step.

“You could have let it fall.”

Minh looked at the two cases.

“You could have let people leave.”

The old man raised the pistol.

Minh kept walking.

## Chapter 24: Keep the Receipt

Rook fired from twelve feet away.

Minh stepped behind the bridge's steel door. The shot punched through its square window, spraying glass across the empty wheelhouse. He caught the door's outer edge and shoved it back toward Rook.

The door hit the old man's gun arm against the railing.

The pistol fell into the water.

Rook pulled his arm free before Minh could close the last three feet. He had moved quickly enough to preserve the elbow. He drove his other hand into Minh's injured shoulder, fingers stiff and together, and followed with a knee to the abdomen.

Minh grunted.

Rook hit him again, stepping into the punch with his whole body. The old man's polished shoes gripped the wet deck. His jacket had torn beneath one arm. He still looked determined to be photographed from his good side.

“You should have taken the ten million.”

Minh caught the next punch.

The cloth around his left hand darkened. Blood ran between their joined fingers. Rook tried to pull away and could not.

“You should have given it to me earlier,” Minh said.

He turned Rook's fist downward. The old man bent at the waist, resisting with both legs, and struck at Minh's ear with his free hand. Minh moved his head. The blow glanced off his cheek.

“You can still walk out with it.”

“I already have eight.”

“Eight isn't ten.”

“I'm good at subtraction, Calvin.”

He let go and hit Rook once in the chest.

The old man flew backward through the wheelhouse entrance. His shoulders struck the captain's chair and tore its base from the floor. Chair and man traveled together until the chair's back hit the control console. The metal frame folded around his hips.

The ship's horn sounded.

It continued sounding because Rook's left shoe had landed on the button.

Minh came through the doorway and lifted the shoe away.

Silence returned except for a slow electrical ticking and Rook's effort to breathe.

“That's enough announcements.”

Rook looked down at the chair around him.

He pushed against one armrest. It held.

He tried the other. A small movement in his chest made him stop.

“Help me out.”

Minh crouched and checked the space between the chair's frame and Rook's ribs. The steel had trapped his jacket and belt. It had not entered his body.

“Stay there.”

“I can't breathe.”

“You keep finding enough air to negotiate.”

He went outside and brought in the cases.

***

The smaller case held the diamonds.

Minh recognized the broad necklace from the auction catalog Mai had printed. The stones lay in a red velvet curve beside three watches and two loose packets. Rook had packed them without their display stands. A large yellow stone occupied a separate compartment.

Minh picked it up between two bloodied fingers.

“This one yours?”

Rook watched him.

“They're all mine.”

“You said they belonged to your guests.”

“They were being sold on consignment.”

Minh wiped the yellow stone on a clean patch of his trousers and set it back.

“That sounds like a guest with extra steps.”

He shut the case.

Below the bridge windows, Moss's boat had come alongside the stern. Harbor officers were boarding by the service ladder. Minh could see Carter behind the first two uniforms, one hand holding the rail and the other pressing his hat against the wind.

Rook saw him too.

“Ray doesn't understand what happened here.”

“Then talk slowly.”

“You think they won't ask where the money is?”

Minh looked at the larger case.

“There's some right there.”

Rook's expression changed. For a second the anger left it. What remained was an older and uglier calculation.

“I know what you are. You put on the family dinner and the little wedding, but you're going to want another ship. Another street. Men to stand up when you enter a room. You won't be fixing motorcycles forever.”

Minh leaned against the open door. His shoulder throbbed. Salt had dried across his lips, and his left shoe made him stand unevenly.

“I like fixing motorcycles.”

“You like being the man who can afford to.”

Minh considered that.

“Yeah.”

The answer seemed to trouble Rook more than an argument would have.

Minh pointed through the broken window toward the boats.

“I also like that one. The blue one with the two engines.”

“Moss doesn't give things away.”

“Neither do I. He'll get something.”

“You could have had all of this through me.”

“Calvin. Look where you're sitting.”

Rook looked down despite himself.

One arm of the chair had caught the chain of his pocket watch. The watch hung beside his knee, still ticking.

He tucked it into his pocket with great care.

***

Carter stopped in the doorway.

He looked at Minh, the ruined console, and the seated man.

“Is he stuck?”

“Yes,” Rook said.

“I was asking the person who put you there.”

Minh nodded.

Carter came closer. He did the same practical inspection Minh had done, looking for where the steel pressed against Rook's body. Then he turned to the two officers behind him.

“Get medical up here. Tell them we need something for the chair.”

“Bolt cutters?” one asked.

“Start with optimism.”

Minh took the chair's two bent arms and pulled them apart.

The left one snapped loose at its mounting. The right straightened enough for Rook to move. Minh held it while Carter helped the old man stand.

Rook's legs shook. He hid it by straightening his jacket.

“I want my attorney.”

“That's an excellent plan,” Carter said.

He turned him toward the wall.

Rook looked over his shoulder at Minh.

“My son will come to his senses.”

“He's twenty-nine,” Minh said. “If you're still waiting, bring a chair.”

Carter glanced at the wrecked seat.

“A different chair.”

One officer failed to suppress a laugh. Rook stared at him long enough to memorize his face. The officer stopped laughing, then remembered where Rook's hands were and resumed looking thoroughly unimpressed.

Minh gave Carter the smaller case.

“The auction jewelry.”

Carter opened it and let out a low breath.

“You know whose?”

“Mai printed the catalog. She has the list.”

“And that one?”

He indicated the cash.

“He took it from me.”

“It comes with us tonight.”

Minh sighed.

“You always arrive when the shopping is over.”

“Try inviting me before the shooting.”

“Nobody dresses properly.”

Carter shook his head and sent an officer for the case.

He lowered his voice.

“All thirty-one accounted for. Navarro's ankle is ugly, but he's talking to everybody about it. Your people are clear.”

Minh looked out at the water again.

Mai stood on the lower deck beside Sơn, speaking into the radio. She had one of Hòa's clean cloths over her shoulder. She looked up as if she had felt him watching.

He raised his unwrapped hand.

She counted his fingers from below and raised her own.

Carter followed his gaze.

“Go let somebody look at those hands.”

Minh started for the door.

Rook spoke behind him.

“Tell your wife's grandfather I haven't forgotten him.”

Minh turned.

“He remembers you every time his boat needs paint.”

***

Mai met him halfway down the stairs.

She looked at his face first. Then she took his right hand carefully between both of hers and turned it palm upward. The skin had split across two knuckles. His nails were intact. His fingers closed when she asked them to.

“And the other.”

He offered it.

“That cloth was white.”

“Your father packs good cloth.”

“My father packs for you like you're a natural disaster he likes.”

She tightened the loose end of the bandage, gently enough that he did not have to pretend it didn't hurt.

Sơn remained three steps below, looking out over the deck with the strained concentration of a man guarding a private moment.

“You can turn around,” Mai told him.

He turned.

“He's coming,” she said.

“Good.” Sơn looked at Minh's shoulder. “Can you climb down?”

Minh stared at him.

Sơn spread his good hand.

“I'm asking because she's standing here.”

Mai nodded approval.

“Keep asking.”

They took the service ladder to Moss's boat. Minh went down first. Mai followed, refusing his offer to carry her, then put her foot on his shoulder when the ladder swung too far from the rail.

“You said no carrying.”

“This is a step.”

He steadied her ankle and helped her onto the deck.

Leon waited there in the gray jacket, his sling damp and his expression grave.

“Before anybody says anything,” he began, “I have a financial question.”

Minh sat on a bait cooler.

“Naturally.”

Leon reached into the jacket pocket with his good hand and produced the bundle of cash Minh had taken from the case.

“Does this come with the suit?”

Mai closed her eyes.

“That's Felicia's jacket.”

“Then she is a hell of a tailor.”

Minh held out his hand.

Leon put the bundle into it reluctantly.

“I wasn't stealing. I was checking the care instructions.”

Minh peeled off several notes and passed them back.

“Dry cleaning.”

Leon looked at the money.

“Nigga, I could dry-clean the ocean.”

***

The ride back took twenty minutes.

For the first five, everyone spoke at once. Reggie wanted to know if the camera had caught the ramp from the pier. Tú insisted the foam cannon had saved more people than anyone was admitting. Duy tried to tell the part where he had backed the recovery truck between two parked trailers without touching either. Sơn told him he had touched one. Duy said touching wasn't hitting and received no support.

Then Moss brought the boat around the breakwater, the water became calmer, and the noise gradually thinned.

Minh sat with Mai beside the cabin. She had cleaned his face and put a folded towel behind his shoulder. A harbor medic had wrapped both hands before they left. The bandages made his fingers look too large for the cup of water she gave him.

“Drink.”

He did.

“More.”

He did.

Leon watched from the opposite bench.

“See, that's marriage. Same thing the police say, but they bought you the cup.”

Mai pointed toward the bow.

“There's a beautiful view up there.”

“I'm enjoying this one.”

She kept pointing.

Leon stood and went forward, carrying the cash for the cleaning in his jacket pocket.

Minh rested his head against the cabin wall.

“Eight days.”

“I know.”

“You'll still have me?”

Mai looked at his torn shirt, the bandages, and the shoe missing its heel.

“At the moment you look discounted.”

“Buy now.”

She leaned over and kissed the unbruised side of his mouth.

“I already paid a deposit.”

He moved closer, letting his shoulder settle against hers. The lights of Bell Street appeared beyond the harbor warehouses. Someone on Bách's boat behind them sounded a horn. Moss answered with two blasts, and Leon immediately asked whether that was something a passenger could control.

“No,” Moss said.

“I'm not a passenger. I'm luxury transportation.”

“Then transport yourself away from the horn.”

Mai laughed into Minh's neck. He felt it through his whole body and closed his eyes for a moment.

At the landing, Hương waited with three cars and enough food to suggest they had been lost for a month.

Tín stood beside her holding Minh's other shoe, the good pair he had left at the house that morning. Hòa held a clean shirt over one arm.

Minh stepped from the boat.

Hương took one look at him.

“Hospital first.”

“I'm hungry.”

“You can eat in the car.”

Tín handed him the shoes.

“You owe me a ride tomorrow.”

Minh looked up.

“Where?”

“Your wedding tailor. I don't trust your friends to explain sleeves.”

Hòa held out the shirt.

Minh let Mai help him into it. Leon climbed into the nearest car and opened a food container before anyone could assign seats. Tú tried to sit beside him and was told that particular seat was occupied by rice.

Hương put the rice in Leon's lap.

“Now it isn't.”

The first car pulled away with all its windows open and Leon trying to eat one-handed without spilling anything on Felicia's jacket.

Minh watched it go, then took Mai's hand as carefully as the bandages allowed and followed her to the next car.

## Chapter 25: Everybody Brought Something

The emergency room gave Minh a plastic bracelet and a bill.

“You haven't done anything yet,” he told the woman at the desk.

She took the clipboard back.

“That's why it's still small.”

Mai laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Minh went through the examination with her beside him. The doctor pressed along his shoulder, made him turn his head, and stared at the cuts in his palms with a puzzled expression. He asked what had fallen on Minh.

“Part of a ship.”

“Which part?”

“The part that opens.”

The doctor looked at Mai.

She nodded.

“He's being accurate. It's unusual.”

They cleaned his hands, closed the worst cuts, and took pictures of his shoulder. Nothing was broken. The doctor studied the films twice, then asked Minh to raise his arm.

He raised it.

“Does that hurt?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop doing it.”

Mai pointed at the doctor.

“I want that written down.”

By the time they were allowed to leave, Leon had convinced a vending machine attendant to refund a dollar for crackers he had already eaten. Duy slept upright beneath a magazine about sailing. Tú had told three strangers they were waiting for Master Minh, and all three had moved to the other side of the room.

Hương stood as soon as the examination door opened.

“Home.”

Nobody argued.

***

The next morning, someone delivered a hospital bed to the garage.

Minh watched it come through the roller door on a lift gate. It had controls on the rail, a polished wooden footboard, and a card from Bách.

Leon read the card.

“For the comfort of a giant among men.”

Mai took it from him.

“He spelled giant wrong.”

“He bought the big bed. The meaning is there.”

Moss arrived ten minutes later with a massage chair.

The chair had leather arms, a padded cradle for the head, and more switches than Minh's motorcycle lift. Moss had brought a man to explain it. Bách's delivery driver remained to defend the bed.

“This one reclines,” the chair man said.

“So does this,” the driver said.

“Heated back.”

“Wheels.”

“Three massage programs.”

“He can piss without getting up.”

Mai put down her coffee.

“Both of you stop selling my fiancé a lifestyle.”

Minh sat in the chair.

The chair man hurried over and pressed two switches. The padded back began moving. Minh leaned into it, closed his eyes, and let out a satisfied breath.

Moss smiled at Bách's driver.

“There.”

The hospital bed's driver took out his phone.

“I need to call my boss.”

Leon lay down on the bed and raised the headrest.

“Tell him this one's also doing numbers.”

***

Duy came in carrying a paper bag and a pair of trousers on a hanger.

The trousers were clean. Their crease was sharp. A dry-cleaning tag dangled from the waist.

“For Dante,” he said.

Minh opened one eye.

“You giving them back?”

“I don't want him saying I owe him.”

“You owe him a beating.”

“That's why I had the pockets checked.”

He set the hanger against the wall and offered the paper bag to Mai. It contained sweet rolls from the bakery on Bell Street. She took one and pointed him toward the empty stool beside Minh.

Duy sat.

For a while he watched the chair knead Minh's shoulders.

“How much is one of those?”

“Try getting shot at by a millionaire. They arrive.”

Duy picked at the paper bag's folded rim.

“Carter said I have to go back tomorrow. With the lawyer.”

Minh nodded.

“Go.”

“I'm going. I just wanted you to know.”

The chair hummed. Outside, somebody tested the hospital bed's wheels on the driveway and was immediately told by Mai that it was not a skateboard.

Duy looked down at his hands.

“I thought if I came out of that first job with money, I'd stop being the guy who borrowed it.”

“Then you gambled the Cadillac.”

“That was after.”

“Strong system.”

Duy made a small, unhappy smile.

Minh opened both eyes and looked at him.

“You drove well at the yard.”

“I know.”

“Don't ruin a compliment.”

“Sorry.”

“You drove well at the pier too.”

Duy nodded, more carefully this time.

“Moss needs somebody who can move that recovery truck without folding his fence. He asked me.”

“A real job?”

“Mostly.”

Duy looked up.

Minh smiled.

“You live here, Duy.”

Mai came back through the garage door.

“He starts Monday,” she said. “And if he borrows money from you before Friday, tell me.”

“Why Friday?” Duy asked.

“I want to enjoy four days.”

He took the empty paper bag, folded it flat, and stood.

“I'll do it.”

Minh held out his wrapped fist. Duy touched it gently with his own.

Then he reached for the trousers.

“Leave them,” Mai said. “His lawyer's coming by.”

Duy looked relieved.

“Good. Because he still doesn't like me.”

“He took your pants off in a car wash,” Minh said. “You're allowed a complicated friendship.”

***

The lawyer arrived with a box of cigars, a bottle of expensive wine, and a handwritten note from Dante.

Mai opened the note.

She read it silently, then handed it to Minh.

It contained four sentences. Dante thanked them for letting him leave the television station alive. He apologized for the flower van and the men at the dress shop. He said his lawyer had advised him not to discuss details in writing. The final sentence said that he had ignored this advice because the lawyer had never met Mai.

Minh passed the note back.

“He's learning.”

The lawyer stood beside the massage chair in a suit that looked too warm for the morning.

“My client would like to know whether there is anything further he can do.”

Mai gave him a folder.

“Three estimates for the front windows. One for the roof. A letter for Felicia's landlord confirming those men came for us. And the name of the jeweler who owned the yellow stone. Two people have called pretending it's theirs.”

The lawyer opened the folder and looked through it.

“All right.”

“Also, these are his trousers.”

She handed over the hanger.

The lawyer looked at the tag, then at the wine he had brought.

“I see.”

Leon raised his head from the hospital bed.

“No, you don't. Be thankful.”

The lawyer took the trousers and left.

Minh watched the sedan pull away.

“Good cigars?”

Moss opened the box and smelled one.

“Very.”

“Give them to my guests. Outside.”

Mai took the wine indoors before Leon could decide his recovery required it.

***

Minh went to the print shop in the afternoon.

Mai drove the Rolls-Royce. He kept looking at the scratch along its front wing when they stopped at lights. She caught him doing it for the third time.

“It'll get fixed.”

“I liked that paint.”

“I liked that street without men shooting at it.”

He nodded.

“Paint loses.”

The print shop smelled of paper, warm machinery, and the lunch somebody had hidden behind the counter. Mai's assistant had kept the orders moving. Completed invitations stood in labeled boxes. A stack of restaurant menus waited beneath a metal weight.

Felicia came through the door carrying the gray jacket between two fingers.

“Who put cash in this?”

Minh raised his wrapped hand.

“Who put fish in this?”

He looked at Mai.

Mai looked at the ceiling.

“We were on a boat.”

“I know where fish live.”

Felicia laid the jacket on the counter and opened its lining. A strip of dried bait clung inside the lower seam.

“Leon sat on something,” Minh said.

“Leon sits on everything. That's not a description.”

She folded the jacket, set it in a bag, and pointed at him.

“Your wedding suit stays with me until the morning. You come to my shop. I put it on you. You go directly to the ceremony. If somebody waves a gun, you tell them you're dressed.”

“What if they're rude?”

“Then Mai can handle it. Her dress has a train.”

Mai leaned against the counter, laughing.

Minh looked from one woman to the other.

“I paid a lot to be supervised this well.”

“You got a neighborhood discount,” Felicia said.

***

The storefront beside Mai's had been empty for four months.

Its former owner had sold office furniture and left behind two desks, a broken filing cabinet, and a picture of a sailboat nobody liked. The landlord met them at the door with three keys and a smile large enough to make Minh dislike the price before hearing it.

Felicia walked through the space with Mai. They measured nothing. They simply stood in different places, looked at the light, and began arguing about where the dividing wall should go.

“Fitting room here,” Felicia said.

“That blocks the window.”

“My customers take their clothes off.”

“Then they'll appreciate the wall I already suggested.”

The landlord watched them with the patient expression of a man increasing a number in his head.

Minh picked up the edge of the broken filing cabinet and moved it away from the wall. Behind it, a dark water stain ran down to the floor.

“Roof leaks.”

“Old damage,” the landlord said.

Minh pressed one finger against the plaster. Water came out around it.

The landlord stopped smiling.

Mai and Felicia turned.

“Interesting weather,” Minh said.

The price came down.

Then the landlord mentioned a deposit, a second deposit for alterations, and a fee for the keys.

Minh held up one of the keys.

“How much is this?”

The landlord named a number.

Minh bent the key into a right angle between his thumb and forefinger and set it on the desk.

“It's defective.”

Mai covered her face with her hand.

Felicia turned toward the window.

The landlord looked at the remaining keys.

“Those are included.”

“Good.” Minh took a checkbook from his shirt pocket and placed it in front of Mai. “You two pick the wall.”

She looked at the checkbook, then at him.

“I'm paying rent from the business.”

“I know.”

“And she's paying her part.”

“I know.”

Felicia folded her arms.

“But you can buy the good mirrors.”

Minh smiled.

“How many?”

“Now you're talking like a fiancé.”

***

On the way home, Mai stopped outside a narrow restaurant with a red awning.

Minh recognized it and sat forward.

“They're still open?”

“New owner. Same cook.”

She parked and came around to his side before he could open the door.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing. I'm opening your door.”

“People will talk.”

“They already have a film.”

Inside, the booths had been recovered in dark blue vinyl. The old jukebox remained near the bathroom, its lower panel held shut with silver tape. Two teenagers shared fries at the counter. A waitress wiped a table beneath the same crooked clock that had been crooked four years earlier.

Mai slid into the booth by the window.

Minh sat opposite her and set his bandaged hands on the table.

“You remember this one?” she asked.

“I remember every second.”

“That's a terrible burden. You said some stupid things.”

“I was twenty-three.”

“You were twenty-three for a whole year. You should have practiced.”

He looked toward the kitchen door.

The cook came out carrying two plates. He was older and heavier than Minh remembered, but the gold tooth appeared when he smiled.

“Look who finally came back.”

Mai raised her hand.

“We're getting married.”

The cook looked at Minh's bandages.

“She make you ask twice?”

Minh laughed and leaned back against the booth.

The cook set down the plates without asking what they wanted.

Four years earlier, he had done exactly the same thing.

## Chapter 26: Before the Good Shoes

In the summer of 1996, Minh borrowed a tie from Leon and immediately regretted it.

The tie was green. Small yellow horses ran across it in several directions. One of them appeared to be jumping over the knot.

“Women like confidence,” Leon said.

“Do they like horses?”

“That's a separate question. Don't lead with it.”

Minh stood in the garage bathroom and tried to loosen the knot. Leon had tied it while giving advice, and the advice had somehow tightened it further. At twenty-three, Minh could pull the engine from a car without a hoist. He could not persuade the small horse beneath his chin to move.

Leon leaned against the doorway.

“Where you taking her?”

“Restaurant.”

“Which one?”

“The expensive one.”

“That doesn't narrow it down. You're always hungry.”

Minh finally got two fingers under the knot and pulled. The tie came loose with a sound that made Leon stand upright.

“Don't tear my shit.”

“It's fine.”

“That's my interview tie.”

“For what job?”

Leon took it from him.

“The right one hasn't appeared.”

Minh wore an open collar.

He had spent the afternoon polishing a dark blue coupe that belonged to a bookmaker named Ernie. Ernie had offered to pay him to frighten a man who was late with a debt. Minh had looked at the man's photograph, recognized the barber who sometimes cut his hair for five dollars, and told Ernie to collect his own money.

Ernie had asked why he kept Minh around.

Minh had picked up the front of Ernie's car so a mechanic could remove a jack trapped beneath the chassis.

“Oh,” Ernie had said.

Then he had offered the coupe for the date.

It waited outside with fresh wax, half a tank, and a cassette player that only worked if the passenger door was shut firmly.

Leon watched Minh lock the garage.

“How old is she?”

“Twenty-one.”

“She know how old you are?”

“Why wouldn't she?”

“Because you look thirty until somebody tells you no.”

Minh got into the car.

Leon bent to the window.

“Listen. You like this girl, ask questions. Let her talk. Don't tell the story about the radiator.”

“She asked about the radiator.”

“Everybody asks about the radiator. It's stuck in a tree.”

***

Mai opened her front door before he could knock.

She wore a white blouse, dark trousers, and small earrings. Her hair was pinned up loosely at the back. She looked at the polished car, then at the open collar he had spent ten minutes making appear unconsidered.

“Where's the green tie?”

Minh stopped.

“Leon called?”

“He asked my mother if you had mentioned a horse.”

Hương appeared behind her, holding a dish towel.

“You brought a car.”

“Yes.”

“Whose?”

“Ernie's.”

“Does Ernie know?”

“Yes.”

She nodded and moved aside.

“Better than last time.”

Minh had once taken Mai home from a late print job on a motorcycle belonging to a man who had lost it to him at cards. The man had disputed the result loudly outside the house. Hòa had come out, listened to both accounts, and told the man to find a bus. The motorcycle had remained a topic at dinner for three months.

Mai took a small bag from the table.

“Ready?”

Hương touched her arm.

“Your father wants him inside for a minute.”

Minh looked past them into the house.

Hòa sat at the dining table repairing a small electric fan. A screwdriver lay beside a bowl of screws. Tín occupied the chair by the open window, trimming the edge of a newspaper with a pair of scissors for reasons Minh had never understood.

Hòa looked up.

“Have a seat.”

Minh sat.

Mai remained standing behind his chair.

Hòa turned the fan on. It rattled once, then settled into a steady rotation.

“What time?”

“Eleven,” Minh said.

“I'm twenty-one,” Mai said.

“I asked him.”

“He's twenty-three. We can both tell time.”

Tín put down the scissors.

“Then why are we talking about it?”

Hòa looked at his father.

Tín folded the newspaper to the page he wanted.

“I need the table for cards.”

Mai kissed Hòa on the cheek, caught Minh by the hand, and pulled him toward the door.

As they left, Hòa called after him.

“The passenger tire is low.”

Minh stopped on the porch and looked at the coupe.

Hòa had not left his chair.

Mai kept walking.

“It probably is.”

***

The expensive restaurant had a fountain in the entrance and a man paid to open the door.

Minh liked the arrangement immediately.

He handed the valet twenty dollars, then handed him another twenty when the man called him sir. Mai watched the exchange with interest.

“You know he says that to everybody.”

“He said it well.”

Inside, a waiter led them to a table near the kitchen passage. Minh looked at the empty tables by the windows.

“One of those.”

“They're reserved.”

Mai glanced at the card on the nearest table. It had no name written on it.

“For who?”

“Guests arriving later.”

She picked up the card and turned it over.

“They're going to have trouble finding it.”

The waiter looked at Minh. Minh looked at Mai. She set the card down exactly where it had been and smiled at the waiter with enough patience to make him nervous.

“We'll wait while you check.”

They got the window.

Minh sat down, delighted.

“I was going to give him money.”

“I know.”

“That usually works.”

“So does reading.”

She opened the menu.

For the first few minutes, he obeyed Leon. He asked about her printing work. She told him about a customer who had ordered two hundred business cards with his own name misspelled, approved the proof, and then blamed the typeface. Minh asked what she had done.

“Printed him two hundred more.”

“For free?”

“Of course not. He needed to learn his name.”

He laughed. She looked pleased and went on, describing the press she wanted someday, the shop she would run, the customers she would refuse even if they waved cash.

“Everybody says that until somebody waves enough,” he said.

“You refused Ernie today.”

He lowered his glass.

“Who told you?”

“The barber came in to order appointment cards. He called you a beautiful young man with terrible friends.”

“He cut my ear last month.”

“He didn't mention that.”

“Put it on his cards.”

The waiter returned with a bottle Minh had ordered by pointing at the middle of the wine list.

He poured a little into Minh's glass and waited.

Minh tasted it.

“Good.”

The waiter continued waiting.

“Is it a test?” Minh asked.

Mai made a small noise behind her napkin.

The waiter filled both glasses and withdrew.

“What?” Minh asked.

“Nothing.”

“You laughed.”

“You looked ready to fight the bottle.”

“It was taking too long.”

She put down the napkin.

“You don't have to know everything.”

“I'm trying to make a good impression.”

“Then stop checking whether I'm impressed.”

He sat back. Outside the window, traffic moved slowly beneath the evening lights. The car he had borrowed was parked near the valet stand, gleaming beneath a lamp. He could see the low passenger tire now that he knew to look for it.

Mai reached across the table and straightened the edge of his collar.

“This is good.”

He looked at her hand.

“The collar?”

“Dinner. You. So far.”

“How do I lose points?”

“Ask that again.”

***

Their food arrived on plates wider than the garage sink.

Minh's steak occupied the middle of his plate beside three narrow pieces of vegetable and a decorative line of sauce. Mai looked at it, then looked at his face.

“Don't.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“Your eyebrows did.”

He ate slowly for three bites. On the fourth, the steak was gone.

Mai still had most of her fish.

He set down his fork and tried to appear occupied by the view.

She pushed half the fish toward the empty side of her plate.

“No.”

“You haven't heard my question.”

“You're going to ask if I'm finishing that.”

“I was going to ask about your mother.”

“My mother would have fed you more.”

He laughed, and this time she laughed with him instead of hiding it.

Then somebody behind him said his name.

Ernie stood in the aisle with a woman in a silver dress and two men Minh knew from the card room. He wore a jacket the color of red wine and a smile that widened when he saw Mai.

“There's my man.”

He put a hand on Minh's shoulder.

Minh looked at it.

Ernie removed it.

“Car running good?”

“Yes.”

“Beautiful machine.” He addressed Mai now. “I told him, take the best. Nothing cheap for a beautiful lady.”

Mai smiled politely.

Ernie took that as an invitation to remain.

“He tell you what he does for me?”

Minh set his napkin down.

“Ernie.”

“I'm praising you.”

“From here it sounds crowded.”

One of the men behind Ernie laughed. Ernie turned his head just far enough to stop him.

“I need the car back tonight.”

“You'll have it.”

“Now, actually. Something came up.”

Mai glanced through the window at the valet stand.

“He has a woman with him,” she said to Minh.

Ernie blinked.

“Yes.”

“Then he needs an audience. That's why he came over.”

The woman in the silver dress looked down at her purse. Her shoulders moved once.

Minh stood.

The two men behind Ernie straightened. One moved his jacket away from his belt. Minh caught his wrist before the hand reached anything beneath it and laid the man's palm flat on the table.

He did it gently enough that the water glasses stayed upright.

The man bent his knees and stopped moving.

“I'm eating,” Minh said.

“You're done,” the man whispered.

Minh looked at his empty plate.

“That's a separate problem.”

He released the wrist.

Ernie took a step back.

Mai folded her napkin and stood too.

“Bring us the bill,” she told the waiter, who had appeared with the urgency of a man hoping nobody would break a window.

Ernie's smile had disappeared.

“You're making this ugly.”

“You brought three people to ask for car keys,” Minh said.

He took the keys from his pocket, placed them on Ernie's palm, and closed the man's fingers around them.

“Ask next time. From a distance.”

The valet came running through the entrance as they reached it.

“Sir, there's a tow truck.”

Ernie swore.

***

The coupe's front wheels were already raised.
