A tow truck idled at the curb, orange lights turning. The driver stood beside the controls with a clipboard. He looked from Ernie to the car and then to the woman in the silver dress.

“Mr. Ernest Bell?”

“You can't do this here.”

The driver looked at the street.

“It's a public road.”

Ernie lowered his voice, but Minh remained close enough to hear every word. Three payments were late. The lender had called twice. Ernie had promised a check that morning. The driver had heard the promise before.

Mai stood beside Minh with her bag under one arm.

“Beautiful machine,” she said quietly.

He pressed his lips together.

Ernie turned on him.

“You could help.”

Minh looked at the tow truck.

“You want me to?”

The relief appeared too quickly on Ernie's face.

“Of course.”

Minh walked to the back of the coupe, placed both hands beneath its rear bumper, and raised the rear wheels off the road.

The tow driver stared.

“Where are you taking it?” Minh asked him.

“Yard on Fourth.”

“Good people?”

“I work there.”

Minh carried the rear of the car sideways until it lined up cleanly behind the truck, then set it down. The tires landed without a bounce.

“There. It was crooked.”

The woman in the silver dress laughed aloud.

Ernie looked at her as if he had just discovered another overdue payment.

Minh tipped the tow driver twenty dollars.

“Passenger tire's low.”

***

They walked six blocks before Mai admitted she was hungry.

Minh stopped so abruptly she bumped into his arm.

“You too?”

“I had a piece of fish and some decorated water.”

“I thought you liked it.”

“I liked sitting with you. I didn't say the food was enough.”

He looked around and found the red awning across the street.

The restaurant had a hand-lettered sign advertising a plate large enough to require two lines of description. A man with a gold tooth stood in the doorway, smoking and watching a basketball game through the front window.

Minh asked if the kitchen was open.

The man looked at him, then at Mai.

“You got money?”

Minh took out his wallet.

“Then it's open.”

They took the booth by the window. The cook brought water in thick glasses and asked what they wanted. Minh began reading the menu. Mai watched the cook watching Minh and started smiling.

“Bring him whatever fills the biggest plate.”

The cook nodded.

“And you?”

“The same.”

The jukebox clicked. An old love song played through one working speaker. A bus stopped outside, released two passengers, and moved on.

Minh rested his forearms on the table.

“I should have brought my own car.”

“You don't have a car.”

“That's the problem.”

“You have a motorcycle.”

“You deserve better than the back of a motorcycle.”

She looked at him for a moment.

“Minh. I like the back of your motorcycle.”

He stopped talking.

“I get to hold on to you, and nobody from the card room can sit at our table.”

The cook brought two large plates and set them down hard enough to make the water jump. Minh looked at his food with such naked happiness that Mai laughed before he lifted the fork.

“That's the face I wanted,” she said.

“You should have ordered potatoes earlier.”

They ate. He told her about arriving in Eastbridge at seventeen, trying to get work in three garages, and discovering Leon asleep in the back seat of a car he was supposed to repair. She told him about arriving at twelve, being furious that adults expected her to know which fears were temporary, and learning the neighborhood through the places her mother sent her for groceries.

Neither story arrived in a polished speech. They interrupted each other, asked about people they both knew, and argued over which market sold the worst fruit with the greatest confidence.

When the plates were empty, Mai put her hand palm upward on the table.

Minh took it.

“Next time,” she said, “your motorcycle.”

“There's a next time?”

“Don't make me withdraw the offer.”

He turned her hand and kissed the inside of her wrist.

The cook walked past carrying a pot of coffee.

“Get married somewhere else. I need that booth.”

***

Four years later, the same cook stood beside them with a fresh pot.

“I told you,” he said.

Mai held up the small wedding invitation she had brought in her bag.

“Somewhere else.”

He took it, read the date, and looked at Minh's wrapped hands.

“You going to be able to hold the ring?”

“I'll manage.”

“Good. I'm not working the ceremony too.”

He tucked the invitation into his apron and went back to the kitchen.

Mai reached across the table, palm upward.

Minh laid his hand in hers.

“The motorcycle,” she said. “When those heal.”

He nodded.

Outside, the yellow Rolls-Royce occupied almost the entire space beneath the red awning. A passing man stopped to admire it. Minh watched him for a second, then looked back at Mai and took another bite.

## Chapter 27: The Practice Dinner

Seven days after the Monarch lost its ramp, Leon arrived at the garage wearing a tuxedo and carrying a live chicken.

Minh looked up from the motorcycle on his lift.

“Why?”

“Before you judge me, this was not my first choice.”

The chicken moved beneath Leon's good arm. He adjusted his grip and looked at the bird as though it had failed to honor a verbal agreement.

“Curtis said he knew a man who had white doves.”

“That's not one.”

“I can see that, Minh.”

“Can Curtis?”

“Apparently the man knew another man. By the time I got there, the story had feathers.”

Minh set down his wrench. His hands had healed enough to work, though a narrow dressing still crossed his left palm. The shoulder had stopped hurting unless he slept on it. Mai had caught him testing it by lifting the front of the Rolls-Royce and made him put the car down before finishing her sentence.

The wedding was tomorrow.

The garage contained no gunmen, no sinking machinery, and one confused chicken. Minh considered this a considerable improvement.

“Take it to Hương.”

Leon looked alarmed.

“I already named him.”

“Then tell her the name.”

“It's Reggie.”

From the open doorway, Reggie lowered his camera.

“Nigga, why?”

Leon held up the chicken.

“Look at him. Always looking around like he missed something.”

Reggie stared at the bird.

The bird stared back.

“I'm not filming your speech.”

“You weren't going to get my good side anyway.”

***

Bách's banquet hall stood three blocks inland from the harbor.

For the wedding, he had replaced the sign outside with a photograph of Minh and Mai large enough to be seen from the next intersection. Mai had approved a modest portrait. Bách had added a gold border, two painted lions, and the words A UNION OF GREATNESS in letters a foot high.

Felicia stood on the sidewalk looking up at it.

“The lions again.”

Minh came beside her.

“These have the right number of fingers.”

“Lions have paws.”

“Then we're improving.”

Inside, the hall smelled of floor polish, flowers, and broth simmering in the kitchen. Tables stood in broad circles around a dance floor. The stage held a piano, two microphones, and a backdrop Mai had printed herself. Every name on it was spelled correctly.

Bách met them in a white dinner jacket.

“Look at this room.”

Minh did.

“You moved the bar.”

“Closer to your table.”

“Good man.”

Bách beamed.

Mai took his arm and turned him toward the far end.

“Put it back.”

His smile faltered.

“It's a gesture.”

“So is walking.”

He signaled two employees, and the portable bar began its return journey across the room.

Moss arrived as they moved it. He wore a dark suit and carried a long narrow box.

“For the groom.”

Bách watched him approach with immediate suspicion.

Minh opened the box. Inside lay a polished brass key fixed to a small wooden plaque.

“Boat's yours,” Moss said. “I put your name on the papers.”

Minh looked at the key.

“Both engines?”

“You think I take one back?”

“I know people.”

Moss laughed and clapped his uninjured shoulder.

Bách disappeared into his office.

Mai closed the box gently.

“You understand what you've started.”

Moss watched the office door.

“Absolutely.”

***

The rehearsal began with the officiant asking everybody to stand where they would stand tomorrow.

It took twenty minutes.

Leon believed the best man belonged beside the groom at all times, including when the groom walked to the bathroom. Tú had assigned himself security at a doorway nobody intended to use. Duy kept moving away from the photographer because he assumed he was in the shot by mistake.

Mai placed him back beside Sơn.

“You were invited.”

“I know.”

“Then stop hiding behind him.”

Sơn looked over his shoulder.

“He's not hiding. He's looking for the food.”

“Both can be true,” Duy said.

The officiant, a small woman with glasses on a chain, waited until the room quieted.

“When I ask for the rings, the best man hands them over.”

Leon patted his jacket.

Mai stared at him.

“Those are the practice rings.”

“I know.”

“The real ones are with me.”

“I know.”

“Because you put a parking receipt in the box yesterday.”

“That receipt proved I was present.”

The officiant took off her glasses.

“Are you going to talk during the actual ceremony?”

Leon looked at Minh.

Minh looked at the ceiling.

“He'll try,” Mai said.

“Then I will wait,” the woman said. “I have performed this ceremony for thirty years. I have outlasted louder men.”

Hương applauded once from the front row.

The rehearsal improved after that.

***

When they practiced the walk back down the aisle, Minh put a hand at Mai's waist and started too quickly.

She slowed him with two fingers on his wrist.

“We're leaving a ceremony.”

“I know.”

“You look like you heard the garage alarm.”

He shortened his stride.

The musician at the piano began playing their chosen song. Mai turned toward him at the edge of the dance floor and put one hand on his shoulder.

“Now this.”

Minh looked down at their feet.

“We practiced.”

“Yes. At home. Where you kept moving the sofa into my way and calling it a turn.”

He took her hand.

The first two steps went well. On the third, she moved left while he moved right. They stopped together, laughed, and started again.

Leon watched with the tense enthusiasm of a man about to give advice about a skill he did not possess.

“Bigger steps,” he called.

“No,” Mai said.

“I was talking to him.”

“So was I.”

Tín rose from his chair.

He wore a plain gray jacket and shoes polished enough to reflect the floor lights. Bích watched him approach with an expression suggesting she had seen this exact decision many times.

“Give me your hand,” he told Minh.

Minh did.

Tín placed his other hand at Minh's upper arm and turned him through a short half circle.

Minh tried to set his feet against the turn. His soles slid across the floor anyway. Tín moved him another half circle, neatly returning him to where he had started. The old man's jacket had not shifted.

“There.”

Minh looked down at the two pale marks his shoes had left.

Mai covered her smile with her fingers.

“He follows beautifully,” Tín said.

“I wasn't following.”

“I noticed. It was rude.”

Bích stood.

“Now try it with somebody who knows where her feet are.”

Tín offered her his hand. They moved onto the floor together, and the pianist changed the pace to suit them. Bích corrected his collar once while they turned.

Minh watched with Mai beside him.

“He dragged me.”

“You looked graceful.”

“You're lying.”

“Practice hearing it. Tomorrow everyone will.”

***

The piano's front caster broke just as the song ended.

It happened with a small crack and a sudden tilt toward the dance floor. The pianist jumped away from the keys. Minh took a step forward, but Hòa was already beside the instrument.

He put one hand beneath its lower edge and held it level.

Bách ran from the office carrying a red envelope.

“Don't scratch it.”

Hương looked at him.

“The man or the piano?”

“Both.”

Hòa looked underneath the instrument while holding its weight in one hand. His expression remained thoughtful. With his free hand, he picked up the broken caster and examined the stem.

Minh came beside him.

“I'll take it.”

“Get something for that corner.”

Minh looked around, found a solid wooden riser beside the stage, and brought it over. Hòa lowered the piano onto it without letting the strings sound.

Tín stood at the edge of the floor, watching his son.

“You could have moved it farther from the wall.”

“You could have asked before I put it down.”

For a second neither moved.

Then Bích came between them and pointed to the dinner tables.

“You can both move yourselves.”

They went.

Minh stayed beside the piano, looking at the broken steel stem in Hòa's hand. It had twisted into two clean spirals before snapping. Hòa put it in his pocket and caught Minh looking.

“Bad wheel.”

“I saw.”

“Then eat.”

Mai took Minh's arm and guided him toward their table.

***

Bách's red envelope contained another key.

“The hall,” he said, placing it beside Minh's plate.

Moss set down his fork.

Mai looked at Bách.

“You're giving us the building?”

“Access,” Bách said quickly. “Whenever you want. Family occasions. Business. Private entertainment.”

Moss picked up his fork again.

“So a key.”

“A key to an institution.”

Minh put it in his pocket.

“Thank you.”

Bách relaxed.

“You see? He understands.”

Moss leaned toward him.

“My key starts engines.”

“My key feeds three hundred people.”

“Only if somebody else works.”

Mai passed them a platter.

“Here. Compete quietly.”

Across the table, Tú's mother watched her son refill everyone's water with unusual efficiency. He had put on a dark suit. The gold letters on his shirt were covered. For once, he was allowing somebody else to be the most visible person in the room.

His mother beckoned Minh closer.

“He's been getting up on time.”

“Good.”

“And paying for things.”

“Also good.”

She lowered her voice.

“He still calls himself Master.”

Minh looked at Tú, who was struggling to remove a tight cap from a water bottle.

“He's developing.”

The cap came loose. Water splashed his sleeve. He looked around to see who had noticed and discovered his mother already holding a napkin.

She handed it to him without a word.

***

After dinner, Minh found Leon outside beside the silver convertible.

The chicken had gone home with a kitchen assistant who kept birds. Reggie had made the assistant promise not to use his name. Leon had changed the bird's name to Curtis at the last second, which seemed to satisfy everybody except the bird.

Now Leon stood alone with his good hand on the car's roof.

Minh came beside him.

“You rehearsing the speech?”

“No.”

“That's a relief.”

Leon smiled faintly.

For a while they watched traffic pass the hall. Somebody slowed to look at the enormous wedding portrait. A passenger leaned out to point at it, and Minh heard his name through the open window.

Leon tapped the roof with one finger.

“Sometimes I hear that shot again.”

Minh turned toward him.

Leon kept looking at the road.

“Not all day. Just when it's quiet. I was holding a plate, then I wasn't. I keep remembering the plate.”

“You dropped it.”

“I know. It was good food.”

Minh leaned against the car beside him.

The hall door opened behind them. Music drifted out, followed by Bách telling somebody the bar had wheels for a reason. The door closed again.

“You don't have to come on the next one,” Minh said.

“Nigga, I didn't ask for a retirement party.”

“I know.”

“I just wanted to say it out loud.”

Minh nodded.

Leon rubbed the edge of his sling.

“You showed up.”

“You were loud.”

“I'll stay loud, then.”

“Please don't.”

Leon laughed properly this time.

Minh put his hand on the man's uninjured shoulder and squeezed once.

“Tomorrow, you stand beside me.”

“Where else?”

“Apparently in the bathroom.”

“Somebody has to make sure you don't run.”

They stayed outside another minute. Then Leon opened the driver's door, took a folded sheet of paper from the seat, and handed it over.

“Look at the speech.”

Minh unfolded it.

The first line read: I have known this beautiful nigga since he was poor enough to listen to me.

Minh began laughing before he reached the second.

Leon took the paper back.

“Exactly. That's how it starts.”

***

When Minh returned to the hall, Mai waited near the stage with her shoes in one hand.

Most of the guests had gone. The staff were clearing glasses. Hòa and Tín argued quietly over the best way to stack two folding tables while Hương and Bích ignored both proposed systems and carried the chairs away themselves.

Mai put her free hand on Minh's chest.

“One more time.”

The pianist had left. There was no music except a radio in the kitchen.

Minh took her hand.

This time he waited for her first step. She moved close, and he followed the pace they had practiced in their living room. They crossed the empty dance floor without bumping the stage or stepping on each other.

At the far side, she turned beneath his raised arm and came back laughing.

“There.”

He drew her closer.

“Tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow.”

Behind them, Leon opened the hall door and began to say something.

Felicia caught the back of his jacket and pulled him outside again.

The door shut before he finished the first word.

## Chapter 28: The Man at the Door

On his wedding morning, Minh woke to somebody knocking on the apartment door with the certainty of a person who owned the street.

He put on trousers and went into the hall.

Tín stood outside holding a paper bag.

“You're late.”

Minh looked at the clock.

“For what?”

“Breakfast. I started.”

The old man stepped past him and put the bag on the table. Hòa followed with a garment bag over one shoulder and a small box in his hand. He closed the front door before Minh could ask why everybody had arrived two hours early.

“Eat,” Hòa said.

Minh sat.

They ate in the kitchen with the windows open. Tín took the chair nearest the breeze. Hòa poured tea. Minh listened to the two men discuss a neighbor's attempt to repair his own roof and gradually understood that neither intended to deliver a solemn talk about marriage.

He was grateful until Tín asked whether he had practiced the dance.

“Yes.”

“Without dragging her?”

“Yes.”

“Good. She's small. People would notice.”

Hòa opened the little box. Inside was a plain silver tie bar.

“My father gave me this.”

Minh looked at Tín.

“You did?”

“He needed something to hold his tie down. It kept arriving before he did.”

Hòa ignored him and pushed the box across the table.

“For today.”

Minh picked it up carefully. The silver had been polished, but a small dent remained near one end.

“Thank you.”

Tín drank his tea.

Hòa looked toward the hallway, where the garment bag hung from a hook.

“Felicia said if you put that on without her, she will come here.”

“Everybody keeps threatening me with the tailor.”

“She's punctual,” Hòa said.

***

At Felicia's shop, the suit waited on a stand beneath a clean sheet.

She removed the sheet as if unveiling a machine she did not expect the owner to maintain properly. The jacket was dark, the cloth soft without looking delicate. The shoulders fit Minh exactly. She had left room for him to move and had told him several times that this was a courtesy, not permission.

Leon stood near the mirror with a new sling under his tuxedo jacket.

“Look at this motherfucker.”

Felicia held up one finger.

“Let me finish.”

She adjusted Minh's collar, straightened the tie, and attached Hòa's silver bar. Then she put Tín's gold cufflinks through the cuffs. The dark stones caught the light when Minh turned his wrists.

For a moment nobody spoke.

Reggie lifted his camera.

Leon leaned closer to the mirror.

“Yeah. Mai's about to make a terrible decision with excellent evidence.”

Minh laughed.

Felicia stepped back and looked at her work.

“There. Hands down. Stop checking whether you can punch in it.”

“I wasn't.”

“Your shoulders were.”

She put a small brush into Leon's good hand.

“Keep him clean.”

Leon looked at the brush.

“For how long?”

“Today.”

“That is a major contract.”

“You're wearing my suit too.”

He slipped the brush into his pocket with immediate professionalism.

***

The street outside the hall had filled before the doors opened.

Guests stood beside polished cars and delivery vans carrying flowers. A man Minh had once helped recover a stolen truck arrived with a whole roasted pig. Marisol came with an envelope and told Leon she was deducting nothing from it, which made him visibly suspicious. Veronica brought her husband and informed Minh that the arcade machines had never earned so much money as the week everybody came to see the damaged pool table.

“That's your gift?” Leon asked.

She handed Minh a wrapped box.

“This is his gift. That was information for your broke ass.”

“I'm not broke.”

“Then pay Marisol.”

Marisol held out her hand without looking at him.

Leon took money from his pocket.

Minh watched the exchange with great satisfaction.

At the entrance, Sơn stood beside Tú. The fighter's left wrist remained in a brace, but his suit sleeve had been fitted around it. Tú had finally abandoned the gold-lettered shirts for the day. His mother had kept all three at home as insurance.

Minh approached them.

“Eat when the food comes.”

Sơn nodded.

Tú looked down at the guest list.

“What if somebody tries to get in?”

“Ask their name.”

“What if they lie?”

“Then you'll have met somebody.”

Leon put a hand on Tú's shoulder.

“Don't worry. I wrote down the cousins.”

Minh took the list from him.

Half the final page consisted of men named Curtis.

He looked up.

Leon spread his good hand.

“Different branches.”

Mai's voice came from behind the closed dressing-room door.

“Minh.”

He handed the list back and went.

***

She stood in front of a long mirror with Hương beside her.

The dress he had glimpsed during the fitting now seemed unfamiliar because she was wearing all of it: the finished neckline, the fitted waist, the train Felicia had kept clean through a week in which almost everything else they owned had touched harbor water. Her hair was pinned back. Her earrings moved when she turned toward him.

Minh stopped inside the door.

Hương watched his face and smiled.

“Good. He noticed.”

Mai looked at her mother.

“Can we have a minute?”

Hương kissed her cheek, touched Minh's arm, and left. Felicia followed after checking the hem one final time.

Minh came closer.

“You look—”

“Careful. Everybody used the good words already.”

He took her hand.

“I want to take you home.”

She laughed softly.

“We paid for food.”

“They can eat without us.”

“Leon can. The others will have questions.”

He looked at her for another moment, then kissed her forehead because he was afraid of disturbing anything Felicia had arranged.

Mai touched the tie bar.

“My father's.”

“He gave it to me.”

She ran a finger over the little dent.

“I used to play with this when he came home. I'd stand on his shoes and try to reach it.”

Minh looked down at the silver, then back at her.

“I'll take care of it.”

“Good. He'll ask.”

Somebody knocked.

Leon spoke from the other side.

“They said it's time. I told them you were probably discussing taxes.”

Mai closed her eyes and laughed.

Minh opened the door.

“Go stand where the woman told you.”

Leon looked at both of them, and for once the next joke did not arrive.

“Yeah,” he said. “All right.”

***

The ceremony went exactly as rehearsed until the rings.

Leon produced the real box promptly, opened it correctly, and handed it over without dropping anything. The officiant looked surprised enough that several guests began laughing before he spoke.

He held up his good hand.

“I can grow.”

She waited.

He lowered the hand.

Minh looked at Mai. Her mouth trembled with the effort not to laugh, and he knew his own looked the same.

When the officiant asked them to speak, Mai went first.

“You brought groceries the night a hundred thousand dollars was in your car,” she said. “Somehow the milk still got put away first.”

A laugh moved through the room.

“I know what your days can look like. I know how many people want a piece of them. I want a home with you, and work I'm proud of, and dinners where you tell me what actually happened before somebody arrives with a refrigerator.”

Bách looked at Moss. Moss looked straight ahead.

Mai squeezed Minh's hand.

“I love being with you. Even when you're impossible to dress. I choose you.”

Minh took a breath.

He had written three versions of his vows. One remained in his pocket. Another had been rejected by Leon for insufficient jokes and by Hương for precisely the opposite reason. The third had come to him that morning while Hòa poured tea.

“The first time we went out, I thought I needed a better car. A better table. I spent half the night trying to look like a man who knew what he was doing.”

Mai smiled.

“Then you told me you liked my motorcycle. You still do. So I'll keep a place for you, whatever I'm driving. I'll come home. I'll listen when you tell me I'm being an idiot. I may need you to say it twice.”

“I have experience,” she said.

He laughed, steadied himself, and went on.

“I want all the ordinary days with you too. The shop being busy. The sink leaking. You falling asleep before I finish a story. I love you, Mai. I choose you.”

She put the ring on his finger with care around the healing skin.

He put hers on without needing any help.

When the officiant finished, the room rose before she could invite it to.

Leon shouted first. Reggie kept filming and shouted through the side of his mouth. Hương cried openly. Hòa stood with one hand on her shoulder. Bích held Tín's hand between both of hers, and Tín smiled without trying to hide it.

Minh kissed his wife.

Somewhere behind the applause, Tú yelled that he had secured the whole door.

Nobody asked which one.

***

Before the meal, Minh and Mai went to the family table.

Hòa rose as they approached. Minh stopped in front of him and bowed his head, slowly and deliberately. Then he did the same before Tín.

Neither man had asked him to.

Tín looked at the cufflinks, straightened one with his thumb, and patted his wrist.

“Better when I don't have to help.”

Minh laughed.

Hòa drew him into a brief embrace, careful of the shoulder even though Minh had said it was fine. When he stepped back, Hương had already taken Mai into her arms.

Bích reached for Minh next.

“Sit down before someone gives a speech.”

It was excellent advice, delivered several seconds too late.

Leon had reached the microphone.

***

He began with the line Minh had read outside the hall.

The room laughed. Mai leaned against Minh's shoulder, and Leon, encouraged, unfolded a second page nobody had approved.

Felicia sat forward.

“I knew this nigga when he had one jacket and three plans,” Leon said. “All three plans involved the jacket looking more expensive.”

Minh covered his eyes.

“Then he met Mai. Suddenly the jacket got cleaned. Suddenly he knew what time the print shop closed. Suddenly I couldn't borrow his motorcycle because apparently love had transportation needs.”

The laughter grew.

“Now look at him. He's got cars. A boat. A refrigerator bigger than my first apartment. People send him furniture because they're scared to send opinions.”

Moss raised his glass. Bách raised his higher.

Leon lowered the paper.

“And he still answers when I call. That's my brother. Mai, I know you already know what you got. I just wanted everybody else to hear it.”

He swallowed, looked briefly annoyed with himself, and lifted his glass.

“To both of you. Be happy. Stay rich. And please buy something with a back seat.”

They drank.

Mai wiped the corner of her eye and whispered to Minh.

“He gets to keep the speech.”

Minh nodded.

“I'll frame the first page.”

***

The food arrived in such quantity that the argument about the two keys ended.

Duy ate beside Sơn and explained why a recovery truck required more judgment than a sports car. Sơn listened for three minutes, then asked whether the judgment happened before or after Duy backed into the trailer. Tú's mother made her son take off his jacket so he would not spill sauce on it. He complied without being reminded of his rank.

At the next table, Sergeant Carter sat beside Navarro, whose swollen ankle was propped on a spare chair. Carter had come off duty and wore a suit that made Leon accuse him of hiding money. Navarro kept describing the ship's damaged engine to the cook from the red-awning restaurant. The cook listened politely until he realized nobody was going to serve the engine and changed the subject to lunch.

Rook remained in custody. Carter mentioned it only when Minh came over to thank him for attending.

“His attorney says he's uncomfortable.”

Minh looked toward the padded chair beside Carter.

“Send him a brochure.”

“I'm off duty.”

“Then enjoy your food.”

Carter raised his glass.

Minh touched his own to it and moved on.

He took pleasure in every table. People stood to shake his hand, pulled out chairs for Mai, slipped envelopes into their palms, and called them back for photographs. A jeweler whose necklace had come out of Rook's case gave Mai a small velvet box and refused to discuss its price. She opened it just enough to see earrings, thanked him, and put it safely beside her plate.

Marisol told Minh that his photograph was staying above her counter.

“Use the wedding one,” he said.

“No. In that one you look available for conversation.”

***

The only trouble at the door arrived after dessert.

Ernie stood outside in a red jacket that had survived four years of fashion by ignoring all of it. He carried a bottle with a ribbon around its neck and looked offended by Tú's clipboard.

“Tell him I supplied the car for his first date.”

Tú looked through the list again.

“What name is that under?”

Minh heard the exchange while walking toward the bathroom and came outside.

Ernie spread his arms.

“There he is.”

Minh looked at the bottle.

“Is it paid for?”

“You're never going to let that go.”

“The tow truck did.”

Tú looked from one man to the other with intense interest.

Ernie held out the bottle.

“Congratulations. I mean it.”

Minh took it. Through the doorway, he could see Mai watching from their table. She recognized Ernie, raised one eyebrow, and waited.

“You got something to say to her?” Minh asked.

Ernie looked into the hall.

“I'm sorry about the restaurant.”

“Louder.”

Ernie drew a breath.

“I'm sorry about the restaurant, Mai.”

Several nearby guests turned. Mai looked at him for a moment, then pointed toward an empty seat beside the cook.

“There's food left.”

Ernie nodded quickly and went inside before she changed her mind.

Tú lowered the clipboard.

“That's it?”

“That's it.”

“I thought something was going to happen.”

Minh put the bottle in his hands.

“You're going to eat cake.”

He held the door open while Tú went through, then followed him back to his wife.

***

Their first dance went well.

Minh waited for Mai's step. She moved close, her hand resting lightly on his shoulder, and they crossed the floor in a slow turn. The room softened around them. People still spoke, glasses still touched tables, but Minh heard the music and Mai's quiet laugh when he successfully avoided the edge of her train.

“See?” she said.

“I was always good.”

“There he is.”

He turned her beneath his arm and brought her back against him.

Leon applauded too early. Felicia pulled his hand down. Reggie moved sideways with the camera and nearly backed into Bách, who was attempting to remain in the background of every important photograph.

When the song ended, Minh did not immediately release her.

“Motorcycle?” he asked.

She smiled.

“Later. I have another dress.”

***

They left after dark.

Mai changed into a shorter white dress and low shoes. Minh took off his tie, put Hòa's bar carefully into its box, and gave the wedding jacket to Felicia with a formal promise that it had encountered no fish.

His motorcycle waited at the side of the hall. He had cleaned it himself that morning before Leon arrived with the chicken. Two helmets rested on the seat.

The guests gathered around them. Hương put a package of food into the small rear case. Bích added another. Tín watched until Minh latched it and then tested the fastening with one finger.

“Good.”

Hòa shook Minh's hand.

“Tomorrow, sleep.”

“That's the plan.”

Mai kissed her mother and grandmother, hugged her father, and touched Tín's cheek. Then she came to the motorcycle and fastened her helmet.

Leon leaned toward Minh.

“If you need anything—”

“Tomorrow,” Mai said.

Leon stepped back.

“A healthy boundary. I respect it.”

Reggie laughed behind the camera.

Minh started the engine. Mai settled behind him and wrapped her arms around his waist. He felt her hands join over his shirt, exactly where they had been on rides home four years earlier.

He pulled away slowly enough for everybody to wave.

At the corner, the light turned red. They stopped beneath it while a bus passed through the intersection. Mai rested her helmet against his back.

“Husband,” she said.

He turned his head a little.

“Wife.”

She squeezed him once.

The light changed.

He took the long way home, along the water, with the city lights on their left and the dark harbor on their right. Nothing chased them. The motorcycle ran cleanly beneath him. When they reached their street, he slowed for the familiar uneven patch in the pavement so she would not bounce against his shoulder.

At home, he parked beneath the shop's outside light and helped her down.

Mai took the food from the rear case. They climbed the stairs above the garage together, and he unlocked their door. He opened it wide, stepped aside, and watched her carry the packages into their kitchen.

Then she set them down, came back to him, and took his hand.

“You too.”

Minh went inside.

---

# Book III: The River’s Weight

## Chapter 1: The Refrigerator Gets a Better Offer

The refrigerator came with a free ice tray, a three-month warranty, and two men trying to steal it.

Tín had paid extra for delivery. He had lived in Eastbridge, California, for five years. In the summer of 1992, he still believed paying a man forty dollars meant the man would carry something.

He stood on the sidewalk outside Vân's grocery, holding the receipt while one of the men wrapped a chain around the axle of Bình's pickup. The other pressed a yellow notice against the windshield and smoothed it with his palm.

“Commercial loading violation,” the second man said.

The pickup occupied Vân's loading space. Vân stood beneath the sign authorizing customers to occupy it. She had owned the sign longer than either man had been shaving.

“That's my space,” she said.

“City jurisdiction.”

“Then go tell the city to buy its own refrigerator.”

The man ignored her. He wore a black polo shirt with HARBOR SECURITY sewn over the breast. Beneath the lettering, a little gold crown leaned to one side.

Tín examined the notice.

Three hundred dollars. Cash settlement available.

“You accept a check?” he asked.

“Cash.”

“Of course. Very advanced city.”

At the pickup's tailgate, Bình stood with his hands open. His right cheek had begun swelling. He was twenty-three, wore his hair high enough to require its own weather report, and had brought Tín a refrigerator strapped to a truck he was still paying for.

“I told them we were unloading,” he said.

The security man turned toward him.

“And I told you to shut up.”

Tín folded the receipt and placed it in his shirt pocket.

“Who hit him?”

The man at the chain looked up. He was broad, red-faced, and pleased with a morning in which nobody had made him work hard.

“He got mouthy.”

“I asked who.”

“Me.”

“Thank you.”

Tín walked past him to the refrigerator. He wore a white undershirt beneath an open short-sleeved shirt, brown trousers, and sandals Bích had bought because the previous pair embarrassed her in restaurants. His hair had gone almost entirely white. A paper birthday crown stuck from Vân's shopping bag beside the door.

Seventy today. Vân had insisted on the crown.

He had hoped the refrigerator would distract her.

“Where you going, Grandpa?” the chain man asked.

“Home. They're making lunch.”

Tín loosened the strap, slid his hands under the refrigerator, and lifted it out of the pickup.

The truck's springs rose.

Bình stepped backward.

Vân stopped opening the paper crown.

Tín held the refrigerator against his chest, its cardboard corners brushing his shoulders. A loose strap dangled across his sandals. He shook it away with one foot and stepped onto the sidewalk.

The security man stared at the empty truck bed.

“You can't remove seized property.”

“Then move the truck. My arms are occupied.”

He carried the refrigerator toward the corner.

From across Bell Street, Darnell Jackson came out of his tow shop holding a coffee mug. Everybody called him Boots. He had once arrived at a neighborhood basketball game wearing expensive cowboy boots and had spent twenty years attempting to make people remember anything else.

He watched Tín pass.

“You know they invented wheels.”

“I paid for them. They're being arrested.”

Boots looked at the truck, the two men, and Bình's face. His mug came down slowly.

“Oh. These motherfuckers again.”

The man with the notices reached under his shirt.

Tín stopped.

“Leave that there.”

The man's hand froze near his belt.

“I said leave it.”

Behind Tín, the refrigerator door clicked open. He leaned it against his shoulder and closed the door with his chin.

Boots set his coffee on the hood of a customer's car.

“My nigga carrying a whole kitchen appliance and you still picked the wrong moment.”

The chain man pulled a steel bar from the tow truck. He came forward with it held low beside his thigh.

Vân stepped into her shop and pulled the door mostly shut.

“Outside,” she called. “If you're doing this, do it outside.”

Tín set the refrigerator carefully on the sidewalk. He checked that its base rested flat, moved the receipt from one pocket to another, and turned.

The bar came across at his head.

He caught the attacker's wrist. The bar stopped a few inches from his ear. Tín twisted the man's arm outward and down. His knees hit the pavement. The bar struck the curb and rang.

Tín took it.

The other man drew his pistol.

Tín threw the bar through the open passenger window of the tow truck. It punched across the cab, struck the pistol man's forearm, and knocked his hand against the door. The gun dropped. He bent after it.

Boots kicked it under the refrigerator.

“Now you got a fucking situation.”

The kneeling man tried to stand. Tín pressed two fingers into the soft place above his collarbone. His knees returned to the concrete.

“You hit the boy with this hand?”

The man sucked air through his teeth.

“You can't—”

“I've been hearing that all morning. Answer something useful.”

“Yes.”

Tín bent his wrist until the man's face lost its color. He released it before the joint broke.

“Apologize.”

The man looked at Bình.

“Sorry.”

Bình touched his cheek.

“You made me swallow my gum.”

“I'm sorry about the gum.”

“And my face.”

“And your face.”

Vân opened the door a little farther.

“Tell him about the truck.”

“I don't know what you want me to say.”

“That you're a thief,” she said. “We can work on pronunciation later.”

Boots laughed so hard he had to hold the refrigerator.

The pistol man climbed into the tow truck. His partner looked over his shoulder and realized he was being left.

“Hey!”

The engine started.

Tín released the kneeling man and walked to the truck's front bumper.

The driver locked the doors.

Tín put his hands beneath the bumper and lifted the front of the truck off the street.

Inside, the driver slid backward against his seat. His cap fell into the space behind him. He tried the gas. The rear tires squealed, made two black marks, and stopped when Tín lifted higher.

The cab tilted toward the sky.

Boots picked up his coffee.

“I've been buying the wrong equipment.”

Tín carried the truck sideways until its front wheels hung over the curb. He set them down with the bumper touching a lamp post. The rear wheels remained in the street. The driver looked through the windshield at four inches of painted steel.

Tín tapped the glass.

“Unhook the pickup.”

The driver nodded.

“Leave the gun.”

Another nod.

“And the bar. It belongs to the neighborhood now.”

The man worked the door handle. The lamp post blocked it. He tried the other side. Vân's newspaper box stood there.

“I can't get out.”

Tín looked at his watch.

“I can wait.”

The window opened. The man squeezed through it, one shoe coming off inside the cab. He landed on the sidewalk in his socks and hurried to the pickup's axle.

A bus had stopped at the corner. Its driver opened the doors. Three passengers leaned out to watch the chain come away.

Somebody applauded.

The applause spread along the sidewalk. A woman outside Loretta's salon whistled through her fingers. The bus driver held out a folded transit pass.

“For your birthday, Mr. Tín.”

“How do you know it's my birthday?”

Vân pointed at the enormous banner hanging inside her window.

HAPPY 70TH, MASTER TÍN.

Beneath it, in smaller letters, Marcus Jackson had added: STILL TAKING APPLICATIONS FOR A WORTHY OPPONENT.

Tín looked at Boots.

“Your son needs employment.”

“I keep telling him. He says promotion is employment.”

The bus driver waved the pass again.

“Take it. Unlimited rides.”

Tín accepted it.

“Does it cover refrigerators?”

The driver looked at the white machine and then at the truck pressed against the lamp post.

“Yours does.”

Vân emerged carrying the crown and a bag of groceries. She put the bag on top of the refrigerator.

“Eggs, fish sauce, fruit. Birthday gift.”

“I ordered one appliance.”

“Now you have food to put in it. Stop making generosity difficult.”

She placed the paper crown on his head.

The kneeling security man rose at last. He cradled his wrist against his chest.

“You don't know whose truck that is.”

Tín looked back at the tilted vehicle.

“Currently, the lamp post's.”

“Duke Mercer.”

Boots stopped smiling.

Tín noticed.

“The man with the boat?” he asked.

“The River Queen,” the security man said. “You ever want to move anything through this neighborhood again, you come see him.”

Tín lifted the refrigerator. Vân steadied the groceries on top.

“Tell him I'm seventy. If he wants to threaten me, he should come before my nap.”

He started down Bell Street. The bus passengers applauded again. The driver closed the doors and followed at walking speed for half a block, apparently unwilling to let the afternoon become ordinary too soon.

Boots caught up beside him.

“You want help?”

Tín tilted his head toward the grocery bag.

“Take the eggs.”

Boots took them.

“Duke's not just some asshole with a boat.”

“Then he'll be pleased I remembered the boat.”

“Calvin Rook runs half the waterfront through him.”

“Which half?”

“The half that sends men to punch Bình over a parking space.”

Tín walked around a crack in the pavement so the refrigerator would stay level.

“Then we should introduce them to the other half.”

Boots looked up at the crown.

“That thing makes you worse.”

“I think it's working.”

At the house, Bích stood on the front steps holding a wooden spoon. She wore a clean blouse and an apron with a small burn near the pocket. Behind her, Hương crossed the hallway carrying a stack of plates. The smell of pork and warm bread came through the open door.

Bích looked at the refrigerator in her husband's arms.

“Delivery cost forty dollars.”

“I know.”

“Did you get the forty back?”

“There was a complication.”

“There's always a complication carrying something expensive up my steps.”

She moved aside. Tín brought the refrigerator into the house. Boots followed with the eggs held solemnly in both hands.

Hòa came from the kitchen, saw the appliance, and moved a chair out of the way without asking why his father was carrying it.

“Turn left,” he said.

“I know where our kitchen is.”

“The door frame doesn't.”

Tín turned. The refrigerator cleared the frame by less than an inch.

Mai stood beside the old refrigerator with a screwdriver in one hand. She had removed the decorative magnets and arranged them across the table in rows. One showed a smiling cartoon dog under the words HAVE A NICE DAY. Someone had drawn fangs on it.

“You wore the crown outside,” she said.

“I was conducting official business.”

She bowed deeply.

“Your Majesty. The freezer leaks.”

He bowed back without lowering the refrigerator.

“We shall investigate.”

Bích pointed with the spoon.

“Put it there, King of Back Problems.”

He did. Hòa pulled the old refrigerator away from the wall. Its rear feet scraped once, then rose clear as he shifted it. He carried it to the back door with one hand against its side and the other holding a glass of water.

Boots watched him pass.

“Does this family own a dolly?”

Hòa looked over his shoulder.

“My wife says we don't have room.”

Hương took the eggs from Boots.

“We don't.”

Nobody offered an explanation. Boots drank his cold coffee and stared at the empty space where the old refrigerator had been.

Tín plugged in the new one. A small light came on when he opened the door. Mai put the cartoon dog on the front, then moved it so the paper warranty would fit beside it.

“Happy birthday,” she said.

He kissed the top of her head.

“Thank you.”

She handed him an envelope.

Inside lay a photograph. Tín and Bích stood outside their house, both caught in the middle of laughing at something beyond the frame. He had one hand on his wife's shoulder. She had turned toward him with her mouth open and her eyes almost closed.

“When was this?” he asked.

“When Dad dropped the cake.”

From the back steps, Hòa called, “It was a difficult cake.”

Bích took the photograph. Her expression softened before she caught herself doing it.

“Good picture.”

“I developed it myself,” Mai said.

“You made me handsome,” Tín told her.

“That part was already a problem.”

He laughed and put the photograph on top of the refrigerator.

They sat down to lunch. Boots claimed he could stay only a minute, then accepted a plate, a second helping, and instructions from Bích to stop eating over his lap. Bình arrived with an ice bag against his cheek and a small wrapped box under his arm.

“A watch,” he said when Tín opened it. “I got it from a guy.”

Tín examined the face. The second hand moved in little uneven jumps.

“An honest guy?”

“He was honest about the price.”

“It's beautiful.”

Tín put it on beside the watch he already wore.

Mai leaned over.

“They disagree.”

“We'll give them time.”

The telephone rang as Bích brought out the cake. Hương answered in the hall. She listened, covered the mouthpiece, and looked toward the table.

“A Mr. Mercer. He says your birthday present is waiting at the roller rink.”

Boots set down his fork.

Bích looked at Tín's two watches.

“You have enough presents.”

Tín took a knife and cut the cake.

“Tell him I'll come after dessert.”

“He says it may not be there later.”

Tín passed the first slice to his wife.

“Then he should eat slowly.”

## Chapter 2: Everybody Bet Against the Old Man

The roller rink had a red carpet because Duke Mercer disliked entering buildings on flooring available to everybody else.

Tín found three boys standing beside it, each wearing a rented tuxedo jacket over shorts. The middle boy held a brass trumpet. The other two appeared to be waiting for him to improve.

“For Duke?” Tín asked.

The trumpet boy nodded.

“Does he pay extra when you stop?”

Boots coughed into his fist. Bình looked away.

The boy lifted the trumpet. One uncertain note came out.

Tín put five dollars in his pocket.

“For the silence after that.”

The boy lowered the instrument. His friends immediately began negotiating their share.

Inside, a painted moon hung above the skating floor. Colored lights moved across empty lanes and a row of arcade machines. The bowling alley occupied the back of the building, separated from the rink by a low rail. A snack counter faced both. Somebody had installed a chandelier over the shoe rental desk.

Boots looked up.

“Duke's mother told him to be classy once. This is what happened.”

At the rental desk, a woman offered Tín a pair of bowling shoes.

“Nine?”

“I'm here to see Mr. Mercer.”

“Everybody is. Nine?”

He accepted them.

She looked at his paper crown.

“Birthday boy?”

“Apparently.”

“Shoe rental's on the house.”

She stamped his hand with a purple star. Tín held it away from his shirt while the ink dried.

Behind him, Boots paid for his own shoes.

“I know the birthday boy.”

“Then buy him a drink.”

“Everybody getting rich off my friendship.”

A man in a green velvet tracksuit sat at the first bowling lane. He had a shaved head, a broad face, and a gold chain carrying an anchor large enough to catch a small boat. His shoes matched the tracksuit. Two women sat on either side of him with drinks in tall glasses. A third occupied her own chair several feet away, studying the score sheet.

“Mr. Tín,” Duke said. “I expected you sooner.”

“The cake was good.”

“Happy birthday.”

“Thank you. Where's my present?”

Duke spread his hands.

“We need to talk about what you did to my truck.”

“That's a disappointing present.”

The woman with the score sheet looked up. Her hair was tied back, and a pencil rested behind her ear. She wore a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow. When Duke shifted his glass toward the sheet, she moved the paper before it could get wet.

“Sable,” he told her, “bring our guest a chair.”

“There are six beside him.”

“A good chair.”

“They're all the same chair, Duke.”

Tín took one and sat.

Bình remained standing. Duke looked at the ice bag against his cheek.

“My men say you were uncooperative.”

“Your men asked for three hundred dollars to stand outside a grocery store.”

“Security is expensive.”

Boots leaned against the rail.

“Apparently health insurance is too. How's the wrist?”

Duke's smile narrowed.

He picked up a bowling ball with two fingers and turned it in his hand. The ball was black, with a white crown painted between the holes.

“I'm willing to call this a misunderstanding.”

Tín looked at Bình's face.

“Then understand it differently.”

Duke stood. He was taller than Tín by almost a head, and the tracksuit concealed very little of the body beneath it. People at the neighboring lanes turned to watch him walk to the line.

He swung the ball once and released it.

It struck the pins so hard that the pinsetter jumped. One pin came back onto the lane spinning on its head. Another disappeared somewhere inside the machinery.

The people behind him applauded.

Duke turned with both hands spread.

“I keep the neighborhood moving.”

From the machinery, something expensive fell over.

Sable made a mark on her sheet.

“That's the third repair this month.”

“Write down a strike.”

“I can write both.”

Tín picked up a ball from the rack. He looked at the finger holes, tried two fingers, and put it back.

“Too small.”

A young man beside the next lane snorted.

“Old man got special hands.”

Tín selected another ball and weighed it in his palm.

“I was referring to the conversation.”

Boots bent at the waist, laughing. Bình lowered the ice bag long enough to grin and regretted it immediately.

Duke came back to the table.

“You want something?”

“My friend's truck left alone. Your men off Bell Street. An apology from somebody whose apology matters.”

“That's a lot to ask over a refrigerator.”

“It has an ice maker.”

Sable covered her mouth with the score sheet.

Duke saw it.

“You know who owns the River Queen?” he asked.

“The river?”

“Me.”

“Congratulations.”

“Three bars. Two dance floors. A kitchen bigger than your house.”

Tín placed the ball on the table. The plastic tabletop bent beneath it.

“My wife would like the kitchen.”

“Your wife can buy a ticket.”

“She dislikes waiting in line.”

Duke looked around at the people watching. A few men stood now. Two had brought their drinks closer. The trumpet boy had entered through the front doors and was trying to find a place to put his instrument where Duke would not notice him abandoning it.

“Let's make this interesting,” Duke said.

Sable lowered the paper.

“Duke.”

“One throw.”

“Duke.”

He held up a finger without looking at her.

“You keep interrupting a beautiful idea.”

“I'm trying to catch it before it becomes expensive.”

He pointed toward the far lane. Its machinery had been removed. At the end stood a steel safe painted white, with a crown across its door. A thick chain ran through a ring welded to the top and down to two anchors in the concrete.

“Crown Lane,” Duke said. “Ten thousand to knock it over.”

Boots stared at the safe.

“That motherfucker got a foundation.”

“Anybody can try.”

“Anybody can try flying. Doesn't make the roof an airport.”

Duke ignored him.

“Mr. Tín knocks it over, I'll apologize to his friend. He misses, I get the three hundred and he comes down to the dock tomorrow to apologize to my men.”

“And my refrigerator's delivery fee,” Tín said.

“What?”

“Forty dollars. My wife asked.”

Duke laughed.

“Fine. Ten thousand and forty.”

Tín looked at the safe. The white paint had scuffs across the bottom where somebody had tried a very different kind of bowling ball. A small crack ran from one of the anchors to the side of the lane.

“If I knock it through the wall?”

The laughter stopped in pieces.

Duke looked toward Sable.

She shook her head once, firmly.

He looked back at Tín.

“Then I'll give you the boat.”

Sable stood.

“No.”

“It's my boat.”

“I know. I schedule repairs for it. Sit down.”

Duke's jaw set.

Tín smiled at her.

“What kind of stove?”

She stared at him.

“On the boat.”

“Six burners. Two ovens.”

“We should put that in writing.”

The crowd came closer. Someone shouted for odds. A man at the snack counter began taking money with a speed suggesting he had come prepared for several kinds of evening.

Boots took out his wallet.

Bình caught his sleeve.

“Against him?”

Boots looked offended.

“I've seen the refrigerator.”

Sable found a blank page. She wrote the terms, read them aloud, and made Duke sign beneath his own offer. Tín added his name. His handwriting was small and tidy. The pencil had a little rubber flamingo on its end.

“You can keep that,” Sable told him.

“Another birthday gift.”

“If you lose, I want it back.”

She went to the far lane and opened a side door. Two employees carried boxes away from behind the safe. She sent them outside, checked the service yard herself, and returned.

“Empty,” she said. “Nobody behind the wall.”

Duke rolled his shoulders.

“You really preparing for this?”

“I'm preparing for whatever stupid thing you say afterward.”

Tín walked to the line holding an ordinary red bowling ball. He had kept the paper crown on. A small child beside the rail waved at him with both hands.

He waved back.

“Don't encourage him,” Boots told the child. “He came like this.”

Tín set one foot at the line and looked down the lane.

Duke folded his arms.

“You want a practice throw?”

“I want the stove cleaned.”

He swung the ball.

It left his hand low, struck the lane once, and flew the remaining distance without touching the polished wood. The safe door folded inward. Both anchors ripped out of the concrete. The chain snapped taut, tore through the ring, and lashed across the empty lane.

The safe went through the wall.

Bricks burst into the service yard. Daylight opened behind the pins painted on the plaster. The safe struck a dumpster outside and shoved it across the pavement until it hit a fence.

The red ball came back through the hole.

It rolled slowly down the lane and stopped against Tín's shoe.

He picked it up.

One finger hole had become much larger.

“I'll pay for this,” he said.

Nobody answered.

At the snack counter, the man taking bets put both palms flat on the money.

Boots turned toward him.

“Don't even think about becoming religious.”

The child began applauding.

Then the whole building went up.

People shouted Tín's name. Somebody started chanting “Master! Master!” while Duke stood beneath the chandelier with his hands still folded over his chest. The trumpet boy finally found a note he could hold and put everything he had into it.

Tín raised the damaged ball.

“Thank you. Please don't stand in the yard.”

Boots approached the betting man with both hands open.

“My money has company now. Bring all of them.”

Bình laughed until his cheek hurt. Sable walked to the new hole, looked outside, and came back holding the signed paper.

She placed it in Tín's hand.

“The stove is clean.”

Duke moved at last.

He came toward Tín with his face hard and his right hand closing.

Boots stopped counting money.

Tín put the ball down on the return rack.

Duke swung.

The punch crossed the space where Tín's head had been. Tín stepped inside the arm, caught Duke by the tracksuit at the waist, and lifted him until both green shoes left the floor.

The anchor necklace swung between them.

Tín turned and sat him on top of the ball return.

The plastic housing cracked. Balls shifted beneath Duke's weight. One rolled out beside his leg and dropped into the rack with a clunk.

Tín kept one hand on his shoulder.

“We can finish the bowling first.”

Duke looked down at him. His face worked through several expressions, none of them helped by the fact that his heels no longer reached the floor.

Sable held out the pencil.

“Sign the receipt.”

“I already signed.”

“That was the wager. This is acknowledgment that you lost.”

Duke stared at the paper.

“You enjoying this?”

“I have waited six years to bill you for something personal.”

He took the pencil.

Tín removed his hand from the man's shoulder. Duke signed, climbed down from the cracked return, and faced Bình.

“My people shouldn't have touched you.”

Bình lowered the ice bag.

“Or my truck.”

“Or your truck.”

“Or charged Mr. Tín for delivery he delivered himself.”

Duke pulled forty dollars from his pocket and placed it on the table.

“Everybody has become very specific.”

“It helps,” Tín said.

As they left, the snack-counter owner pressed a box of pretzels into his hands. The woman at the shoe desk offered him the bowling shoes. A stranger tried to give him a gold watch and became briefly upset when Tín showed him that both wrists were already occupied.

“Then give it to your wife.”

“She knows what time it is.”

The stranger put it in the pretzel box anyway.

Outside, Boots carried the winnings in a paper bag. Bình held the bowling shoes. Tín had the pretzels, the watch, and ownership of a boat with six burners.

He stopped at the pay phone beside the entrance.

Bích answered on the fourth ring.

“Did you get the forty dollars?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Come home.”

He looked at the paper in his hand.

“There's one more thing.”

Boots leaned against the wall, smiling.

“How much room do we have for a nightclub?” Tín asked.

## Chapter 3: Your Grandmother Owns the Dance Floor

Bích took one look at the River Queen and asked where the grease trap was.

Duke had prepared a speech about chandeliers.

“You don't want to see the ballroom?” he asked.

“After the grease trap.”

“It's an elegant vessel.”

“Then the grease trap should be elegant.”

She went up the gangway carrying a market bag. Hương followed with a tape measure around her neck. Mai came behind them with her camera, stopping halfway to photograph the boat's name.

Tín waited on the landing while Duke stood beside a brass post with a rope looped through it. A square of dark water separated the barge's hull from the timber pier. Beyond the pier, the river opened east toward the harbor bridge. Cranes rose along the far bank. A tug passed carrying three men and a dog who appeared to outrank them.

The River Queen had once carried freight. Now a two-story white structure sat on its steel deck. Red trim ran beneath the windows. The lower doors opened onto a dance floor and three bars. Above them, a balcony wrapped around a smaller lounge beneath a striped awning.

“She doesn't have engines,” Duke said.

“My house doesn't either.”

“You need a tug to move her.”

“Then I won't lend her to the children.”

Duke looked at the signed papers in Sable's hands. She had brought a folder, a ring of keys, and the expression of a woman determined to finish one bad transaction before lunch produced another.

“Title and registration,” she said. “The operating business is separate. You get the vessel and what Duke listed on the attached inventory.”

“The stove?”

“Yes.”

“The chandelier?” Duke asked.

Sable turned a page.

“You wrote all fixtures.”

“I was under emotional pressure.”

“You were holding a pencil.”

Tín accepted the keys.

“Does the trumpet boy come with it?”

“Absolutely not,” Duke said.

“Good. I was going to release him.”

They went aboard.

Inside, Loretta Jackson was already standing in the middle of the dance floor. She wore a yellow dress, carried a handbag the size of a small overnight case, and had brought two women from the salon to help decide whether the room deserved them.

“We can put the band there,” she said, pointing at the stage. “Food along the windows. People can sit outside if they want to pretend they came for the view.”

“Who invited you?” Duke asked.

Loretta looked him up and down.

“The new administration.”

Boots entered carrying a box of records. Marcus followed with a speaker on one shoulder and an extension cable trailing from his hand.

“Grandmaster's birthday cruise,” Marcus announced. “I got the flyer designed in my head.”

Tín looked at the speaker.

“My birthday was yesterday.”

“We're extending the season.”

“Without asking?”

“You bought a boat without asking. We're communicating at your level.”

Hương laughed from the kitchen doorway.

Duke turned toward Sable.

“They've invaded.”

“You're standing on their dance floor.”

Mai took a photograph of him beneath the chandelier. He straightened automatically, then realized what she had done.

“Give me that one.”

“Five dollars when it's printed.”

“I used to own this place.”

“Then you can afford six.”

Tín watched his granddaughter put the camera away and open a notebook. She and Marcus began arguing over the name of the event. Marcus wanted THE GRANDMASTER'S SUMMER REIGN. Mai wanted people to know there would be food.

“People understand reign,” he said.

“They understand lunch better.”

“You can't put lunch in gold letters.”

“Watch me.”

Bích emerged from the kitchen.

“The grease trap is filthy.”

Duke closed his eyes.

“Sable.”

“You fired the last cleaner for leaving during your speech.”

“He had a bad attitude.”

“He had another job.”

Bích put down the market bag.

“We need volunteers.”

Everyone looked at Duke.

“No,” he said.

Tín smiled.

“An elegant vessel.”

Ten minutes later, Duke knelt in the galley wearing rubber gloves while Bích supervised from a stool. Loretta's friends carried tablecloths upstairs. Boots checked a socket with a little tester he distrusted. Marcus set a record on the turntable and immediately received three different instructions about volume.

Tín stood at the window facing the pier.

Two black cars had stopped beside the landing.

A young woman stepped out of the first. She wore a gray suit and carried no handbag. Her dark hair was cut just below the jaw. Two men got out behind her. The second car remained running, its windows closed.

Sable came beside Tín.

“Iris Rook.”

“Calvin's wife?”

“Daughter.”

“He named her after a flower and sent her to collect his boat?”

“He sends her when he'd like people to keep their teeth.”

Tín looked at the men following Iris.

“Whose teeth?”

Sable did not answer.

Iris stepped onto the gangway. Its boards barely moved beneath her. She entered the ballroom, glanced at the speakers and tablecloths, and stopped beneath the chandelier.

Marcus took the record off the turntable.

The sudden silence annoyed Loretta more than the arrival.

“Put that back,” she told him. “She didn't rent the air.”

He lowered the needle. Music resumed quietly.

Iris faced Tín.

“Mr. Lê.”

“Tín is fine.”

“My father would like to resolve an error.”

“He should speak to his doctor.”

One of the men behind her laughed before he could stop himself. Iris turned her head a fraction. He looked down at the floor.

She produced an envelope from inside her jacket.

“Twenty-five thousand dollars. You return the vessel, keep the money, and enjoy your birthday.”

Tín looked into the kitchen. Duke had stopped cleaning.

Bích tapped the grease trap with her spoon.

“We're all enjoying our birthday,” Tín said.

Iris placed the envelope on the bar.

“My father controls this berth. He has uses for it.”

“We'll send him a flyer.”

“You think this is a neighborhood party.”

“We haven't decided the name.”

“I'm trying to keep you from making a mistake.”

Hương stepped out from behind the serving counter.

“Then ask your men to stop touching the doors.”

One of Iris's men had moved toward the kitchen corridor. His hand rested on the handle of a locked service door. He took it away.

Tín watched him. The man's jacket hung unevenly over his right hip. The second man had positioned himself where he could see both the gangway and the stairs.

Tín set the boat keys on the bar beside the envelope.

“Take your money home.”

Iris's eyes moved toward the keys.

“You should meet my father.”

“He should bring a dish.”

“He doesn't cook.”

“Then he can learn from Duke.”

From the kitchen came the sound of a rubber glove snapping.

Iris picked up the envelope.

“We won't offer twice.”

She turned toward the gangway.

The man beside the service door drew his gun.

Hương slammed the serving hatch down on his wrist.

The shot tore through the wooden partition above Tín's head. People ducked. Marcus dropped behind the turntable. Loretta seized one of her friends and pulled her through the stair doorway.

Tín caught the gunman's trapped hand and drove the muzzle down against the counter. The second shot went into the floor. He hit the man's jaw with his open palm. The man went backward, pulling his wrist free, and struck a stack of folded chairs.

The other bodyguard reached inside his jacket.

Tín took the bar stool by one leg and threw it low.

It hit the man's knees. Both legs folded. His gun skidded under a table as he struck the deck face-first.

Outside, a car door opened.

“Kitchen!” Tín shouted.

Bích was already pulling Mai behind the galley wall. Hương followed them, then leaned back to drag the box of knives out of the passage so nobody would fall across it.

Tín moved toward the window.

A third man stood beside the second car with a long gun braced against his shoulder.

Tín grabbed the round tabletop nearest him and raised it.

The burst came through the windows.

Glass scattered over the dance floor. Three rounds punched into the table. One cut across Tín's upper arm, hot and quick. He lowered his shoulder, drove the table through the broken window, and jumped after it.

The tabletop struck the gunman across the chest. He fell against the car. Tín landed on the pier, caught the barrel before it turned toward him, and bent it down against the edge of the door.

The man let go.

Tín hit him once in the ribs. His body folded sideways. Tín caught his collar before his head reached the timber and laid him beside the wheel.

Iris stood at the bottom of the gangway.

Her right hand held a small pistol pointed at the man Tín had just put down.

“I said no shooting,” she told him.

The man tried to breathe.

Tín looked at her weapon.

“You're having trouble with your staff.”

She lowered it slowly.

Blood ran down Tín's forearm. He pressed his thumb against the cut and looked through the car's open door. A heavy tow cable lay across the back seat beside a pair of bolt cutters.

He pulled out the cable.

“What are you doing?” Iris asked.

“Improving your transportation.”

He looped the cable through the car's front wheel and around a steel bollard. Then he took the bolt cutters, cut their handles off against the edge of the pier with a short hard bend, and tossed the broken pieces onto the seat.

The driver stared through the windshield.

Tín tapped the hood.

“You can walk.”

Iris looked from the secured wheel to the barge's shattered windows. She put the pistol away.

“My father didn't authorize that.”

“Then you can both enjoy the surprise.”

He turned back toward the gangway.

“Take your men. If one reaches for anything except his injuries, I'll put him in the water.”

Inside, Duke stood over the two fallen guards holding a frying pan. One man had attempted to sit up. The dent in the pan explained why he was reconsidering.

“You brought guns into my kitchen,” Duke told him.

Bích took the pan away.

“My kitchen.”

Duke looked at her, then down at the man.

“You see how quickly circumstances change?”

Tín returned through the ballroom door. Mai came from the galley and looked at his arm. She stopped smiling.

“Sit down.”

“It's a scratch.”

She pointed at a chair.

He sat.

Hương brought clean cloth. Bích took the bowl of water from Marcus before he could spill it. Around them, the crew moved the injured men outside while Iris called for another car from the telephone at the bar.

Sable watched her use it.

“Local calls are free,” she said. “Everything else goes on your father's bill.”

Iris stared at her for a moment, then returned to the receiver.

Mai cleaned the blood from Tín's arm. He watched her hands stay steady even when she saw the torn skin.

“You learned that at school?”

“No. At home.”

She pulled the bandage tight enough to make him look at her.

“Hold still.”

Through the broken windows, people had begun gathering at the landing. Rosa Méndez came aboard carrying a foam cooler. She took in the overturned chairs, the blood on Tín's sleeve, and Duke kneeling beside a bucket.

“I brought shrimp,” she said.

Boots leaned against the bar and closed his eyes.

“Thank God somebody understands business.”

Bích opened the cooler. After inspecting its contents, she looked toward her husband.

“We need a bigger party.”

Tín lifted his bandaged arm.

“I thought we were closing.”

“With all this food?”

Outside, Iris's replacement car arrived. She paused at the gangway and looked back toward the ballroom.

Tín raised his good hand.

“Tell your father Saturday next week. Bring an appetite.”

She left without answering.

Marcus placed the needle back on the record.

This time, nobody told him to turn it down.

## Chapter 4: The Man with Two Tow Trucks

Calvin Rook brought a wheelchair to Boots's garage.

It was red, had a padded seat, and carried a ribbon across the back. Two men unloaded it from a van while Rook watched from beneath the shop's awning. His suit was cream. His shoes had never been near anything Boots would call honest work.

Tín sat on a folding chair beside the open bay while Bình changed the oil in his truck. His bandaged left arm rested across his lap. On the floor beside him stood a paper bag containing the forty dollars he had retrieved for Bích and a pair of peaches Vân had insisted he take on the way over.

Rook looked at the chair, the bandage, and the paper crown hanging from the truck's mirror.

“Something more appropriate for your age.”

Tín leaned forward.

“Electric?”

Rook's smile paused.

“Yes.”

“Excellent.”

He stood, walked to the wheelchair, and examined the controls. Boots came out of the bay wiping his hands on a rag.

“You bring the charger?” Boots asked.

Rook looked at him.

“What?”

“These things need a charger. You can't give a man half a present.”

One of Rook's men returned to the van and fetched a cardboard box.

Tín tested the seat with his palm.

“Mr. Benítez will love this.”

Across the street, the cobbler looked up from a shoe clamped between his knees. He was sitting outside his shop because Loretta had told him to stop spending the whole day beneath a fluorescent tube.

“What's that?” he called.

“A birthday present.”

“For who?”

“You're about to have one.”

Boots wheeled the chair across the street. Rook watched the ribbon bob over the uneven pavement.

“It was for you.”

“I'm sharing.”

Mr. Benítez transferred from his stool into the padded seat with Boots holding the frame steady. He tried the control. The chair moved forward. He released it, turned, and came back with a grin spreading beneath his gray mustache.

“How fast?” he asked.

“Don't start,” Boots said.

“I'm asking academically.”

Tín took a peach from the bag and offered it to Rook.

“Thank you. You've made a friend.”

Rook left the peach in his hand.

“We need to discuss my river.”

Tín bit into it.

“I thought you owned half.”

“Who told you half?”

“A friend. He was trying to frighten me economically.”

Rook looked around the garage. A blue tow truck occupied the second bay. An older white one stood outside with its boom raised and a sign beneath the windshield: DO NOT TOUCH THE RADIO.

Boots returned before Rook could read the smaller handwriting beneath it.

“Don't touch the radio,” he said.

Rook looked at him once, then back at Tín.

“You won a foolish wager. Duke will regret it for years. I'll pay you fifty thousand dollars, and we can all enjoy watching him learn.”

“My wife has begun cleaning the kitchen.”

“I'll pay her as well.”

“That's between you and her.”

“You don't seem to understand what you've taken.”

Tín ate another piece of the peach.

“A stove, mostly.”

Rook's eyes hardened. He had pale eyes, almost the color of the sky reflected in the van's windshield. A small scar crossed the bridge of his nose. When he moved his head, the scar stayed white against his tan.

He stepped closer.

“People use that berth because I permit it.”

“You can come on Saturday next week. We haven't printed invitations.”

“I am offering you a profitable ending.”

“I'm offering you lunch.”

The van's side door slid open.

A large man stepped down onto the pavement. The van rose a little behind him. He had short dark hair, a thick neck, and a narrow silver plate visible along the side of his jaw when he turned. His black shirt was buttoned to the throat despite the heat.

Boots glanced toward Bình. The younger man put down his wrench and moved away from the open truck hood.

“Tom,” Rook said.

The man came forward.

Tín looked at the silver plate.

“Dental work?”

“Nail,” the man said.

“Unfortunate dentist.”

Boots made a strangled sound and pretended to cough.

Nail put one hand on the blue tow truck's fender. His fingers pressed into the metal. The fender crumpled beneath his palm with a soft series of clicks.

Boots stared.

“That was painted Tuesday.”

Nail looked at him.

“Now it's Wednesday.”

Tín set the peach on a clean piece of paper beside the chair.

He took Nail's wrist.

“Take your hand off.”

Nail tried to keep it there.

The fender bent farther. Tín lifted the wrist. Nail's fingers came free one at a time. His shoulder rose until he had to straighten to follow it.

For several seconds they stood facing each other beside the truck. Nail's forearm trembled. Tín's expression remained mildly disappointed, the look he gave Bình when the young man claimed a car's strange noise was probably temporary.

Nail brought his other fist up.

Tín pushed his captured arm across his chest. The fist struck Nail's own elbow. Bone hit bone with a crack. Nail staggered back into the van and dented the sliding door.

Rook caught his arm before he could come forward again.

“Enough.”

Nail looked at him, breathing through his nose.

Tín picked up the peach.

“The fender,” Boots said.

Rook removed a roll of cash from his pocket. He peeled off several bills and placed them on the hood.

Boots counted them without touching them.

“Labor.”

Another bill.

“Paint matching.”

Another.

“Pain and suffering.”

Rook looked at him.

Boots pointed at the fender.

“I've named that truck. We're close.”

Rook added one more bill and turned toward the van.

“Enjoy your party, Mr. Lê.”

“Tín is fine.”

“For now.”

He climbed inside. Nail followed, forcing the dented door closed with his shoulder. The van pulled away from the curb.

Across the street, Mr. Benítez drove his new chair in a careful circle.

“Tell your rich friend thank you!” he called.

Tín raised the peach.

“He heard you.”

Boots gathered the money from the hood.

“That nigga came here to threaten us and paid for my whole week.”

“Keep some for the fender.”

“I'm emotionally attached to the money too.”

Bình came out from behind the pickup.

“Nail's the man from the dock fights.”

Tín looked at him.

“What dock fights?”

“Under the warehouse. They charge admission.”

“Of course they do.”

“He put a man through a shipping crate.”

Boots examined the van's disappearing shape.

“Was it painted Tuesday?”

Bình did not laugh.

Tín saw it and put a hand on his shoulder.

“You boxed there?”

“Once.”

“Against him?”

“No. I'm ambitious, not suicidal.”

“Did you get paid?”

Bình hesitated.

“They said the purse was being settled.”

Boots shut his eyes.

“Baby, that's rich-man language for theft.”

A horn sounded at the corner.

The white tow truck began rolling.

Tín turned.

Someone sat behind its wheel. The driver's head was low, his cap pulled down. Behind him, another man climbed onto the rear platform carrying a crowbar.

Boots ran toward it.

“Hey! Hey!”

The truck accelerated.

Its raised boom swung toward the pickup. The hook caught the pickup's front bumper and tore it sideways. Bình jumped away as the truck lurched out of the bay.

The man on the platform swung the crowbar at Boots.

Tín caught Boots by the back of his shirt and pulled him clear. The bar struck the metal door frame, showering old paint across the pavement.

The tow truck dragged the pickup toward Bell Street.

Bình ran after it.

“My truck!”

“Stay back,” Tín said.

He caught the rear corner of the pickup and lifted. The hooked bumper tore away. The pickup stopped across the garage entrance. The tow truck shot forward with the loose bumper swinging beneath its boom.

Tín jumped onto the pickup's hood, then to the roof, then across the gap to the departing truck.

He landed beside the man with the crowbar.

The man swung again. Tín ducked beneath it, drove a shoulder into his stomach, and pushed him against the towing boom. The crowbar fell into the street. Tín pulled the man's jacket over his face and tucked both sleeves through the hook's retaining loop.

The man hung bent forward, swearing into his own lining.

Tín climbed along the boom to the cab.

The driver saw him in the side mirror and swerved.

The truck mounted the curb beside Loretta's salon. Women scattered away from the doorway. A rolling rack of wigs toppled. One landed on the swinging bumper and rode with it, glossy black hair blowing behind the chrome.

Loretta came outside.

“You motherfuckers better bring that back!”

Tín reached the cab roof.

The driver fired upward through it.

Tín moved his foot. The bullet punched a hole beside his sandal. He drove his hand through the thin roof panel, caught the gunman's wrist, and pulled the arm up through the torn metal.

The pistol fell onto the roof.

Tín kicked it away from the crowd and into the open bed of an empty parked truck.

“Stop,” he said.

The driver pressed harder on the accelerator.

Ahead, Mr. Benítez sat in his new chair at the curb, unable to reverse around two pedestrians who had frozen in front of him.

Tín dropped from the roof to the driver's window. He put both feet against the door and pulled.

The steering wheel came off the column with the driver's hands still around it.

For an instant, the man stared at the wheel in his lap.

“That complicates it,” Tín said.
