He jumped to the street, caught the front bumper with his good arm, and lifted the entire front of the truck. The rear wheels squealed. He turned the truck away from the curb and shoved it sideways across the road.

Its rear tires struck the gutter. The vehicle stopped facing the empty wall of a closed furniture store.

The loose bumper swung forward and hit the brickwork.

The wig remained attached.

Tín set the truck down.

Inside, the driver held the detached wheel against his chest.

“Get out.”

The man opened the door.

“Bring that,” Tín said, pointing at the wheel. “Boots will be angry.”

Boots arrived in the blue tow truck, its crumpled fender shaking above the front wheel. Bình stood on the rear platform, holding a length of rope.

They tied the driver and his companion beside the furniture store. Loretta came to retrieve the wig, inspected it, and slapped the driver with it twice before Boots persuaded her to stop adding hair to the evidence.

Tín leaned against the white truck. His bandage had loosened. A line of blood ran down toward his elbow.

Boots looked at it.

“Your wife is going to kill me.”

“She knows whose arm it is.”

“That makes it worse.”

The furniture-store owner emerged from a side door carrying a key ring. He stared at the truck, the tied men, and the steering wheel on the sidewalk.

“This your doing?” he asked Tín.

“Partly.”

The owner looked toward Mr. Benítez, who had finally found a clear route back to his shop.

“He would've been right in front of that thing.”

Tín nodded.

The man took a brass key from the ring.

“You need chairs for that party? Take twenty. Tables too.”

Boots put a hand over his face.

“I need to start having birthdays like this.”

Tín accepted the key.

“Thank you.”

The owner opened his doors. Inside, stacks of folding chairs lined the wall.

Loretta picked one up, tested its weight, and looked at the tied driver.

Boots gently took it from her.

“Party first.”

She let him have it.

Down the block, a siren began approaching. Tín sat on the curb while Bình brought water and a clean rag from the garage.

He looked at the white truck's torn roof.

“Tell Duke,” he said, “I'd like to see the downstairs room.”

Bình understood which downstairs room he meant.

“Tonight?”

Tín checked both watches. Neither agreed with the clock above the furniture store.

“After supper. These people keep interrupting meals.”

## Chapter 5: Nobody Ordered This Much Shrimp

By three o'clock, six businesses had offered to sponsor the party.

By four, Bích had rejected four of their banners.

“His face is too big,” she told Marcus.

Marcus stood on the River Queen's stage holding a rolled sheet of paper. The drawing showed Tín emerging from the river with a boat in one hand and a mountain in the other. A pair of sunglasses covered half his face. Behind him, letters promised THE GRANDMASTER'S SUMMER REIGN.

“It's an artistic interpretation.”

“He has never worn those glasses.”

“He could.”

“And where did he get the mountain?”

“Mrs. Lê, you're approaching this literally.”

Mai took the sheet from him and laid it on a table.

“We're putting the actual boat on the flyer.”

“The boat doesn't sell tickets.”

“We aren't charging admission.”

Marcus stared at her.

“Then what am I promoting?”

“An event.”

“For free?”

“The food stalls pay for their spaces. The bar makes money. People come.”

He considered this, then turned toward Tín.

“Can we charge to meet you?”

Tín sat beside the window while Bích replaced the bandage on his arm. His old shirt lay folded on the next chair with three spots of dried blood along the sleeve.

“Ask the people who've tried.”

“That's going on the flyer.”

“Nothing else goes on the flyer,” Mai said.

Bích tied the bandage and pressed two fingers against the knot.

Tín winced.

“You could use less enthusiasm.”

“You could bring home fewer holes.”

“This is the same hole.”

“Then you're falling behind on repairs.”

She handed him the clean shirt Hương had brought. He put it on carefully, then reached into his pocket and offered the forty dollars.

Bích took it.

“Thank you.”

“I got it back yesterday.”

“I know. I wanted you to remember.”

He watched her place the money in a little purse she kept inside her apron. She had used that purse when they arrived in California five years earlier. Its clasp had been repaired twice. Hương had offered her a new one last Christmas. Bích said this one still knew where everything belonged.

“We'll buy you a better stove at home,” he said.

She glanced toward the galley.

“I have two ovens now.”

“I noticed.”

“You think I want to give them back because some man wore a suit to a garage?”

“I was thinking about safety.”

She took his chin between finger and thumb and turned his face toward hers.

“Think about it before you jump through the next window.”

She released him and went to inspect a crate of vegetables.

Boots came aboard with Detective Vega beside him.

She wore a dark jacket over a plain blouse, and her short hair had been pushed behind one ear. She carried a small notebook. Boots carried the detached steering wheel from his truck.

“She wanted to see it,” he said.

Vega looked at him.

“I wanted you to leave it at the garage.”

“I don't trust those motherfuckers around evidence. They'll steal the wheel separately.”

Vega approached Tín.

“You were on the truck?”

“For part of the journey.”

“On top?”

“Eventually.”

“The driver says you pulled the steering wheel out through the window.”

Boots held it up.

“The window was open. That's important.”

Vega ignored him.

Tín nodded.

She looked at his bandage.

“That from today?”

“Yesterday.”

“Which incident was yesterday?”

“The boat.”

She looked around at the patched windows. One still had a square of plywood covering it. Behind the bar, Hương had taped a handwritten warning over a hole in the floor so nobody would step into it carrying hot food.

Vega closed her notebook for a moment.

“How long have you owned this place?”

“Since Monday.”

Boots set the steering wheel on the bar.

“He's been busy.”

Vega opened the notebook again.

“Duke confirms the sale. He also confirms Rook's people were here. Iris says three men acted against her instructions.”

“They were very energetic about disobeying,” Tín said.

“One of them has a broken jaw. Another says a table fell out of a window.”

“It did.”

“With you behind it.”

“I was concerned about where it would land.”

For the first time, Vega almost smiled.

She looked past him to Mai and Marcus, who had returned to arguing over the flyer.

“Keep the kids out of whatever this becomes.”

Mai looked up.

“I'm standing right here.”

“Then you heard me.”

“I'm making a flyer.”

Vega examined the enormous drawing of Tín with the mountain.

“That's going to need a bigger printer.”

Mai pushed the drawing toward Marcus.

“Thank you.”

Rosa came through the ballroom doors carrying two buckets. Behind her, three men wheeled coolers down the gangway. One wore a shirt reading MÉNDEZ FISH in blue letters. The others wore the strained expressions of men discovering that shrimp remained heavy after being called a donation.

“Where do you want them?” Rosa asked.

Bích pointed toward the galley.

The first cooler rolled past. Then the second. Then a third appeared on the gangway.

Tín stood.

“How much shrimp?”

“Enough,” Rosa said.

“Enough for what?”

“People.”

Boots opened a cooler and looked inside.

“Which people? We inviting the coast?”

Rosa set down her buckets.

“My cousin heard the story about the truck. He said a man who saves Arturo doesn't pay for shrimp.”

“Arturo bought him shoes once,” Loretta explained to Vega.

“Who bought who shoes?”

“It was a long time ago. The important thing is we have shrimp.”

The men moved the first two coolers into the galley. The third wheel caught on the lip of the doorway. Tín lifted the cooler, set it inside, and returned for the buckets.

One contained live crabs.

A claw closed on the edge as he reached for the handle.

He moved his hand.

“That one hasn't heard my reputation.”

Rosa put a lid on the bucket.

“He doesn't read.”

Vega accepted a cup of coffee from Bích and remained at the bar while the deliveries continued. She asked about the men from the truck. Tín answered what he had seen. Boots supplied names for two of them and descriptions of three unrelated men Vega did not ask about.

“You can call me if you remember something useful,” she told him.

“I got a lot of information.”

“I noticed.”

Outside, a metal clang came from the service side of the deck.

Sable emerged from the office.

“Who's working on the galley fuel?”

Bích looked up.

“Nobody.”

Sable was already moving.

Tín followed her through the side door.

The narrow walkway ran between the galley wall and the river rail. At its far end stood a steel cabinet secured to the deck. Its door hung open. A man in a delivery shirt crouched beside it with a tool bag at his feet.

He turned when Sable spoke.

Tín saw the small flame before he understood what the man had done.

“Inside,” he told her.

The man threw something toward the cabinet and ran.

Fire flashed along its lower edge.

Tín seized the man's collar as he passed, lifted him off his feet, and threw him through the open doorway into the ballroom. He landed on his back between two tables.

“Hold him!”

Boots dropped on him with the steering wheel across his chest.

Outside, the fire climbed the cabinet.

Tín gripped the steel frame with both hands and tore it away from the deck. The bolts came up through the boards. Something hissed. Flame washed across his clean sleeve and browned the cloth.

He heaved the entire cabinet over the rail.

It struck the river twenty feet from the barge, vanished, and blew apart beneath the surface.

Water erupted past the upper balcony. A piece of the cabinet door spun into the air and landed against the far bank with a crash. The River Queen rocked. Inside, people shouted as tables slid and glasses fell.

Tín held the rail until the deck settled beneath him.

Then he looked at his sleeve.

“I just put this on.”

Sable returned with a fire extinguisher. She sprayed the burning patch of deck beside his feet until it disappeared under white powder.

Vega came through the doorway holding her pistol low.

“Is there another man?”

Tín pointed toward the service stair. A second delivery worker had reached the pier and was running for the street.

Vega shouted. The man kept going.

Tín picked up a loose mooring rope, swung its heavy knotted end once, and sent it across the gap. The knot caught the runner behind the knees. He hit the pier on his stomach and slid into a coil of wet line.

Vega ran down the gangway.

Tín looked into the ballroom.

Mai and Hương were helping one of Rosa's delivery men sit up. He had slipped when the deck rocked and cut his palm on a broken glass. Bích pressed a towel around his hand. Marcus held the man's elbow and looked unusually quiet.

Boots still had the first attacker under the steering wheel.

“You pick a seafood delivery to get stupid,” he told him. “We got buckets. We can lose you in themes.”

Tín stepped inside.

Sable caught his burned sleeve.

“Let me see.”

He showed her his arm. The skin above the bandage had reddened. She touched the unburned edge and shook her head.

“Cold water.”

Bích came over with a clean bowl before he could protest.

This time he did not.

Vega returned with the second man. She put him beside his companion and called for officers from the bar telephone. The two men refused to look at each other.

Rosa opened the first man's tool bag with the toe of her shoe. A delivery receipt slid out, blank except for the Crown Shipping stamp across the top.

Tín looked at it.

Vega picked it up by one corner.

“I'll take that.”

“You'll want the wheel too,” Boots said.

“Please take the wheel,” Loretta added.

Boots looked wounded.

“It held the suspect.”

“It also needs to hold your truck.”

The officers arrived. They took the men down the gangway while the kitchen crew began cleaning the broken glass. Rosa's injured worker insisted he could carry another cooler. Bích told him to sit down and earn his dignity by eating something.

Tín stood beside the burned service door, watching the last pale powder settle into the grain of the wood.

Sable came beside him.

“Rook's getting impatient.”

“He can come clean up.”

“He needs the berth open by next week.”

“For what?”

She looked toward the river, then at the doorway behind them.

“Ask him about the midnight train.”

“Why don't you tell me?”

“Because I want you to see where he keeps the answer.”

Tín studied her face.

She held his gaze, then stepped away to help Hương move the unbroken plates.

Bích called everyone to eat before the food went cold.

The stove still worked. She had checked it herself. Whatever Rook had hoped to accomplish, fourteen people were about to have supper in his former kitchen.

Tín sat beside his wife. She placed a plate in front of him and rested one hand briefly on the back of his neck.

“You're going out tonight.”

He nodded.

“Wear the ugly shirt.”

“Which one?”

She looked at him.

“You know.”

He did.

## Chapter 6: The House Asked for Another Table

The ugly shirt had peacocks on it.

Tín had bought it in 1988 because the salesman said it suited his confidence. Bích said the salesman had correctly identified the problem. Four years later, the peacocks remained blue, orange, and impossible to forgive.

Duke looked at the shirt when Tín arrived at the warehouse.

“You came to distract them?”

“My wife selected it.”

“She angry with you?”

“She wants me to come home.”

“In that shirt, they'll send you back.”

Duke wore a dark coat over his tracksuit. He had removed the anchor necklace. Without it, his neck seemed unexpectedly practical.

Bình stood beside Tín with his swollen cheek uncovered. He had insisted on coming after hearing that Rook kept the fight purses downstairs. Boots had wanted to come too, but Loretta had hidden the keys to both tow trucks and told him to develop a hobby that did not require police statements.

The warehouse doors opened onto a ramp. At the bottom, music and warm air rose from a basement larger than Tín expected. Tables stood beneath low lights. Men and women leaned over cards, dice, and stacks of colored chips. Along the far wall, a small boxing ring occupied a raised platform.

A waiter passed carrying drinks in glasses with Crown Shipping etched near the rim.

“Convenient,” Tín said.

Duke looked at him.

“What?”

“When the police arrive, they won't have to ask who bought the glasses.”

A woman at the nearest table recognized Duke and waved. Then she saw Tín.

“That's him.”

The dealer looked up.

“Who?”

“The bowling man.”

By the time they reached the bar, a path had opened through the room. People turned in their chairs. A man in a silk vest came forward holding a drink he had clearly purchased for himself and presented it with both hands.

Tín accepted it.

“What is it?”

“Whiskey.”

“Thank you.”

The man pointed at the peacocks.

“Incredible shirt.”

Duke turned away and stared at the ceiling.

“Don't do this to him,” he muttered.

Calvin Rook sat at a round table beneath a green lamp. Iris stood behind his chair. Nail occupied the space beside the ring, watching a smaller fighter skip rope. The rope stopped when Tín entered.

Rook set down his cards.

“I didn't invite you.”

“I didn't invite the fire.”

Around the table, chips stopped moving.

Iris looked at her father.

He kept his eyes on Tín.

“Accidents happen on old boats.”

“Two of yours are discussing it with Detective Vega.”

Rook's mouth tightened slightly.

Tín pulled out a chair.

“You owe Bình his purse.”

Bình stepped beside him.

Rook looked at the young man's cheek.

“You lost.”

“You paid for me to fight,” Bình said. “I fought.”

“You lasted two rounds.”

“The other man lasted one and a half. They carried him away.”

“There were expenses.”

Tín took a chip from the stack nearest him. It was black, heavier than he expected, with a gold crown stamped at the center.

“How much is this?”

“Five thousand,” Rook said.

Tín handed it to Bình.

Rook caught his wrist.

The table shifted toward them.

For a moment, glasses trembled beneath the green lamp. Rook's fingers tightened. Tín looked down at the hand on his wrist, then up at the man across from him.

“That's more than his purse,” Rook said.

“There were expenses.”

Rook let go.

Tín placed both palms on the table and pushed it gently back to its original position. A little whiskey spilled over one glass. He moved a napkin beneath it.

“The midnight train,” he said.

Iris stopped turning the ring on her finger.

Rook watched Tín for several seconds.

“You should concern yourself with your family.”

“I am. We have a boat in your way.”

“You have a boat in everyone's way.”

“Everyone has been giving me presents.”

Rook glanced toward the crowd. The man in the silk vest raised his glass before remembering whose room he was in.

“Popularity is cheap,” Rook said.

“Then stop overpaying to be disliked.”

A laugh escaped from the card table behind them.

Rook stood.

“Tom.”

Nail climbed into the ring. The smaller fighter hurried out between the ropes.

Tín looked at the raised platform.

“You want your money back?”

“I want you to understand the room you're in.”

“It has a ring, twelve tables, and one exit everyone keeps watching. I understand it.”

“Then make a wager.”

Duke put a hand on Tín's chair.

“He doesn't fight clean.”

Tín looked up at him.

“Have you seen the shirt?”

Duke took his hand away.

Rook held out a stack of black chips.

“Fifty thousand. You last three minutes, it's yours.”

“And Bình's five thousand stays his.”

“Fine.”

“And if I finish early?”

Rook smiled.

“Then you can go home early.”

Tín stood and finished the whiskey. He placed the empty glass in front of the man who had given it to him.

“Thank you. You chose well.”

The man put a hand over his heart.

Tín climbed into the ring.

Nail rolled his neck. Up close, the silver plate along his jaw showed little dark screws at either end. His left hand had swollen slightly where Tín had caught it at the garage. He flexed it once and dropped both arms to his sides.

“No gloves?” Tín asked.

Nail shook his head.

“You should ask for some.”

The bell rang.

Nail stepped in with a straight right aimed at Tín's throat.

Tín turned his shoulder. The fist passed his cheek. He struck Nail's ribs with his left palm and stepped away as the bigger man's elbow came down toward his wrist.

Nail followed, driving a knee at his stomach.

Tín caught the thigh, lifted it, and pushed. Nail struck the ropes backward. The nearest corner post bent an inch toward the crowd. People moved their drinks out of the way.

Nail came off the ropes with both hands reaching.

He caught Tín's shirt at the shoulders and slammed him into the corner.

The post broke through the platform.

Pain flashed across Tín's burned arm. He tucked his chin as Nail's forehead came forward. The blow struck the top of his head instead of his nose. Nail grunted. Tín drove two short punches into the man's stomach, then lifted both elbows between the gripping arms.

The shirt tore.

One peacock left in Nail's right hand.

Tín looked at it.

“My wife will send flowers.”

He struck Nail under the chin.

The big man rose onto his toes. Tín hit him again before his heels came down, this time across the body. Nail stumbled sideways into the sagging ropes. He tore one loose and swung its metal hook toward Tín's face.

Tín ducked.

The hook passed over his head and buried itself in the green-shaded lamp outside the ring. The lamp fell onto Rook's table. Glass burst across the cards. Rook moved back so quickly his chair went over.

The crowd scattered from that side of the platform.

Nail hauled the rope back. Tín stepped onto it, pinning it beneath his sandal.

Nail pulled harder.

The far corner of the ring tore away from its supports.

Tín stayed where he was.

The platform tilted. Nail lost his footing and dropped to one knee. Tín crossed the sloping boards and kicked him in the chest.

Nail went through the remaining ropes and onto a card table.

The table collapsed under him.

Chips flew across the floor. A woman caught a stack against her dress and held it there, staring down as if money had chosen her personally.

Nail rolled off the broken table and came up holding one of its legs.

Tín stepped down from the ring.

Rook moved toward him.

“Stay on the platform.”

Tín pointed at the wreckage.

“It left first.”

Nail swung the table leg across his body. Tín caught it in both hands. Wood split between their grips. Nail drove forward behind the broken end.

Tín turned, let the point pass his ribs, and caught the man's forearm beneath his elbow. He put his heel behind Nail's ankle and pushed the arm across his chest.

Nail hit the floor on his back.

The boards beneath him cracked.

He tried to rise. Tín knelt on his right wrist and put two fingers against the silver plate beside his jaw.

“Does this come off?”

Nail went still.

His eyes moved from Tín's face to the hand beside his head.

“Enough,” Rook said.

Tín looked up.

“He can tell me.”

Nail swallowed.

“Enough.”

Tín released him and stood.

For a moment, the room held its breath.

Then somebody on the far side shouted, “Pay that nigga!”

The chant spread between the tables. People struck the rail with their hands. The woman holding chips against her dress began laughing. Duke stood beside Bình with a broad grin he no longer tried to hide.

Rook took the fifty thousand from the unbroken end of his table and handed it to Tín.

Tín passed it to Bình.

“Carry that.”

Bình stared at the stack.

“All of it?”

“It would look strange if you left some floating.”

Sable appeared from a side corridor. Tín had not seen her enter. She took one look at the ring and stopped beside the bar.

“I asked for another table,” she said. “Singular.”

Duke began laughing so hard he had to sit on the edge of the platform.

Rook pulled Tín aside by the torn sleeve.

Tín looked down at the grip.

Rook let go before he had to ask.

“The berth is mine,” Rook said quietly. “Whatever papers Duke signed, whatever applause you collected, that apron behind the boat stays mine.”

“Then why burn the kitchen?”

Rook's eyes narrowed.

“Move the vessel by Friday.”

“Our party is Saturday next week.”

“Then find another view.”

Tín leaned close enough that Rook could smell the whiskey.

“Send another man with fire, and I'll bring the kitchen to your house.”

Rook looked at the broken ring. His mouth opened, then closed.

Tín turned away.

At the stairs, Sable caught up with him.

“The apron,” she said. “You heard him.”

“Rail loading?”

She nodded.

“A delivery train comes through after midnight. He needs trucks where your gangway stands. That's only the part you can see.”

“What's underneath?”

“Ask Duke how he kept the liquor bill so low.”

She returned to the floor before he could stop her.

Outside, Duke sat on the warehouse steps with his coat open. Bình counted the chips for the third time.

Tín held out the torn piece of his shirt.

“I may frame this.”

Duke looked at the missing peacock.

“Best thing Nail ever did.”

“Tell me about the liquor bill.”

Duke stopped smiling.

From below them came another burst of cheering. Somebody had begun selling small pieces of the broken card table.

Tín sat beside Duke on the step.

“Quickly,” he said. “I'd like to hear it before they start selling the stairs.”

## Chapter 7: Mai Brings Her Own Camera

Mai made him stand in front of a bedsheet.

“Should I look dangerous?” Tín asked.

“You should look where I'm pointing.”

“I can do both.”

She lowered the camera.

He looked where she was pointing.

The sheet hung from the garage door at Boots's shop. Marcus had painted a river across its bottom and several gold stars at the top. Between the stars, a new banner read GRANDMASTER CHIGGA PRESENTS.

Tín examined it.

“What happened to my name?”

Marcus held up both hands.

“That is your name. For entertainment purposes.”

“My wife calls me something else when entertained.”

Boots leaned against the blue truck and laughed.

“My nigga got promoted. Don't fight the blessing.”

Mai took the banner down.

“Nobody is being promoted. We're advertising food, music, and boat rides.”

Marcus took it from her before the wet paint touched the ground.

“You're very restrictive for an artist.”

“You're very expensive for a volunteer.”

Tín wore a plain dark shirt. Bích had chosen it after seeing the remains of the peacocks. He had expected her to be angry about the torn cloth. Instead she had held it up, looked through the largest hole, and asked whether Nail needed a thank-you card.

The burn on his left arm had formed a red patch above the healing graze. He kept the sleeve loose. Mai noticed whenever he adjusted it and waited without making him announce that it hurt.

She lifted the camera again.

“Smile.”

He smiled.

“Normally.”

“This is my normal smile.”

“You look like you know where somebody is buried.”

Boots turned away from the camera.

“Baby, use the other lens.”

Mai finally caught the picture when Tín laughed at him. She lowered the camera, satisfied, and waved Marcus over to help take down the sheet.

“You're free.”

“How much do I owe?”

“A ride to the printer.”

“I have a bus pass.”

“We're carrying boards.”

“It covers refrigerators.”

“Grandpa.”

He took the keys to Bình's pickup. The bumper had been replaced with a temporary steel bar Boots promised was stronger than the original. Bình had painted a little crown at one end while Boots wasn't looking.

Mai put the layout boards between the seats. Marcus climbed into the back with the camera bag and a box of paper.

“Where's your father?” Tín asked.

“School. He said you could take me.”

“He did?”

“He said you'd ask that.”

Tín started the engine.

At the end of Bell Street, they passed Duke standing beside the River Queen's landing with a stack of empty liquor crates. He had come before sunrise to show Tín the service door that opened from the barge toward the rail apron. The crates arrived there cheap because their proper owners were still looking for them. Duke had accepted them without asking enough questions. Sable had kept count of the deliveries and the nights when trucks came for something other than liquor.

Tín had asked what else.

Duke had opened one empty case. Inside, dark foam held the impressions of six handguns.

That had ended the tour.

Now Duke lifted a crate toward the pickup.

“These go back,” he called.

“To who?” Tín asked.

Duke looked into it.

“I'm working on that part.”

Mai turned toward her grandfather as they drove on.

“He works there now?”

“Your grandmother is deciding.”

“He used to own it.”

“She's considering that a gap in his experience.”

The printer occupied a narrow shop near the old rail bridge. Its windows displayed wedding invitations, church programs, nightclub cards, and a faded poster promising FAST TURNAROUND. Inside, two machines ran at once, making conversation require determination.

The owner, Mr. Chen, looked at Mai's layout and adjusted his glasses.

“You did this?”

She nodded.

“The spacing here is wrong.”

Marcus opened his mouth.

Mai caught his sleeve.

“Show me,” she said.

Mr. Chen took a pencil and marked the page. Tín stood beside a shelf of paper samples while his granddaughter watched the correction. She asked three questions. The first made Mr. Chen grunt. The second made him take out another sheet. By the third, he had invited her behind the counter.

Marcus leaned toward Tín.

“He's stealing our designer.”

“She appears to be improving the terms.”

They waited while Mai and Mr. Chen adjusted the lettering. Outside, a train moved slowly across the service line behind the shops. Tín could hear its wheels even through the machines.

A flatbed truck followed the narrow street beside it.

On the truck lay three long wooden cases and a polished brass pipe bent at one end. The pipe slid against the side rail when the driver braked.

Marcus looked through the window.

“That's from the Orpheum.”

Tín glanced at him.

“The theater?”

“They took out the organ last week. My music teacher went down there and got mad. Said they sold it to some church.”

The truck stopped beside a shuttered warehouse across the road. Two men pulled open the rear doors. A third came out carrying a clipboard.

He wore a Crown Shipping jacket.

Tín watched him point toward the wooden cases.

Mai appeared beside the window with her camera bag.

“We're waiting for the first sheet,” she said.

Marcus pointed at the brass pipe.

She lifted the camera.

“For the music page,” she said, seeing Tín look at her.

She took two photographs through the glass, then stepped outside for a clearer angle.

Tín went with her.

Across the road, one of the men dropped the end of a case. The lid sprang open. Beneath the brass fittings lay black weapons wrapped in cloth.

Mai's shutter clicked.

The man with the clipboard looked up.

“Hey!”

Tín put himself between Mai and the road.

“Inside.”

She took one step backward.

The clipboard man reached into his jacket.

Tín picked up the printer's sandwich board and threw it across the street.

It struck the man at shoulder height and carried him through the open warehouse doors.

Mai went inside.

“Back door,” Tín called.

Mr. Chen was already pointing. Marcus grabbed the layout boards. Mai caught his wrist and pulled him toward the rear passage.

The truck driver fired from behind his door.

Tín dropped behind the pickup as the windshield burst. Glass sprayed across the seats. He caught the truck's temporary bumper, pulled it free of its mounting, and rose with it across his chest.

Another shot struck the steel bar.

He ran forward.

The driver tried to swing his door shut. Tín jammed the bar through the opening and pushed. The door folded inward against the man. His pistol dropped into the footwell.

Tín left him trapped and turned toward the warehouse.

The second loader came out with a short shotgun.

Tín reached him before the barrel cleared the doorway. He caught the weapon with his left hand and drove his right elbow into the man's nose. Blood struck the white loading sheet taped to the wall. The man fell against the door track and slid down it.

The third loader ran along the side of the building.

Tín heard a shout behind the printer.

He threw the shotgun onto the warehouse roof and ran for the alley.

Mai and Marcus had reached the rear courtyard. Mr. Chen stood in the doorway behind them with a heavy paper cutter held in both hands. The escaping loader came around the corner and caught Marcus by the shoulder.

The layout boards fell.

Mai struck the man's wrist with her camera bag. He swore and shoved her aside. She hit the fence, caught herself, and came forward again.

“Stay back!” Tín shouted.

He jumped onto a stack of pallets, caught the top of the dividing wall, and vaulted across it.

He landed between the loader and the courtyard gate.

The man pulled Marcus against him and produced a knife.

Tín stopped.

Marcus's eyes widened. His hands gripped the man's forearm below the blade.

“Put it down,” Tín said.

The loader backed toward the far gate.

“You stay there.”

Mai moved to one side, keeping the camera bag in her hand. Tín saw her looking at Marcus's feet, the gate, the broken chair beside the wall.

He shook his head once.

She stayed where she was.

The gate opened behind the loader.

Hòa stood on the other side carrying a stack of exercise books.

He looked at Marcus, then at the knife.

“You're blocking the path.”

The loader swung his elbow backward.

Hòa caught it against his ribs with one arm. He put the exercise books on the wall, took the man's knife wrist, and turned it outward.

The blade fell.

Marcus stumbled free.

Hòa moved his foot behind the loader's heel and guided him down until both knees touched the ground. The man's face went gray. Hòa held his arm at an angle that made any attempt to rise end immediately.

Tín watched his son's hands.

The man's wrist had stopped trembling. So had the rest of him.

“Dad,” Mai said.

Hòa looked at her.

“I came to see your first print.”

Marcus bent over with his hands on his knees.

“The review process got aggressive.”

Mr. Chen lowered the paper cutter.

“Call police,” he said to his assistant inside.

Hòa turned toward Tín.

“Are there more?”

“Across the street.”

“Go.”

Tín looked once more at the captured arm, then went back through the alley.

The driver remained trapped behind his bent door. The man beneath the loading sheet was trying to sit up. The clipboard man had crawled out from under the sandwich board and was considering the far exit.

Tín pointed at the floor.

He sat.

When Vega arrived, Tín stood beside the open case. She looked at its contents and called to an officer before greeting him.

“An organ,” Tín said.

She looked at the brass pipes.

“A loud one.”

Behind them, Mai brought the camera from the printer's shop. She held it against her chest.

“I have photographs.”

Vega looked at her, then at the broken windshield across the road.

“You okay?”

Mai nodded, then shook her head a little.

“Mostly.”

“Good enough for now. We'll talk somewhere away from this.”

Mr. Chen emerged carrying the first printed flyer.

He gave it to Mai.

The lettering was clean. Tín stood beside the River Queen's name, smiling at something beyond the frame. Beneath him, a simple line promised food, music, and a place to dance.

Mai ran a thumb along the edge.

“Thank you.”

Mr. Chen looked toward the ruined sandwich board.

“Your grandfather pays for that.”

“Of course,” she said.

Hòa retrieved his exercise books from the courtyard wall. As they waited for Bình to bring another car, he stood beside Tín beneath the shop awning.

“You didn't know?” he asked.

“No.”

“She came for printing.”

“I know.”

Hòa watched Mai show the flyer to Marcus. The boy's hands had stopped shaking enough to hold one corner.

“Then don't tell her the problem was leaving the house.”

Tín looked at his son.

Hòa met his eyes, calm and tired from a day that had acquired an armed man in the middle of it.

“I wasn't going to.”

“Good.”

Across the street, officers closed the weapon case. One of the brass pipes had rolled beneath the truck. It shone in the gutter while the afternoon traffic moved carefully around the scene.

Mai came to stand between them.

“Mr. Chen said I can work Saturdays.”

Hòa looked down at her.

“You want to?”

She nodded.

Tín took the flyer and examined it again.

“You'll have to tell your grandmother.”

“About the job?”

“That she has competition for your Saturdays.”

Mai smiled at last.

Hòa put an arm around her shoulders. With his other hand, he carried the exercise books home.

## Chapter 8: A Very Inconvenient Wedding

The groom was late because somebody had tied a ribbon around his engine controls.

“It's a boat wedding,” Denise said. “The boat should look married.”

Mateo Méndez stood in the wheelhouse of the Little Mercy with a pair of scissors between his teeth. White satin ran around the steering wheel, across the throttles, and down to a brass bell someone had polished until the lettering nearly disappeared.

“The boat would like to move,” he said around the scissors.

Denise looked through the wheelhouse window.

“You can complain after you get me to the ceremony.”

She wore a cream dress Hương had finished that morning, three days ahead of the emergency Denise had expected to invent. A small veil rested above her dark curls. Her bouquet lay on a bench beside a toolbox and a pair of work gloves.

Tín held the gangway while the last guests came aboard. The Little Mercy was a squat tug with a green hull, a broad rear deck, and a name Mateo defended whenever somebody suggested Big Mercy might pull harder. Today, an arch of white flowers stood behind the cabin. Folding chairs faced it in two short rows.

Rosa stood at the bottom of the gangway checking people against a handwritten list.

“We have twenty places,” she told Boots.

“I am one person.”

“You brought a cooler.”

“The cooler doesn't require a chair.”

“You tried to give it one.”

Boots looked at Tín.

“It's a wedding. I'm thinking about dignity.”

Tín took the cooler and carried it aboard.

“I'll stand with it.”

Rosa pointed at him.

“You're sitting. My brother wants you in the photograph.”

“I can be photographed standing.”

“Everybody knows. We want variety.”

Bích took his arm and led him to a chair beside hers. His left sleeve covered the fresh dressing. The burn had begun to itch. He had been forbidden to scratch it by his wife, granddaughter, daughter-in-law, and a woman at Vân's grocery who had overheard enough to join the decision.

Mai stood near the rail with her camera. Hòa helped Marcus secure a small speaker beneath the cabin awning. Hương checked Denise's hem one last time and removed a loose thread with the concentration of a woman capable of finding imperfections during an earthquake.

Mateo freed the controls.

The engine started.

People on the pier cheered. Mr. Benítez raised a little flag from his red chair. Vân stood beside him holding a tray of pastries nobody had room to carry. She had already distributed half of them to strangers who made the mistake of watching the boat.

The tug moved into the river.

Duke remained on the pier, waving from beside the River Queen's gangway. Bích had left him a list of cleaning tasks. He held it in his other hand, and even from the water Tín could see how badly he wanted the tug to come back and take him away.

“You could have invited him,” Tín said.

Bích adjusted his collar.

“I did. He said weddings make him emotional.”

“He was looking at the grease trap.”

“Then he should have answered faster.”

They went west, past the rail apron and the old cannery inlet. Mateo wanted to marry in front of the little lighthouse at the river bend, where he and Denise had eaten sandwiches on their first date. Denise remembered the sandwiches as cold. Mateo remembered that she had stayed for a second one.

The officiant was Denise's uncle Frank, who had brought his remarks in a blue folder and was now holding it against the wind with both hands.

“We should begin,” he said as the tug slowed.

Marcus pressed play.

The wrong cassette started.

A voice through the speaker announced a discount on used tires.

Boots reached across Hòa and hit stop.

Everyone turned toward him.

“I support his career,” he said.

Marcus found the right cassette. Denise came through the wheelhouse door on Rosa's arm. Mateo stood beneath the flowers with his jacket buttoned crookedly. Tín caught his eye and pointed at the button. Mateo looked down, swore under his breath, and fixed it before Denise reached him.

She saw anyway.

“You look handsome,” she said.

“You look expensive.”

“I am.”

Frank opened the folder.

The ceremony made it through two paragraphs before the speedboat appeared.

It came from the cannery inlet, low and dark, with three men aboard. A second boat followed farther back. The first cut across the tug's wake and came alongside its starboard quarter.

Mateo looked past Denise toward the water.

The man at the speedboat's bow raised a pistol.

“Shut the engine off!”

Frank stopped reading.

Denise turned slowly.

“Absolutely fucking not.”

Tín rose.

“Down,” he told the guests.

Bích pulled Frank behind the cabin before he could ask where they had reached in the remarks. Hương took Denise by the elbow and moved her toward the wheelhouse. Hòa lifted the nearest row of chairs and set them against the rail, forming a low barrier between the guests and the gun.

The first shot struck one of the chairs.

Tín jumped from the tug to the speedboat.

He landed on its bow hard enough to bury it beneath the water. Spray washed over his sandals. The gunman staggered backward. Tín caught the pistol wrist and drove it down against the windshield frame.

The gun fired into the water.

Tín hit the man in the throat with his other hand. The gunman fell into the footwell, clutching his neck.

The driver turned sharply.

Tín caught the frame above the windshield. The boat tilted beneath him. Its stern swung toward the tug, bringing the third man close enough to throw a metal hook at the rear rail.

The hook caught beneath the floral arch.

The line tightened.

The arch tore out of its supports and leaned toward the river.

Mai ducked beneath it. Her camera struck the deck. She caught the rail with both hands as flowers swept over her head.

Tín let go of the windshield and stepped onto the speedboat's gunwale. He caught the falling arch with one hand and held it above the water.

The boat rolled under the weight.

The third man reached for a knife to cut his own line.

Tín swung the arch back onto the tug.

It landed against the wheelhouse with a crash of wooden lattice and white flowers. Hòa caught the far end before it struck the guests. He set it across the deck, expression unchanged, while Marcus crawled underneath to reach Mai's camera.

Tín turned back to the speedboat.

The knife came up.

He caught the attacker's forearm, twisted, and struck him across the face with the back of his hand. The man hit the rail and went over. Tín caught his belt before he reached the water and hauled him back aboard by it.

“Stay where people can find you,” he said.

The driver reached beneath his seat.

Tín put his palm against the man's forehead and drove him backward into the padded chair. The headrest broke. The driver slumped with his hands empty.

Tín pulled the throttle back.

The second speedboat came alongside the tug on its other side.

Two men rose behind its windshield. One carried a short shotgun. The other lifted a canister with a rag burning at its mouth.

Mateo turned the Little Mercy toward them.

The tug's heavy side struck the speedboat's bow. The man with the canister fell against his companion. Fire splashed across the water and burned in a brief floating sheet.

The shotgun went off.

Glass burst from the wheelhouse.

Denise ducked behind the controls. Mateo fell against the door frame with blood spreading along his upper leg.

“Mateo!” Rosa shouted.

Tín jumped back onto the tug's rear rail. From there, he crossed the deck in three strides and leaped over the opposite side.

He struck the second speedboat beside its engine.

The stern went under. Water poured into the cockpit. The shotgun man turned toward him. Tín seized the weapon and pulled the man forward until his chest hit the rail.

He drove his elbow into the side of the man's head.

The body went limp. Tín let it fall inside the boat.

The remaining attacker stood with his hands raised. Fire had burned through one sleeve. He stared at Tín and shook his head rapidly.

“I'm done.”

“Good.”

Tín caught the tug's trailing line and secured the sinking boat beside it. He climbed back aboard as Mateo tried to stand.

Denise had torn the lower lining of her dress and pressed it against his thigh. Hương held the cloth in place while Rosa tied a strip above it. The wound was bleeding steadily, but Mateo remained awake and furious.

“My wedding,” he said.

“I noticed,” Denise answered. “Hold this.”

She placed his hand over the cloth.

Tín knelt beside him.

“Can you move your foot?”

Mateo did.

“Good. We're going ashore.”

“The ceremony—”

“Will fit on land.”

Denise took her husband's face between both hands.

“You are marrying me with all the blood you have left. Stop negotiating.”

He nodded.

Hòa had taken the controls. The tug turned toward the nearest landing, towing the disabled speedboat. Boots hauled the first boat close enough to secure it behind the second. Its surviving men remained where Tín had left them.

Marcus crouched beside Mai. A shallow cut ran across her forearm where the arch had scraped her. He offered her the camera with both hands.

“It still works.”

She took it, then looked toward Mateo.

“Is he okay?”

“He needs help,” Tín said. “We're getting it.”

She nodded and put the camera away.

At the landing, men ran from a repair shed to catch the tug's lines. Someone called for an ambulance from the office. Tín lifted Mateo from the wheelhouse and carried him ashore while Denise walked beside them holding the cloth against his leg.

The nearest worker pulled off his jacket and laid it on a bench.

Tín set Mateo down.

Frank came up the gangway carrying his damp blue folder.

Denise looked at him.

“How much is left?”

Frank blinked.

“The vows. The rings. A reading.”

“Skip the reading.”

“Your aunt chose it.”

“She can read it to us at the hospital.”

Mateo started laughing, then winced and pressed harder against the wound.

Frank opened the folder.

They married on the repair-yard bench with Rosa holding the flowers that had survived the arch and Boots standing behind the couple with both rings in his palm. The ambulance arrived during Mateo's vows. Its crew waited long enough for him to finish, then moved in while Denise said hers.

She put the ring on his finger as they lifted the stretcher.

“You may kiss,” Frank began.

She kissed him before the sentence ended.

The repair crew applauded. One man blew the tug's horn. Another tried to hand Tín a hundred-dollar bill.

“For what?” Tín asked.

“Whatever the hell I just watched.”

Tín pushed the bill back into his hand.

“Give it to the couple.”

The man tucked it into the bouquet.

More money followed. By the time Denise climbed into the ambulance, Rosa's flowers looked as if somebody had tried to grow a bank.

Vega arrived with two patrol cars. She took in the towed speedboats, the bullet holes, and the floral arch lying across the tug's deck.

“Wedding?” she asked.

Bích nodded.

“Congratulations.”

“Tell the man in the ambulance.”

Vega went to speak with the crew before they left. Tín stood at the rail beside the surviving attacker with the burned sleeve.

“Who sent you?”

The man looked toward the police.

“Ask them.”

Tín picked up the length of hook line and held it in his hand.

The man's eyes followed it.

“Bishop,” he said. “Bishop Price.”

“Working for Rook?”

“I don't ask who pays Bishop.”

Tín laid the line down.

Behind him, Bích touched his back.

“Come here.”

He followed her to the other side of the deck. She held a damp cloth and wiped a streak of blood from his cheek. It belonged to someone else.

“Mateo will live,” she said. “The medic told Rosa.”

Tín closed his eyes for a moment.

“Good.”

She took his hand.

“I still want the party.”

He looked at her.

“I know.”

“I want you at it.”

He squeezed her fingers.

On the landing, Marcus had found the correct cassette again. He played it quietly through the tug's speaker while Hương gathered the ruined flowers. Mai took one photograph of the empty bench, the blue folder, and the hundred-dollar bill somebody had missed beneath the cushion.

Then she put the camera away and helped clean up.

## Chapter 9: Duke Gets His Shoes Wet

Mateo's hospital room contained twelve flower arrangements, four coolers, and a wife who had begun charging admission to opinions.

“How is he?” Tín asked from the doorway.

Denise held out her hand.

“You're free. You carried him.”

“What are the others paying?”

“Whatever makes them leave before he gets tired.”

Mateo lay against two pillows with his injured leg raised. A bandage disappeared beneath the sheet. He had shaved, apparently at Denise's insistence, and looked offended by the gown.

“They cut my trousers,” he said.

“They were full of blood,” Denise told him.

“Hương hemmed those.”

“Then stop getting shot in tailored clothes.”

Tín placed a bag of fruit on the cabinet.

“Bích sent this.”

Denise looked inside.

“Tell her thank you.”

“She'll be here later. She didn't trust me with the soup.”

Mateo smiled and reached for his hand.

Tín took it.

For a moment neither spoke.

“You got everybody off?” Mateo asked.

“Everybody from the tug.”

“Mai?”

“A scratch. She's angry about the camera strap.”

“Good.”

Denise moved the chair closer with her foot. Tín sat.

The surgeon had cleaned the wound and removed fragments of cloth. Mateo would stay a few days, then go home on crutches. He listened to Denise explain this with the expression of a man being assigned a punishment for attending his own wedding.

“Can I go to the festival?” he asked.

She looked at him.

“You can sit.”

“On the tug?”

“On something that isn't trying to be useful.”

Tín laughed. Mateo squeezed his hand once and let go.

Outside the room, Rosa waited beside the vending machine. She had slept poorly. Her hair had been pinned up twice and was escaping for a third time.

“Bishop Price,” she said.

Tín nodded.

“I know where he buys his fish.”

“Rosa.”

“I'm just saying.”

“Don't.”

She stared at him, then looked through the open door at her brother.

“Then you do something.”

“I am.”

She pressed her lips together and handed him a paper cup of coffee.

“It's terrible.”

“Why give it to me?”

“I'm angry.”

He accepted it and drank while she went back inside.

Duke waited in the hospital parking lot wearing white shoes and a dark red suit. He held a large gift basket wrapped in clear plastic.

Tín looked at it.

“For Mateo?”

“For Denise. I understand who survived the inconvenience.”

“Room twelve.”

Duke handed him the car keys.

“Don't go anywhere.”

“We have somewhere to go.”

“Then wait five minutes before being impatient beautifully.”

He went inside.

Tín stood beside the car and drank the rest of Rosa's coffee because he had already suffered enough of it to become stubborn. When Duke returned, his gift basket was gone and he carried a wedding favor tied with a white ribbon.

“She gave me candy.”

“You must have behaved.”

“She said it was for leaving quickly.”

They drove to the River Queen.

The landing was quiet. Bích had kept the galley closed for the morning, and the festival volunteers would not arrive until afternoon. Hương had left a note taped to the door telling Marcus exactly which decorations he was allowed to move. Beneath it, Marcus had written YES MA'AM in letters large enough to be read from the pier.

Sable stood beside the service stair with a flashlight.

She looked at Duke's shoes.

“You brought those.”

“I wasn't briefed about mud.”

“I said underneath the dock.”

“A man can hope.”

Tín took the flashlight. Sable unlocked the service gate and led them down a narrow stair to the old rail apron. At low water, a concrete ledge ran beneath its outer edge. Damp lines marked the pilings above it. A steel door sat where the apron met the barge's mooring platform.

Duke pointed.

“Deliveries came through there.”

Tín looked at the distance between the door and the River Queen.

“You thought they carried cases underwater?”

“There was a walkway.”

“You never went down?”

Duke looked at his shoes again.

Tín opened the door.

Inside, a short passage ran under the pier toward a freight lift. The lift platform stood level with the passage floor. Beyond it, another door opened onto the barge's lower storage deck when the vessel sat at the right height beside the apron.

The room smelled of oil, wet wood, and cardboard that had been kept too long near water.

Three empty liquor cases stood beside the lift.

Tín moved the flashlight over the walls. Scratches marked one corner at shoulder height. A fresh tire track crossed the damp concrete and disappeared beneath a sheet of canvas.

He lifted the canvas.

A wheeled frame stood beneath it carrying a heavy locked steel chest.

Duke leaned over his shoulder.

“I don't own that.”

“You're becoming a careful man.”

Sable crouched beside the frame. She touched one wheel with a finger and showed them the wet black residue on it.

“It came from the cannery dock. Same sealant on their loading ramp.”

“What is it?” Duke asked.

Tín pulled the lock apart.

Inside lay bundles of cash wrapped in clear plastic.

Duke stopped breathing for a moment.

Sable whistled once.

Tín moved the top bundle aside. Beneath it sat two pistols and a ring of keys with a yellow plastic tag.

“That's Rook's transfer cash,” Sable said. “He keeps it moving until the shipment arrives.”

Duke looked at her.

“You knew about this?”

“I knew he paid drivers. I didn't know he used your basement as a bank.”

“My former basement.”

Tín picked up the yellow tag.

WEST COLD STORE.

He put it back and closed the lid.

Behind them, the outer door slammed.

The lift began moving.

Sable turned toward its controls.

The platform rose, blocking the upper exit. Water burst through a low opening beneath the passage wall.

Duke stepped back as it reached his shoes.

“Those motherfuckers.”

Tín put the flashlight in his teeth and crossed to the door. He pulled the handle. It moved a fraction, then stopped against something secured outside.

A man's voice came through the steel.

“Rook says leave the money.”

Tín took the flashlight from his mouth.

“Open the door and ask politely.”

A gunshot struck the other side.

He stepped away as the metal dented inward beside his head.

Water rose around their ankles.

Sable climbed onto the lift's lower frame and reached for a switch above the gate. Her fingers fell short. Duke lifted her by the waist. She caught the switch housing, pulled it open, and looked inside.

“No power to the lower controls.”

“Can you open it?” Duke asked.

“If you stop shaking.”

“My shoes are full.”

Tín gripped the door's lower edge.

He pulled.

The hinges tore out of the concrete one after another. Water slapped against his calves. He drew the door into the passage, turned it sideways, and pushed it ahead of him through the opening.

The first gunman fired.

The shot struck steel. Tín shoved the door into the man and carried him backward across the ledge until his back hit a piling.

The second gunman stood on the stair above them.

Tín tilted the door upward as the man fired again. The bullet struck its upper corner and vanished into the concrete overhead. He threw the door up the stairs.

It hit the gunman's legs and pinned him against the rail.

Tín climbed after it.

A third man waited at the top with a long wooden pole. He drove the end at Tín's face. Tín caught it, pulled, and brought the man down the first three steps on his knees.

He struck him across the back with the pole.

The man went flat.

From below, Duke shouted.

Tín looked back.

The ledge beneath the outer stair had begun breaking away. Water rushed through the old cavity behind it, taking loose concrete and rotten timber toward the river. Inside the passage, the wheeled chest rolled as its supports shifted.

Sable jumped from the lift frame onto the chest. Duke caught her arm before she slipped.

“Come out!” Tín called.

They reached the doorway together.

The ledge dropped beneath Duke's foot.

He fell to his waist in the river, catching the threshold with both hands. Sable went to one knee and grabbed his coat. The cloth tore beneath his weight.

Tín came down the stairs, seized Duke by the back of the collar, and lifted him clear.

The shoe on Duke's right foot remained in the mud.

He looked down at the empty sock.

“Fuck.”

Tín set him on the stair above the trapped gunman.

“Stay.”

“I wasn't planning a swim.”

Tín went back for Sable. He took her hand and helped her across the broken gap. Behind her, the chest rolled into the doorway and tipped toward the water.

He caught its handle with his free hand.

Sable stared at him.

“You're taking it?”

“It's in my basement.”

He lifted the chest, stepped across the gap, and carried it up the stairs. At the top he set it beside Hương's decoration note.

Duke sat on the pier with one white shoe and one black sock. Water dripped from his trousers. He held the wedding favor in his hand, checking whether the candy had survived.

Sable came up beside him.

“There's a spare pair in the office.”

“They don't match the suit.”

“Neither does the river.”

Tín returned for the men on the stairs. He dragged the door clear, moved the injured gunmen to the upper landing, and tied their hands with the loose end of a dock line. The man struck with the pole remained conscious and complained about his back.

“You should have used a shorter stick,” Tín told him.

From the far end of the pier, the sound of applause reached them.

Marcus stood with a small group of volunteers, each carrying a box or rolled banner. They had arrived in time to see Tín emerge with a steel chest under one arm and Duke dripping river water beside him.

“Tell me that's treasure,” Marcus said.

Duke held up the wet candy.

“We have all suffered differently.”

Tín opened the chest.

Marcus sat down on his box.

One of the volunteers took off his sunglasses and cleaned them before looking again.

Tín counted several bundles into a paper bag and closed the lid.

“The kitchen needs new fuel equipment,” he told Sable. “The windows need glass. Mateo needs a wedding without gunfire.”

“And the rest?” she asked.

“Rook and I will discuss storage charges.”

Duke looked up.

“Now you're running a nightclub.”

Tín handed Sable the bag.

“Buy Duke some shoes.”

“Black,” she said.

Duke pointed at her.

“Don't let this become a personal campaign.”

Tín took the yellow-tagged keys from the chest and put them in his pocket.

Across the river, a line of gulls rose from the cannery roof. A truck moved along the loading ramp beneath them. Its side carried the same little gold crown he had first seen beside Vân's grocery.

He shut the chest and picked it up.

“I'm going shopping tomorrow,” he said.

Marcus looked at the money, then across at the distant warehouse.

“For what?”

Tín carried the chest through the ballroom doors.

“Whatever they're storing for me.”

## Chapter 10: The Cannery Has Visitors

Rosa drove the truck because she knew where the cannery kept its loading doors and because nobody had succeeded in taking the keys from her.

“You can wait outside,” Tín said.

“You can walk.”

He adjusted the seat belt.

Behind them, Duke sat between Bình and Sable with a clipboard balanced on his knees. Rosa had given him the clipboard because every delivery needed someone willing to look disappointed at a number.

“I owned a nightclub,” he said.

“Then count the boxes dramatically,” Rosa told him.

The truck carried empty fish crates, two ice chests, and a stack of folded canvas tarps. Tín had brought Rook's yellow-tagged keys. Sable wore an old Crown Shipping jacket she had found in the office. She had removed the little crown with scissors, leaving a pale shape where the stitching had been.

“You could have covered it,” Duke said.

“I wanted it to look missing.”

They entered the cannery yard through the west gate. A guard sat beneath an awning with a portable television on his lap. He looked at Rosa, then at the fish crates, and waved them through without standing.

Rosa stopped beside him anyway.

“Open the loading door.”

“Delivery goes around.”

“Then stand up and tell the building.”

He sighed, set the television down, and walked toward the side entrance.

Tín got out of the truck.

The guard stopped with his hand on the door.

He looked from Tín's face to the paper crown hanging from the rearview mirror.

“Oh, shit.”

“Good morning,” Tín said.

The guard ran.

Rosa watched him disappear around the corner.

“Well, that was discreet.”

Tín used the yellow key to open the loading door. It rose slowly, revealing a long room lined with idle conveyor belts. Hooks hung from overhead rails. Stainless tables occupied the center. At the far end, three men stood around an open crate with pistols laid across its lid.

One reached for a gun.

Tín pulled the bottom of the loading door down with both hands and tore it from its tracks.

The door struck the concrete between them with a crash.

“Get behind that,” he told his companions.

The first shots rang against the metal.

Rosa crouched beside the truck's front wheel. Duke took Sable by the shoulder and moved her behind the fallen door. Bình picked up a length of packing timber and held it across his chest.

Tín went left, behind the nearest conveyor.

A gunman followed him with the muzzle. Shots punched through the conveyor's thin side panels. Tín pulled a steel sorting tray from the table, raised it against the next burst, and jumped over the belt.

He landed beside the open crate.

The first gunman tried to turn. Tín struck him across the face with the tray. His teeth hit the crate lid before his body reached the floor.

The second man fired at Tín's back.

Tín bent beneath the shot, caught the crate by its lower edge, and tipped it forward. Wrapped weapons spilled across the floor. The crate's heavy lid struck the gunman's knees and trapped him beneath it.

The third man ran toward a stair at the far wall.

Bình came over the conveyor ahead of him.

He hit the man once in the mouth, twice in the body, and stepped sideways as the pistol swung toward his ribs. His packing timber struck the wrist. The gun fell.

The man caught Bình's shirt and drove him against the stair rail.

Bình's shoulder hit steel. He cried out but kept his feet. He hooked the man's ankle, pulled him forward, and drove his knee into the man's stomach.

Tín caught the attacker as he fell and put him down hard on the concrete.

Bình leaned against the rail, holding his shoulder.

“I had him.”

“You did.”

“Then why—”

“I wanted a turn.”

Bình tried to laugh and found it hurt.

Sable came from behind the door. She took the loose guns away from the fallen men while Duke dragged an empty pallet across the loading entrance to stop it becoming a shooting lane again.

Rosa climbed into a small forklift parked beside the cold room.

“Keys,” she called.

Tín tossed her the ring.

She tried two, started the engine, and lowered the forks beneath the fallen loading door.

Duke watched her lift it.

“You can drive everything?”

“I sell fish. Fish don't walk into the truck.”

She moved the door against the yard entrance and set it upright between two concrete posts. Outside, the fleeing guard shouted to somebody beyond the truck.

Tín climbed the stairs.

At the top, a glass-walled office overlooked the work floor. A man in a striped shirt stood behind the desk holding a telephone. He watched Tín approach and began speaking faster.

“He's upstairs. He's here now.”

Tín opened the office door.

The man put the receiver down.

“I'm just the dispatcher.”

“Then dispatch yourself to that chair.”

He sat.

Tín picked up the telephone.

A voice on the other end said, “Who the fuck is this?”

“The man in your cannery.”

A pause.

“You got an invitation?”

“I brought a key.”

“This is Bishop Price's property.”

“You should tell him to come collect his men.”

The voice laughed.

“I am Bishop Price.”

Tín looked through the office glass at Bình sitting on a crate while Sable checked his shoulder.

“You shot a groom.”

“I sent men to bring you in. They got excited.”

“Then come yourself. You sound calm.”

“You want me?”

“Bell Street. You can ask anyone where I live.”

“I already know.”

Tín took the telephone cord in his hand and pulled it free of the wall.

He placed the dead receiver on the desk.

The dispatcher stared at it.

“That'll be difficult to explain.”

“Try honesty first. It will surprise him.”

On the wall behind the desk hung a harbor map. A red line ran from the rail apron behind River Queen to the eastern terminal. Beside it, somebody had pinned a photograph of a bridge section suspended from a crane. The new steel was painted gray. A board in the foreground identified it as the replacement span for East Channel Bridge.

Tín took the photograph down.

“When do they move this?”

The dispatcher looked at the picture.

“Friday night.”

“This Friday?”

“Yes.”

“The train comes then?”

The man swallowed.

Below them, an engine revved in the yard.

Tín turned toward the window.

A large loader drove around Rosa's truck with its bucket raised. Behind its windshield, a man in a hard hat leaned forward over the controls. Two gunmen walked behind it, using its steel body as cover.

The loader struck the blocked doorway.

The fallen door moved inward against its concrete posts.

“Down!” Tín shouted.

Rosa reversed the forklift away from the entrance. Duke pulled Bình behind the cold-room wall. Sable went with them carrying the first-aid box she had found beneath the office stairs.

The loader struck again.

One concrete post broke.

Tín jumped from the office window onto the conveyor below. Glass fell behind him. He ran along the belt, leaped over a gap, and landed on the loader's bucket as it pushed through the doorway.

The driver raised the bucket sharply.

Tín caught its upper edge. His feet left the steel for an instant, then struck it again as he pulled himself over. The driver tried to lower it and throw him forward.

Tín tore the hydraulic arm from its mounting.

The bucket dropped sideways with a shriek of metal.

He jumped to the cab, drove his fist through the side window, and pulled the driver out by his shirt.

The man came through the opening amid broken glass and landed across the hood.

One of the gunmen behind the loader fired upward.

The bullet cut Tín's trouser leg and scored the skin beneath it.

He dropped behind the cab roof, ripped the driver's seat free, and threw it at the shooter.

The seat struck him across the chest. He went down beneath it, his gun sliding under Rosa's truck.

The second gunman stepped clear of the loader and aimed toward the cold room.

Rosa brought the forklift around the conveyor.

Its forks caught the man's belt and coat. She raised them before he could fire. His feet left the floor. The gun dropped as he grabbed the nearest steel tine with both hands.

Rosa kept lifting until he hung above the worktables.

“Everybody looks down on fish,” she said. “Who's up there now?”

Tín came off the loader and crossed to the dangling man.

“You should let go of the trigger hand,” he told him.

The man opened his fist. A small knife fell to the floor.

Rosa lowered him onto a pile of empty nets.

Duke came forward with a coil of packing strap.

“I'm beginning to enjoy logistics.”

They secured the remaining men beside the loader. The dispatcher came down the stairs with both hands raised, having decided the office offered too much glass and too little career advancement.

Sable brought Tín a towel for his bleeding leg.

“Sit a minute.”

“In a minute.”

“That's what I said.”

She pointed at a crate.

He sat.

Bình came beside him, his shoulder supported in a sling made from one of Rosa's clean towels. He looked at the ruined loader.

“We taking that too?”

Rosa walked around it once.

“Parts,” she said.

Tín smiled, then winced as Sable cleaned the cut along his calf.

“You all enjoy this part too much.”

“Hold still,” she said.

When she finished, he stood and opened the nearest cold-room door.

Inside, rows of crates filled the space where fish had once waited for trucks. Some held stolen sound equipment. Others contained boxed televisions, unopened tools, and cartons of liquor. At the rear sat the missing pieces of the Orpheum organ, their polished wood wrapped in moving blankets.

Duke entered behind him and stopped beside a crate of stage lights.

“These are good.”

“They belong to someone,” Sable said.

“I'm admiring them ethically.”

Tín walked to the organ console. He lifted one edge of the blanket and touched the polished wood beneath it.

Marcus's teacher had wanted this saved.

He lowered the blanket.

“Rosa. Can the truck take it?”

She looked from the console to the rows of pipes.

“Some of it.”

“Then we'll make trips.”

Sable stared at him.

“You're going to steal the stolen organ?”

“I'm moving it to a better performance.”

Outside, a police siren sounded beyond the yard wall.

Duke looked toward the loading entrance.

“Vega?”

“I called before we came,” Sable said.

Tín glanced at her.

She held his gaze.

“You got your turn. She gets hers.”

He considered that, then handed her the bridge photograph.

“Show her this. Tell her the dispatcher knows what arrives Friday.”

“And you?”

Tín took the organ console by its lower frame and lifted it clear of the floor.

“I'm helping with the music.”

He carried it out through the ruined loading door. The first officer through the gate stopped beside Rosa's truck and watched him pass with several hundred pounds of polished wood against his chest.

The officer looked at Duke.

“Is that normal?”

Duke adjusted his cuffs.

“He usually starts with an appliance.”

## Chapter 11: Auntie Sets the Price

Bích auctioned her husband's photograph before he finished breakfast.

“Twenty dollars,” Vân said.

“Twenty-five,” Loretta answered.

Tín looked up from his bowl.

“It's a photograph.”

“Then stop moving,” Bích told him. “You're interfering with the comparison.”

Mai's first print stood on a small easel beside the stove. She had caught him laughing in front of Marcus's painted river. His shirt was clean, his eyes narrowed with amusement, and the top of Boots's hand remained visible at the edge of the frame.

“Crop that out,” Boots said from the doorway.

“You can pay for editing,” Mai told him.

“That's my hand.”

“Then you can pay for publicity.”

He looked toward Hòa, who sat at the table marking exercise books.

“Your daughter becoming dangerous.”

Hòa turned a page.

“She's been practicing.”

The bidding reached forty dollars. Vân won, paid in bills taken from three different pockets, and asked Tín to sign the bottom.

He wiped his hand, accepted the pen, and wrote his name.

“Should I put anything else?”

“Something inspiring.”

He added: PLEASE REFRIGERATE AFTER OPENING.

Vân read it, slapped his shoulder, and took the photograph anyway.

By noon, Bell Street had become a market.

Rosa set up fish beneath a blue awning. Loretta's salon offered appointments and sold raffle tickets beside a rack of hats. Mr. Benítez drove between the stalls in his red chair collecting shoes for repair. Bình sat under Boots's awning with his injured shoulder in a sling, teaching two boys how to wrap their hands while refusing every suggestion that he demonstrate on somebody larger.

Marcus had built a stage from borrowed platforms and hung the approved festival banner across its front. He had also hung the rejected GRANDMASTER CHIGGA banner at the side, where he hoped Mai would mistake it for storage.

She did not.

Tín watched her make him take it down, then helped Bích carry trays from the house to her stall. His calf had been bandaged beneath his trousers. It pulled when he climbed the steps, a small sharp reminder of the cannery floor. He stepped over the gutter carefully, keeping the tray level.

Bích noticed.

“You can sit.”

“I can carry food.”

“You're better at eating it.”

“Years of training.”

She took the tray from him and placed it beneath the awning.

Hương emerged from the house with a red apron folded over her arm. Across its front, she had sewn AUNTIE IN CHARGE in white letters.

Bích held it up.

“Who paid for this?”

“Your son.”

Hòa stood behind Hương, carrying a stack of bowls.

“I thought we should label the equipment accurately.”

Bích put the apron on. Tín tied it behind her, then leaned close enough to speak beside her ear.

“Very commanding.”

“You've had time to notice.”

He kissed her cheek.

Vân saw and immediately began charging more for the photograph.

At the far end of the street, a long white car stopped beside the temporary barrier. A man stepped out carrying a gold-tipped cane. He wore a black suit, a purple shirt, and a broad-brimmed hat. Three others followed him, each dressed almost as well and appearing unhappy about the difference.

Marcus stopped adjusting the microphone.

“Bishop Price.”

Tín set down the empty tray.

Bích caught his wrist.

“He can buy food like everyone else.”

Bishop came through the stalls smiling. He shook hands with two men who had not offered theirs. At Rosa's table, he picked up a piece of fried fish, ate it, and nodded as though passing judgment on a business he intended to acquire.

Rosa held out her hand.

“Three dollars.”

He reached for another piece.

She moved the plate.

“Six if your memory is going.”

Bishop placed a twenty in her palm.

“Keep it.”

“I was going to.”

He continued toward Bích's stall.

Tín stood beside the table with his hands resting on its edge.

“You found the address,” he said.

Bishop lifted his cane slightly.

“I heard there was food.”

“You heard there was a groom. That didn't go well.”

The men behind Bishop stopped smiling.

Bích placed a plate in front of him.

“Eat before you start.”

Bishop looked at her, then at the food.

“You must be Mrs. Lê.”

“Auntie is fine if you behave.”

“And if I don't?”

She pointed at the apron.

“Read slowly.”

Someone at the next stall laughed.

Bishop took the plate. His cane rested against the table while he ate one bite.

He chewed, looked down, and took another.

Bích waited.

“Good,” he admitted.

“Fifteen dollars.”

“The sign says eight.”

“The sign hasn't met you.”

He smiled at last, a real smile briefly breaking through the performance.

“You run a hard business.”

“You should try running one.”

Tín watched Bishop decide how much pride he could afford in front of the growing crowd. The man took out his wallet and paid fifteen dollars.

Bích gave him a napkin.

“Now you can speak.”

“I represent people with interests along this street.”

“Which stall?” she asked.

“The waterfront.”

“That's down the hill.”

“Mr. Tín understands me.”

Tín nodded.

“You want money from people who are working.”

Bishop set the plate down.

“I want respect.”

“Then pick up your napkin. It's blowing into Rosa's fish.”

Bishop caught the napkin against the edge of the table.

Behind him, one of his men moved toward Bình's chair. He was tall, with a narrow scar through one eyebrow. He looked at the sling and smiled.

“Still getting paid to lose?”

Bình stood halfway before Tín lifted a hand.

The young man sat back down, furious.

Tín stepped away from the food table.

“What's your name?” he asked the man with the scar.

“Wade.”

“Wade, carry those chairs.”

Wade looked toward the stack beside the stage.

“What?”

“People are standing. Be useful.”

Wade laughed and reached inside his jacket.

Tín caught his hand through the cloth, pressed it flat against his stomach, and pushed him backward into the stack of chairs.

Metal clattered across the pavement.

The crowd moved away from them. Bishop's other two men reached for their belts.

Hòa stepped between them carrying a tray of bowls.

“Careful,” he said.

One man tried to push past him.

The tray remained level. The man stopped as if he had walked into a closed door.

Hòa looked down at the hand pressed against his chest.

The man withdrew it.

Tín took the small pistol from Wade's jacket and laid it on the stage. Then he pulled the man upright and put a folded chair into his hands.

“That one goes beside Vân.”

Wade stared at him.

Tín picked up a second chair.

“You can carry two.”

Wade carried two.

Bishop watched him walk through the crowd toward the grocery stall.

“You're making a joke out of my people.”

“He was standing beside the chairs. I didn't plan that.”

Bishop picked up his cane.

“Tomorrow night. My hall.”

“I'm busy.”

“Then I'll come back here.”

Tín looked toward Mateo's wedding photograph, which Mai had propped beside a box collecting gifts for the couple. Denise sat beside the hospital bed in the picture, holding her husband's hand. The torn hem of her dress showed beneath the chair.

He looked back at Bishop.

“Come at seven. Bring everyone whose opinion matters to you.”

Bishop smiled.

“You'll regret giving me an audience.”

“So far, they keep bringing food.”

The man with the scar returned empty-handed. Vân had kept one of his chairs and made him open the other for an elderly customer. He looked as if the afternoon had become personally insulting.

Bishop left with his men. At the barrier, Rosa stopped him and pointed to the plate in his hand.

“That stays.”

He gave it back.

She looked at the last piece of food on it.

“You can finish.”

He did, standing beside his car, before returning the plate again.

Marcus watched the car disappear.

“That nigga paid fifteen dollars to get threatened over lunch.”

Bích turned toward him.

“Sixteen. He wanted another napkin.”

The market continued.

Tín helped put the fallen chairs back in their stack. Bình remained beneath the awning, looking at the hand wraps in his lap.

Tín sat beside him.

“You wanted to hit him.”

“Yes.”

“With which arm?”

Bình looked at the sling.

“The optimistic one.”

Tín laughed and handed him a cup of tea.

“Heal first. There's a long supply of fools.”

“You never wait.”

Tín lifted his bandaged arm.

“Your auntie has mentioned it.”

They drank while the two boys Bình had been coaching argued over which wrap looked more professional. Bình corrected one of them with his good hand, his attention returning to the work.

Across the street, Hương measured a woman for a jacket while Hòa held the order book. Mai brought the finished flyers from the printer and divided them among the stalls. She had earned her first afternoon's wages helping Mr. Chen finish another job. She kept the folded bills in a separate envelope and refused when Marcus tried to borrow two dollars for a soda.

“Business expense,” he said.

“Your business.”

Tín watched her pass the flyers to Bích. His wife held one at arm's length, checked the date, and smiled.

“Good,” she said.

Mai looked more pleased by that single word than she had by all of Marcus's complaints.

Near sunset, the man from the furniture store brought another stack of chairs. He had painted a small crown beneath each seat.

“For the boat,” he told Tín.

“You already gave us twenty.”

“People keep asking where you got them. I'm having a good week.”

Tín shook his hand.

Behind them, Bích counted the day's stall money with Loretta and Rosa. They argued briefly over who had paid for ice, settled it with three bills and a promise, then began discussing how much food a floating party could reasonably hold.

Tín took the last tray home.

At the door, Bích caught his sleeve.

“Seven tomorrow?”

He nodded.

“I'll have dinner ready at six.”

“You don't have to organize around him.”

“I'm organizing around you. Eat first. Then do your stupid thing.”

She went inside before he could answer.

He followed her carrying the empty tray.

## Chapter 12: Bishop Brings a Choir

Bishop Price arrived at seven with eleven men, two singers, and a portable organ nobody had asked him to explain.

Marcus stood beside the stage with the microphone hanging from one hand.

“You booked entertainment?” he asked Tín.

“He said he wanted an audience.”

“This nigga brought witnesses with harmonies.”

Bishop wore a white suit with a purple handkerchief folded above his breast pocket. The gold-tipped cane was gone. In its place, he carried a small black bag. Behind him, his men spread across the street in matching dark jackets while the singers argued quietly over where the extension cord went.

Loretta pointed toward an outlet beneath the salon window.

“You trip anything, you pay for the dryers.”

One singer nodded.

“We professional.”

“Then you'll understand the rate.”

Tín stood at the center of the cleared section of Bell Street. Boots had moved the trucks away, and the market tables had been stacked along the curb. Neighbors watched from doorways, windows, and the folding chairs Bích had decided were too useful to leave empty.

At six, she had served dinner exactly as promised. Tín had eaten two bowls while she explained which shirt he would wear and where she expected him to put his shoes if they came home wet.

Now she sat beside Hương outside the house, holding a cup of tea.
