“Keep moving. Leave the boxes. If it's not a person, stop carrying it.”

Duke brought the tug toward the barge's outer side.

“How close?”

“Closer.”

The fenders touched.

Tín jumped aboard.

He landed beside a stack of empty food trays and went through the ballroom. Smoke hung beneath the repaired skylight. People sat against the far wall, coughing. Two men helped a woman with a burned hand. Ruth stood beside the organ console, refusing to move until Ellis left it alone.

“It survived one fire,” she told him. “It can manage another. Walk.”

Ellis looked at Tín.

Tín pointed toward the outer deck.

The technician walked.

Bích came through the galley door carrying a large cooking pot.

Tín stopped in front of her.

She stopped too.

They looked at each other.

“People first,” he said.

“Everyone from the kitchen is out.”

He took the pot.

It was full.

“You brought soup.”

“They'll be hungry.”

He set it on the cold stove, kissed her forehead, and pointed toward the outer deck.

“Stay where the air is clear.”

She went, carrying the ladle.

Tín crossed to the gangway.

The fire had cut the pier off from the shore road. Flames filled the passage between the warehouse and the old ticket booth. People who had tried that route were coming back toward the barge. Behind them, the pavilion roof glowed orange through its smoke.

Hòa helped Ruth's dockhand across with one arm around the man's chest. The dockhand's right foot dragged. His shoe had melted along one side.

“How many left?” Tín asked.

“Rosa's checking the far end. Mai's with her.”

Tín looked toward the pavilion.

His granddaughter emerged through the smoke carrying a little girl against her hip. Rosa followed with the child's father, whose leg was bleeding through his trousers. They moved quickly until a section of the overhead awning dropped in front of them.

Mai stopped short.

Tín ran down the gangway.

He caught the burning beam before it reached her. Heat struck his face. The sleeve on his left arm began smoking. He lifted the beam above his head and turned it toward the water.

Mai passed beneath his arms with the child.

Rosa dragged the father after her.

Tín threw the beam over the rail.

It hit the river and vanished beneath a cloud of steam.

He went toward the pavilion.

“Nobody back there,” Rosa called.

He looked through the smoke anyway, searching the spaces beneath the tables and along the far wall. A white shape moved behind the organ pipes.

Tín crossed the open boards.

The saxophone player from the night market crouched beneath the temporary pipe frame. His jacket had caught on a protruding bolt. He was pulling at it with both hands, unable to reach the fastening behind his shoulder.

Tín tore the cloth free.

The man staggered up with the instrument case against his chest.

“I came for the music,” he said.

“It's on the boat.”

Tín guided him toward the gangway.

Behind them, a sharp burst came from the warehouse. Windows shattered along the upper wall. Burning fragments fell onto the pavilion roof.

The boards beneath Tín's feet shifted.

He felt the movement run toward the gangway.

“Go!”

The saxophone player ran.

Tín turned back as a long section of the pier began sinking toward the river. One support had burned through near the waterline. The pavilion leaned with it, drawing the gangway's shore end sideways.

On the barge, people stumbled against the rail.

Tín dropped through the broken boards.

He landed waist-deep in black water beneath the pier. The heat above him became a low red ceiling. He put his shoulder beneath the main beam and stood.

The sinking platform rose.

On it, the gangway leveled enough for the last people to cross.

Hòa appeared at the barge rail.

Tín could see only his shoes and one hand gripping the steel.

“Clear the gangway,” he called.

“Almost.”

The weight shifted again as the pavilion roof came down onto the supported beam.

Tín's feet drove into the mud. Water rose to his chest. He lifted harder, pushing the pier back toward level.

His ribs burned with each breath.

Above him, someone shouted his name.

“Move them!”

The last feet crossed overhead. He heard the gangway scraping, then the clatter of its lower end coming free.

Hòa called down.

“Clear.”

Tín stepped toward the open water and shoved the beam away from the River Queen.

The pavilion folded into the gap he left.

Burning timber struck the river. Steam and sparks rose together. A piece of the roof swept past him, and he ducked beneath it before surfacing beside the barge.

Hands reached down.

He caught the lowest rail and pulled himself aboard without taking them.

For a moment he knelt on the wet deck, water running from his shirt. Mai crouched beside him. She had the little girl's hand in hers.

“Grandpa.”

He looked up.

“I'm here.”

She nodded quickly, then stood to take the child back to her father.

Duke shouted from the tug.

“The moorings!”

Two lines still held the River Queen to the burning pier. One had tightened against a falling support. The other ran beneath the broken gangway and could no longer be reached from shore.

Tín took the first in both hands and pulled until its shore fitting tore free. He dropped the loose end onto the deck.

The second line dragged the barge's stern toward the fire.

He ran aft.

A man climbed over the rear rail in front of him.

The man wore a dark wet jacket and held a knife.

Tín stopped.

Behind the attacker, a small launch hugged the barge's stern. Another man stood at its controls. A third crouched beside a fuel can.

Tín looked at the flames on the pier.

Then at the knife.

“You should have stayed ashore.”

The attacker lunged.

Tín caught his knife wrist, bent it outward, and drove the blade into the wooden rail beside the man's own hand. He struck the attacker beneath the jaw with his other palm.

The man fell backward onto the deck.

The crouching man in the launch rose with a burning bottle.

Tín tore the barge's rear ladder from its brackets and threw it down across the launch.

The ladder struck both men and crushed the windshield. The bottle broke inside the boat. Fire spread across the driver's seat.

The driver jumped into the river.

The second man tried to follow and became tangled beneath the ladder.

Tín dropped from the barge, caught the man by his jacket, and pulled him clear. He threw him toward the River Queen, where Wade and another volunteer caught his arms and hauled him aboard.

The launch drifted away burning. The patrol boat turned to collect the driver swimming clear of it.

Tín climbed back up and seized the remaining mooring line.

He pulled.

The line cut into his injured palm. Blood mixed with river water and ran down his wrist.

He pulled again.

The fastening beneath the broken gangway came away with a section of timber attached. Tín swung it over the rail and let it fall into the clear water beyond the burning pier.

The River Queen moved free.

Duke increased the tug's power. Rosa brought her fishing boat along the barge's stern to keep it from swinging. The vessels turned east, away from the fire and toward the open harbor.

Onshore, fire engines had reached the road. Their lights flashed through the smoke. A patrol boat came alongside and began taking the most badly injured people aboard.

Tín stood at the aft rail until the burning pier had fallen behind them.

Then he went inside.

Bích had begun serving soup.

People sat on the floor with bowls in their hands. Some were shaking too badly to hold them alone. Hương helped a young mother feed her child. Ruth had taken off her hat and was using its box to collect broken glass from beneath a bench.

The saxophone player sat near the door with his case unopened beside him.

Tín stopped in the middle of the ballroom.

Bích looked up.

She brought him a bowl.

He took it with both hands.

“You see?” she said.

He looked at the soup, then at her face.

“I see.”

She sat beside him on the edge of the stage while the boat moved through the dark.

For several minutes, he ate without speaking.

Then the radio called his name.

Vega's voice came through the open office door.

“Tín. Stay west of the bridge. Rook's men have taken the crane.”

## Chapter 21: Three Boats and a Bad Idea

Duke cut the tug's speed when he heard the warning about the bridge.

The River Queen continued moving behind him, its heavy hull carrying its own opinion about stopping.

Rosa brought her boat against the barge's rear quarter and pushed it back toward the center of the channel. The patrol boat stayed on the opposite side, transferring injured people one at a time while its crew watched the dark water ahead.

Tín stood beside Duke in the wheelhouse.

“Can we turn?”

Duke looked toward the burning waterfront behind them. A loose timber raft had drifted out from Hollis Pier and was turning slowly across the path they had just used.

“Not here.”

Rosa's voice came over the radio.

“Hold straight. I need room to get the stern around.”

Duke acknowledged her.

The first launch came from beneath the bridge's western approach.

It ran dark until it cleared the piling. Then a lamp snapped on, throwing a white circle across the River Queen's windows. A gunman stood behind the light.

The patrol boat's crew shouted for him to lower his weapon.

He fired.

Shots struck the barge's upper balcony. People inside dropped to the floor. The patrol boat turned between the launch and the barge, its crew returning fire from behind the cabin.

A second launch came out behind the first.

Tín took the little black bag from the wheelhouse floor.

Duke looked at it.

“What's left in there?”

“A flashlight.”

“That seems optimistic.”

Tín stepped onto the tug's forward deck and threw the bag at the lamp.

The flashlight struck the lens through the canvas. Glass burst. The launch's bow vanished into darkness again.

Tín jumped.

He landed on the launch's forward rail, bent it beneath his feet, and drove his shoulder into the gunman. Both men crashed through the windshield frame. Tín came up first, took the rifle by its barrel, and pulled it out of the man's hands.

He struck the driver with the stock.

The driver fell sideways, dragging the wheel with him.

The launch turned sharply away from the barge.

Tín caught the controls and straightened it before it reached the patrol boat. He pushed the driver onto the floor beside the gunman and looked toward the second launch.

Nail stood at its bow.

He held a long boat hook in his good hand. His injured wrist was tied against his chest. Behind him, the launch's driver brought the vessels close enough for him to leap.

Nail crossed the gap and landed beside Tín.

The little boat lurched under them.

The hook drove toward Tín's stomach. He turned sideways. Its point cut through his shirt and scored his ribs. He caught the shaft beneath his arm and pulled Nail close.

Their foreheads struck.

Nail grunted, twisted the shaft, and tore it free.

Tín stepped back against the engine housing.

The second thrust went through the housing beside his hip.

He drove his knee into Nail's chest, caught the enforcer behind the neck, and slammed his face against the metal cover.

The silver plate struck steel with a sharp crack.

Nail reached around Tín's waist and lifted.

They went over the side together.

Water closed over Tín's head.

The boat's engine thudded above him. Nail held him around the ribs, driving them deeper with heavy kicks. Tín planted both palms against the man's chest and pushed.

The grip opened.

Tín caught the trailing line from the launch and hauled himself toward the surface.

Nail caught his ankle.

He turned underwater and struck the man's wrist with his heel. The hand loosened. He kicked again and felt it release.

He broke the surface beside the launch.

Nail came up with him, coughing water and blood. He seized the lower rail and pulled himself onto the deck.

Tín climbed after him.

For a moment both men knelt on opposite sides of the engine housing. Water poured from their clothes. The disabled gunman lay against the bow, staring at them with his mouth open.

“Get off,” Tín told him.

The man looked toward the water.

“The patrol boat,” Tín said.

He pointed to the officers drawing close enough to reach him.

The gunman crawled toward them. The driver followed on his hands and knees. An officer threw a line and helped both men across while keeping a weapon trained on the two men still aboard.

Nail stood.

His right hand held the broken end of the boat hook.

Tín rose slowly.

The cut along his ribs burned where river water had entered it. He could feel the split skin on his knuckles when he closed his hand.

Nail came forward.

Tín caught the broken shaft as it thrust at his throat. He turned it aside, stepped across Nail's lead foot, and drove his elbow into the man's jaw.

The silver plate came loose at one end.

Nail reeled back.

Tín struck him in the chest, then across the temple with the heel of his hand.

The big man fell against the rail.

He tried to raise the broken hook again.

Tín took it from him, threw it overboard, and caught him by the front of his shirt.

He drove Nail backward onto the engine housing.

The cover collapsed beneath his body. Metal folded around his shoulders. Tín pulled him up once, turned him onto his side, and looked into his face.

Nail's eyes no longer followed him.

Tín checked his neck.

Nothing.

He lowered the man onto the deck and stood over him, breathing hard.

An officer called from the patrol boat.

“Sir. Hands where I can see them.”

Tín raised his empty hands.

The officer looked at the dead man, then toward the River Queen, where people crowded behind the intact windows watching them.

“Stay there.”

The radio at his shoulder spoke before he could continue.

Vega's voice came through, urgent enough that Tín heard it across the water.

“The crane's moving. Get everyone clear of the lower passage.”

Above the bridge, the great gray span rose from its supports.

Work lights swung across it. Cables tightened beneath the crane's boom. A man stood on the operator's platform with a gun pointed into the cabin.

Rook.

He turned toward the water.

The span began moving across the lower passage.

Duke sounded the tug's horn.

The River Queen was still turning. Its stern had cleared the floating debris, but the current carried it toward the narrow opening beneath the suspended steel. Rosa's boat pushed against its side, engine straining. The patrol boat could not pull away without leaving the injured people it was taking aboard.

Tín looked from one vessel to the other.

Then he pointed toward Mercy's Cousin.

“Take this boat's men. I need that tug.”

The officer began to answer.

Tín jumped to the patrol boat's forward rail, crossed its bow in two strides, and leaped onto Duke's deck.

Duke stared at him through the broken wheelhouse window.

“You look terrible.”

“Closer to the crane.”

“That's a terrible destination.”

“It matches.”

Duke turned the wheel.

Mercy's Cousin moved toward the repair barge.

Above them, the suspended span swung slowly across the channel. Its shadow passed over the River Queen's upper windows, covering the people inside.

Rook leaned from the operator's platform and looked down.

Tín stood at the tug's bow.

He lifted one hand and pointed at him.

Rook stepped back into the cabin.

The crane's boom lowered.

## Chapter 22: Forty Tonnes before Breakfast

The crane operator had both hands above his head.

Tín saw him through the cabin glass as Mercy's Cousin came beneath the work platform. The man was young, with a narrow face and a fluorescent jacket. Blood ran from his scalp down beside one ear. Rook stood behind him holding a pistol against the back of the chair.

The gray span descended another foot.

On the water behind Tín, Duke sounded the horn again. Rosa had almost turned the River Queen away from the opening, but a loose timber raft had caught across its rear quarter. The barge's stern could not swing until the raft moved. Its forward windows faced the hanging steel.

Tín climbed onto the tug's rail.

“Keep clear of the crane,” he told Duke.

“That's where you're going.”

“I dislike company while working.”

He jumped to the low repair platform beneath the crane's boom. His sandals struck wet steel. He caught an upright, pulled himself over its top, and reached the first ladder as a gunman appeared above him.

The gunman fired down.

Tín swung beneath the ladder. The shot struck a rung beside his hand. He kicked upward through the frame, catching the man under the chin with the sole of his sandal.

The man fell back from the opening.

Tín climbed through after him, seized the gun, and threw it into the empty water beyond the repair barge. He put the gunman against a stack of coiled hoses and looped one over his chest and arms.

“Stay behind that.”

The man nodded, coughing.

From the cabin, Rook watched him reach the upper walkway.

He spoke to the operator.

The operator shook his head.

Rook hit him with the pistol.

Tín ran.

The span stopped descending and began swinging toward the River Queen. Its broad side passed through a beam of work light, revealing the long gray web and the heavy lower flange. The markings on it were clean enough to read. Forty tonnes. The number that had stood on the little board at the salt spur now moved across the dark above a boat full of people.

Tín reached the cabin door.

It opened toward him.

The operator fell out.

Tín caught him under the arms before he reached the edge of the walkway. The man's boots scraped across the steel grating. His eyes were open but unfocused.

“Can you stand?”

He tried. One knee folded.

Tín put him over his good shoulder and turned toward the ladder.

Rook fired through the doorway.

The shot struck the railing at Tín's hip. A sharp fragment cut his side. He kept moving, carrying the operator down to the lower platform while the crane continued its slow turn above them.

Duke brought the tug close enough to hear him.

“Take him.”

“How?”

Tín lowered the operator over the platform's edge. Duke caught his legs while Rosa, who had left a deckhand at her fishing boat's controls and come aboard the tug, reached for his shoulders. Together they got him onto the deck.

The operator gripped Tín's wrist before letting go.

“He's over the stop.”

Tín looked up.

“What stop?”

The man pointed toward the crane's turning base, then the four cables holding the span.

“He keeps pulling. It'll twist the rig.”

Tín followed his hand.

One cable no longer hung at the same angle as the others. The span had caught against the edge of the old bridge approach. As the crane turned, the cable pulled sideways across a sharp corner.

A metallic crack rang over the water.

The operator's hand tightened.

Tín let him hold on for one breath, then gently freed his wrist.

“Duke. Back away.”

He climbed.

Rook appeared at the top of the walkway with the pistol raised. Tín tore a loose steel panel from the railing and held it in front of him. Three shots struck it, each sending a hard impact through his arms.

He threw the panel upward.

It hit the cabin door and drove Rook back inside. The pistol skidded across the floor and vanished beneath the controls.

Tín reached the walkway as the first suspension cable broke.

The span dropped at one end.

People on the River Queen screamed. The barge had cleared most of the timber raft, but its bow remained beneath the outer edge of the falling steel.

Tín jumped from the walkway onto the old bridge approach.

He landed beside a low service cart and kicked it out of his path. The suspended span swung toward him, its lower flange descending across the gap between the approach and the repair platform.

He stepped beneath it.

His hands met the steel.

The impact drove him onto one knee. The concrete beneath his sandal cracked. He turned his shoulder under the flange as another cable snapped overhead.

The span rolled toward the river.

Tín stood.

The third cable tore free with a sound like a gunshot. The fourth dragged across the crane boom, pulled a row of fittings out of line, and broke.

The whole span settled onto him.

Forty tonnes of steel rested across his shoulders and raised hands.

On the crane, Rook stopped moving.

Tín took one step.

The concrete under his foot broke into pale pieces. He placed the next foot farther back on the approach, where the old roadway was broad and solid. His ribs flared with pain. Blood ran from his split palm along the underside of the flange.

He took another step.

The span cleared the River Queen's bow.

Below him, Duke shouted something toward Rosa. Both tug engines rose. The barge moved forward into the open water beneath the space the span had occupied.

Tín turned with the steel across his shoulders.

The near end passed over the repair barge, forcing men on its deck to duck behind machinery. The far end swept clear of the bridge's old masonry. A work lamp struck it and broke, sending white sparks across the water.

Tín looked toward the empty staging pad where the replacement span had rested that afternoon.

It lay beyond a narrow strip of water, flat and clear except for two wooden supports. Every worker had already run behind the barrier at its edge.

He bent his knees.

Rook began shouting from the crane.

Tín did not listen.

He drove upward and forward.

The span left his shoulders.

For an instant, the entire gray length hung against the harbor lights.

Then it crossed the water and struck the empty staging pad.

Concrete dust burst beneath it. The two wooden supports flattened. The span skidded several feet and came to rest against a low mound of gravel, rocking once before settling.

The sound rolled over the harbor and returned from the warehouses on both banks.

Tín stood on the old bridge approach with his arms lowered.

His shirt hung in wet strips around one shoulder. Blood dripped from his fingertips. He looked down at the River Queen as it passed beneath him.

Faces filled the windows.

Nobody spoke at first.

Then Marcus appeared on the balcony with the microphone in his hand.

“THAT'S MY FUCKING GRANDPA!”

From somewhere behind him, Mai shouted, “He's my grandpa!”

“WE'RE SHARING TONIGHT!”

The barge erupted.

People cheered, pounded the rail, and raised their hands toward the man above them. A woman who had been crying covered her face and laughed into her palms. The little girl Mai had carried from the pier waved both arms from her father's lap.

At the staging pad, one of the bridge workers took off his hard hat and threw it high into the air.

Another caught it, looked toward Tín, and threw it again.

Duke stood in the tug's broken wheelhouse with his mouth open.

Rosa pushed his chin upward with two fingers.

“Drive.”

He took the wheel.

On the River Queen's rear deck, Hòa stood beside a steel bollard that had begun pulling loose during the turn. A mooring line still ran from it to the trailing timber raft. He put one hand around the bollard's base and drew it back into place.

The raft stopped turning.

For a moment the barge seemed to hang between the moving river and his quiet hand. Then he took the line in the other, lifted it free, and let the timber drift away.

Tín saw only the end of it from above: his son standing upright, the line dropping, a deep crease left across the steel beneath his palm.

Hòa looked up.

He raised one hand briefly.

Tín returned the gesture.

Neither gave the crowd an explanation.

The patrol boat passed after the barge, carrying the injured toward the clear eastern basin. Its crew looked up as they went. One officer touched two fingers to the brim of his cap. The other kept both hands on the controls and grinned so broadly that Tín could see it from the bridge.

Behind him, metal clattered.

Rook had left the crane cabin.

He climbed toward the upper service ladder with a small case in one hand. His suit jacket was gone. Blood marked the side of his face where the door had struck him.

Tín turned.

Rook looked back once, saw him coming, and climbed faster.

“Calvin,” Tín called.

The man kept climbing.

Tín walked to the base of the crane.

Each step hurt now. The cut at his ribs had reopened. His calf throbbed above the sandal strap. His hands wanted to remain half-closed around an absent beam. He flexed them once, leaving small dark marks against his palms, and took hold of the ladder.

Below him, the River Queen's band began playing.

He could hear the organ beneath the brass, rough and loud and entirely unwilling to wait for the rest of the evening to improve.

Tín climbed toward Rook.

## Chapter 23: The Man at the Top

Rook dropped the case halfway up the ladder.

It struck the walkway below Tín, burst open, and scattered cash across the grating. Bills lifted in the wind. Some caught against the rail. Others drifted toward the water, turning pale beneath the work lights.

“Take it,” Rook called down. “There's enough for your boat.”

Tín kept climbing.

“You've misunderstood the damage.”

“You want more?”

“I want you to stop moving.”

Rook reached the upper platform and kicked the ladder outward.

Its lower fastenings tore free. The metal frame swung away from the crane with Tín still on it. He let it travel, put one foot against an upright as it passed, and jumped to the next service rail.

Rook backed toward the crane's long boom.

Below, the ladder fell onto the empty walkway and folded in half.

Tín climbed over the rail.

The wind was stronger up here. It pushed his wet shirt against the cuts along his side and carried the smell of smoke from the western waterfront. He could see the River Queen beyond the bridge now, its lights moving steadily toward the clear basin. A patrol boat accompanied it. Another had stopped beside the repair platform below him.

Rook looked down at the police, then back at Tín.

“We can make an arrangement.”

Tín put one hand on the rail and walked toward him.

“You tried that with my son.”

Rook picked up a heavy tool from beside the crane's upper motor housing. He held it behind his leg, watching Tín's injured calf as he approached.

“Your son walked away.”

“He bought soap.”

“What?”

“It was on the list.”

Rook swung the tool low.

Tín lifted his leg. The steel head struck the platform where his ankle had been. He caught Rook's wrist and drove his other fist into the man's stomach.

Rook folded, then slammed his forehead into Tín's face.

Pain burst across the old man's nose. His grip loosened for half a breath. Rook tore free and struck him in the ribs with the tool's handle.

Tín hit the rail behind him.

The rail bent.

Rook came after him, both hands on the tool now, bringing it down toward his shoulder.

Tín caught the shaft above his head.

He pulled Rook forward until their faces were inches apart.

Blood ran from Tín's nose over his upper lip.

Rook tried to pull the tool back.

Tín bent it between their hands.

The steel shaft took a slow, ugly curve. Rook's fingers opened before the bend reached them. Tín threw the ruined tool onto the motor housing and hit him across the mouth.

Rook fell against the crane boom's lower brace.

He caught it with one hand and swung around the outside of the platform. His shoes found a narrow beam beyond the rail. He began climbing toward the boom's outer walkway, away from the ladder and the officers below.

Tín wiped his nose on his sleeve.

“Calvin.”

The man climbed faster.

“You're making this expensive for your tailor.”

Rook reached the walkway and ran.

Tín stepped over the rail after him.

The boom extended above the lower passage like a dark road with nothing beneath it. Loose cables hung along one side. The remains of the span's broken rigging swung at the far end, striking metal whenever the wind pushed them back.

Rook ran toward those cables.

Tín followed, one hand brushing the outer rail.

Halfway along, Rook stopped and turned.

He had found a knife.

Tín looked at the small blade.

Then he looked at the enormous crane around them.

“You keep choosing smaller equipment.”

Rook lunged.

The blade cut across Tín's forearm. He turned his wrist, caught the knife hand, and pushed it down against the rail. Rook kicked at his injured calf.

Tín's knee bent.

Rook drove his shoulder into him.

The rail broke behind Tín's hip.

For a moment both men tipped toward the water.

Tín caught an overhead brace with his cut hand and held on. Rook hung against him, one foot still hooked around the walkway's lower bar. The knife dropped into the dark.

Tín pulled them both upright.

He put Rook against the crane beam and struck him twice in the chest. The man's breath went out in wet bursts. Tín caught his shirt before he could collapse, turned him, and drove him to his knees.

Rook gripped the walkway with both hands.

“Enough.”

Tín stood over him.

The word sounded different without Nail there to spend it on.

“Look down,” Tín said.

Rook did not move.

Tín took him by one ankle and lifted.

The man's hands tore free of the grating. Tín raised him over the broken rail and held him upside down above the harbor.

Rook shouted once, a raw sound that cut through the engines below.

His tie hung toward the water. Loose money fell from his pocket and followed the bills from the broken case. His remaining shoe slid halfway off before he curled his foot to keep it on.

Tín held him steady.

“Look.”

The River Queen had turned in the clear basin. Its windows faced the bridge. People stood behind them, watching the high dark shape of the crane and the two men at its end.

Beyond the barge, the lights of Bell Street rose above the warehouses. Smoke drifted across some of them. Others burned clean and small, ordinary kitchen windows where people had waited all evening for somebody to come home.

Rook's hands opened and closed in the air.

“Put me up.”

“You wanted them watching.”

“Tín.”

“Now they're watching.”

Rook tried to lift his head. Blood ran toward his forehead and dripped from his hair.

“I'll pay.”

“For what?”

“Everything.”

“Name it.”

“The boat. The pier. The hospital bills.”

“The shop windows. The trucks. The wedding.”

“Yes.”

“Your men leave Bell Street.”

“Yes.”

“Your boats leave its water.”

“Yes.”

Tín looked at the man's remaining shoe.

“Your shoe's coming off.”

Rook made a small desperate movement with his foot.

Tín brought him back over the rail and set him on the walkway.

The man lay on his side, breathing hard, one hand wrapped around the shoe as if it were the only possession he still understood.

Tín crouched beside him.

“That promise doesn't cancel what the police want.”

Rook closed his eyes.

“I know.”

“Good. I dislike repeating prices.”

He stood.

Rook tried to rise and nearly fell through the broken rail. Tín caught his collar, hauled him onto his feet, and put one arm behind his back.

They walked toward the platform together.

At the crane's second access ladder, which remained intact, the operator had returned with an officer behind him. His head was bandaged. He looked at Rook, then at Tín's bloody face.

“The span?” he asked.

Tín pointed toward the staging pad.

The operator followed his hand.

He stood very still.

“You put it back.”

“Near enough for tonight.”

The man laughed once, abruptly, then covered his mouth with one hand. The officer beside him shook his head and reached for Rook.

Tín handed the man over.

The officer secured Rook's wrists, checked the broken walkway behind them, and spoke into his radio. He kept his body between the prisoner and the ladder while the operator helped clear the route down.

Rook looked back once.

His face had changed from anger to something smaller and harder to spend.

“You could have taken the fifty thousand.”

Tín wiped blood from his chin.

“I did.”

The operator made a choking sound and turned away.

They took Rook down the ladder.

Tín remained on the platform until they reached the repair barge safely. The adrenaline that had carried him across the boom began leaving in small, unpleasant installments. His hands shook when he opened them. The cut beside his ribs pulled with every breath. His nose had stopped bleeding, but the blood drying above his lip made his face feel like somebody else's.

He looked toward the River Queen.

The microphone cracked through the night.

Marcus's voice came across the water.

“Grandmaster, your wife says get your ass down.”

Tín closed his eyes.

The officer below looked up, smiling despite himself.

“Sounds official.”

Tín began climbing down.

The descent felt longer than the climb. At the bottom, his injured leg refused one step. He stopped, let the pain settle, and moved it deliberately to the next rung.

Duke waited on Mercy's Cousin.

He held out both hands.

Tín accepted them.

The nightclub owner helped him onto the deck and guided him to the wheelhouse chair.

“Sit.”

Tín sat.

“Rosa teach you that word?”

“Everybody's been using it on me. I wanted a turn.”

He brought a clean cloth and a bottle of water. Tín washed his mouth, spat over the side, and wiped the blood from his hands as well as he could.

The crane operator came alongside in a workboat before they left. He carried his hard hat, the little weight board, and a pair of heavy gloves.

He offered the gloves first.

Tín looked at his torn palms.

“Late.”

“I know.”

The man held out the board marked FORTY TONNES.

“The crew wants you to have it.”

Duke leaned through the wheelhouse window.

“Where's he supposed to put that?”

Tín took the board.

“Over the refrigerator.”

The operator laughed, shook his hand carefully, and returned to the workboat.

Mercy's Cousin moved toward the River Queen.

The sky beyond the eastern warehouses remained black. Tín watched the work lamps along the basin slide past while the barge's lights grew larger ahead of them.

Bích waited at the rail.

She wore the red apron over a blanket someone had put around her shoulders. Her hair had come loose. She held a cup in one hand and the ladle in the other.

Tín stood when the tug touched the fenders.

The movement hurt everywhere.

He climbed across anyway.

Bích put down the cup and caught his face between both hands.

She inspected the split lip, the bruised nose, the new cuts.

Then she pressed her forehead against his.

“You're late.”

“There was traffic.”

She laughed once, close enough that he felt it through her hands.

Then she pulled him inside, where Hương was waiting with towels and Hòa had already found a chair sturdy enough to survive the rest of the morning.

## Chapter 24: The Afterparty Has Stitches

The nurse took one look at Tín and pointed at the chair.

He sat before she finished pointing.

Bích looked pleased.

“You should come to the house,” she told the nurse.

The emergency department had filled with people from the harbor. Some needed treatment. Others had arrived with the injured and refused to leave. A man near the desk held three pairs of shoes in a plastic bag and kept asking who belonged to them. Ruth Hollis had lost her hat but retained the silver bird pins, which she carried in a paper cup like very small survivors.

Tín sat beneath a fluorescent light while the nurse cut away the remains of his shirt.

She held up one sleeve.

“Was this already torn?”

Bích answered before he could.

“Several times.”

“Any part you want saved?”

“No.”

Tín watched the cloth fall into the bin.

“I liked that shirt.”

“You liked the peacocks too,” Bích said. “Your opinions have been examined.”

The nurse cleaned the cuts along his ribs and forearm. He stayed still while she worked, his hands resting open on his knees. The skin across his palms was torn where he had held the steel and mooring lines. Each touch of the damp gauze made the muscles in his jaw tighten.

Bích sat beside him and held the paper cup of water he kept forgetting to drink.

The doctor came in carrying a chart.

She was a compact woman with tired eyes and a pen clipped so securely to her pocket that Tín suspected someone had tried to steal it recently.

“Seventy?” she asked.

“Since Monday.”

She looked at the injuries, then at Bích.

“Eventful birthday.”

“We bought a refrigerator,” Bích said.

The doctor paused with the pen above the chart.

“I'm going to need more than that.”

Tín gave her the short version. She examined his breathing, the bruises across his ribs, his injured calf, and the cuts that had accumulated over the week. When he reached the part about the bridge span, she stopped writing.

“You lifted it.”

“Yes.”

“The steel span outside?”

“It was in the way.”

She looked toward the open doorway.

Two bridge workers stood there, still wearing their reflective jackets. One held the gloves he had given Tín. The other nodded solemnly.

The doctor turned back to the chart.

“Fine. I'm writing harbor accident.”

“Accidents,” Bích said.

“I see that.”

They took him for pictures of his ribs and leg, cleaned the wounds properly, and put stitches where the deeper cuts needed them. Tín endured it with less dignity than he had carried the bridge. When the doctor told him to relax his hand, he looked at the needle and asked whether she had considered using smaller equipment.

“This is the small one.”

Bích laughed into her cup.

The doctor glanced at her.

“You can stay. He's behaving better with an audience.”

“That's usually the problem.”

Afterward, they put him in a clean gown and kept him for observation. He objected to the gown's open back. The nurse gave him a second one to wear over it in reverse.

He examined the result.

“A complicated suit.”

“Don't tear this one.”

Bích tied the upper strings herself.

“You look handsome.”

“You're being cruel.”

“I'm being married.”

Down the hall, Boots occupied a bed with his arm bandaged and his shirt folded in a bag beside it. Loretta sat in a chair near his feet. She had been crying before Tín arrived and now appeared determined to make everyone believe she had merely been furious the entire time.

“He said you were useful,” she told her husband as Tín entered.

Boots looked toward him.

“My brother.”

“He also said you worried about a sandwich.”

Boots closed his eyes.

“Brother.”

Tín took the small black bag from Duke and placed it on the bedside table. Inside, beneath the folded scarf, lay the sandwich in its paper wrapping.

Boots opened one eye.

“You brought it.”

“I made a promise.”

Loretta looked at both of them.

“You think this is touching.”

Boots nodded.

“Deeply.”

She took the sandwich out, checked it, and put it where he could reach it with his good hand.

“After the nurse says you can eat.”

He caught her hand before she moved away.

For a moment the jokes stopped.

“I'm here,” he said.

“I noticed. You keep making noise.”

She leaned forward and kissed his forehead. He held her fingers against his cheek until she let herself sit closer.

Tín remained by the door while they had that moment. Duke stood beside him, both hands in the pockets of Rosa's dry jacket.

“He'll keep the arm,” Duke said quietly.

Tín nodded.

“The doctor told us.”

He nodded again.

Duke looked at the clean bandages on his hands.

“You can breathe now.”

Tín took a slow breath. It hurt, but it entered.

At the next room, Mateo sat up in bed listening to Denise describe the bridge.

“Forty tonnes,” she said.

“People exaggerate.”

Tín appeared in the doorway.

Mateo looked at his two hospital gowns.

“Apparently they don't exaggerate the fashion.”

Denise rose and hugged Tín carefully, finding the narrow space between injuries with an instinct Hương would have admired.

“Thank you,” she said.

“You already paid admission.”

“This is separate.”

He patted her back.

Mateo pointed at the chair.

Tín sat again. The whole building seemed to have agreed on the word.

Rosa came in with coffee, followed by Bình, whose shoulder had been checked and put back in its sling. He had slept in a chair for two hours and looked insulted by everyone else's determination to call that rest.

“I heard Nail's dead,” he said.

The room quieted.

Tín looked at him.

“Yes.”

Bình stood beside the window, his good hand wrapped around the coffee cup.

“He never paid the other fighters either.”

Tín waited.

The younger man looked at Mateo's raised leg, then at Boots's room across the hall.

“I thought I'd feel good hearing it.”

“How do you feel?”

Bình considered the question.

“Tired.”

Tín nodded toward the empty chair.

“There's a cure in this building.”

Bình sat.

Denise brought him a pillow without making a speech about it. He accepted it, leaned back, and closed his eyes while the room resumed talking around him.

By midmorning, the waiting area had acquired so many gifts that a volunteer found a cart.

There were flowers, food, replacement shirts, a box of good cigars Tín did not smoke, and three different hats. Mr. Benítez sent a pair of soft shoes with a note promising that the soles would survive ordinary walking. Vân sent groceries because, as she explained to the nurse, the refrigerator should not become lonely during a family emergency.

One envelope held five hundred dollars and a card from the father whose daughter Mai had carried through the fire.

Tín read it twice.

He asked Hương to return the money and keep the card.

“He'll argue,” she said.

“Tell him to spend it on her.”

Hương nodded and put the envelope in her bag.

Ruth arrived with a small group from the Orpheum. Ellis carried a photograph of the organ before it had been dismantled. The saxophone player came with them, his instrument case held in both hands.

“We're playing tonight,” Ruth announced.

Tín looked at Bích.

His wife had been expecting it.

“At the eastern basin,” she said. “The old excursion landing. There's room beside the barge.”

“Who decided?”

Ruth, Bích, Hương, and Loretta looked at him.

He lifted one bandaged hand.

“A strong committee.”

The doctor returned while they were discussing food. She listened for a moment, then looked at the patient.

“You're planning a party.”

“They are.”

“Good. You can sit at it.”

Bích nodded.

“We've already discussed the chair.”

The doctor gave them her instructions, checked the fresh dressings, and told Tín she would see him again before he left. He listened this time. Bích noticed and did not make a joke of it.

When the room finally emptied, Hòa remained beside the window.

He held the board from the bridge crew beneath one arm. FORTY TONNES faced the wall, as if he had decided the number had enjoyed enough public attention for one morning.

Tín looked at his son's hands.

There was a dark bruise across one palm.

“The bollard?” he asked.

Hòa glanced down.

“It moved.”

“I saw.”

His son said nothing.

Tín leaned back against the pillow.

“You've been keeping busy.”

“I have a family.”

The answer settled between them without challenge.

Hòa put the board beside the gift cart, straightened the blanket over his father's feet, and moved the water cup within reach.

“Sleep,” he said.

Tín looked at him for a long moment.

Then he closed his eyes.

In the corridor, someone began arguing with Marcus about whether the hospital permitted a rehearsal. Hương's voice joined the discussion. A moment later the argument ended abruptly.

Bích sat beside the bed and took Tín's uninjured fingers in hers.

He slept while she held them.

## Chapter 25: Rook Signs the Receipt

Iris brought the check in a white envelope and placed it on the table as if it might bite her.

Tín sat opposite her in a quiet room off the hospital corridor. Bích had permitted the meeting because the doctor had not yet permitted him to leave, and therefore someone else would have to do any climbing involved.

Sable stood beside the window. Vega waited near the door. Rook's lawyer occupied the remaining chair and had arranged his briefcase on his knees with the care of a man hoping it would count as a barrier.

“An initial payment,” the lawyer said.

Tín looked at the envelope.

“You can say the number.”

“Two million dollars.”

From the corridor, Boots said, “Goddamn.”

Loretta's voice followed.

“Stop listening at the door.”

“He said the number loudly.”

Vega stepped outside long enough to move them farther down the hall. When she returned, the lawyer had begun adjusting his tie.

Tín opened the envelope.

The check lay inside beside a short letter listing the damaged properties and medical expenses Rook had agreed to address. Tín read it once, then passed it to Sable.

She read it more slowly.

“The tug?” she asked.

The lawyer opened his briefcase.

“Separate document.”

“Duke will be thrilled you found another page.”

Tín looked toward Iris.

Her father had remained at the hospital under guard through the morning. His injuries had been treated. His accounts and businesses were being pulled into questions that neither this envelope nor the money inside it would settle. Iris had spent several hours telling Vega which deliveries she had arranged and which orders had come directly from him. She looked tired enough to be angry with furniture.

“He wants to see you,” she said.

“I saw plenty of him last night.”

“He said five minutes.”

Tín looked at Bích, who had come to stand in the doorway.

She folded her arms.

“He said ten minutes at the cinema.”

“That was me,” Tín said.

“I'm establishing a standard.”

Vega considered them, then nodded toward the corridor.

“Five. With us present.”

They took him down the hall in a wheelchair because the nurse had decided walking remained a privilege he had abused. Tín looked at the chair's plain gray frame and thought of Arturo's red machine back on Bell Street.

“Calvin bought a nicer one.”

Bích pushed him a little faster.

“Then next time ask him before you spend the night fighting.”

Rook sat upright in a private room with one hand cuffed to the bed rail. A dressing covered the cut above his eyebrow. His lip had swollen. Someone had brought him a clean shirt, but he wore it open at the collar because the bruising around his throat made anything else uncomfortable.

He looked at the wheelchair.

For a moment, he almost smiled.

Tín saw it.

“Don't become hopeful.”

The smile disappeared.

Bích stopped the chair beside the bed. Vega remained at the foot, and the lawyer took a position near the wall where he could see both men without being within either one's reach.

Rook looked toward the envelope in Tín's hand.

“You received it.”

“Yes.”

“My daughter will handle the rest.”

Iris stood at the door.

“The legitimate accounts,” she said. “You can explain the others.”

Rook looked away from her.

Tín took the check from the envelope and examined it again.

“You signed this sitting down.”

“Naturally.”

“Much neater than upside down.”

The lawyer stared at the wall.

Rook closed his eyes briefly.

“Must you?”

“I've paid for entertainment. I like to receive it.”

Bích touched the back of his chair.

“Five minutes.”

Tín put the check away.

Rook opened his eyes.

“You think you've won the waterfront.”

“I won a boat.”

“You took a route worth more than the boat.”

“Then you should have offered Duke a better bowling ball.”

“There will be other men.”

Tín looked at him without smiling.

“Send them your photographs from last night.”

Rook's jaw worked.

Vega shifted slightly at the foot of the bed.

Tín continued before anyone needed to speak.

“You have businesses away from Bell Street. Keep your people there. Duke runs the tug. My wife runs the kitchen. The people whose homes you tried to burn get to decide when they're finished being angry.”

Rook glanced toward Bích.

“Mrs. Lê—”

“No,” she said.

He stopped.

“You can pay for what you broke. You don't get a conversation with me because the check is large.”

She turned the wheelchair toward the door.

Tín let her.

As they passed Iris, the young woman stepped aside. She watched Bích push her husband down the corridor, then followed them to the quiet room.

The lawyer remained with Rook.

Sable sat on the window ledge with the tug document in her hands.

“Mercy's Cousin,” she read. “They've put the new name on it.”

Tín looked at her.

“Duke works quickly when encouraged.”

“Rosa encourages him loudly.”

Iris came through the door and closed it behind her.

For a moment she stood with both hands at her sides.

“I'm selling the eastern office,” she said.

Vega looked up.

“You'll tell us before moving anything.”

“I know. I mean after.”

She looked toward the window, where the harbor cranes stood against the pale morning sky.

“I don't want to sit behind his desk and explain why everything smells like smoke.”

Sable folded the tug paper.

“There are desks without his name on them.”

Iris gave her a tired look.

“You found one quickly.”

“I spent years learning where the bad ones were.”

Tín watched them without interrupting.

Iris turned back to him.

“When the captain fired at the lighter, you pulled me down.”

“You were in front of me.”

“You knew who I was.”

“You introduced yourself very formally.”

She smiled despite herself.

Then the smile went.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

“Tell Vega everything you saw.”

“I am.”

She left with the detective a few minutes later, carrying none of her father's papers. Tín watched the door close and sat back in the wheelchair.

Bích took the envelope from him and put it in her bag.

“You don't need to carry this around.”

“It's my first two-million-dollar receipt.”

“Then we'll keep it flat.”

Sable stood.

“There's something else.”

She placed a smaller envelope on the table.

Tín looked at it.

“You've been busy.”

“My wages. The part Rook kept promising and moving into another month.”

“How much?”

She told him.

He nodded toward the envelope.

“Keep it.”

“I took it from the chest before I gave you the rest.”

Bích looked at her directly.

Sable held the look.

“I'm telling you now because I want to work somewhere I don't have to keep doing that.”

Tín considered her. She had brought him to Rook's ring, shown him the passage beneath the pier, called the police before the cannery raid, and kept finding the one door that a room full of men had forgotten to watch. She had also worked for Rook while his crates passed beneath Duke's dance floor.

He pushed the envelope back across the table.

“We discuss pay before the month begins.”

Sable looked at Bích.

“With you?”

“With me,” Bích said.

Sable let out a breath.

“Good.”

Bích stood and moved behind Tín's chair.

“Now he needs to rest.”

“I slept.”

“You slept once. Don't treat it as a completed project.”

She wheeled him back toward his room.

In the corridor, Bishop stood beside Boots with a large paper bag. Boots had been allowed into a chair and was eating the rescued sandwich while Loretta watched every bite as if personally responsible for its medical suitability.

Bishop held out the bag.

“Fresh clothes.”

Tín looked inside.

A plain dark shirt, loose trousers, and soft shoes lay folded together. Beneath them was a gold-colored sash.

Tín lifted one corner.

Bích took it from him.

“No.”

Bishop looked disappointed.

“It came with the crown.”

“Then return half the kingdom.”

Boots began laughing and immediately regretted moving his wounded arm.

Loretta steadied his cup.

“Laugh on the other side.”

Tín looked around at them: the nightclub owner dressed like a pilot, the street boss holding a rejected royal sash, his oldest Bell Street friend guarding a sandwich, and his wife directing traffic through a hospital corridor with an envelope worth two million dollars in her bag.

He smiled.

Bích saw it.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That's never true with you.”

He took her hand where it rested on the chair handle.

“We should buy the good refrigerator next time.”

She bent until her mouth was near his ear.

“There is no next time.”

Then she kissed his cheek and pushed him toward the clean bed waiting at the end of the hall.

## Chapter 26: Nobody Bought Enough Chairs

The festival opened without him.

Tín learned this from a radio in the hospital hallway, where Marcus was giving an interview with the confidence of a man whose entire business plan had survived being set on fire.

“We have food, music, the recovered Orpheum organ, and a special appearance by the Grandmaster himself.”

The interviewer asked when Tín would arrive.

“When he's finished being medically admired.”

Tín looked at Bích.

She kept folding his clean clothes.

“I told you people would come.”

“He's charging admission to my stitches.”

“No admission. We agreed.”

From the radio, Marcus added that photographs would be available at a reasonable price.

Bích paused.

“I'll discuss reasonable with him later.”

They left in Hương's sedan after the doctor checked the dressings one last time. Tín sat in the back beside his wife, wearing the loose dark shirt Bishop had brought. His soft shoes looked almost painfully ordinary beneath the new trousers. He appreciated them every time he moved his feet.

Hòa drove. Hương sat beside him with a basket of food on her knees, because somehow leaving the hospital for a food festival still required carrying something to eat.

On Bell Street, people came out as the car passed.

Vân waved a kitchen towel from her doorway. Mr. Benítez sounded a little bicycle bell he had attached to the arm of his red chair. The bus driver from Monday leaned out of his window and held up Tín's folded transit pass, which had been found beneath a chair after the market and returned to him for safekeeping.

Hòa stopped long enough to take it.

The driver looked into the back seat.

“Still covers refrigerators.”

Tín lifted his bandaged hand.

“I'm between appliances.”

Bích leaned across him.

“He's retired from delivery.”

The driver nodded solemnly.

“I'll tell the city.”

They continued toward the eastern basin.

The old excursion landing had become a small fairground. Banners hung between lamp posts. Food stalls lined the broad quay, leaving a clear path to the River Queen. The barge's repaired windows reflected the afternoon light, and a temporary cover lay over the broken skylight. Mercy's Cousin rested beside it with Duke's uneven lettering now outlined in gold.

Someone had tied a tiny family tree beneath the tug's new name.

Rosa stood on the deck staring at it.

“You're making the joke official.”

Duke came from the wheelhouse with two cups.

“The paperwork agreed.”

“The paperwork needs supervision.”

He offered her a cup.

She took it.

When Tín's car stopped, Marcus called his name through the loudspeaker.

The crowd turned.

Tín closed his eyes for a moment.

Bích touched his knee.

“You can still get out.”

“I'm considering the bus.”

Hòa opened the door.

Applause rose along the quay as Tín stood. People moved aside to make a broad path toward the boat. Several tried to shake his hand, saw the bandages, and changed the gesture into a careful touch on his shoulder or a little bow from the waist.

Tín returned each greeting as well as his ribs allowed.

A boy of about eight stood near the gangway holding a toy crane.

He looked up at the old man.

“Mine broke too.”

Tín stopped.

One wheel had come off the toy's base. The boy held it in his other hand.

Tín looked toward Hòa.

His son took the wheel, crouched beside the boy, and pressed it back onto the axle. He rolled the crane across his palm, tested the wheel once, and handed it back.

The boy stared at him.

“You can do it too?”

Hòa smiled.

“Small jobs.”

Tín watched his son's hand close around the little toy, then open again. He said nothing as they continued aboard.

Inside, the ballroom looked better than it had when Duke owned it.

Hương had hung clean fabric along the damaged wall. The new glass was clear. Tables stood with enough space between them for people to move without climbing over a stranger's knees. Flowers from the wedding had been mixed with fresh ones in jars along the bar. Near the stage, the organ console shone beneath its polished cover while Ellis made an adjustment to the little pipe frame behind it.

Ruth met Tín at the door.

“You look less alarming.”

“They threw away my shirt.”

“Good hospital.”

She took his arm and led him to a broad chair near the stage. A cushion had been placed on it, and a small table held water, tea, and a bowl of fruit.

Above the chair hung the board from the bridge crew.

FORTY TONNES.

Tín looked up at it.

“I said refrigerator.”

Mai stood beside the chair with her camera.

“We considered the traffic.”

He sat.

Marcus approached carrying the gold-plated crown.

Bích stepped into his path.

“One photograph.”

Marcus looked toward Mai.

She lifted one finger.

He placed the crown on Tín's head and stepped away.

The flash went off.

Bích removed the crown.

“Finished.”

The crowd laughed. Marcus opened his mouth, saw her expression, and decided the microphone needed adjusting somewhere else.

People came to greet Tín in small groups. The printer brought a stack of good paper for Mai and shook Tín's uninjured fingers carefully. The theater manager delivered the annual pass in a little frame. The furniture-store owner counted the chairs in the ballroom and looked almost tearful at how many people were sitting in them correctly.

“I sold eight sets this morning,” he told Tín.

“Then you'll have to buy food.”

“Already did.”

He held up three tickets for the stalls outside.

“My wife thinks I'm investigating the competition.”

“Are you?”

“Thoroughly.”

The father of the little girl from the fire came aboard with his daughter. He had received his envelope back from Hương and carried a paper bag instead.

“She chose it,” he said.

The girl took a small framed drawing from the bag.

It showed a man holding a bridge over his head. The bridge had six windows and a chimney. Beneath it, tiny boats floated among blue lines. The man wore a crown almost as large as his body.

Tín accepted it with both hands.

“You gave me a house.”

She nodded.

“Bridges don't have enough rooms.”

He laughed and put the drawing beside the fruit bowl.

When they left, Bích leaned toward him.

“That one can go over the refrigerator.”

He nodded.

On the outer deck, Duke had begun offering short rides around the basin in Mercy's Cousin. Rosa stayed with him for the first two, then stepped ashore and let him take the third alone with an experienced deckhand.

Tín watched from the ballroom window.

Duke stood straight at the wheel, concentrating so hard that he forgot to look impressive. He brought the tug back to the landing without scraping anything. Rosa caught the line, secured it, and waited while he came down from the cabin.

“Well?” he asked.

“You arrived where you intended.”

“High praise.”

“Don't get greedy.”

He leaned against the rail beside her.

“Dinner?”

She looked toward the food stalls.

“We're surrounded.”

“With me.”

She considered him for a moment.

“You paying?”

“I still have money.”

“After the boat?”

“I lost a barge. I acquired education.”

Rosa smiled and took his arm.

They walked toward Bích's stall together.

Tín turned back from the window to find his wife watching him.

“You look pleased.”

“Duke may survive.”

“Rosa will decide.”

At the bar, Sable had already begun running the room. She moved between staff with a pencil behind her ear and a little pad in her hand. When somebody tried to open a tab under Tín's name, she pointed toward the chair where he sat.

“Ask him.”

The man looked at the bandaged hands and the board above his head.

“Cash is fine.”

Bích heard and gave Sable a small approving nod.

Outside, Bishop's men carried tables, cleared plates, and discovered that helping a festival run involved more bending than guarding a doorway. Wade had been assigned to supervise the chairs. Vân corrected him twice and then promoted him to carrying the heavier ones.

Tín watched Bishop stand at the end of the quay with his hands in his pockets.

The street boss came aboard a few minutes later and stopped beside the chair.

“My people are working.”

“I can see.”

“They're good at it.”

“You should tell them.”

Bishop looked toward Wade, who was holding a chair open for the woman who had taken it from him at the market.

“They're going to ask for more money.”

Tín smiled.

“You have a hundred thousand from Rook.”

Bishop sighed.

“Nothing stays private on this street.”

The first full song began at four.

The band had rehearsed beneath smoke, through power cuts, and around a half-assembled organ. Now it had a whole afternoon, a room full of people, and every piece of equipment Marcus had managed to persuade someone to donate.

The sound filled the ballroom and spilled across the basin.

Tín leaned back in his chair.

Bích sat beside him at last.

For one song, nobody brought either of them a problem.

They held hands beneath the table and listened.

## Chapter 27: The Bride Comes Back

Denise arrived at the festival pushing Mateo in a wheelchair he had decorated with a small green pennant from the Little Mercy.

“Temporary,” he told everybody who looked at it.

“Marriage too, if you keep announcing that,” she said.

He looked up at her.

She bent and kissed the top of his head.

The hospital had released him that afternoon with instructions Denise could recite more accurately than the staff. His leg remained wrapped and supported. He would use crutches at home, the chair for the crowded quay, and his wife's patience only where absolutely necessary.

Rosa came down the gangway to meet them.

She put both hands on her brother's shoulders and looked into his face.

“You look better.”

“They gave me trousers.”

“That helps everyone.”

Denise wore a new dress Hương had finished while supposedly resting. It had a simple cream skirt and sleeves that let her move freely. The damaged wedding dress was folded at home. She had decided to keep it, bloodstains and all, because she refused to let anyone tell her later that she had been dramatic about the day.

Hương met her at the ballroom door and inspected the hem.

Denise turned slowly so she could see it all.

“Good?”

“Good.”

“Can I eat now?”

“Carefully.”

They laughed and embraced.

Tín rose from his chair when the couple approached.

Bích put one hand against his chest.

He sat again.

Mateo watched this with satisfaction.

“Even the bridge man gets parked.”

Tín pointed at his wheelchair.

“We have a club now.”

“Do we charge?”

From the stage, Marcus said, “I can help.”

Three women answered him at once.

“No.”

Mateo rolled his chair beside Tín's. Denise sat on the other side, and Bích brought them plates of food before anyone could begin another public speech.

For a while, they ate.

Mateo closed his eyes over the first bite.

“We should have started with this.”

“You wanted a lighthouse,” Denise said.

“I made several ambitious choices.”

“One of them married you.”

He took her hand beneath the table and kissed her fingers.

Tín looked away long enough to let them believe nobody had noticed.

The wedding cake had survived in Rosa's shop refrigerator through every emergency. Now she brought it aboard with two men walking beside her as if escorting a valuable prisoner. Its icing leaned slightly to one side. The little bride on top had lost an arm during transport, and the groom's painted face had acquired a smear of frosting that made him look suspiciously like Mateo after surgery.

Denise studied the figures.

“Accurate enough.”

Mateo nodded.

“Leave them.”

Frank appeared with the blue folder from the ceremony.

Denise saw it and raised a finger.

“We are already married.”

“I know.”

“No reading.”

He looked disappointed.

“Your aunt has been asking.”

“Then read it to her.”

Frank considered this, turned toward the older woman seated near the window, and went to join her. A few minutes later, Tín heard the reading begin quietly behind him. The aunt listened with both hands folded over her handbag. Frank looked relieved to have finally used the page.

Marcus brought the microphone to Denise.

“Anything you want to say?”

She looked at the room, then at Mateo.

“Thank you for coming back.”

She handed the microphone away before the sentence could become a speech.

The applause came gently this time.

Mateo wiped his eyes with a napkin and pretended the food had been too hot.

Bích let him.

The band began the song that should have played on the tug. Denise stood beside Mateo's chair and took both his hands. He pushed himself upright on his good leg with her help, leaning against the table while she held him close.

They moved only a little.

It was enough.

People made room around them. Rosa stood beside Duke near the door. He offered his arm. She looked at it, looked at the crowded floor, and accepted.

“No showing off,” she told him.

“I lost my best opportunity at the bowling alley.”

“You keep finding smaller ones.”

He smiled and led her into the music.

Tín watched them pass the couple, then turned toward Bích.

She shook her head before he asked.

“You can dance later.”

“When?”

“When standing stops being an argument.”

He leaned back, defeated by terms he could not improve.

Mai moved through the room with her camera. She took the photograph of Mateo and Denise first, then Rosa and Duke, then Frank finally reading his page to the aunt. When she reached Tín and Bích, she paused.

“Together,” she said.

Bích leaned against her husband. He put his good arm behind her shoulders and looked at the camera.

“Don't do the burial smile,” Mai warned.

He laughed.

The shutter clicked.

She lowered the camera, checked the remaining film, and looked pleased.

“That one.”

“How do you know?” Tín asked.

“I was looking.”

She went to find Marcus, who had begun explaining to an impressed visitor how much effort it took to make an event look spontaneous. Mai stood beside him until he noticed her.

“You missed the best part,” she said.

“Which?”

She took his hand and pulled him onto the dance floor.

For once, he followed without negotiating a title.

Late in the afternoon, Loretta arrived with a message from Boots. He remained at the hospital for another night and had begun organizing the other patients into an audience for a story in which his role grew every time the nurse changed shifts.

Loretta handed Tín a folded note.

It read: TELL THEM I SAVED THE SANDWICH.

Below it, in smaller writing: Glad you home, brother.

Tín read the second line again.

He folded the note and put it in his pocket.

“We'll take him cake.”

“The nurse already said no,” Loretta replied.

“Then we'll take it to you.”

She smiled.

“That's legal.”

Ruth came by with Ellis and the saxophone player. They had decided which parts of the organ needed a workshop and which could stay aboard for future performances. Ruth wanted music at the pier again once it was rebuilt. Bích wanted enough notice to plan food. Sable wanted somebody to tell her the dates before posters appeared in the windows.

Marcus heard the word posters from across the room and lifted one hand.

Mai pulled it back down.

Tín watched the small group argue over Saturday nights, Sunday lunches, and whether Duke's new tug could provide rides without him calling them royal excursions.

“It was one flyer,” Duke said when accused.

Sable held up three.

He took them from her.

“Early drafts.”

Rosa looked over his shoulder.

“You spelled cousin wrong.”

Hòa, passing with a tray of empty cups, stopped long enough to point at the missing letter.

Duke looked at him.

“Your family enjoys corrections.”

Hòa smiled.

“You provide opportunities.”

Tín laughed until his ribs asked him to reconsider.

Bích handed him water and waited for the pain to pass. Then she took the empty cup and sat close again, her shoulder warm against his.

Outside, the river moved past the excursion landing. Children watched it through the rail while adults stood close enough to catch a sleeve if anyone forgot the water was real. The repaired tug came and went, carrying short trips around the basin. People returned windblown, happy, and newly willing to believe Duke had always intended to become a captain.

Near sunset, Mateo and Denise prepared to leave.

Rosa packed enough food for them to avoid cooking for several days. Hương folded a blanket over Mateo's lap. Frank gave Denise the blue folder, and she accepted it at last, laughing as she tucked it beneath her arm.

At the door, Mateo turned his chair toward Tín.

“Next anniversary, land.”

“A sensible start.”

“Somewhere quiet.”

Tín looked at the ballroom, the band, and Marcus already approaching with another idea.

“Don't tell anyone here.”

Denise laughed and pushed her husband down the gangway into the warm evening.

Tín stayed in his chair and watched them go.

This time, they reached the car without anybody reaching for a gun.

## Chapter 28: Hòa Keeps His Own Hours

On Monday, Duke delivered the safe from the bowling alley to Hòa's school.

He had painted it blue.

The red bowling ball remained lodged inside its ruined door.

“A teaching aid,” Duke explained.

Hòa stood beside the loading bay with a cup of tea in his hand.

“For what subject?”

“Consequences.”

Tín sat in the truck's passenger seat with Bích's permission to leave the house for one hour. She had made Duke repeat the limit before handing over the soft shoes. The bandages beneath Tín's sleeves itched, and the stitches at his side pulled whenever he turned too quickly. He was learning to turn slowly. He disliked being good at it.

Duke climbed onto the truck bed and looked at the safe.

“We need equipment.”

Hòa set his cup on the loading-bay ledge.

“Where does it go?”

“I thought the courtyard.”

“The principal will want to see it first.”

Duke looked toward Tín through the open window.

Tín lifted his bandaged hands.

“I'm on holiday.”

Hòa stepped onto the truck's rear platform, put one hand beneath the safe's lower edge, and drew it toward him.

Duke moved aside.

The safe slid across the bed. Hòa lifted it clear, stepped down to the pavement, and carried it toward the loading bay with the red ball pointing away from his shirt.

The truck rose on its springs.

Duke watched him go.

Then he looked at Tín.

Tín watched his son set the safe beside the wall and pick up the cup of tea.

“Should I ask?” Duke said.

“He has classes.”

“After classes?”

“He has a family.”

Duke closed his mouth.

Hòa returned to the truck.

“Come in. The office has chairs.”

Tín sighed.

“Everyone keeps offering me furniture.”

“You've been hard on theirs.”

They went inside.

The principal was a tall woman with gray hair and a stack of papers that appeared to grow whenever she looked away. She came out to inspect the safe, heard Duke's explanation, and decided it could remain in the courtyard if someone made sure no child could close the damaged door on a hand.

Duke promised to have it fixed open.

“And remove the ball?” she asked.

He looked at the red curve inside the steel.

“I'd prefer to preserve the artistic integrity.”

She looked at Hòa.

Hòa smiled.

“I'll handle it.”

The principal returned to her papers.

Tín sat outside Hòa's classroom while his son finished the last part of a lesson. The door stood open. Students worked at their desks, some bent intently over the page, others wearing the expression of people hoping arithmetic might become embarrassed and leave them alone.

Hòa moved between them without raising his voice.

At one desk, a boy pointed toward the corridor.

“That's your father?”

“Yes.”

“He threw the bridge.”

“He moved part of it. Finish the problem.”

“Can you do that?”

Hòa looked at the boy's page.

“I can do this. So can you.”

He tapped the unfinished line and moved on.

Tín smiled to himself.

When the bell rang, several students came into the corridor slowly enough to make their intentions obvious. One carried a notebook open to a clean page.

“Could you sign?” he asked.

Tín took the pencil.

“For school?”

“For my brother. He doesn't believe you came here.”

Tín signed his name and handed the notebook back.

The boy looked at it, then at Hòa.

“Your dad's famous.”

Hòa began collecting the exercise books.

“His teacher was very strict,” Tín said.

The boy looked from father to son, laughed, and hurried after his friends.

Duke went to arrange the safe's mounting with the caretaker. Tín remained in the classroom while Hòa stacked books into a canvas bag.

“You waited in the trunk,” Tín said.

His son looked up.

“Yes.”

“After the latch was broken.”

Hòa folded the bag's flap over the books.

“The men outside kept shouting. I was curious what they wanted.”

“They wanted me.”

“They chose an indirect approach.”

Tín studied his son's face.

Hòa held his gaze without challenge.

“You could have left.”

“I could have.”

The classroom was quiet now. Outside, Duke could be heard telling the caretaker that the ball had traveled faster than anyone in the building had expected. The caretaker asked whether the bowling alley was still open.

Tín rested his hands on his knees.

“When did you start keeping so much to yourself?”

Hòa considered the question before answering.

“When I found work I wanted to come home from.”

Tín nodded slowly.

His son took the bag from the desk.

“You know where I live.”

“Your mother makes that difficult to forget.”

“Then come for tea without a damaged vehicle.”

Tín looked toward the loading bay.

“Duke brought this one.”

“You're improving.”

They walked back outside together.

The safe stood beside the courtyard wall, its blue paint still glossy in the sun. Duke had found a sheet of cardboard and written a sign for it.

DO NOT CHALLENGE THE TEACHER'S FATHER.

Hòa read it.

He took the marker and added a second line.

PLEASE FINISH YOUR HOMEWORK.

Tín laughed until he had to hold his ribs.

Duke looked between them.

“This is why nobody on Bell Street knows how to act normal.”

Hòa handed back the marker.

“You're welcome to practice.”

They drove home before the hour ended.

At the house, Bích checked the clock, inspected Tín's shirt for fresh damage, and allowed him inside. Duke received a container of food for bringing the patient back in the same general condition.

“Rosa gets half,” she told him.

He looked at the container.

“She'll know?”

“I called her.”

He accepted his fate and went down the steps.

Tín found Mai at the kitchen table sorting photographs. The new prints lay in careful rows: the repaired ballroom, Denise beside Mateo's chair, Ruth at the organ, Duke trying to look casual beside Rosa, and Hòa carrying cups through the crowd.

Mai held up the photograph of Tín and Bích.

“This one's for home.”

He took it.

His wife leaned against him in the picture, looking directly at the camera. His own face had turned toward her. The bandages were visible. So was the ridiculous board above the chair, cropped at the edge so only part of the number remained.

“You didn't get the whole sign,” he said.

“I got the important people.”

He looked at her.

She met his eyes and smiled.

“Mr. Chen said I can learn the presses properly. Not just carry paper.”

“What did you say?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She returned to the photographs. He stood beside the table for a moment, then placed the picture gently on top of the new refrigerator.

Bích came to look at it.

“Better than the crown.”

Tín put his arm around her shoulders.

“You can say both are good.”

“I can say many things. I choose carefully.”

She leaned against him just as she had in the photograph.

Behind them, the refrigerator hummed steadily, pleased at last to be the least troublesome large object in the house.

## Chapter 29: The Long Way Home

Three weeks later, Bích allowed him to walk to the river without an escort.

She came anyway.

“You said I could go alone,” Tín reminded her.

“I wanted air.”

“In the same direction?”

“It's a small street.”

She took his arm as they went down the steps. The wounds along his side had closed. The stitches were out. His palms remained tender where the deeper cuts had healed, and a pale line crossed the bridge of his nose. He wore the soft shoes Arturo had made and carried no crown, weapon, or object requiring two men to explain why he was holding it.

At the gate, Mai called after them.

“Be home before dinner.”

Tín turned.

“Who is making it?”

“Dad.”

“We'll be punctual.”

Hòa appeared behind her holding a kitchen towel.

“I heard that.”

“Then improve accordingly.”

His son smiled and went back inside.

Bell Street had repaired its windows. The new glass looked a little too clean beside the older panes. Boots's garage had a fresh section of roofing, and the white tow truck's cab no longer admitted daylight from above. He had insisted on keeping the torn steering wheel, mounted on the wall beneath a small plaque reading ADVANCED DRIVER TRAINING.

Boots sat outside the shop with his recovering arm supported against his chest.

Loretta stood beside him holding a cup.

“You're walking,” Boots said when he saw Tín.

“I've done it before.”

“Without a vehicle in your hands.”

Tín looked toward the white truck.

Boots lifted one finger.

“Don't admire anything mechanically.”

Loretta handed Bích the cup she had been carrying. The two women stepped into the salon doorway and began discussing somebody's daughter, a dress, and a decision that had apparently been made without enough consultation.

Tín sat beside Boots.

For a while they watched the street.

A customer came out of the garage and stopped beneath the mounted steering wheel. He read the plaque, looked at Tín, and opened his mouth.

Boots pointed at the cash register inside.

“Pay for your repair first. Story afterward.”

The man laughed and went back in.

Tín looked at his friend.

“You charging now?”

“Only people with warranties.”

He shifted his arm carefully and let out a breath through his nose.

“Still hurts,” Tín said.

“Some days.”

“You sleeping?”

“Loretta says I am. Apparently the whole house knows.”

They smiled.

Boots looked down the hill toward the river.

“You ever think about that first year?”

“Here?”

“You came in asking if I could fix the little fan.”

Tín remembered the fan. It had rattled so loudly that Hương said the neighbors would think they were keeping a motorcycle in the bedroom.

“You said you worked on cars.”

“You said a fan was a car with limited ambition.”

“You fixed it.”

“You sat there for two hours telling me which screw sounded loose.”

Tín laughed.

Boots looked at him, then at the steering wheel on the wall.

“Should've known.”

“You did know. You kept inviting me back.”

“You brought food.”

From the salon doorway, Bích said, “I brought food.”

Boots raised his good hand.

“And we have been grateful under the correct management ever since.”

She nodded, satisfied, and returned to Loretta's story.

When they left, Boots stood long enough to embrace Tín with one arm. Neither squeezed hard. Both pretended this was a matter of style.

“Come by tomorrow,” Boots said.

“Something broken?”

“Probably. Come anyway.”

Tín promised.

At Vân's grocery, the birthday banner had finally come down. In its place hung a framed photograph of Tín beneath the words PLEASE REFRIGERATE AFTER OPENING. Vân had enlarged the writing rather than crop it out.

Bích stopped to look.

“You're encouraging him.”

Vân came to the doorway.

“It sells cold drinks.”

Tín examined the photograph.

“I should receive a percentage.”

Vân handed him a bag of fruit.

“Your quarterly payment.”

“Generous.”

“There's a bruised peach. That's tax.”

Bích took the bag before he could start negotiating.

They continued downhill.

The old berth at Pilgrim Slip had new pilings and a half-finished landing. Rook's damage payments were turning into wood, glass, medical bills paid, and men arriving on time with tools instead of guns. The remaining claims would take longer. Tín had left Sable to argue with the people who enjoyed numbers written on several different pages. He preferred seeing the boards become a place where someone could stand.

Rosa and Duke waited beside the repaired gangway.
